en: Auspicious Invocation (Maṅgalācaraṇa)

Constantly meditating upon the Supreme Brahman and repeatedly recollecting the words of my guru, I compose this *Prakriyā-prakāśa*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, entitled the *Prakriyā-prakāśa*. (Alternatively: ...I compose the *Prakriyā-prakāśa*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, known as the *Prakriyā-prakāśa*. (Note: The provided text contains a slight ambiguity regarding the title; "prauḍhamanoramā" is the name of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita's own commentary, while "prakriyā-prakāśa" is the name of his sub-commentary. The translation above reflects the more common scholarly understanding of the intent of such introductory verses, though the literal reading of the provided Sanskrit suggests he is composing a work called *Prakriyā-prakāśa* that serves as a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī*.)
Now begins the section on technical designations (saṃjñā).

The instruction of the letter *ha* in the sequence *hayavaraṭ* is for the purpose of including the letter *ha* in the rules concerning *aṭ*, *aś*, *haś*, and *iṇ*. [Examples: In *arheṇa* ("by one who deserves"), there is the substitution of *ṇa* by the rule *aḍvyavāye 'pi*. In *devā hasanti*, there is the substitution of *ya* for the *ru*-sound by the rule *bho-bhago-*. In *devo hasati*, there is the substitution of *u* by the rule *haśi ca*. In *lilihiḍhve* or *lilihidhve*, the substitution of *ḍha* optionally occurs by the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ*.

The mention of *hal* in this sūtra is for the purpose of including the letter *ha* within the categories *val*, *ral*, *jhal*, and *śal*. In *rudihi* and *svapihi*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* because they belong to the *valādi* group. In *snihitvā* and *snehitvā*, there is optionally the status of being *kit* by the rule *ralo vyupadhāt*. In *adāgdhām*, there is the elision of the *sakāra* by the rule *jhalo jhali*. In *alikṣat*, the suffix *ksa* is applied by the rule *śala igupadhāt*.

Regarding the phrase "the last in the sūtra": the intention is that in the analysis *hali antyam* (the last [sound] before a consonant), the compound is formed either by the rule of *yogavibhāga* ("[a word ending in a locative case may be compounded with another]") or by the rule *sup-supā* ("a word ending in a case affix may be compounded with another word ending in a case affix"). Alternatively, this is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound. It might be argued: let there be one of the options—tantra, repetition (*āvṛtti*), or *ekaśeṣa*—specifically for the *ekaśeṣa* of *hal*. It will be explained as *ha-l* (the letter *ha* and the letter *l*). The meaning of the genitive case here is proximity. Or rather, let there be no tantra and so forth; let it be a collective dvandva compound: *hal-ca-l-ca* (the consonants and the *l*). If it is asked: "Does this not result in the elision of the final member of the conjunct *lakāra* according to the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*?"

Not so; for in the first case, the compound would be strained (*kliṣṭa*). Indeed, in expressions such as *brāhmaṇakambala* ("the Brahmin’s blanket"), one does not perceive a blanket belonging to someone else that is merely near the Brahmin; nor is a tree or similar object perceived from the word *citragu* ("possessing brindled cows") as being near brindled cows. For this very reason, it is clearly stated in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that there is no compound in cases such as *anantara* ("immediately following"), due to the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). What more need be said? Even the analytical constructions (*vyasta-prayoga*)—namely, *brāhmaṇasya kambalaḥ* ("the blanket of the Brahmin") and *citrā gāvo'sya* ("his cows are brindled")—are undesired in those instances.

In the second case as well, the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would be difficult to achieve, because of the commencement of the prohibition regarding *yaṇ* sounds. Even on the view that this [prohibition] is rejected, the elision is prescribed for a *jhal* sound by drawing down the mention of *jhal* from the rule "jhalo jhali. Furthermore, since the understanding of the meaning of a sentence is impossible without the understanding of the meanings of its constituent words, and since the comprehension of the meaning of this sūtra would not occur prior to the establishment of the *hal*-pratyāhāra, this effort is made to resolve that difficulty.

In such a state, if the meaning of the word *hal* were not established, even a *dvandva* compound would be difficult to obtain, because the requirement of simultaneous intention (*sahavivakṣā*) would be impossible. Therefore, what has been stated above alone is logical.

Regarding the phrase *madhyagānām* ("of those situated in the middle"): the whole (*avayavin*), which is the aggregate (*samudāya*), is implied by its two constituent parts—the initial and the final. Since it is impossible for that [whole] to be applied simultaneously to the objects of indication (*lakṣya*), the technical name (*saṃjñā*) descending upon its constituents comes to rest upon those situated in the middle, and not on the initial and final [elements]. The sense is that because they are included within the very form of the name itself, their status as subservient to another (*pārārthya*) is determined.

Regarding the phrase *svasya ca* ("and of itself"): this is due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *svaṃ rūpam*. And "its own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*) is understood to belong only to the initial [element], not to the final one, because of the mention of the instrumental case in the subordinate term *antena*; for pronouns (*sarvanāman*) generally refer to the principal element.

Regarding the phrase "the first utterance": although it has been explained in the Bhāṣya, the Vṛtti, and other works that *upadeśa* (instruction) refers to the *śāstra* (the treatise) based on the instrumental derivation (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*)—meaning "that by which something is taught"—nevertheless, that is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). This is because the suffix *ghañ* is difficult to obtain in the sense of an instrument, as it is superseded by *lyuṭ*. Nor can *gha* be used here, because [the rule for *gha*] does not apply to non-technical names (*asaṃjñā*). Furthermore, the interpretation that [the rule for *gha*] applies "mostly to technical names" (*prāyeṇa saṃjñāyām*) is strained; moreover, there is the disregard shown by the author of the Bhāṣya in such statements as "for a limiting condition (*upādhi*) cannot itself be a limiting condition. For this very reason, even *ghañ*—which is an exception to *gha* under the rule *halaśca*—is not applicable here.

The principle of *bāhulaka* (exceptional usage) is a resort for those who have no other way out. For this very reason, even the instrumental derivation—meaning "those by which words are formed"—is refuted. Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "In opposition to [the rule for] feminine suffixes in *-a* and *-ap*, the suffixes *strī*, *khal*, and *na* [apply]; and in opposition to the feminine suffixes, *khal* and *na* [apply].
Therefore, the intended meaning is that it is logical for the suffix to denote the abstract state (*bhāva*) alone.

Regarding what they read beginning with "In the *Dhātusūtra*," and what they explain: "By the derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇa*), the status of being an *upadeśa* belongs to those [categories] included in the first half [of the verse]; however, by the derivation based on the object (*karman*), it belongs to the *āgama*s and so forth. Since the *uṇādi*s, the *liṅga* rules, and the *anuśāsana*s are also *sūtra*s, their separate mention is according to the maxim of 'the cow and the bull' (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Likewise, since the *dhātu*s are already established as such by virtue of being *gaṇa*s, [they are mentioned separately]," and so on—here this must be said: Do these possess the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *upadeśa*, or is it merely a formal connection (*yoga*)?

The first [alternative] is not tenable: because no technical name (*saṃjñā*) has been assigned by the authors of the treatise; because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya* that since it is not a name, the suffix *gha* does not apply; and because if names created by people like us were to establish the system of the treatise, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, there would be contradiction with one's own and others' works, such as the statement, "The *ām* [suffix] is *am-it* because it ends in *a*"; for it is not the case that *ām*, when its *anubandha* has been dropped, ceases to be a suffix, such that it would not possess the property of being *mit*.

Furthermore, if the ablative case in the rule for suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*) were to imply a genitive case, one might suspect that the substitute *san* itself should be designated as *san*; however, this would contradict what was stated by the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa, namely that because there is no formal instruction (*upadeśa*), the technical name (*saṃjñā*) would not apply. Moreover, this would conflict with the Bhāṣya on the rule *na dhātulopa-* which asks, "What is the purpose of the mention of 'root' (*dhātu*)? [Consider] *lūñ* [becoming] *lavitā*, and *pūñ* [becoming] *pavitā*," as well as Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, which intends to show that "the designation of root (*dhātusaṃjñā*) occurs only after the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) have been elided during the very act of formal instruction."

Furthermore, in the rule *ghvasoreddhau*, the mention of *lopaśca* contains two *ś*s; [if your view were correct], this would contradict the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule *alontya* regarding the second *ś* being *it*. Nor is the second alternative [correct], because if the *yoga* itself were prioritized, the enumeration [of specific cases] would be redundant. Moreover, it would be difficult to justify the disparity that the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "instrument" applies to roots (*dhātu*) and so forth, but not to augments (*āgama*) and so forth. Finally, it would contradict your own text, which states that the meaning is: "the *hal* [consonant] that is final in a collection delimited by a qualifying property (*upādhi*) such as 'being a root' (*dhātutva*), which serves as the cause for its status as an *upadeśa*."

In both cases, the instruction on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) is irrelevant to the present subject; furthermore, the letter *ś* is not included in the rule "and [the elision] of *lopaś*" (*lopaś ca*). Moreover, in rules such as "of *ādic*, in the original enunciation" (*ādeca upadeśe*) and "in the original enunciation, of that which has *at* as its penultimate" (*upadeśe'tvataḥ*), it is universally accepted that the meaning of the term "original enunciation" (*upadeśa*) is simply the initial utterance. This is the general direction of the argument.

*Upadeśe 'janunāsika it*. Although it would have been more appropriate to state the definition of *anunāsika* first here, since it is that upon which this [present rule] depends, nevertheless, because its meaning is already established by the etymological derivation (*yoga*) "that which follows the nose" (*nāsikām anugataḥ*), the sūtra defining *anunāsika* is of little practical utility; thus, it is not introduced here. Why specify "in the *upadeśa*"? Consider: *abbhra ām̐ apaḥ*. Although one could easily argue here—just as in the case of *uñaḥ* and *ūm̐*—that the *it*-designation does not apply due to the force of the specific rule, the term *upadeśe* is nonetheless included here for the sake of clear understanding, even though it must necessarily be employed for subsequent purposes.

What is the purpose? It is so that [the substitution] does not apply to the *makāra* of *manin*. [The analysis is as follows: "It is promised (*pratijñāyate*)" thus it is "a promise" (*pratijñā*). By the rule "ātaścopasarge," the suffix *aṅ* is applied in the sense of the object. The analysis of the compound is: "those for which nasality (*ānunāsikya*) is promised. And in this way, one need not resort to the strained interpretation that "the word *pratijñā* has a figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to what is to be understood through a promise," because it can be explained without resorting to figurative meaning, just as in expressions such as "grammar is Pāṇini’s discovery" (*pāṇinyupajñam vyākaraṇam*).

The sense is that although the nasalized reading (anunāsika-pāṭha) composed by the author of the Sūtras has now been lost, it is nevertheless inferred that it existed previously according to its function, on the strength of the usage of the authors of the Vṛtti and others.

One might object: "Is it not the case that [the rule] *ralayoḥ* is deficient, since the letter *ṭa* is also situated between them? To this he replies: "In the *pratyāhāras*. He explains: "They are used (*vyavahriyante*)"—that is, they are "collected" (*pratyāhriyante*), meaning "abbreviated" (*saṃkṣipyante*) therein; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*) by virtue of the rule allowing for diversity (*bāhulaka*). Although the mere etymological connection (*yoga*) is over-extensive when applied to technical names such as *akāra*, the intended sense is that these are "conventional terms based on etymology" (*yogarūḍhi*). Furthermore, the ancients maintain that there are forty-one *pratyāhāras*.

The meaning of that [statement] is that there are forty-one *hal* consonants employed in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, formed by the *it*-markers found in fourteen sūtras. By this, there is no fault even if [the count] includes the *sup* and *tiṅ* suffixes, the *rapratyāhāra*, and the *cay* pratyāhāra found in the Vārttika rule "cayo dvitīyāḥ."

As for the claim that the term "ñam" was employed by the author of the Vārttika in the rules "ñamaṅantāḍḍaḥ" and "yamirñamanteṣvaniḍeka iṣyate," that is a hasty assertion; for the former is a sūtra from the Uṇādi class, and the latter is found in the kārikās of Vyāghrabhūti. Let this matter rest for now. Furthermore, this restriction regarding the number [of roots] is not of much practical utility and has therefore been disregarded.

*Ūkālo’c hrasvadīrghaplutaḥ* is a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*). The masculine gender is according to the rule of the Sūtra. *Vāṃ kāla iva* is a statement of the resultant meaning; the analytical construction (*vigraha*), however, should be understood as *vaḥ kālo yasya* (that whose time is like that of *vām*). By the word *ū*, the duration of its own pronunciation is indicated. Regarding *āye*: the vowel *ā* is udātta by the rule "particles (*nipātāḥ*) are udātta in their initial syllable," while the word *yat* is [udātta] by the Phiṭ-sūtras. In *arvāṅ*, the vowel *a* is anudātta.

Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of that, it is not mandatory": the meaning is that, as with the prefix in the word *upeyivān*, it is not intended to be significant here. If one asks, "Granted that there may be non-intentionality [of the prefix] in that case because we see usages such as *īyivāṃsam atisridhaḥ*, but what is the authority for non-intentionality here?"—understand that the answer is the observation of actual usage and the Prātiśākhya and other such works.

For instance: in the word *yerāḥ*, the vowel *e* is [acute]; and in *tanūnapāt* and *śacīpatim*, it is well-known among all followers of the Ṛgveda that in the *padapāṭha* the vowels *ū* and *ī* are acute and half-toned (*ardhoddātta*). When the initial accentuation of both members of the compounds *tanūnapāt* and *śacīpati* is applied according to the rule "in the case of *vanaspati* and others, both [members] are [acute] simultaneously," the remaining syllables are then rendered grave (*anudātta*) by the rule "a word has one [acute] syllable, the rest are grave. Regarding the final syllable of the first members *tanū-* and *śacī-*, the *Prātiśākhya* states that there is an optional circumflex (*svarita*) accent: "Alternatively, like the *jātya* [circumflex], the two vowels at the end of *tanū-* and *śacī-* [become circumflex] when they are preceded [by another acute]."

Likewise, regarding the acute (udātta) nature of the first half of a circumflex (svarita), the Prātiśākhya also states: "In the case of the coalescence of two monosyllables, the accent of the former two is circumflex (svarita).
Of that [circumflex], the portion higher than the acute (udātta) is one half-mora, or even just half [of that]."
"The remaining [vowel] that follows an unaccented (anudātta) one is heard as accented (udātta), provided that no accented or svarita syllable is uttered subsequently. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: when there is a simultaneous occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the two preceding qualities—namely, acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*)—within a single [syllable], it should be understood as *svarita*. Regarding that *svarita*, it should be understood that its half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) is more acute than an independent (*svatantra*) acute vowel. The phrase "kva vo'śvāḥ" and so forth refers to short vowels; the phrase "or half [a mora]" (*ardhaṃ vā*) refers to long vowels. The particle *eva* is used to indicate that this [definition] alone should be adopted, as it is all-encompassing since it includes even the short vowel by this very [rule].

The statement beginning with “anudāttaḥ” (unaccented) is an explanation of a meaning established by elimination (*pariśeṣasiddha*). That—namely, the remainder (*śeṣa*)—should have the audible quality of the acute accent (*udātta*). Is this without distinction? No; he says “naced” and so forth. The meaning is: excluding that which is followed by an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent.
Śākalya also says:
“But that circumflex (*svāra*) which is non-natural (*aprākṛta*), preceded by a circumflex or an acute...”

"Then, having raised half of this, they strike the remainder while it is trembling. Here, *udādāya* means "having made [the first half] acute (*udātta*). As for the works of Haradatta and others which state that "by the word *ardha-hrasva*, a half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) is indicated," these must somehow be interpreted as referring to other opinions (*matāntara*).

Regarding *kva*: the suffix *at* added to *kim* is *svarita*. Regarding *va*: it is *anudātta* (unaccented) because of the governing rule, "everything [is unaccented] except at the beginning of a *pāda*. Regarding *aśvāḥ*: the word is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) due to the *nit*-accentuation of the suffix *kvun* added to the root *aś*. However, in *saṃhitā*, the vowel *o* is *udātta* by the rule, "a single substitute for an *udātta* [vowel] is *udātta*. Regarding *ye arāḥ*: both words are *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable) according to the *phiṭ-sūtras*. But the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is optionally *svarita*, as stated in the rule, "or it is *svarita* when [the preceding word] begins with an *anudātta* syllable."

In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound "mouth and nose" (*mukhaṃ ca nāsikā ca*), because it refers to parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), it would undergo the rule of becoming a single word (*ekavadbhāva*), resulting in "mukhanāsikam. Therefore, he says: "accompanied by the mouth" (*mukhasahitā*). Regarding the term *tulyāsya*, he explains that it means "occurring in the mouth" (*āsye bhavam āsyam*), intending the rule "the suffix *yat* after words meaning parts of the body, etc. (*śarīrāvayavādyat*). He says "palate, etc. (*tālvādīti*). [He specifies] "internal," and this is understood from the force of the prefix *pra-* (in *prayatna*). What is meant by "having the same place of articulation" (*tulyāsya*)? For example, *tarptā*. Here, when the letter *p* is followed by the letter *t*, let there not be elision (*lopa*) according to the rule "a *jhara* [consonant] is elided before a *jhari* [consonant]" (*jharo jhari*). Why is the mention of "effort" (*prayatna*) included? For example, *vāk ścotati*. Here, there is no elision of the letter *ś*.

Regarding the phrase *ñamaṅaṇanānām*: by the word *ca* ("and") in the expression *nāsikā ca* ("and the nose"), the respective points of articulation such as the palate are conjoined with their own corresponding classes (*varga*). The *Prātiśākhya* of the Taittirīyas states: "The *anusvāra* and the last [consonants] of each class are nasal (*anunāsika*). The *Prātiśākhya* of Kātyāyana states: "The nose is the place of articulation for the *yamas*, the *anusvāra*, and the nasals (*nāsikya*), as well as the last [consonants], which are also nasal (*anunāsika*). And its commentary explains: "The last [consonants] of each class—*ña, ma, ṅa, ṇa, na*—are nasals; by the word *ca* ('and'), the meaning is that the nose is their second place of articulation, without abandoning their own primary places."

In examples such as *edaitoḥ*, the addition of the *t* (taparatva) is for the sake of removing ambiguity, and not for the purpose of including sounds of that specific duration; by this, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is also included.

If this were an independent rule (*svatantra-vidhi*), then one would only obtain the result that "the three final sections (*tripādī*) are non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes them," but a subsequent rule belonging to the three final sections would not be non-existent with respect to what precedes it. Therefore, he says: "This is an *adhikāra* (heading/rule governing a section). If here the non-existence of the operation itself were intended, then in the case of *manorathaḥ* and similar forms, the substitution of *u* (*utva*) would not occur, because the rule *ro ri* would apply subsequently and take effect.

Furthermore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—"In the case of what is not established in the preceding [section], there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because of the absence of the subsequent"—would be contradicted; moreover, forms such as *amū* and *amī* would not be established. Therefore, he says: "the Tripādī," and "the subsequent rule. By this, the statement of the ancients, "an operation prescribed in the Tripādī," and so forth, is refuted.

"They open the throat" means that their effort (*prayatna*) consists of opening (*vivāra*). "Those belonging to the classes and the *yamas*" means those belonging to the classes (*varga*) and those belonging to the *yamas*.
"Kādayaḥ" (beginning with *ka*): this refers to the order well-known in common usage, as it would be impossible for them to end in *ma* within the fourteen *sūtras*.
"Half-*visarga*" (*ardhavisarga*): the similarity should be understood both in pronunciation and in writing.

Regarding "the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*": the analysis is "ā and ā are *ralau*; those two and the *varṇau* [sounds] are *ṛlṛvarṇau*"; or alternatively, "u and ul are *ṛlau*; of those two, the *varṇau* [sounds]" (*tayoḥ rvarṇayoḥ*). This is because of the established principle that an analysis may be made using either a word in the nominative case or a word with its final inflection fully formed. There is no change to the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "ṛtyakaḥ."

Regarding the statement *nājjhalau ākārasahita iti* ("vowels and consonants are not [homogeneous], including the long *ā*"), the indications such as *kāla-samaya-velāsu* serve as evidence for this *praśleṣa* (the inclusion of the long vowel). Nor should it be argued that even so, in forms like *yiyā3so*, the rule *guroranṛta* would still cause the *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) of the *s* of the suffix *san* following the protracted (*pluta*) *ā*—for the explanation is that in the *dvandva* compound *āśca āśca*, by means of the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel resulting from homogeneous vowels), the long vowel is included as being subsequent even to the protracted vowel.
As for the phrase *yaṇādikam*, the meaning of the word *ādi* (etcetera) refers to the *savarṇadīrgha* in the word *śītala*.
Regarding the word *atra*, it means "in this very [context]."

The phrase "even though" (*yadyapi*) implies that the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule for determining which sounds are included in a grammatical term) has not yet been finalized. The rule "ho ḍhaḥ" is merely illustrative; one should understand that it does not apply to the following cases: the substitution of *ṣ* in *ramāsu*, the substitution of *gh* for the vowel *ā* in *vāg-aśīḥ* by the rule "jhayo haḥ," nor the substitution of *gh* for the initial *d* in *dāsīṣṭa* and similar forms by the rule "dādeḥ. However, if it is explained that in the rule "vivṛtam ūṣmaṇām" the word "slightly" (*īṣat*) is carried over [from the previous rule] and then removed in the rule "svarāṇāṃ ca"—thereby accounting for the difference in articulatory effort (*prayatna-bheda*)—then, as established in the *Bhāṣya*, the rule "nājjhalau" need not exist.

In the rule *vṛddhir ādaic*, the diphthongs *ai* and *au* are indeed two-mora (*dvimātra*) because they follow [the definition of] *tātparya*. Therefore, in the expression *kṛṣṇaikatvam*, [the vowel *e*] is not three-mora (*trimātra*). The same applies to the subsequent sūtra as well; thus, in expressions such as *gaṅgodakam*, [the vowel *o*] is not three-mora.

"Bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ" (Bhū and others are roots). "Bhū" and "vā"—this is a dvandva compound. Regarding the two words "ādi," there is a single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) of those expressing both "sequence" (vyavasthā) and "manner" (prakāra). "Those which have 'bhū' and 'vā' as their beginning"—this is a bahuvrīhi compound. Thus, [the meaning is] "those beginning with bhū that are similar to vā. And intending that this similarity is based on being expressive of action (kriyāvācaka), he says: "expressive of action. Why "expressive of action"? [So that] in cases such as "yāḥ paśyasi" ("those which you see"), there may not be the status of a root; for if that status were present, [the rule] "āto dhātoḥ" would apply.

Why [specify] "beginning with *bhū*"? So that it does not apply to words such as *hiruk* or *pṛthak*, nor to forms ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) expressing a state of being, such as *śiśye*. By the addition of the marker *u* to the roots beginning with *stambh* (in the Dhatupatha), the status of these Vedic roots (*sautra-dhātu*) as verbal roots is indicated. As for *culump* and others, they are included by means of the group-rule (*gaṇasūtra*): "This [list] is illustrative in its abundance."

Are particles (*cādayaḥ*) those whose meaning is not a substance (*adravyārtha*)? For example, *paśuḥ*. A substance is that which possesses gender and number. But here [in the following case], it would indeed be a substance: *lodhaṃ naśyanti paśu manyamānāḥ* ("Those who consider Lodha to be an animal perish"). Here, "animal" (*paśu*) is used in the sense of "correctly."

The prefixes *niḥ* and *dur* end in *s*. This is because of the specific grammatical mention in the rule *nisastapatau*, and because in the section concerning the *ayogavāha* sounds, the examples *niṣkṛtam* and *duṣkṛtam* are cited; furthermore, it is stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "the *visarjanīya* that replaces the *s* which has *i* or *u* as its penultimate. Vāmana also holds this view regarding the rule *upasargasyāyatau*. However, Haradatta maintains in that very same rule that they also end in *r*, based on the mentions *niraḥ kuṣaḥ* and *suduroradhikaraṇe*.
Thus ends the section on technical terms (*saṃjñā*) in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now begins the section on technical rules (paribhāṣā).

The phrase "iko guṇavṛddhī" means "by means of the words *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. This is obtained by carrying over (*anuvṛtti*) the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* from the two preceding sūtras and connecting them with the construction: "those which are *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Therefore, it does not apply here: in "diva aut," [the result is] *dyauḥ*; in "tyadādīnām aḥ," [the results are] *saḥ* and *imam*.

Regarding the phrase "ending in the sixth case": since the word ending in the sixth case in the sūtra is an imitation (anukaraṇa), it refers to the actual form of the word; thus, the intention is that there is elision of the nominative suffix *su* after a neuter [noun]. Regarding the word "pada": when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, it is connected in the sequence beginning with "of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in an *iK* vowel. However, in rules such as "there is guṇa for *mid*" and "there is vṛddhi for *mṛj*", because coreferentiality is impossible, it is connected as "the *iK* which is a constituent part of the roots *mid* and *mṛj*."

As for the explanation given by the earlier commentators that "the two [suffixes] stand in the place of *ika* alone," and as for what the author of the commentary on that work stated—that this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) in view of the contingency of non-restriction (*aniyama-prasaṅga*), and so forth—all of that is to be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya. For they say that after refuting the view that [the sūtra] is a supplement to that [preceding rule], the Bhāṣya establishes only the view that it pertains to the presentation of the word-form (*padopasthiti*). Furthermore, we have clarified the removal of objections even against the view that it is a supplement to that [rule] in the *Śabdakaustubha*.

Regarding the phrase "in the middle of these vowels": as for what was stated by the ancients—that [the augment] follows after the final vowel—that is incorrect, because in rules such as *śe mucādīnām* ("after the root *muc* and others when followed by *śe*"), a final vowel is impossible [since the suffix *śe* consists of a consonant]. The phrase "an integral part at the end of that very [suffix]" means that by this [definition], in forms such as *trapūṇi*, the long vowel is established because the stem (*aṅga*) ends in *n*. If [the augment] were initial (i.e., at the beginning of the suffix), that would not be established. However, if it were not a part of the suffix (*abhakta*), then in the case of *vahaṃlihaḥ*—where the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *vahābhre lihaḥ* and the augment *mum* is added by *arurdviṣad*—the anusvāra would not occur, because [the *m*] would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*).

As for the objection that [the vowel] would not be long if it were not a *bhakta* (subordinate element), that has already been effectively refuted by the Vārttika on the definition of *aṅga*: "The mention of 'beginning with that' (*tadādi*) is for the sake of [including] the *si* and *ātmanepada* markers (*num*).

Regarding "in connection with the place" (*sthāne-yoga*): the analysis of the compound is "that which has a connection (*yoga*) with a place (*sthāna*). The change to *e* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

"Of many kinds" means produced by place, meaning, quality (*guṇa*), and measure (*pramāṇa*). "Stronger" means that, therefore, in forms such as *cetā* and *stotā*, the substitute *a* is not the closest match in terms of measure (*pramāṇa*).

In the expression "tasmin," the word ending in the locative case is an *anukaraṇa* (imitation). The prefix *niḥ* signifies "immediacy" (*nairantarya*). The root *diś-* denotes the action of utterance. When it is stated that *yaṇ* [replaces *iK*] "before a vowel" (*aci*), a rule would apply both when there is an intervening element and when there is none; therefore, it is restricted so that it applies only when there is no intervention, and further restricted so that it applies to the preceding [vowel] alone rather than the following one. The phrase "of the non-intervened" (*avyavahitasya*) is a statement of the resulting meaning.

Regarding the phrase *parasya yat*: the rule *tasmād ity uttarasyādeḥ* was not formulated as a sūtra. This is because the portion *ādeḥ* would result in the sublation of all-substitute (*sarvādeśa*) operations. However, according to the final established view (*siddhānta*), he will state immediately below that the status of being a full substitute is the sublater due to its higher priority (*paratva*).

Regarding the rule *anekāl śit sarvasya*, an example of a *śit* [suffix] is *idama iś* (Pāṇini 5.3.3), which results in *itaḥ*. As for the example given by the author of the Vṛtti, *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.20), that is incorrect; for before the status of being a *sarvādeśa* (a substitute for the whole) is established, the status of being *śit* cannot even be obtained. For in that case, as with the suffixes *ḍā* and *ṇal*, the established conclusion is that the status of being a *sarvādeśa* is achieved by this very rule through its sequential application (*ānupūrvyāt*).

Regarding the phrase "ityādau": by the word *ādi*, the rule "ato bhisa ais" (Pāṇini 7.1.9) is included. Regarding the phrase "paratvāt" (because of its being subsequent): for this very reason, it has been stated that the rule "ādeḥ parasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.54) is treated separately. However, the portion "uttarasya" (of what follows) certainly applies even to [the replacements] *auś* and *ais*. As for what was said by the ancient commentators while explaining the rule "ādeḥ"—namely, that it is due to the mention of the ablative case (*pañcamīnirdeśena*) and so forth—that is clearly irrelevant.

Regarding the term *paranitya* (eternally subsequent): it is eternally subsequent as in *tudati* and *ruṇaddhi*. Here, even setting aside the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), the augment *num* is applied by the rule "radhijabhoḥ. Nor should it be argued that this [augment] is also non-eternal because it applies to a different word-form (*śabdāntara-prāpti*); for in some cases, a rule is accepted as eternal merely by virtue of its application being both performed and not performed (*kṛtākṛta-prasaṅga*). Regarding *antaraṅga* (internal): as in *ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ*.

In this case, the designation of *sarvanāman* (pronoun) by the rule "sarvādīni" prevails over even the subsequent option "prathamacarama," because it is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned) due to its independence from case endings (*vibhakti*). Even an exception (*apavāda*) is indeed set aside by an *antaraṅga* rule if that exception has already found its scope elsewhere. For example: *ayaje indram*, *grāme iha*, *sarve ittham*. Here, the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel resulting from the coalescence of similar vowels) is set aside by the *antaraṅga* *guṇa* (substitution). And although that [guṇa] is an exception to both the *yaṇ* and *guṇa* rules, it nonetheless finds its scope of application only when the locus is identical.
And likewise, the Vārttika states: "In the case of *iṇ*, *ni*, and *śī*, there is guna [substitution] because of the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*)."

"It is unestablished" (*asiddham*). Therefore, in forms such as *pacāvedam*, the substitution of *ait* for *et* does not take place. Regarding the rule "those which have not been performed" (*akṛtavyūhāḥ*): although another technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is recited stating that "even what has been performed [is] annulled," and the result is the same, nevertheless "not performed" (*akṛta*) alone is more concise. The sense is based on the maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. "They do not perform [the operation]" means, for example, in the case of *niṣeduṣīm* and so forth, they do not apply the augment *iṭ* to the suffix *kvasu*, even though it would otherwise be required, because they consider that its status as having a consonant beginning with *v* (*valāditva*) will be destroyed by the subsequent internal (*antaraṅga*) semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*).
Thus ends the section on Paribhāṣās in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now begins the section on vowel sandhi (ac-sandhi).

In the case of the inclusion of *pratyāhāras* such as *ika* and *yaṇ*, there is a conventional (nirūḍhā) secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) referring to that which is expressed by those terms. This is established by the *jñāpaka* rule "dīrghājjasi ca" and by the technical designation "lvādibhyaḥ. Consequently, by the word *ik*, sixty-six [sounds] are included, and by the word *yaṇ*, seven. Although, due to being in the process of formation (*bhāvyamānatva*), they do not include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), the nasalized (*anunāsika*) forms of *y*, *v*, and *l* are nevertheless included because the grammatical qualities (*guṇa*) do not cause differentiation. Therefore, there is no correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṅkhya*).

Nor should it be argued that the correspondence (yathāsaṅkhya) may be established by taking the understanding of the literal meaning (*śakyārtha*), which precedes the understanding of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*); for even so, since the thirty [sounds] would be presented individually by the third and fourth vowels, *ṛ* and *ḷ*, there would result the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *r* for the *ḷ*-vowels and the substitution of *l* for the *ṛ*-vowels. Therefore, intending that the desired result is achieved here precisely by the rule "sthānentaratama" (Pāṇini 1.1.50), he says: "on account of proximity in terms of place of articulation."

Regarding the rule *anaci ca dve vā*: Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the sūtra *nājjhalau*, states that the word *vā* (or) is understood from the preceding sūtra *yaro 'nunāsikaḥ*. Thus, the sense is that the sūtra *sarvatra śākalyasya* and the two preceding and following sūtras—which are its elaborations—need not have been composed at all.

As for those who, taking the mention of "Ācāryas" in the rule *dīrghādācāryāṇām* to be for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*), laboriously struggle to find a justification for the alternative form *vāk* cited in the Bhāṣya—that is entirely in vain; for no authoritative scholars have stated that it is for the sake of honor. Otherwise, the same would apply to the mention of Śākaṭāyana in the rule *triprabhṛtiṣu*. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it contradicts the works of Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others—such as their statement in the commentary on *saṃskartā* that there are three *s*-sounds following [the root]—and because it contradicts one's own [stated] texts.

For this very reason, even in the *Prātiśākhya-bhāṣya*, an option for the doubling of the letter *t* is cited in the mantra "ā tvā ratham"; and by Mādhava, an option for the doubling of the letter *s* is stated in the word "āste. Thus, the claim that the doubling of the letter *t* in "dhātraṃśa" is incorrect is itself incorrect; such is the direction of the argument.

Regarding the rule *sthānivadādeśaḥ* ("a substitute is like the original"), the ancient grammarians stated: "Substitutes for verbal roots (*dhātu*), stems (*aṅga*), primary suffixes (*kṛt*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), indeclinables (*avyaya*), case-endings (*sup*), and finite verb endings (*tiṅ*) are [governed by this rule]. Is this an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*) or merely illustrative (*udāharaṇamātra*)? It cannot be the first, because it would fail to include substitutes such as *sic*, *sac*, *caṅ*, *aṅ*, and others, as well as the substitute *śnā* and the affix *śānac*. Nor can it be the second, because the separate mention of "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) from "stem" (*aṅga*) and "word" (*pada*) would be redundant. Furthermore, the example cited by the author of the *Vṛtti*, namely *prastutya*, is weak; for the suffix *ktvā* alone is not an indeclinable, and its status is already established by its being a *kṛt* suffix. With this intention, he says: "the substitute."

What is the purpose of the phrase *analvidhau*? It is so that [the rule] does not apply in the case of an operation (*vidhi*) concerning *tena*, *tasmāt*, *tasya*, or *tasmin*. In this regard, regarding an operation concerning an *al* (phoneme): as in *vyūḍhoraskena*. Here, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (substitution) of the *sakāra*, one might assume it possesses the property of being an *aṭ* (vowel), and thus the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* would be required by the rule *aḍvyavāye*. Regarding an operation concerning what follows an *al*: as in *dyauḥ* and *panthāḥ*. The elision [of *s*] by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* does not take place. Regarding an operation concerning an *al*: as in *dyukāmaḥ*. The elision [of *y*] by the rule *lopo vyor vali* does not take place. Regarding an operation concerning an *ali* (vowel): as in *yajeḥ ktaḥ*, resulting in *iṣṭaḥ*. The substitution of *u* by the rule *haśi ca* does not take place.

In this context, only the *sthānin* (the original element) itself is understood as the constituent part (*avayava*). Consequently, in forms such as *rāmāya*, the lengthening prescribed by the rule *supi ca* is established; for in that rule, the status of being a *yanādi* is relied upon, and [the *yan*] is a constituent part of the substitute (*ādeśa*), not a constituent part of the original element (*sthānin*). Having considered all of this, he says: "but it does not depend on the *al* of the *sthānin*. Here, the requirement of dependence is not restricted to being the primary factor, but may be in any way whatsoever. Therefore, in *prapaṭhya*, the augment *iṭ* characterized by the condition of being preceded by a *val* does not occur. The phrase "due to its prohibition" means due to the prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original).

The statement "the [mention of] *ac* is for the purpose of [indicating that the rule is] not an *al-vidhi*" means that, by this, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the *v* in *vavraśca*. This is because, due to the status of *uraṭ* as a *sthānivadbhāva*, it would be considered a *saṃprasāraṇa*, and thus the prohibition "there is no [substitution] when a *saṃprasāraṇa* follows" (*na saṃprasāraṇe*) would apply. Nor should it be argued that *uraṭ* does not have a subsequent cause (*paranimitta*). For it is prescribed when a suffix is present, which is implied by the term "aṅga"; and after refuting the position that "the section on *aṅga* extends prior to the modifications of the reduplicated syllable" (*prāgabhyāsavikārebhyaḥ*), the position that "it extends up to the end of the *āsupāda*" (*āsupātamasamāpteḥ*) has been established as the final view (*siddhānta*) in the original treatise (*ākara*).

Furthermore, by the preceding sūtra, that which is occasioned by the *sthānin* (the original element) is extended [to the substitute], but that which is occasioned by the *ādeśa* (the substitute) is not excluded; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of rules such as *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* failing to apply in cases like *nāyakaḥ* and *pāvakaḥ*. By this [present] sūtra, however, it is excluded, because it is accepted that—relying on the heading of "words" (*śabdādhikāra*)—this extension applies to both presence and absence. The inclusion of the terms "elision of *y*" (*yalopa*), "lengthening" (*dīrgha*), and so forth in the sūtra *na padānta* is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this. For this very reason, there is no *vṛddhi* in forms such as *gaṇayati*.

Since that [quality] does not exist even in its substitute when it exists in the original locus, its non-existence is extended by the rule of atideśa. And it has been said: "Let it be extended, whether it be existent or non-existent; there is no burden here."

It might be argued as follows: since priority (*pūrvatva*) requires a limit (*avadhi*), it is appropriate that only what is proximate should serve as that limit. And here, three things are proximate: the substituend (*sthānin*), the substitute (*ādeśa*), and the cause (*nimitta*). Among these, the substituend cannot be the limit, because it is superseded by the substitute; nor can the substitute or the cause be the limit, for otherwise in the word *vaiyākaraṇa*, the substitution of *ay* for *ai* would result. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "of that which is seen as preceding the vowel. The meaning is that "preceding-ness" (*pūrvatva*) is a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) and not a defining qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
By this, the Vārttika—"The rule is established for *ai* and *au* through the understanding of 'preceding the vowel'"—is explained.

The term *padānta* does not mean "the final constituent of a word. [Consider the example: from *vṛkṣam veti* comes *vṛkṣavīḥ*; from *vāti* comes *vṛkṣavāḥ*; and one who describes that [action] is *vṛkṣav*, with the suffix *vic*. Here, the elision of *v* by the rule *lopo vyoḥ...* does not occur because of the status of being a *sthānivat*. Nor is there a prohibition by the rule *na padānta...*, because the elision (*lopa*) which is the element to be prescribed here is not a constituent of the word (*pada*). However, if the rule were interpreted as "there is no [application of a rule] when it is prescribed in place of a word-final [element]," then this would not be established, according to the view of Haradatta and others that "after a *subanta*, the suffix *ṇic* occurs," since the internal *sup* [case-ending] would cause the status of being a *pada* to persist.

Nor does the status as a *bha*-stem, which is extended by the rule *iṣṭavad* to the causative (*ṇic*), subvert the status as a *pada*; for the *ṇi* has been elided, and there is no application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule that a grammatical operation conditioned by a suffix applies even when the suffix is elided), because [the substitution] depends on the individual phonemes (*varṇāśrayatvāt*). This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "and in the case of reduplication, etc.": the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) and other such operations. As for the term "in *vare*," it should be explained as: "a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*) occurring in place of *vare* is not like the original (*na sthānivat*). Although there is no intention to express them together (*sahavivakṣā’bhāve’pi*), the compound is a *dvandva* due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), and there is the elision of the locative case ending (*saptamyaluk*).

Now, the examples: at the end of a word (*padānte*)—*kāni santi*, *kau staḥ*. In the case of reduplication (*dvirvacane*)—*suddhyupāsyaḥ*. In the case of the suffix *-vara-* (*vare*)—*yāyāvaraḥ*. [This is formed] by the suffix *-varac* according to the rule "yaśca yaṅaḥ"; there is elision of the *a* (ato lopaḥ). And that [elision] is not treated as if it were in its original position (*na sthānivat*) when the elision of the long *ā* is to be performed by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca. In the case of the elision of *y* (*yalope*)—*yātiḥ*. From the root *yā* with the suffix *yaṅ*, the suffix *ktic* is added; there is elision of the *a*, then elision of the *y*. Because the elision of the *a* is treated as if it were in its original position (*sthānivat*), there is elision of the long *ā*, and then elision of the *y*.

Furthermore, the elision of *ā* (in *cikīrṣakaḥ*) should not be suspected [of being subject to the rules of substitution], because the elision of *ā* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) according to the maxim of *ciṇ* and *luṅ*, and because of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). Regarding accent (*svara*): in *cikīrṣakaḥ*, when the acute accent (*udātta*) is to be applied to the vowel *i* of the suffix *kak* by the rule "the vowel following *san* is acute when *liṭ* follows," the elision of the *a* of *san* is not treated as the original element (*na sthānivat*). Regarding homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*) and the nasal (*anusvāra*): in *śiṇḍhi*. Regarding lengthening (*dīrgha*): in *pratidīvnā*. Regarding the *jaś*-substitution: in *sagdhiśca me*. Here, *gdhi* means eating.

From the root *ad* with the suffix *ktin*, there is the substitution of *ghas* by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (optionally in the Veda). Then, by the rule "ghasibhasorhali" (the penultimate vowel is elided before a consonant), the penultimate vowel is dropped. By the rule "jhalo jhali" (an *s* following a *jhāl* is elided before a *jhāl*), the *s* is elided. Then the change to *gh* occurs, and by the rule of *jaśtva*, *gh* becomes *j*. Following the word *sa* from the sūtra "sahasya saḥ" (the substitute *sa* for *saha*), the rule "samānasyacchandasyamūrdhaprabhṛtyudarkeṣu" (in the Veda, *samāna* is replaced by *sa* except in the words *mūrdhan*, etc., and *udarka*) applies, resulting in *sa*. In the case of *car*, [the forms] *jakṣatuḥ* and so on are derived.

The meaning is that [the word *saṃyogāntasya*] refers to that which ends in such a [consonant cluster], according to the paribhāṣā "of the final [element] of what precedes the vowel" (*alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*). Although it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as *saṃyogasya*, since the extension to that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained through the qualifier, the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) is for the purpose of obtaining a compound with a dual ending—namely, *saṃyogau antau yasya*—in order to prevent the elision [of the final consonant] in forms such as *dṛṣatkaroti* under the view that the technical name *saṃyoga* applies to each individual [consonant]. For it is established in the Bhāṣya that, regarding subordinate members (*upasarjana*), singularity is the default number, whereas duality and so forth must be achieved through deliberate effort.

The term *yaṇ* is either explicitly stated (*vācanika*) or it must be explained (*vācya*). The explanation is twofold: either by drawing down the mention of *jhal* from the rule *jhalo jhali*, it is established that the elision (*lopa*) applies only to a *jhal* sound; or, since the internal (*antaraṅga*) elision is to be applied first, the external (*bahiraṅga*) *yaṇ* substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) at that time. Nor should it be argued that the *asiddha* paribhāṣā of the sixth book (the *pūrvatrāsiddham* rule), being situated within the *tripādī*, does not perceive the internal elision as non-existent; for we accept the *kāryakāla* view of the application of rules.

Nor is there a prohibition based on the rule "nājānantarye bahiṣṭvapraklṛptiḥ" (there is no designation as external when there is immediate sequence with a vowel), because that [designation] is non-permanent and because there is an absence of immediate sequence with a vowel once the elision has taken effect at a later time. Thus says the Vārttika: "There is a prohibition regarding the elision of a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) at the end of a conjunct," "Or rather, not so, because of the elision of a *jhal* [consonant]," and "Or because of its being characterized as external. Here, the distinction is that the first two Vārttikas apply under the *yathoddeśa* view, while the third applies under the *kāryakāla* view.

As for what they say—that the statement belongs to the author of the Vārttika, whereas the two methods of rejection belong to the author of the Bhāṣya—that is baseless, because there is no evidence for a difference of opinion [regarding this]. Furthermore, as for what they say—that one who speaks of *kāvyam*, *kalatram*, and *śālvam* becomes *kāv*, *kalat*, and *śāl* respectively, according to the rule "after the root *adabhra*, the suffix *ac* is applied"—that too is incorrect, because in all three cases, the elision of a consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is difficult to establish.

For the sake of uniformity in the first position, since it can be easily stated that each preceding [element] is internal (*antaraṅga*) and each succeeding one is external (*bahiraṅga*), the non-established status (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of *a* and the elision of *ṇi* is applicable. For this very reason, in the *Kātantra-Parīṣiṣṭa*, "śukl" is cited as the form of the root *śuklayati* after the suffix *kvip*; for otherwise, when *kvip* follows the two forms ending in *vānta* (the *vṛddhi* substitute for *ai* and *au*), the substitution of *ūṭh* would be unavoidable. Nor can there be the application of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (treating the substitute as the original), because that is prohibited with respect to an operation prescribed by *kvip*; furthermore, if *vic* were used instead, the elision of *vyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.66) would undesirably apply.

In the case of *giriveśmayaṭ*, when the suffix *kvip* is applied, if one adopts the position that the rule must be explicitly formulated to prohibit the *yaṇ* substitution, then *giriveḍ* is appropriate; however, if one adopts the position of rejecting the necessity of such a formulation, then it remains as ending in *m* (i.e., *giriveḍm*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. As for the phrase "in both positions," the sense is that both views are established in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the statement "there are four forms": as for what some say—that there are nine forms based on the doubling of both the *dhakāra* and the *yakāra*, the subsequent doubling of both, the optional elision (*lopavikalpa*), and the doubling of only one of the two; specifically: one *dha* in three ways (one *ya*, two *yas*, three *yas*); likewise, two *dhas* in three ways and three *dhas* in three ways.

Furthermore, the external *yaṇ* substitution is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the internal doubling, because it has been established in the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the rule for the *visarjanīya* that the paribhāṣā concerning what is external does not apply to an internal operation within the three final chapters (*traipādika*).

On this point, the following must be said: reduplication is not pure [in this context], because it has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" that a single characteristic applies only once to a single individual instance (*vyakti*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of an infinite regress of reduplications. Nor can the matter be resolved by the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rules "jharo jhari" and "halo yamām," because that elision is optional (*vaikalpika*). Otherwise, how could your own statement—"tridham" and "triyaṃ"—be consistent?

Furthermore, if this were the case, the rule *sarvasya dve* would have to apply again and again. For this very reason, the mention of the term *abhyāsa* (reduplication) in the rule *liṭi dhātoḥ* was rejected in the Bhāṣya. Kaiyaṭa and others, however, have stated that its purpose is to prevent reduplication when a *caṅ* suffix follows a desiderative (*sannanta*) or a *yaṅ*-intensive (*yaṅanta*) after the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Therefore, in this context, it is entirely inconsistent to claim there are only nine forms; one must either abandon the forms beginning with the fifth or accept an infinity of forms. As for the claim that there are eight forms due to the doubling of the letter *s* and sixteen due to the doubling of the *visarga*, that is a separate matter.

As for what was stated—that [the rule] "internal (antaraṅga) [operations take precedence] over those consisting of three feet (traipādika)," etc.—that too is incorrect. For in that very Bhāṣya, the fact that *vṛddhi* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) in order to prevent the visarga in the forms *nārkuṭa* and *nārpatyaḥ* is explicit. Furthermore, the prohibition against the elision of a *yaṇ* (*yaṇaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ*) following the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) has been rejected on the grounds of its being external (*bahiraṅga*). Moreover, you yourself have restated the matter in exactly that same way. Therefore, in this context, the *yathoddeśa* (locus-based) view must be adopted so that the paribhāṣā regarding external operations does not apply.

And likewise, in the Bhāṣya, regarding the doubling of a *yaṇ* following *mayaḥ*, the form "dadhyatra" is cited as an example. Nor should it be argued that even so, another form would arise by means of the Śākala rule (*iko 'savarṇe*); for that [Śākala rule] is prohibited in the case of a compound. Nor should it be argued that its prohibition applies only to obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*), because the mention of "obligatory" (*nitya*) has been rejected in the Bhāṣya; for among the sages, authority increases in proportion to their seniority.

If it is argued that the *yaṇ* substitution is indeed difficult to justify here—since the word *sudhī* is derived from the root *dhyai* with *samprasāraṇa*, and by the rule "after a *samprasāraṇa*" (*samprasāraṇācca*), the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) would result—[we reply]: no, because of the Vārttika statement, "when there is a *samprasāraṇa*-precedent, the term 'identical stem' (*samānāṅga*) is understood," and because that which occupies the place of the *samprasāraṇa* does not possess that [identical-stem] status.

Nor should one fear the prohibition of *yaṇ* by the rule "na bhūsudhiyoḥ," because that rule operates only when a suffix follows an *aṅga*, and because the prohibition applies only to what is obtained through the two rules "eranekācaḥ—" and "ossupi" according to the maxim "anantarasya" (the rule of immediate proximity).

Regarding the word *dhātraṃśa*: here there is no doubling of the *repha* (the letter *r*). This is because, within the section on doubling (*dvitvaprakaraṇa*), the status of being an object of the operation (*kāryitva*) for the *repha* is set aside by its status as a cause (*nimittabhāva*) as explicitly stated in the rule *rahābhyām*. However, Kaiyaṭa maintains that in cases such as *sudhyupāsya*, the status of the *repha* as a cause by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) is not set aside, based on the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) found in rules such as *ikaḥ tasmādityuttarasya*. It has been stated, however, that this applies to the *takāra* (the letter *t*), and since that is optional (*vā*), there are two forms here. But *lākṛti* is only one form.

There may optionally be elision (*lopa*) of *yam* [following a consonant]. This is because the word "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood from the rule "ha after *jhay*" (*jhayo haḥ*). And this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the *laṇ* sūtra.

Regarding the word *māhātmyam*: here, the meaning is that there is no elision of the *m*. However, the rule "there is elision of *y* and *r* after a consonant when followed by a homogeneous *y* or *r*" was not formulated as a sūtra. For if it were, there would result the elision of the letter following the *r* in forms such as *ārdhnot*, *mūrdhnaḥ*, *śārṅgam*, and *ārtnī*. [The rule is stated as] "after a consonant, there is elision of the *yama*s. It may or may not occur; this is because the word *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood from the previous rule "haḥ after *jhayaḥ*. This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the *laṇ* sūtra. Regarding *māhātmyam*: here, the meaning is that there is no elision of the *m*.

However, the rule "halo yarāṃ yari savarṇe lopaḥ" was not formulated as a sūtra; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of elision (lopa) of the letter following the *repha* in forms such as *ādhrnot*, *mūdhrnaḥ*, *śāṅrgam*, and *ārtnīḥ*.

Regarding the phrase *vānto yi yakārādau*: this meaning is obtained through the Vārttika *yasminvidhistadādāvalgrahaṇe*, which serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *yena vidhiḥ*—a rule intended to mean that a designation applies to that which ends with the [specifying] element. As for *odautoḥ*: the meaning is that in the preceding rule, those two (the vowels *o* and *au*) alone were determined to be the substituends (*sthānin*) in relation to the *vānta* sounds. Now, one might raise the objection that in the word *gavyūtiḥ*, there would be elision (*lopa*) either by the rule *hali sarveṣām* or by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*; anticipating this, he says *vāntaḥ*.

Regarding *lavyam*: the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *lū* by the rule *aco yat*. The *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*. Regarding *avaśyalāvyam*: the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *orāvaśyake*.

Regarding *kṣayyam*: by the rule "śaki liṅ ca," the particle *ca* implies that the *kṛtya* suffixes [are also used]. Regarding *kṣeyam*: by the rule "arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca," the suffix *yat* is applied. Regarding *hara ehi*: here, the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpam*) would have been required by the rule "omāṅośca."

"Uraṇ raparaḥ" [means] "by virtue of internal similarity"; that is to say, because the *ar* (the vowel *a* with the *ṛ*-element) which has the letter *r* as its head shares a common place of articulation (*sthāna*) with the letter *ṛ* through the mediation of the *r*.
"In the alternative case, there is doubling"—this refers to the rule *ṛdher dhaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase *lopo vā*: this is because the option (*vikalpa*) from the rule *jhayo ho 'nyatarasyām* is carried over [into the present context]. This is clear in both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *nājjhalau*. However, prior to that [work], there was a deficiency because the carrying over of the option was not mentioned.

As for the argument presented by some commentators—that the *bhāṣya* was cited in support of the rule "śaro 'ci" (Pāṇini 8.4.49) with the intention that this rule serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), such that the *bhāṣya* states: "The option (*vibhāṣā*) from [the previous rule] 8.4.47 carries over; otherwise, this [rule 8.4.49] would prevent reduplication"—that is not correct, because that very indicator has been refuted in the subsequent *bhāṣya*. For if the elision (*lopa*) were compulsory, then the reduplication prescribed by "aco rahābhyām—" (Pāṇini 8.4.46) would constitute an exception (*apavāda*) to that elision. In that case, the purposefulness of the rule "śaro 'ci" would be quite evident.

Therefore, if one follows the alternative view (*vikalpa*), another indicator (*jñāpaka*) must be sought, or else the explanation of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) and others alone must be taken as the refuge. Regarding the phrase "of doubling and elision": as for the claim that by the force of the rule prescribing doubling, only two [consonants] remain, that is not correct; because elision is optional, doubling serves its purpose in the alternative case. Regarding "threefold": it should be understood that if doubling occurs again by another rule, such as *yaṇo mayaḥ*, it becomes fourfold as well.

In the rule *etyedhatyūṭsu*, the term *ec* is understood to carry over from the previous sūtra. According to the ancient commentators (*prāñcaḥ*), this [term *ec*] qualifies only *eti* and not *edhati*, because there is no deviation [in the application of the rule] for *edhati*; nor does it qualify *ūṭh*, because that is impossible. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa states: "[The term *ec*] is also a qualifier of *edhati*, because there is a deviation in the case of *mā bhavān predidhat*. Although this is generally not seen in the manuscripts of Kaiyaṭa, it is indeed found in some instances. And it should not be argued that, once the shortening (*hrasva*) has been applied by the rule *ṇau caṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.41), this is no longer *edhati*, because that which is modified in one part remains essentially the same (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*).

Nor should it be argued that even in this case, by the rule "of the second [element] beginning with 'a'," when the word *dhidhi* is substituted in place of the word *dhi*, there would be a confusion regarding the division between base and suffix—just as occurs with *vas* and *nas*. This is because the *Ṣāṣṭhabhāṣya* has established the principle that "reduplication is a double utterance. Otherwise, the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) would not occur in this very instance. Furthermore, one might argue that in forms such as *jighāṃsati*, when reduplication is applied to the entire element *san* including its *s*-sound, the shortening (*hrasva*) does indeed not take place. However, this is not so, because the fact that the root *oṇ* is marked with the *ṛt* indicatory letter (*ṛdit*) indicates that the shortening prescribed by the rule "ṇau caṅi—" applies first, even though it is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*).

Regarding this, Mādhava states: there is no over-extension [of the rule] in the case of *mā bhavān predidhat*, because the causative (*ṇyanta*) form is a distinct word and is therefore not included by the mention of the root *edh*. For this very reason, it was stated in the rule *na bhābhūpūkamigami-* that there is an extension [of the prohibition] to the roots beginning with *bhā* when they are in their causative forms (*ṇyanta*).

In that very context, Kaiyaṭa, the author of the Nyāsa, Haradatta, and all others have stated that since it is a different word (*śabdāntara*), the rule does not apply and thus an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made. Furthermore, if the inclusion of even the suffix *ṇi* were accepted, then regarding the example *abhiṣāvayati* under the rule *upasargātsunoti-*, an objection would arise as to how there can be the substitution of *ṣ* when *abhi* is connected with the causative (*ṇyanta*) form and is therefore not a prefix (*upasarga*) with respect to the root *su*. The resolution provided by the author of the Bhāṣya and others—that *abhi* qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)—would then be inconsistent.

Nor should one be misled by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *heracaṅi* into thinking that "when a base is mentioned, that which has an additional suffix such as *ṇiC* is also included. This is because the indicator applies only to the domain of *kutva* (the substitution of guttural sounds). Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "The prohibition regarding *he* in the case of *acaṅ* is purposeless because the base is different; however, it serves as an indicator for the absence of *kutva* even in the case of a *ṇiC*-derived form, provided it is other than *acaṅ*. Therefore, Kaiyaṭa’s view is to be disregarded due to its contradiction with reasoning and its conflict with the Bhāṣya, the Vārttikas, the Vṛtti, the Nyāsa, and other works, as well as with his own earlier and later statements.

In this regard, the following must be said: Let it be granted that the qualified [form] is a different word; even so, let it be determined by what means the status of the base (*prakṛti*) portion as *edh* is lost? For in forms such as *upaidhata*, the status of being *edh* does not cease to exist in the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), and thus it is not lost in the base portion. And accordingly, there is a Vārttika on the rule *upasargātsunoti-* which states: "But it is established because of the difference in parts."

As for the objection raised regarding the contradiction with the Bhāṣya on the rule *abhiṣāvayati*, that is the reverse of the truth; for, according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, the aforementioned distinction is established because the form of the root *su* (*sunoti*) remains unchanged from its original state (*prakṛti*). In your view, however, because the form is different and the additional element *ṇiC* would not be included, the previously stated distinction would be entirely untenable. For what indeed is the difference between *edhayati* and *sāvayati*—such that the additional element *ṇiC* is not included in *edhate* but is included in *sunoti*?

As for the proposal that an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) should be made for causative forms such as *bhāpayati* and others, that too is not contrary to our position; for since the specific form is a distinct word (*śabdāntara*), it is necessary to provide an addition because the root portion is separated by the suffix *ṇic*. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Nyāsa or other commentaries on that point, nor with their own statements; on the contrary, the contradiction lies with you alone, because in the sixth [book] of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika, the rule "etyedhatyoḥ—" is split and specifically qualified by the term "eci".
Therefore, the commentary (*vṛtti*) and Mādhava’s work here are indeed inconsistent; [the author] explains with the intention that it refers to the roots beginning with *ej* and *yā*.

Regarding the term *akṣauhiṇī*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has an *ūhinī* (multitude) of *akṣas* (chariots)," namely *akṣāṇām ūhinī*. An army characterized by a specific measure is called an *akṣauhiṇī*. The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 8.4.3). As for the analysis provided by the ancients—"an *ūha* (collection) of *akṣas* exists in this"—that too must somehow be understood as intending a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound with the word *ūhinī*. For if there were a compound with the word *ūha*, and then the suffix *in* were added, the *vṛddhi* [of the first vowel] would not occur, because it would be barred by the internal *guṇa* [substitution].

Even though [the form] *vṛddhi* is an exception (*apavāda*), it has already fulfilled its purpose through the analysis (*vigraha*) with the word *ūhinī*, as was stated previously: "In the case of roots ending in *iṇ*, the suffix *ṅī*, and the root *śī*, there is *guṇa* [substitution] because of the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*). Regarding the rule *svādīreriṇoḥ*: the reading *ireriṇyoḥ* is an occasional corruption. For if it were so, in the case of *svairī*—which ends in the suffix *ṇini*—there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of *vṛddhi* in the feminine. However, in the case of *svairiṇī*, the *vṛddhi* should be understood by taking the portion preceding the suffix *ṅīp*. As for what some commentators have explained—that this is due to the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the metarule concerning words qualified by gender)—that is fruitless.

Regarding the rule *prādūhoḍhoḍhyeṣaiṣyeṣu*: the ancient scholars (*prāñcaḥ*) maintain that the word *ūha* was interpolated by some [commentators], as it is not seen in the *Bhāṣya* and other early works; however, in modern manuscripts, the word *ūha* is indeed found in both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*. As for the phrase *nānarthakasya* ("not of that which is meaningless"): the meaning is that since the presented meaning can function as a qualifier with respect to the word, it is improper to abandon it. Sīradeva, however, says: "In the rule *vraśca*, the separate mention of *bhrāj* apart from *rāj* is the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) for this."

If it is argued that this is incorrect because, due to the association with *rāji* (as in *phaṇādi-rāji*), the mention of *bhrāj* is exhausted by its purpose of signifying *ṣatva* for that specific form alone—[we reply: two forms, *vibhrāṭ* and *vibhrāk*, must indeed be established. And these can be established even by reading "rājṛ" in the *vraśca*-sūtra, since it is possible to assign the vowel *ṛ* to the single root *bhrāj* even prior [to the suffix]. This is because the optional rule (*vikalpa*) "bhrājabhāsa... is based on a scriptural statement (*vācanika*), and the assignment of the vowel *ṛ* results solely in the formation of the Ātmanepada endings.

Furthermore, because it will be mentioned later, the vowel *a* is easier to read in its place [in the rule]. Therefore, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) cited by Sīradeva is also entirely correct. Regarding the word *praiṣya*: due to its association with *eṣa*, the form *eṣya*—provided it is not an indeclinable—is also understood. Consequently, when the suffix *lyap* is applied after the *ktvā* suffix following the causative (*ṇic*) of the root *iṣ*, there is only the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and not *vṛddhi*. Thus: *preṣya gataḥ* ("having sent, he went"). Regarding *pravatsatara*: here, those who follow the Kālāpa school also include the word *vatsara*, and they cite as an example *vatsarārṇam* ("a debt to be paid in a year"). Others, however, also include the word *vatsa*; all of this is contrary to the *Bhāṣya* and other authoritative sources.

*Antādivacca* (P. 6.1.85). Here, the phrase *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (P. 6.1.84) is understood to carry over, as well as the principle of *yathāsaṃkhyam* (correspondence according to order); with this in mind, [the author] says: "as if it were the final element of the preceding. This rule is already established by the *sthānivat* rule (P. 1.1.56). One should not mistakenly think that this rule is for the sake of operations concerning vowels (*alvidhi*), because even in the case of non-vowel operations (*analvidhi*), this [substitution] is undesirable. Otherwise, in the form *ayaje indram*, there would result the occurrence of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*). And thus says the Vārttika: "Or rather, it is not so, because the transfer is of the property of being 'that' (*atādrūpyātideśāt*)."

It is not [the case that] there is no *visarga*. And this is the same even in cases such as "sukhārtaḥ. Furthermore, in this context, according to the view that the time of application is determined by the effect (*kāryakālapakṣa*), one should understand that [the substitution] is non-existent (*asiddhatva*) due to being extrinsic (*bahiraṅgatva*). Nor is there a prohibition by the rule "nājānantarye" (P. 1.1.58), because although that [prohibition] would apply under Haradatta’s view—namely, that it applies wherever there is immediate sequence of vowels (*ac*) whether in an intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) or extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) operation—it does not apply under Kaiyaṭa’s view, which holds that the prohibition applies where the immediate sequence of vowels exists at the time the subsequent [operation] is about to take effect. This is because, although the immediate sequence of vowels exists when the extrinsic *vṛddhi* (which depends on many factors) is present, that sequence is absent at the time when the subsequent [operation] actually takes effect.

Regarding the phrase *upasargeṇa*: the meaning is that since it has been stated that the designations *gati* and *upasarga* apply only with respect to that action (*kriyā*) with which the prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) are connected.

In *prārṣabhīyati*, there is a prohibition of doubling by the rule *śaro'ci*. In *prejate*, the root *ejṛ* means "to shine. However, the sense of "trembling" belongs to the *parasmaipada* form. The explanation of the ancients (*prācām*) that *ejate* means "it trembles" is merely based on an error.

The mention of *para* (in the rule *eṅi pararūpam*), though *eṅyeṅ* would have sufficed, is for the sake of what follows. As for the mention of *rūpa*, its purpose is to be considered; for the result would be established simply by saying *eṅi paraḥ*, just as in the case of *ami pūrvaḥ*.
*Niyoga* means restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). As they say:
"When *eva* is observed in the sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*), it has the form of another [particle] as its scope;
but when it occurs in the sense of restriction (*niyama*), this is the domain of *vṛddhi*."

By this, the explanation that "niyojana is niyoga, which is an activity (vyāpāra)" is refuted; for it contradicts usages such as "when previously [I cast] my body into the fire" and "of my very own sins in another birth," it contradicts the verse cited in the *Vṛtti*, and it contradicts Vedic sūtra usages such as "the *laṅ* [is used] according to Śākaṭāyana alone" and "[the root] *tap* [is used] when its object is the act of penance (*tapas-karman*) alone. As for their claim that this is a *Ślokavārttika*, that is due to haste.

Regarding the rule *śakandhvādiṣu*: the meaning is that in the case of words such as *śakandhu* and others, a subsequent form (*pararūpa*) should be prescribed in accordance with their established usage. For this very reason, he says: "And that [substitution] is of the final vowel (*ṭeḥ*). If, however, by virtue of the governing rule *āt*, the substitution were desired only for the letter *a*, then the form *manīṣā* would not be established. Some, however, maintain that because the words *manas* and *patat* belong to the class beginning with *pṛṣodara*, there is elision of the final syllable, and thus the subsequent form of the letter *a* alone occurs. *Śakandhu* means the well (*andhuḥ* = *kūpaḥ*) of the Śakas—a particular region. It is the well of the Karkas, who are kings.

The word *karkandhū*, meaning the jujube fruit (*badarī*), ends in a long vowel; this will be explained among the *uṇādi* suffixes in the rule beginning with "andhūdṛmbhū-". The term *aṭā* is derived from the root *aṭ* (meaning "to wander") with the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class). A woman who wanders through families is a *kulaṭā*. From the roots *īṣ* (in the sense of "gathering") and *īṣ* (in the senses of "motion," etc.), the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule "garośca halaḥ," resulting in *īṣā*. The "mind's impulse" is *manīṣā*. The "pole of a plough" is *halīṣā*; it refers to the shaft of the plough and has a retroflex (*mūrddhanya*) as its penultimate letter. As for the statement: "The word *īśa* [denotes] a lord or Śaṅkara, and in the feminine, the shaft of a plough."

Thus, when the word *rabhasa* ending in *keśa* follows a word ending in *tālavya*, the rule "ād guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87) applies, resulting in *haleśā*. [The name] *patañjali* is derived from the sense that his hands were joined in *añjali* as he fell (*patan*) because he was worthy of being saluted (*namaskāryatvāt*). [The name] *mārtaṇḍa*: some here claim this is a case of *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous sounds). Vedic usages such as "he ascended to the supreme *mārtaṇḍa*," "he undertook the *mārtaṇḍa* again," and "the universal *mārtaṇḍa* went forth" support their view.

Regarding the rule "otvoṣṭhayoḥ": this operates when the letter *a* and the letters *o* or *u* stand together in a single compound; therefore, it does not apply here in the example: *vṛṣalasutauṣṭhavraṇaste* ("the wound on the lip of the son of a low-born man").

He explains the word *avyakta* (unmanifest) with the words "of sound" (*dhvaneḥ*). "Of the imitation" (*anukaraṇasya*) means that its phonemes, such as the letter *a*, are not clearly articulated; this is the intended sense. And its status as an "imitation" (*anukaraṇatva*) is to be understood through some degree of similarity. As for what was stated by the ancients—"What then? [The rule] should not apply to that which ends in *d*"—and as for the explanation given there, namely that "ending in *d*" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other forms such as *vaṭaka* and *marut*, that is worthless, because both the question and the answer "ending in *d*" would be without foundation.

As for what they have explained—namely, that the question arises because [the rule] is established by carrying over *ataḥ* from "ato guṇe" and relying on the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "word" (*śabda*), such that even when there is "dentality" (*jaśtva*) due to the substitution of *d*, the rule would still apply; whereas the answer is "no," because by repeating the mention of *at*, a literal (*śrauta*) final *t* is intended—this is to be considered doubtful. For, since the rule for *jaśtva* is treated as not having taken effect (*asiddha*), only the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) operation would occur; furthermore, this would lead to the example *paṭat-paṭat* being disconnected [from the prohibition], since the prohibition "not for a reduplicated word" (*nāmreḍitasya*) would then be inapplicable.

For in that case, according to the method you have stated, there is no occurrence (*prāpti*) at all, because [the word] has been tamed (*dāntatva*).
