By this, the following argument is also refuted: "In the expression *paṭat iti*, since one intends to express the non-difference between the original (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*), there is an absence of case-endings; thus, due to its being a non-word (*apada*), as in the case of *gavityayamāha*, the substitution of *jaś* (i.e., *t* becoming *d*) does not occur. This is contradicted by the subsequent portion of the treatise, and furthermore, because the substitution of *jaś* is unestablished (*asiddha*), it is superseded precisely by the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*).

If it is objected: "But even that [word *agni*] is eternal; so how can there be an application [of the suffix] in the absence of another form?", we say no. This is because it has already been explained by [the author] himself that this is an unworldly (*alaukika*) analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*), and because such a construction is possible when the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) is not intended to be expressed. This is the general direction [of the argument].

[The rule] is *akaḥ savarṇe aci paraḥ*. However, when the sūtra *nājjhalau* is rejected on the grounds that the sibilants (*ūṣman*) possess a slight opening (*īṣadvivṛtatva*), then the term *aci* need not be supplied here; it is more appropriately stated as *ako'ki dīrghaḥ*. As for the statement that "two phonemes [consisting of ṛ and ḷ] have two morae (*dvimātra*)," the explanation given by the ancients—that since a long vowel would otherwise be required, the short vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ* are specifically prescribed—is to be disregarded because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*, *Kaiyaṭa*, and other authorities.

Since the rule *eṅaḥ padāntād ṅasiṅasośca* begins [immediately after], this [rule] is already understood to have the domain of word-final elements (*padānta*); nevertheless, the phrase "from a word-final [eṅ]" is placed right here for the sake of clarity and for the purpose of what follows.

Regarding the rule *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ*: although the phrase *chandasi* (in the Veda) is not currently under discussion, one might suspect that this [rule] applies only to the Veda because of the sequence beginning with *yajuṣyuraḥ* ("the substitution of *u* for *ū* occurs in the Yajus"). Therefore, it is said *sarvatra* ("everywhere"). This is explained as: "in both common usage (*loka*) and the Veda (*veda*). Here, by carrying over the term *eṅaḥ* from the previous rule, it should be interpreted as "of *go* ending in *eṅ*. Consequently, there is no [substitution] here in the case of *citragvagram*. Because the *eṅ* is taken in its specific, stated form (*pratipadokta*), there is no [substitution] here either in the vocative *he citrago'gram*. [The term used is] *prakṛtibhāvaḥ* ("the state of being the original form").

This is because the word *prakṛtyā* (in its original form) is carried over from the sūtra *prakṛtyāntaḥ pādam*. Although the reading *nāntaḥ padam* is established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *iko guṇavṛddhī*, and the same is found in the Bhāṣya on the sixth [chapter], nevertheless, since the Bhāṣya on the Śākala-sūtra states that by the word *ca* in *hrasvaśca*, the word *prakṛtyā* is drawn over [from the previous rule], the reading *prakṛtyāntaḥ pādam* is indeed correct. However, it should be noted that if the reading were *na*, then by the rule *sarvatra*, only the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute form) would be optional.

Regarding *avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya*, it should be explained here as well that [the word] *go* ends in *eṅ*. It would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule as *ag*. The mention of Sphoṭāyana is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*), because the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) is understood from the previous context. As for *gavī*: as for the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) given by the ancients as *gave*, that is incorrect. Even if *avaṅ* were applied, the form would be established by the subsequent substitution (*pararūpa*) according to the rule *ato guṇe*. Nor should it be argued that if *avaṅ* were applied, the substitution of *yā* for the case-ending *ṅi* would occur, whereas in the feminine, the suffix *ṭāp* would occur; for by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, both the substitution of *yā* and the suffix *ṭāp* are easily resolved.

Nor should it be said that this [term] is non-eternal (*anitya*), for even by that much, the desired result of its general application is established. Regarding *gavākṣa*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the eye (*akṣi*) of cows (*go*). The compound-ending suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule "after *akṣi*, when not meaning 'eye'. This word is conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) to mean a window; its masculine gender is established by common usage (*loka*).

And in the case of *indra*, this [suffix] is obligatory due to the force of the initial undertaking (*ārambhasāmarthya*). However, the reading "and in the case of *indra* it is obligatory" (*indre ca nityam*) has been disregarded because it is inconsistent with the Bhāṣya.

"Ehi kṛṣṇa" (Come, Kṛṣṇa). Here, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs by the rule "dūrāddhūte ca" (Pāṇini 8.2.84). As for what the Eastern grammarians (*prāc*) stated—namely, "kṛṣṇā3 ehi"—that is incorrect; for in rules such as "dūrāddhūte ca," the governing heading "vākyasya ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.82) applies. In the example "cakryatra," there is no elision of *k* by the rule "skoḥ—" (Pāṇini 8.2.29). This is because, under the view that the application of a rule depends on the time of its operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the elision is rendered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the paribhāṣā regarding external operations (*bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*), and also due to the status of the substitute being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). However, the principle "pūrvatrāsiddhīye na—" (the paribhāṣā stating that this rule does not apply when an operation is considered non-existent with respect to a preceding rule) does not apply here, because of the specific statement: "tasya doṣaḥ saṃyogādilopa—" (the fault of that [paribhāṣā] concerns the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant, etc.).

The word *api* [in the rule] indicates that the prolation (*pluta*) applies both to the final vowel (*ṭi*) of a teacher's name and to that which is not a teacher's name. For example: *devadatta ehi* (O Devadatta, come!), and so forth; the same applies in subsequent cases. Regarding the statement "every prolated vowel": thus, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *agnītpreṣaṇe parasya ca*, it says: "Every prolated vowel must be treated optionally (*vibhāṣā*), even by one who does not wish to commit a rash act. Haradatta explains that a "rash act" (*sāhasa*) is the abandonment of the scripture; therefore, "even by one who does not wish to do so" means even by one who follows the scripture. Others hold that the meaning is: "even by one who does not wish to do so" because the difficulty of performing optional rules—even though they result in an abundance of merit—is impossible to carry out.

By this, the *Bhāgavata* passage—"Dvaipāyana, distressed by separation, called out 'Son!'"—is explained. This is because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is optional. Furthermore, it can easily be maintained that here the word *putra* does not stand at the end of a sentence, since it is possible for a word to be repeated even when it precedes a verb. Moreover, let us grant that there is a protracted vowel; however, let the absence of the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) also be granted, as it too is optional. Thus, the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "ī cākravarmaṇasya" states: "There is no need for the mention of *ī*; [for example,] 'this cow' (*vaśā iyam*) and 'this cow' (*vaśeyam*)."

Every instance of the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) for a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is indeed difficult to justify, according to the rule "aplutavad upasthite. For the meaning of that rule is that when the word *upasthita*—meaning a non-Vedic *iti*—follows, a protracted vowel shall behave as if it were not protracted. Thus, since a clear resolution in four ways [of the objection] exists, Śrīdhara’s assertion that it is an archaic usage (*ārṣaprayoga*) is not to be accepted.

Regarding the phrase *dvivacanam* ("the dual ending"): the intention is that by the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) in the rule *suptiṅantam*, it is indicated that "in a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends with that suffix. Therefore, it does not apply here in cases such as *kumāryor agāram* or *vadhvor agāram*, which become *kumāryagāram* and *vadhvagāram*. This is clear from the Bhāṣya and other sources. The claim of the ancients that "that which ends in a dual suffix should be *pragṛhya*" is merely an error. In the example *harī etau*, there is no application of the *śākala* rule; this is because it has been stated that in the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam*, the mention of *nityam* (always) [prevents the optional application of *śākala*].

Regarding this, the author of the *Vṛtti*—having read the rule as "the prohibition for those who hold the view of *maṇi* and so forth must be stated"—cited *maṇīva*, *rodasīva*, *dampatīva*, and *jampatīva*. However, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that this is not authoritative because it was not stated by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali).

This being the case, he justifies the usage in the *Mahābhārata*: "Like two jewels, my two dear young calves hang from the camel," by stating that the word *iva* is the intended meaning. Regarding the word *va*, the *Medinīkośa* states: "One should know *vaṃ* in the sense of *pracetasa* (the wise one), and it is also an indeclinable used in the sense of *iva*. Furthermore, at the point of explaining the entry in the *Amarakośa*—"*va*, *vā*, *yathā*, *tathā*, *eva*, *evam* [are used] in the sense of similarity"—the learned have cited the usage by Kālidāsa: "They drank up the enemy's fame as if it were water" (*śātravaṃ va papuryaśaḥ*). Thus, the word *va* here functions in the sense of *iva*.

The intended meaning is that this is evident from such observations as, "the lotuses whose petals were torn by *kādamba* birds. As for the alternative reading, "or else, 'vadvā' means 'yathā' (just as)," etc., that is incorrect; for within the context of a treatise on names and genders (*nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*), the secondary derivative suffix *-vat* (*taddhita-vat*) is not appropriate, and furthermore, suffixes such as *-aṇ*, *-phiñ*, and *-vuñ* are not mentioned among the synonyms for "offspring," "collection," and so forth.

Regarding the rule *adaso māt*: the intention here is that the term *ekāra* (the vowel *e*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], because its occurrence is impossible; thus he says, "*īdūtāviti*" (referring to P. 1.1.11). Now, one might object: the carry-over of the vowel *u* is redundant, since in forms such as *striyau* or *phale* in the case *amū āsāte*, the result is already established by the preceding rule (*P. 7.3.109*), even if the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered *asiddha*, because the stem still ends in *e*. To this he replies with the example *rāmakṛṣṇau*. The point is that in the masculine, the result would not be achieved by the preceding rule, because the ending there is *au*. However, with respect to the rule *adaso māt*, both the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) and the substitution of *ī* (*ītva*) are not *asiddha*, due to the specific force of the present rule's formulation. He adds: "*ekāro'pi*" (the vowel *e* also [does not carry over]).
And thus, the intention is that the inclusion of *māt* serves the purpose of ensuring that the vowel *e* does not follow from the previous rule.

Here, this point should be considered: why was it not simply formulated as "the vowels *ī*, *ū*, and *e* [ending] in the sense of the locative case are *pragṛhya*; so too those of *adas*; and the dual ending *e*"? For in this way, the mention of *īt* and *ūt* in the preceding rule and the mention of *māt* in the present rule would be unnecessary, and the difficulty of having to carry over only a portion of the previous rule would also be avoided.

This [form] is Vedic (chāndasa), stated for the sake of the purity of the composition; however, in reality, it is indeed possible even in common usage (laukika) as a mere imitation (anukaraṇa). But in cases such as *tve rāyo me rāyaḥ*, since there would be no purpose in imitating [the forms] *tve* and *me*, [they are not so used]. As for *asme*—it means "to us" (*asmabhyam*). The substitution of *śe* for the dative plural ending (*bhyas*) occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Then, by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ*, the remaining case-endings are elided.

Since the form *aj* (non-*j*) is already obtained by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not *āṅ*," the inclusion of the word "particle" (*nipāta*) is for the sake of what follows; it is placed right here for clarity. *Ā evam iti*: this particle *ā* indicates that the meaning of the sentence previously commenced has changed. The sense is: "Previously you thought thus, but now you think in this way.
*Ā evaṃ kila iti*: this particle *ā* indicates recollection. Regarding the phrase "vākya... and so forth, the Bhāṣya states as follows:

"One should know that this *āṅ* is *ṅit* when it signifies slightness (*īṣadartha*), connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), limit (*maryādā*), or inclusion (*abhividhi*); but it is *aṅit* in the sense of a sentence (*vākya*) or recollection (*smaraṇa*). (Pāṇini 1.1.14). Here, the intention is solely to define what constitutes *aṅit*, for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*). The status of the other [forms of *āṅ*] as *ṅit* is established by implication. The phrase beginning with "īṣadarthe," etc., is a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*). Thus, in the example *abhra ām̐ apaḥ*, because the vowel *ā*—which functions in the sense of the locative case—is *ṅit*, the rule "āṅo 'nunāsikaś chandasi" (Pāṇini 6.1.126) applies; such is the meaning.
What is the purpose of the mention of *nipāta* (particle)? [Consider the example: *devo'si vāyavāhi*.

Regarding the term *sambuddhau* (in the vocative), [the author] says "non-Vedic" (*avaidika*), intending that since we see such usage in passages like "it was said by the *ṛṣi*" (*taduktamṛṣiṇā*), the word *ṛṣi* here refers to the Veda. Why is the condition *sambuddhau* stated? [Consider the example: *aho iti*. Here, because the subsequent rule [P. 1.1.15] would otherwise apply, let there not be an option. As for the counter-example given in the *Vṛtti* and other commentaries on the rule "ot" (*P. 1.1.15*)—where the term *nipāta* is understood from that context and the term *sambuddhi* is mentioned here—to wit, *gavityayamāha*, that is incorrect; for even though the designation *pragṛhya* applies there, the *prakṛtibhāva* (preservation of the original form) does not actually arise.

For it is clear in the commentary on the rule *iko 'savarṇe* that the mention of "the end of a word" (*padānta*) is carried over [from a previous rule]. And thus, its connection is necessary in the rule *plutapragṛhyā*. Furthermore, *gavi* is not a word (*pada*), because no case ending is produced due to the absence of meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), since there is an intention to express the non-difference between the object of imitation and the imitator.
Regarding *uñ*, although the rule "a particle consisting of a single vowel" would have applied, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*).

"Ūm̐ is nasal. Because of this [rule], when this [ūm̐] follows, there is an option according to the rule "yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā. Whether you read it as *yadetanūm̐* or as *yadetanūm̐*, [the rule applies] such that "that [final consonant] becomes long," and so forth. It is precisely for this purpose that the term "anunāsika" (nasal) is mentioned there; otherwise, he would have simply stated "yaro ñami ñamvā" (a consonant before ña, ṇa, na, ma, or va).

The rule *maya uño vo vā* [P. 8.3.32] applies when *mayaḥ* follows. However, the claim that it applies to what follows (*parāt*) is an error of the Easterners (Prācya). This is because the *Mahābhāṣya* states, "Substitutes are prescribed for that which is indicated by the genitive case," and because, in a rule prescribing a substitute, it is logically correct that the original element (*sthānin*) must be indicated by the genitive alone.

Regarding the phrase "because it is not established" (*asiddhatvāt*): for this very reason, this substitution of *v* is prescribed in the final three quarters (*tripādī*) of the grammar. If its purpose were merely to subvert the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), he would have stated *maya uño vā* immediately after *iko yaṇ aci* [P. 6.1.77], and he would have carried forward the term *yaṇ*.

In this context, twenty-eight forms are derived by me when *uñ* is followed by *iti*. To explain: in the case of its status as a *pragṛhya* by the rule "uñaḥ," we have *kimu iti*; in the alternative view involving the substitution of *vat*, *kimviti*; in the case of the substitute *ūm̐*, *kimūm̐ iti*; and by virtue of the substitute being *sthānivadbhūta*, when the *prakṛtibhāva* prescribed by "maya uña—" is set aside due to the closest proximity (*āntaratamya*) resulting in an anusvāra-like nasalized *v*, we have *kimviṃti*.

Regarding the two *v* sounds—one nasalized and one non-nasalized—there is an eightfold set of forms when the substitution of *v* for *m* (by the rule *mayo yaṇ*) and the doubling of *m* (by the rule *anaci ca*) are optional. When these two operations do not occur, there are two forms; thus, there is a total of ten forms.

In the view that the technical designation *pragṛhya* is absent, because the substitution of *v* by the rule *maya uñaḥ* is considered *asiddha*, the *yaṇ* substitution alone applies by the rule *iko yaṇ aci*. Since that [substitution] is *siddha*, the *anusvāra* occurs for the *m*; then, in the alternative where there is *parasavarṇa* by the rule *vā padāntasya*, there is a form with eleven syllables, consisting of two *v*s—one nasalized and one non-nasalized. When the nasalized *v* is doubled, since the elision by the rule *halo yamāṃ yami saṃhitāyām* is optional, in the case of its non-occurrence, there is a twelfth form containing three *v*s.

In the alternative view where there is no *parasavarṇa*, because the *anusvāra* may optionally become a *yara* (semivowel or nasal), there are two [instances] when doubling occurs; thus, by summation, there are fourteen. With the vowel *i* of the word *iti*, there are twenty-eight due to the optional substitution of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) form according to the rule "aṇo'pragṛhrasya."
Thus ends the section on vowel sandhi (ac-saṃdhi).
Now begins the section on the euphonic combination of consonants (hal-sandhi).

The term *stoḥ ścunā* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The masculine gender is a Vedic archaism (*sautram*). Regarding the word *ścunā*: it will be stated under the rule *saha yuktā-* that the third case suffix occurs even in the absence of actual conjunction; the word *yoge* (conjunction) is to be supplied by ellipsis. Here, there is a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) between the substituends (*sthānin*) and the substitutes (*ādeśa*), but not between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*), as indicated by the rule *śāt*. However, in cases such as *alpāctaram*, the substitution of *ścutva* does not occur because it is a Vedic archaism (*sautratvāt*); yet in cases such as *tajjñānam*, it certainly does occur. It would be more appropriately stated as *stoḥ ścau ścuḥ*.

Nor would [the forms] "yajñaḥ," "yācñā," and so forth fail to be established by the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when that [element] is specified [by the locative case]," because that rule does not apply here due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "after *ś*."

In this case as well, there is no one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) between the cause of the operation and the result; this is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *toṣṣi*. It would be more appropriately stated as *ṣṭau ṣṭuḥ*. In forms such as *īṭṭe* and *īṣṭe*, there is no fault because of the *jñāpaka* in the rule *na padāntāt...*.

Regarding *sarpiṣṭamam*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *hrasvāttādau...*. As for the statement "in a suffix in the common language" (*pratyaye bhāṣāyām*), that which was read by the ancients as "it is obligatory in *mayaṭ*," and that which was exemplified in the section on consonant endings as *ṣaṇṇām* and *ṣaḍṇām*, and that which was explained there under the rule *yaro'nunāsike vā'nunāsikaḥ*—all of that should be disregarded due to its contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*.

Regarding the term *yavādigana*: in the reading of the *saṃhitā* according to the rule "in the presence of *yaC*, [a stem ending in] *ta* or *sa* is called *bha* when a possessive suffix (*matvartha*) follows," one can resolve this by eliding a *da* before the *ta* in *tasau*, thereby establishing its status as a *bha*.

Regarding the rule *udaḥ sthā-* and the rule *anusvārasya yayi-*, the intention is that the entire term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) from the latter is extracted here and connected [to the former], because it is promised (*pratijñāna*) that the term is *svarita* (accented) in part; with this in mind, he says: "it shall be the preceding homogeneous sound. By the phrase "of the unvoiced," etc., the works of the ancients which state that "the *s* becomes *t*" are refuted. Furthermore, the citation of the rule *cayo dvitīyāḥ śari* in this context is due to excessive haste.

Regarding the statement *tacchiva* [is the example]: as for what was said by the elder [grammarian] regarding *tat śiva*, namely that after applying *jaś*-substitution, the rule *khari ca* applies—that is not correct, because since *tad-* ends in a dental (*d*), the introduction of *jaś*-substitution would be redundant. As for what was stated by his grandson [Nāgeśa], namely that after applying the *car*-substitution of *tad-* by the rule *vāvasāne*, there is subsequently a connection with *śiva*, whereby *jaś*-substitution occurs by *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* and then *car*-substitution occurs by *khari ca*—that is extremely clumsy; for *car*-substitution in the *avasāna* (pause) position serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to *jaś*-substitution.

Furthermore, because the *jaś*-rule does not depend on the word *śiva*, and because the rule *vāvasāne* has not yet applied prior to the occurrence of the subsequent destruction of the final position (*avasānabhaṅga*), or because there is the possibility of retracting what has already been applied. As it is said: "The followers of Pāṇini do not apply [rules] when the conditions for their application have already been met," and "They cause even an already applied rule to be withdrawn. Otherwise, in the case of *harir ayam* as well, by your own reasoning, who could prevent the visarga from being applied? If you argue that *tat* is derived from the root *tan* with the suffix *kvip*, even so, let the letter *d* arise by the *jaś*-rule.

However, the view that "the substitution of *ścutva* occurs when *cartva* has been performed" is not logical, because *cartva* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to *ścutva*. As for the claim that—by splitting the rule "na mu ne" into two separate rules ("na" and "mu ne")—the non-existence of *cartva* does not apply here; that too is incorrect. For even if *cartva* were non-existent, since the formation of the correct form remains unimpeded, there is no evidence to justify resorting to such a split of the rule (yogavibhāga), which is a desperate measure taken only when no other way out exists.
Regarding the form *ākraṃsyate*: the suffix *taṅ* (ātmanepada) is applied by the rule "āṅ udgamane" (Pāṇini 1.3.40), and the augment *iṭ* is not added by the rule "snukramoḥ—" (Pāṇini 7.2.36).

The rule is one of equal connection (*samasambandhī vidhiḥ*). However, it is not stated as "a prescription involving equal objects" (*samakarmakaṃ vidhānam*), because sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is also desired between two things that are merely being restated (*anuvādya*), as in the rule: *samūlākṛtajīveṣu hankṛñgrahaḥ*.

Because the *kuk* and *ṭuk* augmentations are considered part of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), in the form *prāṅksāye*, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "sātpadādyoḥ" does not apply. In the form *sugaṇṭsāye*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* by the rule "na padāntāt—" does not apply.

One who sits (*sīdati*) at Puṣkara, a particular sacred site (*tīrtha*), is called *puṣkarasat*. His descendant is the teacher *Pauṣkarasādi*. The suffix *iñ* is applied because [the name] belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group; the vowel lengthening of both members of the compound occurs because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* group.

Regarding the rule *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ*, since there is an instruction by both the genitive and the locative cases, the instruction by the fifth (ablative) case is stronger; with this intention, he says: *sasya* ("of *s*"). The use of the locative case (*si*) in the rule, however, is for the sake of brevity. As for the form *ṣaṭtsantaḥ*: the letter *t* arises from the substitution of *c* for the *ṭ* of *dhuṭ*. As for what some say—that according to the view "the second letters of the *cayaḥ* [class] are substituted," there would be *th* instead of *t*—that is not correct, because the substitution of *c* for *ṭ* (*cartva*) is considered *asiddha* (not yet established). For this very reason, in the absence of *dhuṭ*, as in the form *ṣaṭ santaḥ*, there is no substitution of *ṭh* for *ṭ*.

There are sixteen [forms] due to the optional doubling of the *ṭ*, *n*, and *visarga*. When there is doubling of the *s* according to the rule "khayaḥ śaraḥ," there are thirty-two. Nor should one suspect that the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) is not established there, because it is stated: "That which is not established in what precedes does not apply to doubling. Nor should one suspect a prohibition of doubling by the rule "śaro'ci," because that [rule] applies only to doubling within the context of the Sūtra itself. For this very reason, the examples *vatsaḥ* and *apsarāḥ* are established in the Bhāṣya as illustrations of the Vārttika "śaraḥ khayaḥ."

The placement of *dhuṭ* at the beginning [of the *dhātu*] is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *ṣṭu* by the rule "na padāntāt..."; for this very reason, the *tuṭ* augment which will be mentioned later has not been applied here. As for what some say—that even so, for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), it would be more appropriate to apply *tuṭ* alone—that is incorrect; because under the alternative view that "the second consonant of a *caya*-group [is doubled]," it would result in the appearance of the letter *tha*. Regarding the statement "the substitution of *ścu* should be stated as established before a *dhuṭ*," [consider the example]: *aṭ* (from *aṭati*) + *ścotati*; here, *dhuṭ* does not occur.

The suffix *tuk* is applied in the seventh case (*saptamī*) as established previously; however, he states "of *na*" (*nasya*) because he interprets the fifth case (*pañcamī*) "from *na*" (*naḥ*) as a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Now, one might object: let there simply be the augment *dhuṭ* (as prescribed by P. 8.3.29), so what is the need for *tuk*? Do not say so. For the established meaning in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) of the rule "śaścho’ṭi" (P. 8.4.63) is that *cha* replaces *śa* when it follows a *jhay* consonant at the end of a word (*padānta*). If this were not the case, then because *dhuṭ* is added at the beginning of the following element (*parādittva*), the substitution of *cha* for *śa* would not occur in forms such as *sañcchambhuḥ*.

In the word *virapśan* (from the root *rap* preceded by *vi*), with the *śa*-affix in the sense of the *auṇādika* [Uṇādi] suffixes—as in the example, "The honey-drops drip all around, O *virapśan*"—the augment *tuk* is applied as a *pūrvānta* (belonging to the end of the preceding element). If it is objected that, in this case, in the form *kurvañc śete*, the prohibition of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) by the rule "of a word-final [consonant]" (*padāntasya*) would not apply, we say no; for under the *kāryakāla-pakṣa* (the view that the application of rules depends on the time of their operation), the *tuk* augment is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) because it is *bahiraṅga* (external/dependent). Under the *yathoddeśa-pakṣa* (the view that the application of rules depends on the order of their enunciation), the rule *stoḥ ścunā* is divided. The word "not" (*na*) and "ṇ" (*ṇaḥ*) carry over from the previous context. Thus, when *st* (sibilants and *t*-class consonants) comes in contact with *śc* (palatals and *c*-class consonants), the substitution of *ṇ* shall not take place.

This [mention of *nakāra*] is for the sake of the letter *n*. The mention of *sakāra* and the mention of the entire class (*varga*) are for the sake of subsequent rules. From that follows the rule "ścuḥ"; here, the previous [rule] continues. Thus, regarding the sūtra "naśca," the purpose of the prohibition of *ṇatva* (nasalization) in the case of *kurvantsīdati*—based on the view that [the augment] is *parādau* (added after the final phoneme)—is to be understood as the purpose of the *dhuṭ* augment being added at the beginning [of the word], according to the text of the ancients, even under the *yathoddeśapakṣa* (the view that grammatical elements apply where they are taught). As for what they say—that this purpose is refuted because it is already covered by the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* (the maxim concerning external operations)—[that is incorrect].

That [argument] belongs to that side; however, let this matter rest for now, as it contradicts one's own statement regarding the example *suddhyupāsya*, based on the principle that when an internal rule (*antaraṅga*) resides in the same triplet (*tripādī*), this external rule (*bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*) does not apply.

As for *sañcchambhuḥ*: here, one should not suspect the substitution of *r* by the rule *naśchavi* on the grounds that the substitutions of *ś* and *t* are unestablished (*asiddha*), because the substitution of *ch* is itself unestablished.

The *ṅam* [in the sūtra] is a *pratyāhāra* formed from *ṅ* and *m*. Furthermore, the status of being marked with *ṭ* (*ṭit-tva*) applied to the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is, by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), connected with the named elements (*saṃjñin*). Consequently, the augments *ṅuṭ*, *ṇuṭ*, and *nuṭ* are applied respectively. The inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) is for the sake of clarity, since the status of being obligatory is already obtained simply by the fact that it is placed between the two optional rules: "when followed by *m* and another *m*" (*he mapare*) and "the substitution of *v* for *uṅ* optionally after *m*" (*maya uño vo vā*).

Regarding the example *sugaṇṇīśa*: the elision (*allopa*) of the *ṇi* suffix is not treated as if it were in its original position (*na sthānivat*), because that prohibition applies when what precedes is considered *asiddha*. The fact that the augment *ṅamuṭ* is placed at the end [of the word] is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ṇ* in forms such as *kurvann āste*. For this very reason, the rule "ṅamo hrasvād aci dve" was not formulated; otherwise, since the preceding element would be established (*siddha*) with respect to the subsequent *ṇatva*, the substitution of *ṇ* would undesirably occur—so say the ancients. As for the claim that both [the above arguments] are irrelevant because the matter is already covered by the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*, that too is only partially true.

Just as in the case of the word *rājñaḥ*, since it has been stated that the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā* is absent in the *yathoddeśa*-pakṣa pertaining to the three chapters (*traipādika*), the treatises of the ancients (*prācām grantha*) are excellent; otherwise, how could he have himself stated both "two" and "three"? This is the direction [of the argument].

One might object: "In examples such as *paramadaṇḍin-au*, since the status of being a *pada* (word) exists due to the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), the augment *nuṭ* should occur. This is not so, because of the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations based on a suffix) by the rule: "When the subsequent member is a *pada*, [the suffix-status of the preceding member is suspended] except for operations concerning the beginning of a word" (*uttarapadatve cāpadādividhau*). For this very reason, in cases such as *paramavācau*, *paramagoduhau*, and *paramalihau*, the substitutions of *k* for *g*, *gh* for *d*, and *ḍh* for *l* do not take place. As for the statement made by the ancients—that the augment *ṅamuṭ* does not occur because they carry over the word "pada" from the rule *uñi ca pade* and explain it as "of a word beginning with a vowel"—that is refuted by this very argument. For even they would have to follow the aforementioned method in order to prevent the elision of *n* (*nalopa`) in this very instance.

Although the substitution of *m* by *anusvāra* is established by the rule *samaḥ suṭi*, this [sūtra] is nevertheless intended for the sake of establishing its nasalized quality (*anunāsikatva*) and its status as having three *sakāras*.

Regarding this, there is a twofold view: whether this [term *anunāsika*] is an *adhikāra* (a governing heading) or a *vidhi* (an actual rule). In the first case, the mention of *atra* (here) is redundant, because the context of the *ru*-section is obtained from the *adhikāra* itself. However, the word *tu* (but) serves to indicate a distinction from the subsequent subject in the *adhikāra* view—namely, that for the subsequent [element] the substitution of *ru* is obligatory, whereas for the preceding [element] the *anunāsika* is optional; in the *vidhi* view, it would be useless. The inclusion of the word *vā* (or) is for the sake of clarity, since the desired result is already established by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "after an *anunāsika*, [the following *ru* becomes *u*]."

For it is not possible for there to be a position in which the nasalization is absent without recourse to an alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*). To indicate this very point, the words "but" (*tu*) and "or" (*vā*) were not stated in the *Vṛtti*.

He says that the ablative case is used in the sense of "leaving aside" (*lyablope*) because of the nasal (*anunāsika*), stating: "having left aside the nasal. And thus, just as conjunction is a cause for the cognition of a specific [quality], so too is disjunction; therefore, as in the example "let the one without a calf be brought," that which possesses the potential quality of nasality is connected as the limit (*avadhi*) because it is present and required. With this intention, he says: "from what precedes the *r*. Regarding the term "the augment *anusvāra*": its status as an augment is understood precisely by the word "following" (*para*), just as in the rule "but the diphthongs *ai* and *au* are before those two," where the status of being before is understood by the word "before" (*pūrva*). This is the sense.
Regarding the rule *visarjanīyasya kharīti*, this is carried over from the sūtra *kharavasānayoḥ* by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) method of interpretation.

Now, since the *anusvāra* is not a vowel (*anac*), there would indeed be no doubling of the consonant following it; therefore, he says: "The *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, etc. [and] "above the letter *a*. The intention is that if they were recited above the letter *i*, then in forms such as *payaḥsu* and *yaśaḥsu*, there would be the substitution of *ṣ* according to the rule *iṇaḥ parasya*. Regarding the phrase "because it is a vowel" (*actvāt*): even so, there is no risk of the application of *yaṇ* (vowel-substitution) and other rules in cases like *hariḥ kartā* or *hariṃ smaret*, because the *visarga* and others are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to their being located within the last three chapters (*tripādī*). And thus, there is doubling even for the *anusvāra*.

By the word "api" (also), the letter *ka* is included. Regarding the phrase "by another statement": the intention is that even when [the rule] "aco rahābhyām" has been applied, [the rule] "yaṇo mayaḥ" still indeed occurs.

In *pumaḥ* [before] *khayi*, once the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* (conjunction) has been performed, this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the remaining portion. The phrase "due to exclusion" (*paryudāsāt*) refers to the sense that it is intended for the rule prescribing *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*): "idudupadhasya... (Pāṇini 8.3.41). This is according to the opinion of the ancient grammarians who explain [the rule] through a non-co-referential construction (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), namely: "the visarga which belongs to what is not a suffix. However, it should be understood that if the connection is made through a co-referential construction (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the manner that will be explained later, then the application of *ṣatva* would indeed occur.

Regarding the term *khyāñ-ādeśa*: the substitute (*ādeśa*) is indeed *khśāñ* in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). In the section on what is not established (*asiddha-prakaraṇa*), following the rule for *ṇatva*, the substitution of *y* for the *ś* of *khśāñ* is optionally prescribed. Consequently, from *suprakhyena nirvṛttam* we derive *sauprakhyaṃ*; that which exists there is *sauprakhyīyaḥ*. Because the substitution of *y* is considered unestablished (*asiddha*), the suffix *vuñ* does not apply by the rule "from a base ending in *dhanvan* or having *ya* or *va* as its penultimate letter" (*dhanvayopadhāt*); such purposes are maintained in the original treatise (*ākara*). And thus, because the substitution of *y* is unestablished, the condition of being followed by a *m* (*amparatva*) is absent; therefore, by the rule "after *pum*, [there is *ru*] before a *khaya*" (*pumaḥ khayi*), the substitution of *ru* does not occur—this is the meaning.

Regarding the form *puṃkhyānam*: it is derived from the root *cakṣiṅ* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, and the substitution of *khyāñ* occurs. But one might object: "Is this substitution difficult to justify here? If you argue that it is so because of the Vārttika rules "there is a prohibition in the case of exclusion (*varjana*)" and "and in the case of *as* and *san*," that is true. However, the matter is resolved by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("diversely") in the Vārttika: "*bahulaṃ taṇi annavadhakagātravicakṣaṇājirādyartham*. Accordingly, there is a Vārttika enumerating the purposes for the inclusion of the class beginning with *khśādi*, which mentions: the rule for *ru*—as in *puṃkhyānam*; the rule for *ṇatva*—as in *paryākhyānam*; and the rule for the *ṇatva* of the *niṣṭhā* [suffix]—as in *ākhyātam*.

Because of the intervention of the letter *ś*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] by the rule "kṛtyacaḥ" does not occur; likewise, in the word *ākhyātam*, the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule "saṃyogāderāta—" does not occur, because the substitution of *y* (by "ādeśapratyayayoḥ") is unestablished (*asiddha*), and thus the condition of being followed by a semivowel (*yaṇvat*) is absent. Consequently, the meaning is that the mention of the root *khyā* in the rule "na dhyākhyā—" need not be made. Nor should it be argued that this is for the sake of the root *khyā* in the sense of "speaking," for that root belongs exclusively to the domain of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes.

And on this point, the subsequent *vārttika*, "The status of being a *saṣṭhāna* [retroflex sibilant] is for the name *khyā*," is the authority. *Saṣṭhāna* is the designation used by the Easterners (*prācām*) for the *jihvāmūlīya* (the *visarga* before *k* or *kh*). That [designation] does not apply here, because the rule "the *visarjanīya* remains when followed by a *śar* [sibilant] and *par* [velar or labial]" is operative; such is the intended meaning. If the root were also desired independently in the *ārdhadhātuka* domain, then, since the *jihvāmūlīya* would be unavoidable, this *vārttika* would be inconsistent.

As for what Haradatta, Mādhava, and others have stated—that the root *khyā* is also [included] among those beginning with *khśā*, and that the rule for *yatva* (the substitution of *ya*) applies to both [roots, *cakṣiṅ* and *khyā*]—that is to be reconsidered. For in the Bhāṣya, the discussion begins specifically with *cakṣiṅ*; furthermore, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of using forms beginning with *khśā* even in the domain of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. Nor can this be accepted as the intended conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because Mādhava has stated that this [root] beginning with *khśā* belongs only to the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. Moreover, since one would then have to resort to the position that such forms are simply not expressed (*anabhidhāna*) in the *sārvadhātuka* domain, the theory is burdened by unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Let this matter rest for now.

It might be argued: "In the case of *bahupum khyāti* (meaning 'many men are known in this family'), the substitution of *r* [for *s*] should occur; for since the word *pum* is listed among the *uraḥprabhṛti* group only in its singular form, the suffix *kap* does not apply here. Furthermore, the use of the root *khyā* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is entirely unimpeded. If this is said, we reply: this is acceptable, as it is our desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). However, when the formation of *saṃhitā* is not intended, it is clear that the substitution of *r* does not take place. As for what the ancients stated—"some say there is no [substitution of *r*] in the root *khyā*"—if the meaning there is "in the substitute *khyāñ*," then the phrase "some say" (*kecit*) is inappropriate.

If [the prohibition] were to apply to the independent (svatantra) verbal root, then there would be a prohibition even in the domain of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. But this is not an acceptable consequence, because it lacks any basis in the rules. For example, in *cakrim̐strāyasva* ("O Creator, protect!"), that which was stated by the ancients as *trāhi* is incorrect, as it uses the *parasmaipada* ending. This is because the root *trai* is marked with the *ṅit* indicatory letter (*ṅittvāt*). It should be understood that *trāḥ* is derived from the root *trai* in the sense of "one who protects" (*trāyate*), followed by the *kvip* suffix; or alternatively, it is formed by adding *kvip* in the sense of "acting like one who protects" (*trāyata iva ācarati*) to the agentive *kvip*-derived stem. Regarding *praśān*: it is formed from the root *śam* preceded by the prefix *pra*, with the *kvip* suffix. The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "anunāsikasya kvi—" (*Pāṇini 6.4.15*). The change of *m* to *n* occurs by the rule "mo no dhātoḥ" (*Pāṇini 8.2.64*). Because that [substitution of *n* for *m*] is considered non-existent (*asiddhatvāt*) for the purposes of the subsequent rule, the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) does not take place.

In the word *nṝn*, the letter *a* following *pa* is for the sake of pronunciation; by this, forms such as *nṝḥ punāti* are established. With the intention that the option is realized through the recurrence of the term "in both ways" (*ubhayathā*) from the rule "in the case of *ṛkṣu*" (*ubhayatharkṣu*), he says: "ru may optionally occur."

In the rule *kupvoḥ*, there is a visarga because [the sounds] *ka* and *pa* possess the quality of being *khara*; and for the *jihvāmūlīya*, it is because it possesses the quality of being *khara*. By the rule *kharpare śari*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the visarga, because the *jihvāmūlīya* possesses the quality of being *śara*; or, by the rule *vā śari*, there is optionally the visarga itself. The substitutes *ka* and *pa* are used merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). As for the statement "and the visarga," some predecessors have said that "and" (*ca*) implies an option (*vikalpa*); but that is not correct, because when the *ka* and *pa* are absent, there would follow the occurrence of *satva* (the substitution of *sa*) for the visarga.

Regarding the rule for the reduplicated form *kān*, although one could simply have said *kān kān*, the inclusion of the term "reduplicated" (*āmreḍita*) is so that the rule applies only where there is a doubling [of the word], and not here: *kān kān paśyasi* ("Whom do you see?"). Here, one *kiṃ* is used in the sense of a question, while the second is used in the sense of censure; thus, the meaning is "Whom—meaning those who are contemptible—do you see?"

Regarding the *kaskādi* group, it has been stated here by the Easterners (*prācām*) that there is no substitution of *ka* or *pa* for the *visarjanīya*. However, that is not the actual meaning of the rule (*sūtra*), because *ka* and *pa* are not marked as *svarita*, and the negative particle (*nañ*) has not been introduced [as a governing factor]. Rather, that statement is intended to explain the implied sense (*ārthika-artha*). Indicating this, he says: "In the case of *ka* and *pa*. The word *kautaskuta* means "come from where? Although the suffix *tyap* would have applied after an indeclinable (*avyaya*) in this sense, the suffix *aṇ* is used by virtue of the word being included in the *gaṇa* list. The example *sarpiṣkuṇḍikā* is given.

Since the rule would already be established by the statement "nityaṃ samāse," the purpose of its recitation here will be explained in that very place. Regarding the rule "senāsurā-": if there were *tuk* after *ccha*, then, upon the application of *cartva* (the substitution of *ca*) for *ccha*, there would be two *ca*s. However, if *cartva* does not apply due to the *sannipātaparibhāṣā* (the technical rule concerning the non-disturbance of a cause-effect relationship), then the letter *ca* would be heard immediately after the letter *cha*. This is the intended meaning.
Thus ends the section on consonant sandhi.
Now follows the euphonic combination of the visarga (visargasandhi).

This [rule] is an exception to the rule concerning *satva* (the substitution of *s*) when followed by a *śar* (a sibilant) or *par* (a plosive). However, if it were stated simply as "not when followed by a *śar* or *par*," then even though *satva* is prohibited in the present case, the substitutions of *k* and *p* for *ku* and *pu* would still occur, as in *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* ("linen garment") and *adbhiḥ psātam* ("eaten with water"). With the intention that the mention of the *visarjanīya* (the visarga) serves to sublate only the specific modification [of *s*], he says: "but not anything else. He clarifies this very point with the words: "here..."

In the rule *so 'padādau*, the dual ending *-oḥ* is used by way of transference (*vyatyaya*) for the singular. However, if *khaḥ* (the visarga) is qualified as being "in the beginning of a word" (*apadādau*) [and the condition is] "before a *khar* [consonant]," then it is correct according to the literal reading. But this involves the difficulty of having to carry over (*anuvartana*) the term "before a *khar*" across the gap by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*). Nor is such a carry-over necessary for what follows, because since a visarga cannot occur without a *khar*, its carry-over would be fruitless. The commentary states: "In the case of *pāśa*, *kalpa*, *ka*, and *kāmya*. This is an illustration of possible cases rather than an exhaustive enumeration, as no others are possible.

Regarding the term *prātaḥkalpam*: although the word *prātaḥ* primarily denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), in this context of a compound (*vṛtti*), it refers to the possessor of that locus, as in the expressions *doṣābhūtam ahaḥ* ("the day became evening") and *divābhūtā rātriḥ* ("the night became day"). Regarding *gīḥ kāmyati*: here, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] by the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* does not apply, because the restriction *kāmye roreva* ("only after *r* when followed by *kāmya*") continues to apply there as well. If, however, this were read in that very same rule (*iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*), then even if the substitution of *ṣ* were prohibited, the substitution of *s* would still occur by the preceding rule (*iṇkoḥ*).

The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* following *iṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. Both this sūtra and the word "saḥ" carry over (*anuvartate*) to the subsequent rules. The distinction is that *ṣ* replaces *s* when it follows *iṇ*, and in all other cases, *s* remains as *s*, as far as possible. Regarding the form *puraḥ*: the root *pṛ* (meaning "to protect" and "to fill") takes the suffix *kvip* by the rule "bhrājabhāsa—" etc.; from that stem ending in *kvip*, the nominative plural suffix *jas* is added. To make clear that it ends in *jas*, the forms *pūḥ* and *parāḥ* have been cited.

The relationship between *idudupadhasya* and *idutau* is one of grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*): it means that the *visarjanīya* which is a member of a word-group (*samudāya*) that has *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter (*upadhā*). However, in the case of the rule *apratyayasya*, it is connected as "the *visarjanīya* which is not a suffix. This is because, when co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, non-co-referentiality is improper. Nor should it be argued that the status of the *visarjanīya* as a suffix is unestablished; for in examples such as *agniḥ karoti*, that status is established through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Nor should it be suspected that the Tripādī is *asiddha* with respect to *atideśa* (extended application), because its status as *siddha* is made known precisely by the prohibition in the rule *apratyayasya*. For this very reason, the substitution of *visarga* for *ru* in forms such as *agniḥ* is established; otherwise, it would not occur because [the final *r*] would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*). The rule for *visarga*, however, finds its utility in cases such as *punar*. Furthermore, the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) is specific in its scope; therefore, the rule *acaḥ parasmin...* does not apply within the Tripādī.

And thus, we have explained in the *Śabdakaustubha* that the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—"that which is not established in what precedes [is] not like the original form" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*)—is based on reasoning rather than being merely a formal rule (*vācanika*). If it be objected: "In that case, would there not be the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) in forms such as *mātuḥ kāryam*?"—No; for by the inclusion of the word *bhrātuṣputra* among the *kaska*-type words, it is indicated (*jñāpana*) that "there is no substitution of *ṣ* for a letter following the *u* of the *ṅasi* and *ṅas* [case endings] when that *u* follows [the stem-final *r*]. And thus, Haradatta’s statement—that the rule "*apratyayasya*" (Pāṇini 8.3.59) also has a different grammatical locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) [than its immediate context]—need not be given much weight.

Regarding the word *mātuḥ*: here, the rule for single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)—"*ṛta ut*"—is an indirect cause (*paramparayā prayojaka*) for the visarga. However, in the original treatise (*ākara*), the more common reading is "*ekādeśaśāstranimittāt*. In that case, the meaning is: "from that *u*-vowel which has the rule for single-substitution as its cause. Regarding *muhuḥ kāma*: here, the rule "*kupvoḥ ka pau*" applies. Haradatta states that the reading *muhuskāma* with the letter *s* found in some commentaries (*vṛtti*) is due to a scribal error (*prāmādika*).

Regarding the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*: here, because of their association (*sāhacarya*) with the two words ending in the suffix *su* (*dvi-su* and *tri-su*), the word *catur* is also understood as being specifically one that ends in *su*. The mention of the sense of the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "association does not always serve as a restrictive factor. Therefore, in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām*, even though there is association with verbal roots (*dhātu*), the augment *iṭ* is included. This option (*vibhāṣā*) applies in both cases: for *catur*, it applies where the rule *idudupadhasya ca* would otherwise have applied; for the other two, however, it applies where [the rule] would not otherwise have applied.

Nor should it be suspected that the formation of these two [words] is established by the rule *isusoḥ sāmarthye*, because in that rule, the suffix *is* and a meaningful word (*arthavat*) are what are being referred to.

Regarding *catuṣkapāla*: the substitution of *ṣ* is obligatory by the rule *idudupadhasya*. Regarding the phrase "even in the absence of mutual expectancy": this means in cases such as *tiṣṭhatu sarpiṣkuṇḍikām ānaya* ("Let him stay; bring the ghee-pot").

Regarding the phrase "in the case of mutual expectancy" (*vyapekṣāyām*): this means in the example "this [is] the *sarpiṣ-kuṇḍikā*" (*idaṃ sarpiṣkuṇḍikāyāḥ*). As for what the followers of the *Pārāyaṇa* say—"The inclusion of *sarpiṣ-kuṇḍikā* and others in the *kaska-* group is for the sake of the *ṣatva* [substitution of *ṣ*], even when they occur as the second member of a compound"—that should be disregarded because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*.
Regarding *ayaḥsahitā*: it does not mean "a modification of iron" (*ayasaḥ vikāraḥ*), for that would entail the application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule "jānapada-...
(Pāṇini 4.1.42). In *ayaskarṇī*, the ears are like iron (*ayaḥ*). The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "nāsikodarauṣṭha-... (Pāṇini 4.1.55).

Regarding the phrase "adhaḥśirasī etayoḥ": in the sūtra, however, it should be understood that the nominative case is used in place of the genitive. *Adhaspadam* is a compound formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. *Śiraspadam* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Thus ends the section on the euphonic combination of the visarga.
Now, the rules for the euphonic combination of *s* and other sounds (*svādisandhi*).

The phrase *sasajuṣo ruḥ padasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.66) is understood [from the previous rule]. This is qualified by the two words *sasajuḥ*; because it is a qualification, the rule of *tadantavidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the qualified element) applies. Nor should one fear the prohibition regarding the portion of the word *sajuḥ*, namely, "there is no *tadantavidhi* when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix," because that prohibition pertains specifically to the domain of suffix-vidhis. Thus, for a word (*pada*) that ends in *s* or ends in the word *sajuṣ*, there shall be *ru* (the substitution of *r*), and that *ru* replaces the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*). This being established, he states the resulting conclusion: "of the end of a word" (*padāntasya*) and "of the word *sajuṣ*" (*sajuṣśabdasya*).

The meaning is "of that which has that [suffix] as its final element"; by this, there is no over-extension in cases such as *sajuṣaḥ*. Nor should it be argued that there is an under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of *sajūḥ* because of the prohibition "the designation of a thing is not extended [to another] when it is not a nominal stem" (*aprātipadikena*). For this prohibition has been rejected in the *Śabdakaustubha* on the rule *yena vidhis* (Pāṇini 1.1.72).

Furthermore, since both the two *paribhāṣās*—"*vyapadeśivadbhāvo'prātipadikena*" (the designation of a thing as being like itself applies even when it is not a nominal stem) and "*grahaṇavatā-" (when a term is used that includes its own substitute)"—are stated by Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta in the commentary on the rule *diva ut* to pertain to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*), the form *paramasajūrbhyām* and others are likewise free from objection. This being the case, one should note that the statement of the ancients (*prācām*) to the effect that there is no *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to a word ending in the specified element) here with respect to the word *sajuṣ* is merely superficial.

"Regarding *bho-bhago-asaṃdhiḥ sautraḥ*: the meaning is that the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) resulting from the combination of the vowel *o* and the vowel *a* in the words *bhago* and *agho* does not occur because they are *sautra* (belonging to the Vedic sūtras). However, if one were to explain the rule by taking *bhos*, *bhagos*, and *aghos*—ending in either *-s* or *-r*—as the basis for imitation, and then interpret [the rule] as "let *y* be the substitute for the final *al* (vowel) of these three, namely *bho* etc., when followed by a vowel other than *a* and when preceded by *r*," then the absence of sandhi (*asaṃdhi*) would indeed be logical. And this is correct.

Otherwise, in the case of *vibhoridam*, *suprabhā gaur yasya sa suprabhagus tasya suprabhagoridaṃ*, and *raghoridam*, the substitution of *yat* would also result; for the *ru* [substitution] occurs when preceded by the word *bhoḥ* and so forth. Nor can it be argued that the words *bhoḥ* and others are not included here because they are *lākṣaṇika* (derived/metaphorical), since the words *bhoḥ* and others—which are derived from bases such as *bhavat*—are likewise *lākṣaṇika* according to the Vārttika: *vibhāṣā bhavadbhagavadaghavatām occāvasya*. Furthermore, the lack of meaning (*anarthakatva*) is equal in both cases, because only those forms qualified by the *ru* substitution possess meaning.

One might object: since the letter *r* in *roru* is an *anubandha*, the substitute for the *visarga* would be merely the letter *r*; and thus, by the rule "analvidhau," the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) would not apply. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "na hyam" (for it is not as such). The meaning is that just as in the case of *agrahīt*, where the status of *iṭ* [belonging to the long vowel] due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the long vowel in "graho 'liṭi" causes the application of "iṭa īṭi," so too here the substitution of *yatva* (the *y*-sound) would proceed from the *rutva* (the *r*-sound) of the *visarga*.

And likewise, in the Bhāṣya on the *sthānivat* sūtra, it is said: "For this [suffix] relies upon a specific power, namely that called *iṭ*. For this reason as well, it should be understood that the enumeration beginning with "dhātu-aṅga" and so forth is incorrect.

Regarding the term *nipātāḥ*: those [particles] specified in the rule *bho-bhago-* should be understood there as belonging to the *ākṛtigaṇa* (class of words defined by its form). Consequently, the *vārttika* *vibhāṣā bhavadbhagavat-* need not be resorted to. Otherwise, even though forms such as *bho hare* would be established for the singular masculine alone, forms such as *bho hariharau*, *bho vidvadvṛnda*, and *bho gaṅge* would not be established; this is the intended meaning. And this has been stated according to the opinion of Vṛttikāra Haradatta and others.

However, according to the natural tendency of the Bhāṣya, the Vārttika beginning with "vibhāṣā—" must indeed be commenced. But since the word *bhoḥ* is also a particle (*nipāta*), there is no fault regarding the dual number and so forth, nor in the case of the feminine and neuter genders. This is even more appropriate, because the usage *he bhoḥ*—just like *he bhavan*—is desired, and that [usage] is established only by the commencement of the Vārttika; for it is impossible to use together the particles denoting address mentioned by Amara in the verse "syuḥ pyāṭ pāṭ aṅga hai he bhoḥ," etc.

Furthermore, in this context, forms such as *tatrabho* (O venerable one there) are established only when the Vārttika exists—just as *bhavān hariḥ* and *tatrabhavān* [are established]—because the rule "they are seen after others as well" (*itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyante*) intends that the suffixes *-tra-* and *-tas-* are used after words like *bhavat* only when they end in all case endings.

Furthermore, if [the word] is treated as an *āmantrita* (vocative), then the following results are established: the eighth-case *nighāta* (elision of accent) for what follows a word; the status of being "as if non-existent" (*avidyamānavat*) according to the rule "an *āmantrita* preceding [another vocative]"; the injunction "after *āma*, separated by one word"; the doubling [of the vocative] according to "an *āmantrita* at the beginning of a sentence"; and the status of being "like a subordinate member of the subsequent word" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) according to "a *suptiṅanta* followed by an *āmantrita*," and so forth—all of this is accomplished, but not otherwise. This is the general direction. As for the particles *bhago* and *agho*, if they are indeed authoritative, let them remain so;
however, the establishment of the grammatical operations (*kārya*) pertaining to the *āmantrita* depends entirely upon the *Vārttika*, as the wise should observe.

As for what they say—that by adopting these particles as ending in *s*, the rules for *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) and *autva* (the substitution of *au*) were rejected in the Bhāṣya—that is due to excessive haste. This might be argued: if these particles are accepted, only those [ending in *s*] would be included in the rule prescribing *yatva* (the substitution of *y*), because they are taught directly (*pratipadokta*), whereas those ending in the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) would not, because they are derivative (*lākṣaṇika*). If this is said, it is not so; for in the rule "svaritenādhikāraḥ," one may rely on the interpretation that "adhikaḥ kāraḥ" means "adhikāraḥ" (governance), and thus, by resorting to the state of being *svarita* according to the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*), both types are included.

Furthermore, according to Haradatta and others, the inclusion of the term *mahāvyāhṛti* in the sūtra "bhuvaśca mahāvyāhṛteḥ" is for the purpose of indicating that the paribhāṣā rule regarding "that which is taught by its specific form (*lakṣaṇa-pratipadokta*)" is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). Even so, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words such as *prabhoḥ*, because when the particles mentioned in the Vārttika and those [others] are understood through mutual association (*paraspara-sāhacarya*), other [words] are not included.

The *v* [substitute] is lighter (*laghu*) and involves less articulatory effort (*laghuprayatnatara*), meaning it is more lightly pronounced. Because of proximity (*antaratamya*), he states that [the *v* substitute] occurs for *va* where there was *va*, and for *ya* where there was *ya*; thus he says "in *vaya*" (*vayau*). Regarding the rule "for Gārgya, after an *o*-vowel" (*oto gārgyasya*): as for the explanation given by the ancients (*prācā*) that it means "after a stem (*aṅga*) ending in the vowel *o*," that is incorrect, because a "stem" (*aṅga*) has not been introduced as the subject here, and because such a case is impossible. Indeed, in the examples provided, there is no stem ending in the vowel *o*.

The word *hal* [meaning "consonant"] applies to all [the preceding rules], but the word *vakāraḥ* ("the letter *v*") does not recur, because there is no possibility of a *v* being preceded by *bho*, *bhago*, or *agho*. Although a *v* not preceded by those [specific words] is possible—as in *vṛkṣav karoti*—nevertheless, the elision (*lopa*) does not apply there, because the word *aśi* (in the locative case) is understood as a qualifier of the consonants (*hal*). As for forms such as *vṛkṣav hasati*, they are said to be ungrammatical (*asādhu*) due to a lack of attested usage (*anabhidhāna*). In the case of *gavyam*, there is no status of being a word-final (*padāntatva*); however, in *gavyūti*, it has been stated that there is no elision of *v* because of the inclusion of an additional *v* (*praśleṣa*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that in examples such as *devā namyāḥ*, the desired form is already established by the rule *lopo vyoḥ*? [Response: Not so; for in relation to that [rule], the substitution of *y* (for *i*) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent). Furthermore, in the case of *devā yānti*, there is an absence of a following semivowel (*val*). Regarding *ahorātra*: the masculine gender is prescribed by the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ*.

Regarding *aharādīnām*: in both instances, the word *ādi* (etcetera) denotes a class or type. By this, forms such as *svarcakṣo rathinaḥ satyaśuṣmaḥ* and *vipraḥ kaviḥ kāvyena svarcanaḥ* are to be understood.

Regarding *tṛḍha* and *vṛḍha*: because these roots are marked with the indicatory letter *u*, they are optionally subject to the augment *iṭ*; however, by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," the augment *iṭ* is not applied in the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Then, the substitutions of *ḍha* for *dha*, *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭa*, and the elision of *ḍha* take place. As for the counter-example *dṛḍha* cited by the Easterners (Prācā), that is incorrect; for in that case, the elision of *ḍha* simply does not occur. To explain: by the rule "dṛḍhaḥ sthūlabalayoḥ," the elision of the *n* and *h* of the root *dṛṃh*, as well as the substitution of *ḍha* for the *t*, are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*), but the application of the *ḍha*-substitution belonging to the section on "asiddha" rules does not occur here, because it is superseded by the substitution of *gha* for the initial *d* of the root according to the rule "dāder dhātoḥ."

Nor should it be argued that the absence of *iṭ* and the substitution of *ḍha* for *dha* may be treated as irregular (nipātana), while the substitutions of *dha*, *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍha* will simply occur [by other rules]; for if that were so, in the form *paridraḍhayya*, the substitution of *ay* for *ṇi*—governed by the rule "lyapi laghupūrvāt"—would not apply; and in the form *pāridṛḍhī kanyā*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* governed by the rule "aṇiñoḥ—" would also apply, because the elision of *ḍha* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purpose of determining whether the penultimate syllable is heavy (*gurūpottama*). This is established in the Bhāṣya.

As for what was explained by the predecessor—that this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) specifically of the root *dṛṃh*, while *dṛh* in the sense of "growth" is a different verbal base (*prakṛti*), and that this example is to be seen as a counter-example where, due to the non-eternality of rules concerning augments, there is an absence of *iṭ* in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*); and where, by the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the rule "vā druha... being split as a separate yoga (*yogavibhāga*), there is optionally an absence of *ghatva* and the elision of *ḍha*—that is not correct, because both [roots] are accepted as being subject to the *nipātana*.

Regarding this, Vāmana says: "Now, there exists another root *dṛh*, and for that too this [grammatical] substitution applies, with the exception of the elision of *n*. And this is logical; otherwise, the suffix *ṇi* would not yield *aya*, and the suffix *ṣyaṅ* would instead apply."

The meaning is that *utva* alone occurs because, since the established (*siddha*) and the unestablished (*asiddha*) are not of equal strength, the rule "in case of conflict, the latter [prevails]" (*vipratiṣedhe param*) does not apply; thus, being without opposition, *utva* alone takes effect. As it has been said: "When the preceding is unestablished (*pūrvatrāsiddhe*), there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because of the absence of the subsequent. By this, the statement "the operation of the case-ending (*vibhaktikārya*) occurs first, and then *utva* and *atva*" and so forth is explained.

He states that in the sūtra, *su* is a separate word with its genitive case ending elided—namely, *yaḥ suḥ etattadoḥ*. The meaning is: "of that *su* which expresses the number belonging to the referents of *etad* and *tad*. However, if one were to explain it as "prescribed after *etad* and *tad*," then forms such as *paramasa dadāti* and *paramaiṣa dadāti* would not be accounted for. It should be understood that the evidence (*liṅga*) for resorting to a relationship mediated by the meaning [rather than the form] is the phrase "*anañsamāse*" (in a compound other than one with the negative particle *nañ*).

Regarding the question "Why [specify] 'after *a* and *ka*'?": the question arises because there is no possibility of application for the forms with the augment *sak* (*sākackayoḥ*), since they are distinct words.

Regarding the term *eṣaka*: the meaning is that the prohibition [stated] in the rule *akoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.36) itself indicates the existence of the *paribhāṣā* (technical maxim): "That which falls between [two elements] is included by the mention of those two. Regarding the mention of *bahula* (in various cases): for this very reason, even when filling out a metrical foot (*pāda*) without an elision (*lopa*), it occurs in some instances—as in *sāsmā aram*. The analysis (*ccheda*) is *saḥ asmai*.
Thus ends the section on the euphonic combination of *svādi* (the nominative and other case endings).
Thus ends the section on the five types of sandhi in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now begins the section on masculine nouns ending in vowels.

The meaning is that in the sūtra *arthavad adhātuḥ pratyayaṃ pratyayāntaṃ ca*, both [the meanings of "meaningful" and "ending in a suffix"] are intended through the device of *tantra* (simultaneous application), and so forth. For instance, if only the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of a suffix were intended, then the prescription of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix by the rule *kṛttaddhita-samāsāś ca* would be redundant. Nor should it be argued that even there [in that rule] that which ends in [a suffix] is not to be understood; for the inclusion of that which ends in [a suffix] follows from the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *arthavat*. For the suffix *matup* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*).

The fact that [the term *arthavat*] is well-known in common usage through the process of unifying meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is the basis for its commendation. Furthermore, the rule "arthavat" (Pāṇini 1.2.45) does not have its purpose fulfilled by the preceding rule, because that purpose is already obtained simply by excluding verbal roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*). Therefore, it is indeed appropriate to state "and excluding that which ends in a suffix.
If, however, suffixes were not excluded, then the mention of the word *sāti* in the rule "sātpadādyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.111) would be redundant.

Why is it stated that [the term *prātipadika*] must be "meaningful" (*arthavat*)? [It is so that] in examples such as *dhanaṃ* and *vanaṃ*, the designation [of *prātipadika*] does not apply to each individual phoneme. If that were the case, the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) would have to follow. If one objects: "But surely they will not occur because of the absence of number, object, and so forth," we say no; for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the singular number is applied by default (*utsargataḥ*). Furthermore, the suffix *su* would be unavoidable, just as in the case of words like *huṃphaṭ*. Nor should it be argued that [the suffixes] would not apply to meaningless items due to the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of "meaningful" items; for that paribhāṣā pertains specifically to cases where a particular form is explicitly mentioned.

Although meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) is obtained by the force of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule beginning with *adhātuḥ*, it is nevertheless stated [here] for the sake of what follows. This has been indicated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *suptiṅantam*. As for what they say—namely, regarding *adhīte* and *yāvaka*: since the root *iṅ* is used only in conjunction with the prefix *adhi*, it is meaningful only in that specific form, and not in its isolated state. The assignment of meanings such as "the root *iṅ* means study" is due to the superimposition of the meaning of the whole onto its constituent part. Similarly, the suffix *kan* is also meaningless.

This is because the meaning is understood even from the word *yāvat*; and because of the mention of both "vibhakti" (inflection) and "kāraka" (grammatical participant) in the rules "oṣadheśca vibhaktāvaprathamāyām" and "akartari ca kārake," which leads to the assumption that the maxim regarding the connection with *nañ* and *iva* is not universally applicable. To this, it must be said: first of all, to say that a verbal root (*dhātu*) is meaningless is contradictory, since it cannot be a verbal root without expressing an action. If you argue that its [meaningfulness] is merely superimposed (*āropita*), that is true; however, the desired conclusion is established by that alone.

The division between base and suffix, as well as the division of their respective meanings, is entirely conceptual (*kalpita*). For the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the *sphoṭa* alone possesses meaning. And it has been said by Bhartṛhari:
"The means [of grammar] are but consolations for children who are being instructed;
standing upon the path of the unreal, one then seeks the real."

Otherwise, how could there be reduplication for the root *iṅ* (as in *adhi-i-ya*) or the addition of *aṭ* and other augments? Thus, in the section on Pratyāhāra, in the passage beginning "The phonemes possess meaning," it is stated quite clearly in the Bhāṣya regarding the forms *adhyeti* and *adhīta* that the vowel *i* possesses meaning. Likewise, the suffix *kan* also possesses meaning, because even for suffixes added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*), they possess meaning precisely through the meaning of the base. If it is argued that this is merely a conceptual construction, we say no; for the answer has already been given. If it is argued that this construction is not accepted by the author of the Śāstra, we say no.

Regarding the rule "dvitīya-tṛtīya-caturtha-turyāṇi," the fact that the suffix *an* has the sense of "completion" (*pūraṇa*)—rather than its own meaning—is stated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself. This is also the view of the author of the Sūtras, who employs the technical designation "pratyaya" (suffix) as a comprehensive term. As for the argument beginning with "oṣadheśca," that too is not valid.

Even if [the rule] were non-eternal (*anitya*), the desired result would be established through its general application (*autsargika-pravṛtti*); furthermore, if there were no application even in cases where it is desired, the underlying logic (*nyāya*) would fall into the error of being devoid of scope (*nirviṣayatva*). Moreover, if the knowledge of its non-eternality must somehow be established, it is possible for the mention of *arthavat* itself to serve as that indicator (*jñāpaka*). Finally, since the purpose of the subsequent [rule] can appropriately be achieved here by the maxim "something is done here [which serves a purpose elsewhere]" (*iha kiñcit kṛtam atra kim api prayojanam asti*), and because, this being the case, the mention of case-endings (*vibhakti*) and grammatical relations (*kāraka*) in rules such as *oṣadheś-ca* could likewise be dispensed with—this is the direction of the argument.

What is meant by "not being a suffix" (*adhātuḥ*)? [Consider the example: *ahan*. Let there not be the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*). Nor should it be argued that, under the view that the time of application is determined by the presence of the suffix (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the exclusion applies because [the word *ahan*] ends in a suffix; for the aforementioned exclusion does not apply by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule regarding the presence of a suffix), as this is made known by the prohibition "not before a suffix ending in *ṅi* or in the vocative" (*na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*). Otherwise, how could the elision of *n* occur in forms such as *rājā*? What is meant by "not being a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*)? [Consider the examples: *hariṣu*, *karoṣi*. Here, let there not be [the elision of the *n*] in the case of the suffixes *sup* and *sip*.

What is the purpose of [specifying] that which does not end in an affix (*apratyayānta*)? It is so that [the designation *prātipadika*] might not apply to those very forms when they are distinguished by case-endings. Nor should it be argued that by virtue of the treatment as being "like the end" (*antavadbhāva*), the status of *prātipadika* would indeed apply to forms such as *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye*, whereby—by the rule "the short vowel in the neuter"—shortening would occur and the suffix *su* would arise. This need not be said, because the desired result is established through the "time-of-operation" (*kāryakāla*) view. Even under the "time-of-enunciation" (*yathoddeśa*) view, the single-substitute for a case-ending is not treated as "like the end," as evidenced by the formulation of rules such as "and in the locative, when expressing the locus. Alternatively, let the mention of the term *prātipadika* in the rule "the short vowel in the neuter" serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned point, with reference to the general principle.

As for what they say—that the exclusion of the suffix (*pratyaya*) need not be made because the purpose is already served by the exclusion of that which ends in a suffix, since even a simple word is considered "ending in a suffix" through the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva*—that is not correct. For when a suffix is mentioned [in a rule], there is the inclusion of everything beginning with that from which the suffix is prescribed; and a simple word is not such [a thing]. Otherwise, according to the method you have stated, even verbal and nominal endings (*suptiṅ*) would be "ending in those [suffixes]," and consequently, the status of being a *pada* would apply to them as well.

And likewise, in cases such as *hariṣu* and *karoṣi*, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur due to the prohibition in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*. Although the definition could have been established simply by stating "not a root (*adhātu*) or an affix (*apratyaya*)," the employment of two negative particles (*nañ*) is for the sake of clarity.

The use of a technical name (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is in accordance with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). Thus it is recited in the Atharvaveda: "What is a root? What is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? What is an affix?

Examples here are words like *ḍittha*, which are unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*). The ancients maintain that this very point is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the theory of non-derivation (*avyutpattipakṣa*).

As for what Haradatta stated—that even on the view that words are derived (*vyutpattipakṣa*), this [sūtra] is for the sake of particles (*nipāta*) and for the sake of imitation (*anukaraṇa*)—that is to be reconsidered, because even in that case, the postulation of a base (*prakṛti*) and so forth is possible.

In reality, however, even on the view that words are derived, the sūtra is for the sake of forms such as *bahupaṭavaḥ*. Nor should it be argued that one should simply have formulated the sūtra as *bahucpūrvaḥ*; for in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) since it ends in a *kṛt* suffix.
