Nor can one find a solution by claiming that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because without the formulation of the *arthavat-sūtra*, the mention of "compound" cannot function as a restriction. This is the general direction of the argument.

The terms *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa* follow from the [previous rule] "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat*). By virtue of that, there is an application of the rule by way of the final element (*tadantavidhi*). For in a compound where the constituent parts lose their own meanings (*jahatsvārthā vṛtti*), there is no meaning belonging to the *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffixes themselves. However, an interpretation based on what was previously so is not commendable. Even in a compound where the parts do not lose their own meanings (*ajahatsvārthā vṛtti*), the meaning does not terminate with the suffix alone; with this intention, he says: "those ending in *kṛt* and *taddhita*. In cases such as *liṭ* and *dhuk*, the exclusion [by the rule] "not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*) applies; and in cases such as *kartṛ*, the exclusion "not ending in a suffix" (*apratyayāntam*) applies—this present rule is an injunction (*vidhi*) in anticipation of those exclusions.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of restriction" (*niyamārtham*): it should not be suspected that this is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*) because an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) would otherwise apply due to the suffix ending in a *pratyaya*. This is because the entire *vākya* (the compound) does not end in a *pratyaya*; furthermore, when a *pratyaya* is mentioned [in a rule], only that which begins with the element from which that *pratyaya* is prescribed is understood to be included. If it is argued: "But the restriction regarding the beginning of the form (*tadādiniyama*) is prohibited in the case of feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*); therefore, in cases such as *rājakumārī*, let this be for the purpose of an injunction," we say: not so. For even though the elision (*lopa*) of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), it does not take effect in the domain of *luk* elision; thus, the compound formation occurs only while the *sup* suffix is still audible.

And in that case, because the technical name (*saṃjñā*) applied by virtue of not ending in a suffix remains easily available even after the elision of the case-ending (*vibhakti-luk*) by the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), for this very reason, *num* and other such operations do not occur in forms such as *gomatpriya*. However, if they were to apply internally (*antaraṅga*) prior to the elision, they would indeed occur.

[Objection: Even so, let [the rule] apply to an incompetent compound (*asamarthasamāsa*) for the sake of a prescriptive injunction (*vidhi*), just as in the case of "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*) and the like. [Reply: No, because it has already been stated that the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is understood by way of *anuvṛtti* (carrying over from a previous rule). [Question: If that is so, how then is there a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for an incompetent compound? [Answer: Understand that it is due to the very means of proof that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*). For, by the rule "after *asūrya* and *lalāṭa*... (*asūryalalāṭayoḥ...*), the suffix *khaś* is prescribed when the word *asūrya* is an attendant word (*upapada*). And an attendant word is a word uttered in proximity (*upoccāritaṃ padam*), and a word is that which ends in a nominal suffix (*su*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

He states the body of the rule (*niyamaśarīra*): "In which aggregate," and so forth. The phrase "the preceding portion" is an illustration; it should be understood that the subsequent element is not a suffix (*pratyaya*). Otherwise, in cases such as *janmavān*, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would not apply, because the mention of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) would have served its purpose in examples like *aupagava*. Why is it said that "the preceding portion is a word" (*pada*)? So that the designation of nominal stem (*prātipadika*) may apply to that which is qualified by the suffix *-bahuc*.

Therefore, in the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ*, when the nominative plural suffix (*jas*) is elided, the word *bahupaṭu-* receives the *cit-svara* accent; subsequently, when *jas* is added again, the penultimate syllable becomes udātta, as required. Alternatively, let the restriction apply to a composite [form] that has not yet entered into the relationship of base and suffix. Nor should it be argued that, under the first view, a designation such as *puruṣau* would apply to the portion *puruṣau* in forms like *rājapuruṣau*; for this is precluded by the very condition of being "meaningful" (*arthavattva*).

For it is only the specific meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) that undergoes syntactic connection (*anvaya*), and not merely the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*), which would otherwise render *puruṣau* meaningful [as a nominal stem]. He states the result of this restriction with the words "by that," etc. If it is argued: "Even so, in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam*, the designation of a sentence (*vākya*) would be unavoidable, because when a *kṛt*-affix is mentioned, there is a rule for including even those preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or a kāraka"; [The author] says: "Not so. This is because the restriction established by the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) sublates [the previous rule] due to its higher status (*paratva*).

And thus, the truth is that in the rule *kṛttaddhita-*, the restrictive maxim (*paribhāṣā*) regarding *kṛt*-suffixes does not apply at all, because it would be fruitless. As for what they say—that the mention of *samāsa* (compound) is not for the sake of restriction but rather for the sake of an injunction; for "possessing meaning" (*arthavattva*) consists in possessing a linguistic function (*vṛttimat*), and this function is twofold—denotation (*śakti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—and that such [a function] does not exist in a compound—on this point the following must be said: according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted, the claim that there is no function (*vṛtti*) is certainly refuted.
Even in the Mīmāṃsā view, indication (*lakṣaṇā*) certainly exists. As they have said:

For it is established that in every case, the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) is indeed what is indicated (lakṣya). Now, suppose it were argued according to the Naiyāyika method? That too is not [correct], because [in that case] examples such as *bahupaṭavaḥ* would remain unestablished.

If it is argued that the mention of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) refers to that which is qualified by it? No, because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as *pacatakī*. Furthermore, in this way, due to the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt* suffixes, the over-extension to cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam* would be unavoidable; let this matter rest for now.

The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By this, the statement "the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) should be prescribed for a meaningless particle" becomes redundant; this [present rule] is intended for those cases where there is no meaning even to be indicated (*dyotya*). For example: *avadyati*.

However, in the case of imitations (*anukaraṇa*), when there is an intention to express non-difference from the thing being imitated, there is no nominal-stem status precisely because of the absence of meaningfulness, as in: *bhū* in the sense of "existence. But when there is an intention to express difference, the designation would indeed apply, as in: *bhuvo vuk-* (Pāṇini 7.3.88).

Regarding the phrase *liṅgaviśiṣṭasya*: the meaning is "even that which is qualified by a suffix expressing gender. The purpose of this paribhāṣā is as follows: in the word *ayaskumbhī*, there is the substitution of *s* [for *k*] according to the rule *ataḥ kṛkami-*. For that [substitution] is prescribed when words such as *kaṃsa* follow as the final member (*uttarapada*). Furthermore, in the case of *kumārayati* (he treats like a girl), where one says *kumārīm ācaṣṭe*, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix occurs by the rule *ṇāviṣṭavat*. Similarly, in the expression *yāminayantyahāni* (the days act like nights), the formation of the *kvip* suffix in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*) is also a result [of this paribhāṣā].

Regarding the phrase "before the two [suffixes] *ṅ* and *ya*": by this, both *lohinikā* and *āryakā* are established. For instance, because it is an affix applied in its own sense (*svārthika*), the suffix *kan*—which is internal (*antaraṅga*) and subsequent—[in the rule] "after *lohita*, when referring to a gem," would supersede the suffix *ṅīp*. Consequently, only *lohitikā* would result; however, both forms are desired. But by the force of the mention of *ṅīp*, both forms are established when *kan* follows a stem ending in *ṅīp*, since the rule "after a low-pitched vowel denoting a color... is optional.

However, from the word *ārya*, the suffix *kan*—which will be taught as being used even in an absolute sense (*atyantasvārthika*) in the rule "not when expressing a part" (*na sāmivacane*)—does not apply prior [to the addition of *āp*], due to the force of the inclusion of the term *āp*. Consequently, the optional substitution of *it* (the shortening of the final vowel) by the rule "for the *ā* in place of which there is *ya* or *ka* preceding, according to the Northern Grammarians" (*udīcāmātaḥ sthāne yakapūrvāyāḥ*) is established.

It might be argued: "If this were so, the form *bahugomatka* would not be established, because the suffix *ṅīp*—conditioned by the presence of an *u*-vowel or an *i*-vowel (the *ugit* rule)—would apply prior to the addition of the *kap* suffix. This is not correct. For it will be stated that the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) applies as a constituent part of the final member while the compound itself is still unformed, specifically within the non-technical (alaukika) analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*). Regarding its position: some hold that it occurs before the case-ending (*vibhakti*). However, according to the view that it occurs after the case-ending, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because it ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the case-ending is elided (*subluk*); then, once the case-ending has been restored (*sup*), the compound is formed.

Therefore, it is established that the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is for the purpose of ensuring their application prior to the formation of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), even though that suffix would otherwise intervene.

As for what some have said—that the mention of *āp* is for the sake of clarity—that is refuted by this very point. In reality, however, the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* may be omitted. The conclusion is that secondary suffixes arise from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Furthermore, it should be noted that *ṅī* and *āp* apply precisely before the case-suffixes, because it is accepted that operations prompted by meanings such as the primary sense (*svārtha*) occur in a sequential order.

Regarding the term *suṅasyoḥ*: the letter *u* in *su* is for the purpose of distinguishing it in the rule "arvaṇastrasau," for if it were stated simply as *si*, the meaning would be "when [the suffix] begins with *s*. Consequently, the form "vājamarvatsu paya usriyāsu" would not be established. The letter *i* in *ṅasi* is so that there might be no inclusion of this [suffix] in the rule "yuṣmadasmabhyāṃ ṅaso'ś."

If it is argued that, because of the recurrence of the term "pañcamyāḥ" (of the fifth case) in the rule "ekavacanasya ca," the remaining *ṅas* will be understood here by process of elimination, then this [rule] would serve the purpose of "ṭāṅasiṅasām. Furthermore, the letters *ja* and *śa* in *jas* and *śas* are for the sake of distinguishing the scope of the two rules "jasaḥ śī" and "tasmācchaso naḥ. If it is suggested that one of these two [suffixes] should simply be without an *anubandha*, this is not so; for if the *ja* were absent from *jas*, the form *au* would undergo *āv*.

Furthermore, the suffix *pratyaya* might otherwise be suspected of ending in the letter *v*. Similarly, in the absence of the letter *ś* in *śas*, one might suspect that *auṭ* possesses the property of being *ṅit*. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, it is appropriate to include those markers. The *ṭ* in *auṭ* is for the purpose of forming the pratyāhāra *suṭ*. The *ṭ* in *ṭā* is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "*ṭāṅasi*". The *ṅ* in *ṅe* and the subsequent suffixes is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "*gherṅiti*". The *p* is for the purpose of forming the pratyāhāra.

And thus, even though all [the suffixes] are fruitful, the statement of the ancient authors that "they are for the sake of *saṃjñā*" (technical names) is indeed inconsistent. Even if one attempts to explain it by breaking down the term as: *saṃjñā* is correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), and "for the sake of that" means for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*), such an interpretation is merely strained and has therefore been set aside.

He explains that from the rule *supaḥ tiṅastrīṇitrīṇi*, the phrase *trīṇi trīṇi* and the entire rule beginning with *tānyekavacana-* carry over; this he does by stating *supastrīṇitrīṇyetyādinā*. Regarding *ekaśaḥ*: the meaning is "one by one. The suffix *śas* is applied after a word ending in the nominative case to express distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) according to the rule *saṅkhyaikavacanācca*. As for what the ancients stated—that it should be *ekaikaśaḥ*—that is incorrect, because since the distributive sense is already expressed by *śas* itself, a reduplication (*dvirvacana*) would be improper.

According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the suffix *śas* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule of reduplication (*dvirvacana*) by virtue of the principle of non-attainment (*yenāprāptinyāya*). As for what some say—that both forms are correct because of the usage *ekaikaśo dadāti* in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *sarvasya dve*, and because of the author of the Sūtras’ own mention of *ekaśas* in the rule *tāny eka-*—that is not so, because the cited *Bhāṣya* passage pertains to a different subject matter.

Having begun with the statement, "Where the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is not expressed by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), there occurs reduplication," the *Bhāṣya* provides the example: "For instance, *ekaikaśo dadāti* (he gives one by one). Kaiyaṭa explains this as follows: "There is also an *ekaśeṣa* [compound] in the sense of 'few' (*alpa*); when its reduplication occurs for the sake of distributive repetition, the suffix *śas* is applied according to the rule *bahvalpārthāt*. However, this meaning is not possible in the present context, so let it rest for now.

Regarding the word *rāma*: if one holds the view that this is an unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*), its designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is established by the rule "arthavat... (Pāṇini 1.2.45). However, if it is derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) as "that in which they delight" (*ramante 'smin*), then—under the governing heading "and [the suffixes] ghañ and ap are used in the sense of instrument and location"—it is formed by the suffix *ghañ* (as an exception to *ap*) according to the rule "halaśca" (Pāṇini 3.3.121); whereas if it were analyzed using the suffix *ap*, it would be formed by the rule "kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca" (Pāṇini 1.2.46). This is the distinction.

Regarding the rule *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau*: "in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*) refers to those [words] which [possess it]. The case-ending (*vibhakti*) is a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for homogeneity (*sārūpya*), but it is not the cause (*nimitta*) for the single-remainder operation (*ekaśeṣa*). Thus, because it is independent of a cause, the single-remainder operation is internal (*antaraṅga*) and applies even prior to the production of the case-endings. If this were not commenced, then a case-ending would apply to each [word] individually, and a copulative compound (*dvandva*) would also take effect. However, once the single-remainder operation has been commenced, the non-application of the copulative compound is effectively achieved, as there is an absence of multiple words ending in case-endings; such is the intended meaning.

"Only those that are identical in form (*sarūpāṇy eva*). This is understood through the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the particle *eva* from the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 1.2.64]. Consequently, there is no single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) for two words *mātṛ* when one denotes "mother" (the progenitor) and the other denotes "measurer" (a limited quantity), as in *mātṛbhyām* and so on; for although they are identical in form in the dual case, they differ in form in the nominative and accusative singular (*au*, *jas*, etc.).

"It is only one" (eka eva). And this [principle] operates only when there is a desire to express [the members] together; that is to say, within the scope of the *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) *dvandva*. For where there is a mutual connection of several combined meanings, such is its scope. This is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule "The augment *num* is added to a root ending in an *it*-letter," as well as from logical reasoning (*nyāya*). To explain: once it is established that "that which remains denotes the meaning of what is elided," everything presented by the single word that is actually heard must, without distinction, connect in a uniform manner.

Alternatively, one should explain this by carrying over the word "dvandve" from the previous sūtra, meaning "when a dvandva compound is about to be formed. It might be argued that the meaning should simply be "when a dvandva has been formed. This is not so; for in cases such as *panthānau* and *panthānaḥ*, there would be the undesirable application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). In cases such as *karau* and *karāḥ*, there would be the undesirable application of singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*). And in cases such as *sarve* and *sarveṣām*, there would be the undesirable application of both the rules "dvandve ca" and "vibhāṣā jasi. This is the general direction of the argument. As for what the ancients said—that when *rāma-rāma-au* is situated [as the basis], and that "when a single case-ending follows"—[that is incorrect].

In this regard, the possibility of such an explanation is as follows: in the expression *rāma rāma*, the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) applies not only to the individual parts but also to the whole, because the whole possesses meaning when its components are combined. Nor should it be argued that even though the whole has meaning, this cannot be the case because the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). For it has been stated that the restriction applies only to those cases where the preceding portion of the whole is a word (*pada*); furthermore, in accordance with forms such as *bahupaṭavaḥ*, it is more appropriate that the restriction pertains only to items of the same class.

And thus, by the principle of reduplication of a single syllable (*ekāj-dvirvacana*), the dual and other case-endings arise directly from the composite nominal stem (*samudāya-prātipadika*) itself; for even by that much, it is possible to maintain the connection of the number with the meanings of the individual components. If it is objected: "In that case, would not case-endings arise from the composite in examples such as *rāma-kṛṣṇau* even without a copulative compound (*dvandva*)?"—do not say so. For, since the phrase "multiple *subanta*s" recurs in the rule prescribing the *dvandva*, it subverts the application of the principle of reduplication of a single syllable. This is the general direction of the argument.

If it is asked: "Even though such an interpretation is possible, for what reason is the view that 'when a single case-ending follows a group [of words]' (*samudāyāt*) disregarded? Listen: under this view, even in cases such as *mātṛ-mātarau* ("mother and mother"), there would have to be a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*). If one objects: "By repeating the phrase 'when a single case-ending' (*ekavibhaktau*) and drawing forward the particle *eva*, the rule should be explained as: 'those which are similar in form when they possess a single case-ending'"; we say no. For there is no evidence for such repetition, and furthermore, if the case-ending were the qualifier of the single-remainder formation, there would be no resulting benefit.

Furthermore, the exclusion of cases such as "milk digests milk" cannot be the result [of the rule], because the requirement that there be a desire to express [the objects] together (*sahavivakṣā*) is indispensable; otherwise, in the case of "he carries milk-milk," there would be the undesirable consequence of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for both the primary and secondary objects. Moreover, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "God of gods. On the contrary, if [the word] were a qualifier of both through repetition (*āvṛtti*), then the formation of the term *bhaikṣam*—meaning "a collection of alms"—would not be established.

For instance, when *bhikṣā bhikṣā bhikṣā* remains as *ām a*, once the elision (*luk*) has been applied by the rule "an external operation [supersedes] even internal operations," the single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) would not occur because there is no subsequent case-ending (*vibhakti*). This is because, when the suffix has been elided, there is no basis for applying the technical designation of being "as if followed by a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, in forms such as *rāmāu*, since the single-substitute *vṛddhi* (ā) replaces the preceding and following sounds according to the rule "vṛddhir eci" due to its higher status and permanence, the single-remainder formation would not occur because there is no subsequent case-ending; this is because the status of being either the final element of the prior or the initial element of the subsequent does not apply when both sides are relied upon. This is the general direction of the argument.

As for the alternative interpretation proposed by the earlier commentator—that there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the forms including their case-endings—that is not correct; for even if the disappearing elements were to cease along with their case-endings, it would follow that the single form remaining would be heard with the singular ending.

Now, it might be argued that when there is simultaneous denotation of multiple substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*), there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) for words ending in dual or plural suffixes; and the copulative compound (*dvandva*) is likewise so. For indeed, in the *ajahatsvārthā* theory of semantic function, each individual word denotes multiple meanings due to their mutual co-occurrence. Thus, since in the non-worldly (*alaukika*) procedural sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) of both the copulative compound and the single-remainder, only the dual and plural suffixes are introduced, the position that the single-remainder applies to words ending in case-suffixes is entirely unassailable.

That too is not correct, because that [simultaneous expression] is impossible in a *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) compound. Even in the other view (*ajahatsvārthā*), it is impossible to abandon the singular number that was first applied. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of cutting off established compounds such as the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. In those cases as well, since the prior member is subsumed within the meaning of the subsequent member, the use of the genitive case and so forth is untenable. Thus says the Bhāṣya: "This simultaneous expression of multiple substrates is both difficult and hard to justify."

As for what they have explained—that on the view that words denote individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*), since the use of each specific word would apply to every individual instance, this *sūtra* exists so that only one [word] may be used; whereas on the view that words denote forms (*ākṛtipakṣa*), because a single form inherently implies multiple individuals, [the *sūtra*] would be purposeless—this is not correct. For even on the view that words denote individuals, in the case of the injunction "One should not kill a Brāhmaṇa," it is easily stated through a single word, namely "Brāhmaṇa," that the prohibition applies to many [individuals] by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application).

Otherwise, even in the view that [the word] denotes a genus (*jāti*), the rule would be untenable without the Sūtra, because it must conform to various meanings such as "in that [place], by means of dwelling, and through perfect forbearance. Therefore, although the application [of the term] can be sustained through *tantra* (simultaneous reference) in both the views of denoting a genus and an individual (*vyakti*), there is no restrictive rule that it must always be understood through *tantra* alone. Consequently, a disjunctive *dvandva* (copulative compound) is unavoidable without the Sūtra. This is because we observe the use of multiple words, such as "this is a jar, this is a jar," and likewise, the formation of a *dvandva* such as "jar-jars" (*ghaṭa-ghaṭau*) is logically established.

Even so, there is no possibility of the application of the *dvandva* compound in the form "ghaṭakalaśau" (pot-and-jar), because of the Vārttika rule: "Even for dissimilar [words], if they have the same meaning. This is because, by deriving the word *rūpa* as "that which is manifested or understood," one relies on its denoting "meaning" (*artha*), and thus the sense of the Vārttika is already encompassed within the Sūtra itself. Therefore, it should be noted that the Sūtra is necessary in both views in order to prevent undesirable optional forms such as "ghaṭaghaṭau" or "ghaṭakalaśau."

This being the case, keeping the very futility of the Sūtra in mind, they have explained it here as follows: "By this [Sūtra], a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) is not prescribed," and so forth. Furthermore, having rejected the position that [the operation occurs] from a whole aggregate when there is a single case-ending, they say again: "When *rāma rāma au* is situated [as the state of the base]," and so on. This is an inferred non-standard (*alaukika*) procedural sentence (*prakriyāvākya*), and not a standard one. And in a non-standard state, operations such as case-endings and single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*) do not apply, because grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) pertains only to words actually in use (*prayukta*). Thus they argue.

All of that is contrary to the context and contrary to logic. For it is precisely in order to explain those forms already in use that an unreal (alaukika) form is postulated; and all grammatical operations apply only to these unreal forms, not to the final, established (pariniṣṭhita) form. This is because the final form cannot be obtained without the application of rules such as "the single substitute for the first two [vowels] is the homogeneous preceding one," and because it is impossible to justify the application of such rules to a form that is already finalized. Let this matter rest for now.

The term *ami* means "in that which is *ac* following *am*"; that is to say, when there is an *ac* vowel within the constituent of *am*. Consequently, there is no *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) for [the vowel] accompanied by the letter *m*. Similarly, in cases such as *akṣād ūhinyām*, it should be understood that the rule applies when there is an *ac* vowel in *ūhinyām*, and so forth. This is because the inclusion of the term *ac* in the rule "iko yaṇ aci" is beyond dispute. Furthermore, the grammatical indications (*nirdeśa*) such as "padāsvairibāhyā—" serve as evidence here.

Therefore, by the word *tat* (in the rule *tasmācchasaḥ*), the preceding homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) which is in proximity is referred to. The term *śasaḥ* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). And that member [of the suffix] is further qualified by its position as "following"—that is, "of the member of the suffix *śas* that follows the preceding homogeneous long vowel. This is what he states: "the *sakāra* which follows the *śas*. However, it is not stated as "the *śas* which follows," because such a thing is impossible; for once the homogeneous long vowel has been applied, a subsequent *śas* cannot exist.

Since the rule *aṭkupvāṅ raṣābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.2) employs an ablative case (*pañcamī*) indication, this present statement is made because [the application of the rule] would otherwise not apply when there is an intervention. Here, an intervention by all [the letters mentioned] together is impossible; nor does the meaning intend an intervention by each one individually. This is stated with the intention that [the intervention occurs] by separate [letters] as far as possible, or by them combined, based on the force of the inclusion of the word *kṣubhna* in the *kṣubhnādi* group and the usage in rules such as *sarūpāṇām*. Thus he says: "by separate [letters] as far as possible, and by combined [letters]."

But in that case, would there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in examples such as *ādarśena*? Nor can it be said that the restriction applies only when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and so on, because it has been stated that this is an original injunction (*vidhi*) where [otherwise] nothing would have applied. True; however, a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) should be understood here: one rule, "*vyavāye'pi*," is for the purpose of an injunction; another, "*aṭkupvāṅnum*," is for the purpose of a restriction. The elision (*luk*) of *bhis* is Vedic. The phrase "to set aside the prohibition" means that by this, the substitution of *ṇ* in *paryāṇaddham*—by the rule "*upasargādasamāse'pi*"—is established; this is the intended meaning.

The mention of *num* means that it is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both the *num* substitute and the natural (*svābhāvika*) anusvāra. By this, in the case of the root *bṛhi* (in the sense of growth), *num* is added because it is marked with the *it* letter; its *anusvāra* follows. In the case of *tṛṃhū* (in the sense of harming), the *anusvāra* is natural here. Thus, in both *bṛṃhaṇam* and *tṛṃhaṇam*, the substitution of *ṇ* is established. In the case of *ivi* (in the sense of pleasing), we have *prenvanam*. Here, the substitution of *ṇ* does not apply by the rules "after a *kṛt* suffix ending in a vowel" (*kṛtyacaḥ*) or "after a root beginning with *i* or *ī* that has *num*" (*ijādeḥ sanumaḥ*).

Just as in the injunction "one should release speech after seeing a star," the sight of a star serves merely to indicate a specific time; therefore, even if stars are seen during the day, speech is not released because the specific time indicated by them is absent. At night, however, speech is released even if no stars are seen, because that [specific time] exists. The same should be understood here as well. [Objection: But in that case, the inclusion of the term *num* is redundant, since the *anusvāra* is already included by virtue of being an *aṭ* (a vowel or *y*, *v*, *r*, *l*).

If it is argued that in cases such as *uraḥkeṇa*, where there is an intervention by the *visarga* or the *jihvāmūlīya*, this very same [explanation] applies, he says "And that" (*tacceti*), acknowledging it is true.

It might be objected: according to the reasoning stated, the mention of *num* in the rule *anumvisarjanīya* should also be abandoned; for there too, the *anusvāra* is what must be indicated, since otherwise [the rule] would be impossible. Indeed, at the time when the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) is about to take effect in forms such as *sarpīṃṣi*, the *num* is no longer present, because the *anusvāra* occurs prior to that due to the fact that the *ṣatva* is not yet established (*asiddha*).

If it is argued: "Even though [the condition] is indeed possible in the case of *suhinsu*, nevertheless, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that very instance, one must resort to a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) for the *anusvāra* in place of *num*, in accordance with the intended examples (*lakṣya*), because of the explanation [in the commentary]. And since that [substitute] is a *śar*, the substitution of *ṣ* is established even when there is an intervention by it"—we say: not so. Even if, according to the method stated, the inclusion of the *visarga* in that rule could be rejected, the mention of *num* is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*).

For it is thus: if the substitution of *ṣ* occurs upon intervention by an *anusvāra*, it is restricted to that which stands in place of *num* alone. Therefore, in cases such as *puṃsu*, it does not occur; this is the general direction.

Regarding the rule for suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*), the ancient [grammarians] have stated here: "from whatever root or nominal stem (*prātipadika*). That is not correct, because even verbal forms ending in *tiṅ* (conjugated verbs) and others serve as bases (*aṅga*) for suffixes such as *tarap*. Furthermore, there would be no basis for such a restriction, and it would result in the absence of *vṛddhi* substitution in forms such as *āmuṣyāyaṇa*. For this secondary derivative (*taddhita*) does not indeed follow from a nominal stem, but rather from that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*); such is the direction of the argument.

Therefore, let it simply be "ato bhisa ais nanves". Nor does there arise the contingency of *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the latter form) by the rule "ato guṇe", because that would render the pronunciation of the vowel *e* in *ais* redundant. If it is argued that otherwise [the rule] would have prescribed only *is*, that is true; however, since *ed* and *ai* are indistinguishable in having two morae (*mātrā*), *ais* was employed to avoid the complexity [of a longer term]. Thus, there is no suspicion of *pararūpa* at all, which results in great economy. As for what some say—that the formation of *ais* is for the sake of hearing the sound *ai* in forms like *nirjarasaiḥ*—that contradicts the Bhāṣya. For, according to the *sannipātaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the non-disturbance of a cause), the substitution of *jaras* does not apply, and thus *nirjaraiḥ* alone is established as the final conclusion in the Bhāṣya.
"It is not [the case] because of contradiction with the rule *nāmi*. This is clear from both the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rules *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam* and *śnānnalopaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the force of its formulation": the sense is that the rule *supi ca* lacks such force, because it finds scope in forms such as *rāmābhyām*. Thus, what some have said—that the citation of *nāmi* in the word *rāma* is due to a scribal error—is to be considered doubtful.

With the intention that even a single genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is divided according to the difference in its scope, he explains: "the substitute (*ādeśa*) and the portion of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*). However, if the "portion of a substitute" were taken [as the meaning], then there would be a fault in forms such as *tisṛṇām*. And if [the meaning] were "that which is the *sakāra* belonging to an affix," then [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *rāmeṣu*. Although this dual interpretation involving such heterogeneity is not appropriate as a *dvandva* compound due to the absence of a desire to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*), it should nevertheless be understood as being based on the usage of the Sūtra itself (*sautratvāt*).

Regarding the phrase "of the unvoiced [consonant]": as for what some say—that among the unvoiced sibilants (*soṣman*), the dental *ṣ* alone is the most similar substitute for the [dental] *s*—that is insufficient, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the case of *ṭh*. Thus, the Prātiśākhya states:
"In each class (*varga*), the first two are unvoiced; the pair [the second and third] are sibilant (*soṣman*); and the last is nasal."

If it is argued: "In examples such as *dadhi-secaḥ*, the Bhāṣya states that the compound *padādādiḥ padādiḥ* (a genitive compound meaning 'the beginning of a word after [a preceding] word') is employed to prevent the application of *ṣatva* before the addition of case-endings (*sup*). Consequently, would not the prohibition *'sātpadādyoḥ'* also apply here?"—it is not so. This is because the mention of *sāti* indicates that the aforementioned prohibition does not operate by relying on that technical designation of a word (*pada*) which occurs in the rule *svādiṣu*. As for what some say—that this indicates the prohibition does not apply in the domain of suffixes—that is incorrect.

That is not so, because in cases such as *avyatise*, there would result the undesirable application of the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). Now, one might object: "Under the view that [a word] is the beginning of a *pada*, the *ṣatva* in *avyatise* is indeed unavoidable. Nor can it be argued that by the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as what it designates), *se* also possesses the status of a *pada* because it is a *tiṅ*-ending; for when a suffix is mentioned, only that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed is included. Otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence of prohibiting *ṣatva* even in forms like *rāmeṣu*. This is true.

We do not claim that the status of being a word (pada-saṃjñā) belongs to the suffix alone; rather, we extend the designation "word"—which applies to the entire collection of stem and suffix—to a suffix even when its stem has been elided, by means of the maxim of "modification of a part" (ekadeśavikṛtanyāya). For in cases such as *rāmau* and *rāmāḥ*, the status of being a word is established precisely through this maxim of modification of a part, because the designation "word" applies prior to the occurrence of the single-substitute (ekādeśa) operation. It is not the case that the rule "that which ends in a nominal suffix or a verbal suffix" (*suptiṅanta*) applies once the single-substitute has already taken effect, according to the established doctrine that "when both sides [of a grammatical operation] are relied upon, the resulting form is neither like the end nor like the beginning."

As for what they say—that when a *prakṛti* (base) is in proximity, the *pratyaya* (suffix) lacks the status of a *pada*, because of the indications in [Pāṇini’s rules] such as *mantreṣu* and *sarveṣām*—that is weak; for, since the absence of *padatva* is established by the aforementioned reasoning, such an indication would be impossible and useless.

In the rule *sarvādīni sarvanāmāni*, the expression *sarvādīni* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (where the qualities of the members are understood), as evidenced by the indication in the rule *hali sarveṣām*.

Regarding the phrase "dvandve ca": for it will be stated that this is a prohibition of the entire compound (*samudāya*), and not of its individual parts (*avayava*). The intention is that, without the application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (the application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element), there would be no possibility of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applying to the whole compound. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of this designation of the ending element? It cannot be argued that forms such as *paramasarvasmāi* provide the result [of the designation], because even in those cases, the suffixes like *smāi* are established simply by the *tadantavidhi* within the governing context of *aṅga* (the nominal stem). To this, he says: "by that" (*tena*).

Nor should it be said here that, because the term *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem") is understood [in the rule], the designation *tadantavidhi* (application to that which ends with the stem) applies to the pronouns as qualifiers of that [stem], on the grounds of the statement: "There is a prohibition regarding the prescription of compounds and suffixes. This is the intended meaning. Regarding *akac ca*: by virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix *tasil* occurs in *paramasarvataḥ*. Regarding *jasaḥ śī anekāltvāt*: the sense is that it is due to its having more than one *al* (phoneme), and not due to its being marked with *ś* (*śit*). Regarding *avarṇāntāt*: the meaning is "after a stem (*aṅga*) ending in an *a*-vowel. Thus, there is no lack of application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *yeṣām*, *keṣām*, or *teṣām*.

The rule states that *ām* is prescribed after a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). It is not stated as "after [a pronoun] following another [pronoun]," because if it were so, the augment *suṭ* would undesirably apply in the case of *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*. For the prohibition "and in a *dvandva*" applies to the whole compound and not to its individual members. Furthermore, this *ām* is not prescribed after that [individual member], but rather after the entire compound; thus, there is no *suṭ*. The authority for adopting the view that the pronoun is a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*) is precisely the usage in the Bhāṣya: *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*.

Regarding the term *pañcatriṃśat*: it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "five and thirty," or a *tatpuruṣa* meaning "thirty plus five. As for what was stated by those explaining the ancient text of the *Pratyāhāra*—namely, that there are forty-one [phonemes]—it was said: "This is not a *tatpuruṣa* with the middle word elided (*madhyamapadalopa*). For if it were so, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) prescribed by the rules 'in a *dvandva* of many *rājanya*s among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis' and 'in the case of a number' would not apply. Therefore, this is indeed a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective compound)."

Regarding the statement that there is no neuter gender in cases such as *ekaviṃśati* because gender depends upon common usage (*lokāśrayatvāl liṅgasya*), that is to be reconsidered; for when there is a difference in accent due to a difference in compound type, the desired result is achieved. Thus, while explaining the Vārttika on the rule *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye*—"there is an extension [of the neuter] for the numeral in a *tatpuruṣa* for the sake of forms like *niḥ-śatā*, etc., because elsewhere there is the elision of the suffix *adhika*"—the author of the Bhāṣya says: "One more than twenty is *ekaviṃśati*; two more is *dvāviṃśati*. The phrase "for this very reason" means that the dual number alone is logical for the word *dvi*.

But in that case, the inclusion of *ubha* in the list of *sarvādi* (the group beginning with *sarva*) would be useless, because the pronominal operations such as *smāy* and so forth do not occur in the dual. Nor is it correct to argue that the result of this inclusion is the optional third case (*tṛtīyā*) in forms such as *ubhābhyāṃ hetubhyām* or *ubhayor hetvoḥ*, by virtue of the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca*; for that purpose is already covered by the Vārttika: *nimittakāraṇahetuṣu sarvāsāṃ prāyadarśanam*.

Nor should it be said that this Vārttika depends upon the technical designation *sarvanāman* (pronoun) because it is recited by the author of the Vṛtti under the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca*; for it is recited in the Bhāṣya under the rule *hetau*. It is precisely for this reason that Haradatta has cited the examples *annena kāraṇena vasati* ("he dwells for the sake of food") and *annasya kāraṇasya* ("of the cause that is food"). Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "But its recitation here... [is as follows].

Regarding the phrase *ayac-prasaṅgāt*: this is the intended meaning. In the rule *ubhādudātto nityam*, the portion *ubhādudāttaḥ* is separated as an independent rule. From the word *ubha*, which denotes a number and functions to express a part (*avayava*), the suffix *ayac* shall be applied in the sense of a whole (*avayavin*). Thus, *ubhayoḥ maṇiḥ* ("a jewel belonging to both"). Then follows *nityam*. This means that in the context of a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), the suffix *ayac* must necessarily be applied to the word *ubha* in its own sense (*svārthe*). Consequently, just as *ayac* is mandatory in cases such as *ubhayapakṣavinītanidrā* ("one whose sleep has been dispelled by both wings"), it would likewise apply even when the suffix *kap* is used.

If it is argued that even when *akac* is applied, the form *ayac* remains unavoidable, we say: not so. For the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) is intended for the sake of achieving desired results, and because of the specific mention in the rule "ubhau sābhyāsasya," this [application of *ayac*] is explained as occurring only where the dual number (*dvivacana*) is not heard. Thus says the *Vārttika*: "The absence of others [is established] because [the rule] concerns the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Indeed, when *akac* is present, the status of the word *ubhaya* as being within the scope of the dual number is not obstructed by the maxim "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing"; however, when the suffix *kap* is present, that status is certainly obstructed.
Regarding the phrase "it has been stated thus": the words "by the author of the Vārttika" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Although the suffix *ṭāp* was also mentioned in the preceding Vārttika, it is not intended here; for Kaiyaṭa and others have explained that even the status of being the domain of *ṭāp* must be understood as occurring only when followed by a dual ending. With this intention, he explains [the rule] with the words "in the absence of being followed by a dual ending. The sense is that because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for *ṭāp* is also included as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatvena*), the condition of being followed by a dual ending does indeed exist.

Although the status of being followed by a dual suffix (*dvivacanaparatva*) is difficult to establish in cases such as *ubhau*—because when both [the preceding and following elements] are resorted to, the treatment of the end-like-initial (*antādivadbhāva*) is absent—nevertheless, the intended meaning here is that the dual suffix produced from the word *ubha* has not been elided (*luk*) in instances other than those where it is removed; therefore, the suffix *ayac* is applied elsewhere. Although the *Bhāṣya* rejects the inclusion of the word *ubha* on the grounds that the suffix *kap* is also considered "inherently dual" (*svārthika*) since it follows the word *ubha*, that is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*).

For it is appropriate to understand that only the artificial (kṛtrima) dual number is intended here; otherwise, there would be over-extension (atiprasakti) to suffixes such as *tratasil* and others. If it is argued that although *tratasil* are prescribed after a case-ending denoting a kāraka, they do not denote duality even when they are svārthika (denotative of their own meaning), we say no; for the suffix *kap* also conveys the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*), and in the view that [the nominal stem] consists of five elements (pañcapakṣa), it necessarily conveys an additional meaning. This is the direction of the argument.

"It does not exist. The sense is that it is because [the word] is not mentioned [in the grammatical lists]. And thus, since the word *ubhaya* does not produce a dual ending, it would follow that it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by virtue of not possessing all case-endings; however, Kaiyaṭa has introduced the *bhāṣya* on the rule "A *taddhita* suffix that does not possess all case-endings [is also indeclinable]" (*taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ*), stating: "The inclusion of *kṛt* and *taddhita* derivatives occurs only when they are explicitly recited [in the list]. "It exists. The sense is that there is no evidence for its non-mention, because the explicit recitation [of the word in the list] has already served its purpose by excluding forms such as *pacatikalpam* and *pacatirūpam*. "The one ending in the suffix *tayap*. The sense is that this refers to the word *ubhaya*.

Regarding "it is eternal": however, the phrase "the higher, the lower, and both are enemies" should be understood as being due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Regarding "underived": this is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *Paspaśā* section.

Some—the authors of the *Kāśikā*—hold that this is because we observe both the udātta [accent] in "etántvaṃ manye" and the anudātta [accent] in "utá tvaḥ paśyan. One—the first [author]—maintains that although the word ending in *-tām* is not clear in the *saṃhitā* recitation, it must be divided as ending in *-tām*; otherwise, one would recite it only once with a single monotone (*ekaśruti*). Nor should there be any disagreement, for according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra*: "The words *tvat*, *tvas*, *asmat*, and *asme* are anudātta. Thus, there is a Ṛgvedic mantra: "At one time you are barren, at another you give birth."

The commentators on the Vedas have explained it thus: this word *tvat*, listed among the pronouns (*sarvanāman*), is unaccented (*anudātta*) and is a synonym for "another" (*anya*). Jayadeva also employed it in the phrase: "drinking the honey-sweet nectar from your lower lip" (*tvadadharamadhuramadhūni pibantam*). The analysis (*vigraha*) here is "the lower lip of another woman than you" (*tvatto'nyasyā adharaḥ*), and not "your own lower lip" (*tavādharaḥ*). This is because it would result in a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the preceding sentence: "he beholds you in secret in every direction. Furthermore, it is heard in the Vedic text: "In this [cup], Soma was seen by Nema" (*pra nemasmin dadṛśe somaḥ*).

Regarding the word *sama*: thus it is heard in scripture—"May others, all (*same*) alike, perish"; "May we not [fall] to the wolf or the she-wolf, to any such as these (*samasmai*"); "Protecting us from every one who intends evil (*samasmāt*"); and "And also toward every one (*samasmimnā*)" and so forth. Regarding the word *sima*: "It may mean 'entire' (*kṛtsna*) or 'capable' (*śakta*), and it occurs in the senses of 'limit' (*maryādā*) and 'bound' (*avabaddha*)". And it is heard: "Night spreads her garment for everyone (*simasmai*"); "The bright, white [light] rises up from everyone (*simasmāt*)". In both cases, the word *sima* is a synonym for "all" (*sarva*), according to the Vedabhāṣya.

Regarding the term *gaṇasūtra*: although the Vārttika "it should be stated that [the rule applies] except for *puri*" is recited in the Bhāṣya under a sūtra of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, nevertheless, it is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that *gaṇasūtra* and not to the rule prescribing the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) before the suffix *jas*. This is because, with the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from *ata*" (Pāṇini 7.1.11), the substitution of *śī* for *jas* is prescribed; thus, there is no possibility of its application to a word ending in *ṭā*. Regarding *antarāyām*: the meaning is "outside the wall" or "inside it. Alternatively, the application may be understood through the inclusion of the *ekādeśa* (single-substitute) as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavadbhāva*), by virtue of the maxim concerning words qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*).

*tyad* and *tad*—these two refer to what has been previously mentioned. Regarding these, the author of the *Gaṇaratna* states that the first (*tyad*) is Vedic; however, that is not correct, because it would render the mention of "Vedic" (*chandasi*) in the rule *syaśchandasi bahulam* superfluous. The word *eka* is used in the sense of "another," as well as for "the principal," "the first," and "alone.
It is also employed in the senses of "common," "equal," "small," and "number."

"By its own denotation" (svābhidheya): the meaning is that there is a restriction of the limit (avadhi) required by the word "east" and so forth, which is its own denotation. Even in instances such as "be the rival of the South," a restriction certainly exists; however, because it is well-known, a word expressing the limit is not employed. Nor is there a prohibition based on it being a technical name (saṃjñā), for a technical name is indeed a recent convention (ādhunika-saṃketa). And since such a convention does not exist regarding the directions, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain this in the section concerning the suffix *astāti*.

In this matter, the word of the commentator alone is the authority for the fact that the convention [of naming] is ancient in the case of the quarters (diś), but recent in the case of the Kurus. By this, the term "of all the gods" (viśveṣāṃ devānām) is also explained, because it is well-known in the Veda. The sense is that although there is a possibility of connecting the limit (avadhi) here with "skilled in such-and-such a place," there is no fixed rule regarding that. One should also provide counter-examples such as: "the redness of betel on the lower lip" and "capable in the reply."

How then are [the usages] such as Kālidāsa’s “*tathā pareṣāṃ yudhi ca*” (and likewise against others in battle) and “*apare pratyavatiṣṭhante*” (others stand in opposition) to be explained? On this point, they say: the application of the words *para* and *apara* to an enemy or an opponent occurs through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), even though these words primarily denote direction or a state of relative positioning. Nor does this constitute a loss of primary status (*upasarjanatā*). For being figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) does not mean being secondary; rather, it is the transfer of the word's own meaning onto another object qualified by that meaning. And such transfer occurs only within compound formations (*samāsa*) and the like.

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa’s statement in the *bhūvādi* sūtra—"‘These too’ means these things to be explained"—is consistent. In reality, however, the meaning of the words *para* and *apara* is simply being situated in another direction and so forth; their status as enemies and the like is merely an implied (ārthika) meaning. Why [is the condition] “not when it is a technical name” (*asaṃjñāyām*) stated? Consider: *uttarāḥ kuravaḥ* (the Northern Kurus). With reference to Mount Sumeru as a limit, the word *uttara* (northern) applies to the Kurus; thus, there is indeed a fixed convention (*vyavasthā*) here. However, they say that this is merely a modern convention (*ādhunika-saṅketa*).

Regarding the word *sva* when not used in the sense of "kinsmen" or "wealth": the word *sva* denotes the self (*ātman*), that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), kinsmen (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*). Since "kinsmen" and "wealth" are excluded here, with the intention that the "self" and "that which belongs to the self" remain, he explains: "the meaning is 'those belonging to oneself' (*ātmīyāḥ*)," or "the selves themselves" (*ātmānaḥ*).

As for what they say—that the word *sva* when referring to the self (*ātman*) is neuter, and therefore an example such as *sve* (locative dual) or *svāḥ* (nominative plural) is impossible there—that is to be reconsidered; for the word *sva* is masculine even when applied to the self. This is because the very author of the Sūtras, in the section beginning with "vibhāṣā jasi," provides the weighty instruction that one should simply state "svam ātmīye" (the word *sva* is used in the sense of 'one's own'), rather than making a cumbersome specification. Furthermore, regarding the support for his own stated meaning, he says: "Svo jñātāvātmani svaṃ triṣvātmīye svo'striyāṃ dhane" (The word *sva* is used in the masculine in the sense of a kinsman or the self; in the three genders in the sense of 'one's own'; and in the masculine, not feminine, in the sense of wealth).
Thus they cite the statement of Amarasiṃha; however, that too is to be considered. For in the lexicon (*kośa*), "ātmani" connects with what precedes it, whereas "svam" connects with what follows.
Accordingly, Hemacandra states: "Dyauḥ [is used] for heaven and the sky; svaḥ for kinsmen and the self; svaṃ for one's own and wealth."
Medinīkāra also states: "The word *svaḥ* may be masculine when meaning 'self' or 'known'; it is used in three genders for 'one's own,' and in the feminine for 'wealth.
Therefore, it is established that the gloss *ātmānaḥ* (selves) for the term *sve svāḥ* is indeed correct."

Regarding the phrase "jñātidhanavācinaḥ" (denoting kinsmen and wealth): by means of the suffix *ṇini* used in the sense of habitual disposition (*tācchīlye*), it is implied that even when [words] denoting kinsmen or wealth function by prioritizing their relationship to oneself (*ātmīyatva*), they indeed possess the status of pronouns (*sarvanāmatā*). It is precisely for this purpose that the term "ākhyā" (designation) was included in the rule.

Regarding the terms *antara* (inner) and *bahir-yogopasaṃvyānayoḥ* (in relation to what is worn outside and wrapped around): "outside" (*bahiḥ*) refers both to an uncovered space and to that which is external. Taking the first sense, he says: "the meaning is 'external'. In the second sense, however, the meaning should be understood as "internal," for the internal is indeed connected with the external. Both meanings are established in the authoritative source (*ākara*). Furthermore, the word *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition), derived through the agentive (*kartari*) construction, refers to the upper garment (*uttarīya*), whereas derived through the objective (*karmaṇi*) construction, it refers to the inner garment (*antarīya*).

Regarding the nine [words] beginning with *pūrva*, the following should be noted here: this sūtra is to be explained by carrying it over (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule "jas-śī" through a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), just as the rule "vā chandasi" is carried over to the rule "ami pūrvaḥ. In this way, the three sūtras beginning with "pūrva-parā—" in the Aṣṭādhyāyī become redundant in meaning, resulting in great economy of expression (*mahallāghava*). Eight meanings of the word *eka* have been stated; regarding that, he states a specific distinction: "in the sense of number. However, in the other seven senses, there may indeed be another form of declension, as in *eke* and *ekeṣām*; such is the intention.

Once a *bahuvrīhi* has been formed, the prohibition regarding the *bahuvrīhi* would be redundant, because it will be stated later that "words such as *sarva-* do not become *sarvādi* when they have become subordinate members (*upasarjana*). Therefore, he says: "when [the compound] is intended to be formed" (*cikīrṣite*) and "prior to the formation of the compound" (*samāsāt prāg eva*). He explains this by the term "process" (*prakriyā*). Nor should it be argued that the designation [as *sarvādi*] will not occur even prior [to the formation of the compound], because the condition of being non-subordinate (*anupasarjanatva*) is on the verge of being destroyed. This is because the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that a grammatical operation does not take place if its cause is about to be destroyed) is not universally valid (*anitya*). And in this regard, this very sūtra serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that fact.

The phrase *atibhavakān* indicates that this very point is the purpose of the indication (*jñāpana*). The sense is that one might assume the desired result has been achieved. Regarding the statement "having accepted the undesired consequence": the inclusion of the *t* in the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), or the mention of the transformation of the base and the suffix, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rule;

the sense is that the application is determined according to the specific forms to be explained (*lakṣya*). As for the expression *yathottaram*: the sense is that, in the present day, the determination is made precisely by the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya.

As for what was stated by the predecessors: "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) would not apply to words beginning with *sarva*, as in *priyasarvāya*. According to the view of the author of the Sūtras, there is no pronoun-status in a *bahuvrīhi*; according to the view of the author of the Bhāṣya, it is absent whenever there is even a trace of figurative usage (*gauṇatva*). The opinion of the author of the Nyāsa is that this sūtra was formulated for the following purpose: in forms such as *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ*, since the members *yuṣmad* and *asmad* (which are parts of the compound) possess the status of pronouns, the suffix *akac* would apply because they are not part of the inflected word-form (*anaṅgakāryatvena*). To prevent this, so that only the suffix *kap* occurs, this sūtra was composed.

In this regard, the following must be stated: is it intended that the designation (*saṃjñā*) does not apply to the *bahuvrīhi* compound as a whole, or rather to its constituent parts, namely those beginning with *sarva*? It cannot be the first alternative, because that would contradict the subsequent text which states "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they are constituents of a compound," and because there is no possibility of the designation applying to the aggregate [as a whole]. Nor can there be application by means of the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*), because since the constituents of the *bahuvrīhi* are subordinate elements (*upasarjana*), they fall outside the scope of the *sarvādi* group; thus, the possibility of application to a form ending in such a word is far removed. For this very reason, the second alternative is also untenable.

Nor should it be said that the author of the Vārttika stated an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the recitation of the subordinate members (*upasarjana*), but not as being established in the sūtra itself; for by the force of the technical name (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), that [exclusion] is obtained from the very syllables of the sūtra. By this, the view that "in the opinion of the author of the sūtra, the term 'pronominal' (*sarvanāman*) does not apply in a *bahuvrīhi* compound" is also refuted; for its meaning is simply "only in a *bahuvrīhi*. Nor is the claim "in the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya," and so forth, correct; for by the specific mention [of the distinction], it is understood that the views of the author of the sūtra and the author of the Vārttika are indeed different.

This is like saying that when it is stated, "Devadatta sees with his left eye," it follows that he does not see with his right eye; but that is not the case, because even in the Sautrāntika-Vārttika view, a figurative exclusion (gauṇa-paryudāsa) is accepted.

As for the phrase beginning with *tvatkapitṛka*, it has been explained by the ancient commentators as follows: having analyzed the compound as *tvaṃ pitā yasya* (he whose father is you) and *ahaṃ pitā yasya* (he whose father is I), and having formed the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *akac* would undesirably apply to the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*—which are components of the compound and fall within its scope—because they are designated as *sarvanāman* (pronouns) due to their denoting all objects (*sarvārtha*), when there is an intention to express meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, according to the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ*. This is because, unlike the forms *smai* and so on, this suffix is not prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), and thus does not depend upon the designation of a stem.

Consequently, undesirable consequences such as [the application of] *tvakatpitṛka* and so forth would follow. The author of the *Nyāsa*, having raised the objection that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would be excluded by the very force of the etymological definition (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), and thus the suffix *akac* would not occur, stated: "For the composite whole (*samudāya*) functions with reference to a specific [meaning], whereas the prior member (*pūrvapada*) has not yet departed from its universal sense. All of this is merely due to negligence. For instance, in a compound where the constituent parts abandon their own meanings (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), the individual meaning of the members of the compound does not exist at all.

Even in the case of *ajahatsvārthā* (the theory that the word retains its own meaning), its status as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is quite evident, since it functions as another word-meaning qualified by its own meaning. And thus, the passage beginning with "because the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, which fall within the compound, denote all things," as well as the *Nyāsa* passage beginning with "for the aggregate... would be contradicted under both views. Furthermore, in this way, the substitution of *smāy* in the form *atisarvāya* would be unavoidable, because of the rule for taking the final member (*tadantagrahaṇa*) in the context of *aṅga* (stem), and because the word *sarva* retains its status as denoting "all" according to the method you have stated.

Indeed, it is not logical that the word *sarva* possesses the sense of "all" when it is the first member of a compound, but lacks it when it is the latter member. Furthermore, if this were the case and the words beginning with *sarva* were used in a figurative sense, there would be a contradiction with your own statement that these words denote all things; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

As for what they have explained—that in an analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) such as "you are the father of whom" (*tvaṃ pitā yasya*), the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) that would otherwise apply is prohibited—that too is not correct. For is the analytical sentence intended to be worldly (*laukika*) or extra-worldly (*alaukika*)? Not the first, because it contradicts Kaiyaṭa’s statement that this prohibition applies to the *prakriyāvākya* (the formal derivation sentence) and not to the worldly one, and because it contradicts both the preceding and following passages of his own work in the present context. Nor is it the second, because that [extra-worldly sentence] takes the form *yuṣmad su pitṛ su*, and thus it is impossible for it to take the form *tvaṃ pitā*.

Regarding what they have explained: "Now, surely a technical name (*saṃjñā*) does not apply to *atisarva* and similar forms, whereas it does apply to *tvatkapitṛka* and similar forms; what is the determining factor here? To this he replies: "Because it is not an operation dependent on a stem (*anaṅgakāryatvena*). The word *aṅga* refers to the whole (*samudāya*). Therefore, in the case of *atisarva*, the technical name "stem" (*aṅga*) is required because the suffix *smāt* and others are prescribed after a pronominal stem (*sarvanāmnaḥ aṅgāt*); thus, even though the individual part possesses the status of being a pronoun, there is no fault [in applying the rule] since the operation depends on the whole.

It is logical that in a compound (*samudāya*), because the word *sarva* and others are subordinate (*upasarjana*) with respect to the meaning of the whole, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) does not apply to that which ends in them. However, in this case, it is intended for the individual member alone and not for the whole; and since the member has its own primary meaning as its principal referent, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). This is the intended distinction (*vaiṣamya*). But even that is not correct, because since the extension to what ends in [the term] (*tadantavidhi*) within the governing rule concerning "bases" (*aṅga*) is universally accepted, the statement that there is no fault even when the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) exists in the mere member is contradicted.

This is because it would contradict his own statement, "smāy [should] occur by means of the technical definition (paribhāṣā) regarding the governing rule for case endings (aṅgādhikāra). Now, suppose the intention is this: "Even though the designation had already taken effect previously, it has ceased once there is a transition to another meaning. If that were so, then let the suffix *akac* also cease! If you object: "Under the view that the time of application is determined by the specific operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the designation is required again for the sake of *smāy* and so forth, and that [designation] is difficult to obtain"—if this is your intention, let it be so. However, this is not the meaning of the present text. For it contradicts the supplementary statement, "this is the opinion of the author of the Nyāsa," due to its disagreement with the *Nyāsa* text;
the *Nyāsa* text itself will be cited immediately below.

As for what they have explained—that the meaning is that the *aṅga* (the primary member) and the *pradhāna* (the principal element) are to be sublated (*bādhya*), while the *anaṅga* (non-member) which contradicts them is the sublater (*bādhaka*)—and that consequently, since *akac* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *kap*, it will occur; that too is both strained and useless, and moreover, it is not accepted by the author of the *Nyāsa*. For, having explained the commentary (*vṛtti*) passage "tvatkapitṛkaḥ, matkapitṛkaḥ," the author of the *Nyāsa* argued: "But surely, since the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is established according to its literal meaning (*anvartha*), the designation [of 'member'] is already excluded here, and thus *akac* will not occur."

For here, the status of being a *sarvanāman* (pronominal) is not possible, because [the compound] has a specific referent. This is not so; for while the aggregate (*samudāya*) functions as a specific [referent], the first member of the compound does not at all lose its status as a *sarvanāman*. In that case, let these two immediately preceding [compounds] fall within the scope of this sūtra. However, this is not applicable to forms such as *priyaviśvāya*, and so on. For words like *priyaviśva* are not names of all things (*sarvanāman*). Nor is any pronominal operation (*sarvanāmakārya*) applicable to the words *viśva* and the rest, which constitute parts of those compounds.

Because [the suffixes] *smāt* and so forth function as operations (*kārya*) upon the *aṅga* (stem), whereas words such as *viśva* do not function as *aṅgas*. He thinks thus: "This must be undertaken at least for the purpose that the suffix *akac* does not occur in forms such as *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* or *matkapitṛkaḥ*; furthermore, it will serve to clarify the meaning in cases such as *priyaviśvāya*. For by this passage from the *Nyāsa*, the very fact that there is no dependence on the technical designation *aṅga* is obtained as the intended meaning; however, that [meaning] has been utterly discarded in his own speculative commentary.

As for what they have explained—that although this view belongs to both the author of the Sūtra and the author of the Vārttika, it is nevertheless called "the opinion of the author of the Nyāsa" because it was commented upon by him—that too is quite gross; for the author of the Vārttika did not touch upon this point at all, and since the author of the Nyāsa, when stating "when a compound has been formed," and so forth, has moved far away from the meaning you have stated, there is no commentary on that [meaning] by him either.

As for what they have said—that by the word "composer of the Nyāsa," the author of the Sūtras himself is intended, and so forth—that too is not correct. For it contradicts the preceding text beginning with "in the case of a Bahuvrīhi, according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras" (*sūtrakāramate bahuvrīhau*), and because that [preceding view] has been set aside by the text beginning with "but according to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya" (*bhāṣyakāramate tu*). Therefore, let it rest for now that the ancient Prakriyā texts and the works of their commentators are merely superficially pleasing.

If, however, there is a persistent insistence that even the *prakriyā* (grammatical derivation) text must be explained in some way so as not to contradict the *Bhāṣya*, then let it be explained as follows: "Is it not the case that [the form] *priyaviśvāya* has already been accounted for through its secondary (*gauṇa*) application? Therefore, he states the essential point: 'In the opinion of the author of the Sūtras'. Regarding the phrase "in a *bahuvrīhi*": the words "when it is intended to be formed" are to be supplied. Regarding "merely in its secondary application": the word *mātra* is used for emphasis, meaning "only in the state of being secondary, and not prior to that. Thus, the sense is that the Sūtra itself is thereby rendered superfluous (*pratyākhyāta*).

However, because the view of those who advocate *nyāsa* (the method of leaving words unaltered) is extremely trivial, he says "tvatkapitṛka," etc., with the intention that "the very analysis of its own form (*svarūpa*) is itself the supreme analysis. This should be discerned by those well-versed in the study of various ancient treatises. Let us return to the subject at hand. "The operation of a technical name (*saṃjñā-kārya*)" means [operations] such as *smāy* and so forth, which are prompted by the technical designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*). "The operation of a sub-group (*antargaṇa-kārya*)" means [operations] such as *adḍ* for the words beginning with *itarat*, *a-* for *tyad* and so forth, and *s-* for *tad* and *doḥ* before the nominative singular suffix *su*.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the third case in a compound": here, the compound prescribed by the rule "pūrvasadṛśa—" is understood because it is taught as a specific term (pratipadokta), and not the compound [prescribed] by "kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā. Therefore, there is no prohibition in the case of *tvayakā kṛtam*.

Regarding the phrase "of the aggregate" (*samudāyasya*): the connection is that the word *dvandva* (copulative compound) applies primarily to that very aggregate, and not to the case where the rule would mean "those [words] beginning with *sarva* which exist within a *dvandva*," because grammatical factors (*kāraka*) must connect only with an action (*kriyā*). Nor is there a connection meaning "those which exist within a *dvandva*," because such an elliptical supply (*adhyāhāra*) of the verb "to exist" (*vidyati*) would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, it is more logical for the connection to be with the verb "to be" (*bhavati*), which is the primary verb to be negated here. Moreover, there is no *dvandva* compound of words beginning with *tyad* (the pronouns), as it is precluded by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one).

Consequently, there is no distinction between *prācīnāḥ* and *tvadanyaḥ* in that regard; nor should it be argued that, in the case of *na ca dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*, one might as well prohibit the desired *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution). For the inclusion of the word *mātra* in the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre* indicates that *puṃvadbhāva* occurs even when words were previously seen to be sarvanāmas but no longer function as such at the time of composition. Therefore, both by the force of logic and by the evidence of the result, it is appropriate to take the term as referring to the whole compound.

The sense is that although, under the view that the word *tvac* ends in *-t*, the result [of the prohibition] could easily be stated even when the prohibition applies to a constituent part, nevertheless the scope of the treatise (*śāstra*) would be too narrow and the underlying logic (*nyāya*) would be contradicted. Regarding the phrase "the contingency of *suṭ*": the sense is that this would occur in examples such as *varṇāśrametarāṇām*. Nor can the prohibition be justified on the grounds of its own power (i.e., it cannot be argued that the rule is necessary to prevent *suṭ*); for it has already served its purpose by excluding non-aṅga elements such as *tratasil* and others.

Regarding the phrase *jasādhāram*: although the case ending *jas* is removed by the substitution of *śī*, its status as a locus (*ādhāra*) should nevertheless be understood in a figurative sense. Alternatively, *jas* + *i* = *jasi*; [the rule applies] *in that*. He explains this according to the actual meaning—namely, *jasādhāram*—by noting that there is an elision of the locative case-ending (*saptamyā luk*) in the sūtra. The phrase *jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām vibhaktau* follows from the previous rule *aṣ�ṭana ā vibhaktau*. The intention is that, because of this, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) to forms such as *jarāyā idam* or *jāram*. Regarding the word *pade*: both *pada* and *aṅga* are the qualified elements (*viśeṣya*), and through the qualifier, the rule of "specification of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies; this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "by those who follow that": their intention is that, because the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction) applies to both *in* and *ataḥ* as they are contained within a single sūtra, it is appropriate to include the substitution of *syādeśa* as well. Precisely for this reason [it is said]: "For those desiring to attain the supreme, pure state of Brahman, free from birth and decay..."
Thus, considering the separation of the word *bhāra* to be improper, they stated that it should be read as *vītajanmajarasaḥ*. Regarding this:

for the author of the Bhāṣya, in the rule *ṭāṅasi*, having rejected the suffixes *in* and *āt*, he prescribed the substitutes *nā* and *adā*. Then, when *nā* follows, the substitution of *e* was established by means of a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*). First: *bahuvacane jhalyet*; then: *osi ca*. Thus, when *āṅ* follows, there should be the substitution of *e* for *at*: as in *rāmeṇa*. Then: *āpaḥ saṃbuddhau ca*; the substitution of *e* should occur in the vocative, in *āṅ*, and in *osi*. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be elision (*lopa*) of the *an* in *anena* because of the rule *hali lopaḥ*.

Because there is a specific rule for the substitution of *an* when *na* follows an unindicated [stem] (*anādeśa*). To explain: the meaning of "anāpi" is that *an* occurs when *na* or *āp* follows. In the sūtra, the term *a* is a neuter designation for that which ends in *n*. Nor should it be argued that once the substitute *at* has been applied to the ablative case ending (*ṅasi*), the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) would apply; for by the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*, the occurrence of the long vowel is possible.

And likewise, it is stated in the rule *jarāyā jarasanyatarasyām*: "But Gonardīya says that *atijaraiḥ* must be the form, according to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. Thus, the meaning is that everything [such as] "by way of a prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*) is contrary to the Bhāṣya. In the rule *paddanno-* etc., the forms beginning with *śas* are presented as the cause; and since these imply specific bases corresponding to the substitutes such as *pad*, he says: "pāda, danta," and so on.
