Although the term "in Vedic" (*chandasi*) from the rule *śīrṣaṃ chandasi* continues to apply here, it will be stated that it nevertheless occurs in the common language (*bhāṣā*) as well, because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the *vārttika* *māsaśchandasi*, where the mention of "Vedic" serves as a sign [of its broader applicability].

"It is erroneous. For instance, in the mantra "āsno vṛkasya vartikāmabhīke," the meaning is "from the mouth," due to contextual propriety (*aucitya*), and because of corroboration by another mantra: "vṛkasya cidvartikāmantarāsyāt. The same applies to such passages as "havyā juhvāna āsani" and "āsanyaṃ prāṇamūcuḥ. Furthermore, the commentaries in the *Vedabhāṣyas* explain it in that very way. Therefore, one should note that even Haradatta has revealed the erroneous nature of the *Kāśikā* on this point.

Regarding the rule *allopo'naḥ*, the ancient commentators explain it as: "There shall be elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a* belonging to a *bha*-affix which ends in *an*. If this were the case, there would be elision of the vowel *a* even in *takṣṇā* and similar forms [where the *an* is part of the root]. However, if one explains it as "the *a* of *an* belonging to a *bha*-affix which is an *aṅga*," then it would apply to *anasā*, *manasā*, and so on. Even if one explains it through methods such as *tantra* or *āvṛtti* as "the *a* of *an* belonging to a *bha*-affix which ends in *an* and is an *aṅga*," there would still be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases like *anastakṣṇā*. Therefore, he explains it with the words "a member of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgāvayava*), etc.

The sense is that by the word *bhasya* (of a nominal stem), two things—the specific suffix (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*) and the *aṅga* (the base)—are implied as qualifiers; however, this does not apply to the vowel *a*, and therefore the aforementioned fault does not arise. This is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*.

Although the condition of being within a single word (*ekapadatva*) is already established by the force of the rule *raṣābhyāṃ padāntāt* itself, the inclusion of the term *samāna* (identical) is intended so that the rule applies only where the word is truly identical—that is, where it is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). Thus, it applies there, but not in a compound (*samāsa*), as in *rāmanāma* (Rāma’s name). Also, in *yūṣṇaḥ*: *yūṣ* means broth (*maṇḍa*). As seen in the statement, "Broth made of mung beans and āmalaka fruits is digestive, appetizing, and a promoter of digestion."

Regarding the phrase *iti pakṣe tu* ("but in this alternative view"): by this, he indicates that the compound with the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is optional. For instance, in the Bhāṣya, three purposes are stated—namely, *bebhiditā*, *māthitikaḥ*, and *apīpacan*—yet these are established otherwise. In the rule *ekāca upadeśe*, because the word "prescribed" (*vihita*) serves as a qualifier, there is no prohibition of *iṭ* in the case of *bebhiditā*.

In the analysis of the compound *mathitapaṇya* (meaning "whose merchandise is churned"), after the suffix *ṭhak* is applied and the substitution of *ik* for *ṭha* occurs, the elision of the vowel by the rule *yasyeti ca* takes place. However, the substitution of *ka* by the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* will not occur, because the element *ṭha* is no longer present. Nor can the status of *ṭha* be attributed through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, because this is not a rule dependent on an *al* (vowel) substitute (*analvidhi*). Indeed, in the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ*, the vowel *a* in both the original (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is merely for the sake of pronunciation. Furthermore, in the form *apīpacan*, the result is established even without relying on *sthānivadbhāva* for either the elision of the *ṇi* suffix or for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the final *a* of the *caṅ* prefix and the following vowel.

Because of its association with the *vidhi* (prescriptive) suffixes, the substitution of *jus* for the *jhi* of the *laṅ* alone is prescribed even when it follows a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*). Nor should it be argued that, due to its association with *sic*, it might belong only to the *luṅ*; for the association with what follows (*parasāhacarya*) is stronger than the association with what precedes (*pūrvasāhacarya*). This is the general direction of the argument.

Regarding the statement "not when [an operation] is not established in what precedes": we have already stated that this is established by logical necessity (*nyāya*). Since the three final sections (*tripādī*) are considered non-established (*asiddha*), the extension (*atideśa*) rule "when a subsequent [element] follows, [the original] vowel [is treated as if it were still present]" does not apply to an operation to be performed therein. The phrase "of that" refers to that rule, *pūrvatrāsiddhe*. Thus, the meaning is that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) must be asserted in three instances: 1. For the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*): *cakryatra*. 2. For the substitution of *l* for *r* (*latva*): *nigālyate*. 3. For the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* (*ṇatva*): *māṣavapanī*. In the case of *māṣavapanī*, although the elision of the *a* (by the rule *yasyeti ca*) would otherwise cause the *n* to be at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is not so because the elision is treated as a substitute (*sthānivat*); therefore, the substitution of *ṇ* does not take place.

As for what they say—that even in the absence of *sthānivadbhāva* in cases such as *yūṣṇaḥ*, the rule *raṣābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.1) is of no use because the desired form is established by *ṣṭutva*; and that consequently, the mention of *ṣ* in that rule is for the sake of subsequent purposes (*uttarārtha*), as established in the *Ākara*—this very point is a mere rash assertion (*rabhasavāda*). For indeed, the mention of *ṣ* remains necessary here even for the sake of subsequent purposes.

Furthermore, in cases such as *yūṣṇaḥ* and *puṣṇāti*, who could prevent the application of the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) by the rule *raṣābhyām*? If it is argued that this is prevented by the rule for *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣ*), we say no; because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha* (not yet established). Nor can its status as *siddha* be established on the grounds of the authority of a specific statement, since that rule has already served its purpose in forms such as *puṣṭi*. If it is argued that the portion of that rule stating "after *ṣ* in conjunction with *y*" has not yet served its purpose here, we say no; because that [portion] was not stated separately. Moreover, the same logic applies to the claim that the expression "following *ṣ*" in the present context has not yet served its purpose.

For the intended meaning here is that in the source [the *Śikṣā*], there is no failure to establish the desired forms (*lakṣya*) without the inclusion of the letter *ṣ*; it is not, however, meant that rules such as "raṣābhyām" would fail to apply in cases like *puṣṇāti*. This is the general direction [of the argument].

"The elision of *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)," [is stated] with the genitive case marker elided. Because it is a *sūtra*-formulation, it does not refer to the first member of a genitive or locative *tatpuruṣa* compound; for the reason that a compound is impossible when there is mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*), and because the term "nominal stem" functions as a qualifier of the word (*pada*). This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "at the end of that" (*tadantasya*): this is a genitive *tatpuruṣa*. The meaning is: "of that which is the final *n* belonging to it. And Haradatta has said: "'[The word] *anta* (end) is the thing to be qualified (*viśeṣya*),' and thus *na* is without a case-ending; likewise, the word *prātipadika* is a qualifier of the word [itself]."

As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the rule applies] to the *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or at the end of a word (*pada*)—and as for their explanation that the term "at the end" (*antasya*) is connected with both [of those], that is burdened by unnecessary complexity, because it would entail the repetition of the word "at the end" and result in two genitive constructions in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). However, if the word "word" (*pada*) is qualified by the term "at the end" through a relation of identity (*abheda*), just as it is qualified by the nominal stem, then, by means of that qualifier, the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies; thus, the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) in the Sūtra could have been omitted.

The rule *vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ śī* refers to the *śī* prescribed by *napuṃsakācca*, and not to the *śi* [prescribed] for *jaś* and *śas*, because in that case the status of being a *bha*-stem would be impossible. By the rule *bhasya*, there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of only those suffixes beginning with *y* (i.e., *yañ*, etc. that are not *asarvanāmasthāna*; this is what he expresses by saying "not an *asarvanāmasthāna*. "For this very reason" means because of the usage *doṣaṇī*. Although the Bhāṣya could be easily reconciled even if a collective dvandva were formed and then a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) applied, nevertheless, it is more logical that *kakud* be a separate word. Otherwise, the singular number of *kakud* and the dual number of the two arms (*bāhu*) would not be obtained; such is the sense.

"In *Raghuvaṃśa*: 'The night-stalker rushed at him, raising his right arm (*dakṣiṇaṃ dorniśācaraḥ*). Here, 'the right arm' (*dakṣiṇaṃ doḥ*) is connected with 'raising' (*udyamya*) as its object. Regarding 'his arm' (*doṣaṃ tasya*): in the usage of Śrīharṣa, 'Taking the fault (*doṣaṃ*) of such a man who was resorting to the bow (*cāpasya*), while grasping its string (*guṇam*),' the connection is as follows: 'taking the hand (*hastaṃ*)—which is the fault (*dūṣaṇaṃ*)—of the bow that he was resorting to, while grasping the string (*maurvīm*), which is the excellence (*atiśayaṃ*) [of that bow]. "

The commentators on Amara, however, having accepted the word *doṣā* as feminine even though [the base] is masculine, stated *doṣā* by applying the suffix *ṭāp* according to the opinion of Bhāguri; they then cited the *Dhanañjaya-nighaṇṭu*: "The arm is called *dor*, *doṣā*, *bhuja*, *bāhu*, *pāṇi*, *hasta*, and likewise *kara*.

Regarding the expression "occurring in two days" (*dvayor ahnoḥ bhavaḥ*): it is a compound formed by the rule "for the sake of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārtha*). The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule "from time [words]" (*kālāt ṭhañ*). There is elision (*luk*) by the rule "elision after a *dvigu* [compound], except for *apatya*. The suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule "after *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*. The substitution of *ahan* for *ahar* occurs by the rule "for *ahan*, [substitute] *ahna-* after these [words]."

Regarding the term *ahnaḥ sāya*: the word *sāya* is derived from the root *si* (to settle) with the suffix *ghañ*, and it signifies the conclusion [of the day]. According to the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "saṃkhyā-visāya—" (*Pāṇini 2.2.25*), this is an *ekadeśisamāsa* (a compound denoting a part of a whole).
Thus end the words ending in *at*.

*Hāhā*: This is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a specific class of *gandharvas*. However, the followers of Kumāra (the *Kaumārāḥ*), asserting that it is an action-word (*kriyāśabda*) derived from "he abandons" (*jahāti*), thus [becoming] *hāhā*, state that its form is like that of *viśvapā*. According to their view, the counter-example is: "The letter *a* should be Vāsudeva"; those who exist together with him are *sāḥ*; thus, one should understand [the form] as *tān sān*. [Thus end the words ending in long *ā*.]

It was not stated that "after *āṅ*, [the substitute] *nā* occurs in the masculine, but not in the feminine," so that [the form] *amunā kulena* might be obtained. Nor can the correct form be established by means of the augment *num*, because the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of rule application), and thus the *num* augment prescribed by the rule "iko 'ci" (Pāṇini 7.1.73) would not apply. However, in the case of the substitute *nā*, there is no *asiddhatva*, because of the prohibition in the rule "namune" (Pāṇini 8.2.3). Nor should it be argued that the prohibition "namune" applies only to the *num* augment, since the vowel *a* in the word *ne* is merely for the sake of pronunciation; for if this were so, forms such as *amuṣmai kulāya* would result in being unestablished.

With the intention that the three words *idudbhyām*, *ṅeḥ*, and *aut* carry over [from previous rules], he explains [the rule] with the words "of that which follows *i* and *u*" (*idudbhyām uttarasya*), and so forth. It is not stated as "following *ghi*," because in the sūtra the word *gheḥ* is in the genitive case; furthermore, there is no authority for [applying] *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, and so on; and finally, because it is improper to abandon the established relationship between *idudbhyām* and *ṅeḥ* in the preceding sūtra, which is connected to *aut*.

Regarding the form *aut*, they have explained here: the *au* of *aut* is for the sake of the *svarita* accent. The prohibition of *it*-ness by the rule "not in a case-ending" (*na vibhaktau*) does not apply, because that rule is non-eternal (*anitya*). And its non-eternality is understood from the fact that the addition of the marker *u* (in *idamasthamuḥ*) was made for the purpose of protecting the *m* of *tham* from being designated as an *it*; this has been stated in that very [rule]. That [explanation] is to be questioned. For there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows, since you yourself have stated under the rule "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) that the *t* of *aut* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and is not an *it*.

It is logical that [the word *barhis*] serves the purpose of recitation and not the purpose of indicating a svarita accent, because the svarita accent is not observed in such instances as "stīrṇe barhiṣi samidhāne agnau" and so forth.

Regarding the term *at*, they say that the inclusion of *t* as a marker (*taparatvam*) is for the purpose of preventing the application of the suffix *ṭāp* in the feminine after the substitution of *at* has been made in words such as *buddhau*. This too is questionable. For by the inclusion of *t* as a marker, one would prevent a long vowel [resulting from the combination] with *ṭāp*; however, *ṭāp* itself should indeed apply, as there is no evidence to justify the subversion of two grammatical rules simultaneously. For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary on the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* and in the *Vārttika* and its exposition that *ṭāp* does not apply by virtue of the *sannipātaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the destruction of a cause). For if there were an intervention by *ṭāp*, the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) would be disrupted. Therefore, it should be understood that the inclusion of *t* as a marker after *at* is merely for the sake of pronunciation, just as it is in the case of *aut*.

The ancient grammarians maintain that although the form *anaṅ* would be established by the rule "soḥ ḍā" alone, the specific prescription of *anaṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that it may also occur elsewhere. Consequently, they argue that *anaṅ* is thus established in the vocative singular of *uśanas*. This, however, is questionable. For if "soḥ ḍā" were stated, then by the subsequent rule "ṛduśanas-purudaṃso-nehas-ca," the suffix *ḍā* would also apply; as a result, in the case of *uśana*, there would be lengthening by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau," and in the case of *purudaṃsas*, there would be lengthening by the rule "sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya.

Alternatively, the resolution should be understood either through the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory" (*saṃjñāpūrvako vidhiranityaḥ*), or by the paribhāṣā concerning the application of grammatical operations within their own domain (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*).

The rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* is a qualifier specifically for *ṅī* and *āp*, and not for *hal*, because [the latter] is impossible; thus he says, "long" (*dīrghau*). Regarding the word "following" (*param*): this is not a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*), because there would be non-application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *yā*, *sā*, and *kā*. Nor can the requirement be met there by virtue of being prescribed after a *hal*-ending [stem], because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *yaḥ* and *saḥ*, and non-application in cases such as *kartā*; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the word *hal*: its nature as *su*, *ti*, *si*, etc., should be understood through the maxim of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). Regarding the phrase "is elided" (*lupyate*).

Although the word *lopa* (elision) is understood here from the rule *lopo vyoḥ*, and although in that [previous] context it was derived as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), here it is a patientive derivative (*karmasādhana*) because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *hal*, which ends in the nominative case. What is the purpose of mentioning *dīrgha* (long vowel)? [Consider: *atikhaṭvaḥ* (beyond the bed), *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (departed from Kauśāmbī). But surely, in these cases, the entire compound does not end in a feminine suffix (*ṅyāp*). Nor should it be said that "there is no restriction regarding the initial element of a feminine suffix," for such a principle applies only when the suffix is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*).

But here, because [the word] is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the rule regarding the initial element of that [compound] certainly applies. True; nevertheless, since the final member (*uttarapada*) ends in a feminine suffix (*ṅyāp*), its status as following that [suffix] remains unchanged. For we have already stated that this [rule] is not a qualification of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*). Precisely for this reason, there is elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*) in the form *bahuśreyasī*.

It might be argued: [from the root] *gaṅgīyati* [with the suffix] *kvip*, we have *gaṅgīḥ*. Here, because the vowel *i* possesses the status of *āp* by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute for a long vowel), there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) due to its length. True; however, there is no fault, because the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is rejected by reading [the rule] as a *praśleṣa* (conjoined reading): *ṅī-ī, ā-āp*. Why [are the words] *su-ti-si* mentioned? [To exclude] *bhettā*; otherwise, there would be the elision of the *t* of *tās*. Nor does this lead to the undesired consequence of the elision of *sic* in forms such as *abhaitsīt*, because by association (*sāhacarya*) with *su* and *ti*, only a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is understood here.

What is the purpose of the term *apṛkta*? They offer counter-examples such as *bhinatti* and *chinatti*. That [explanation] is to be reconsidered, because [in these cases] the specific [consonant] is not an *ah* (vowel). It is inappropriate to raise an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by providing a strained interpretation of the rule *suti-sīnāṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68). Furthermore, some say: from the root *su* in *surāṃ sunoti*, we derive *surā-sut*; from that, with the suffix *ṇic*, we have *surāsayati*; then, with the suffix *kvip*, we get *surāḥ*, *surāsau*, and *surāsaḥ*. In this case, the mention of *apṛkta* is intended to prevent the elision of the *s* which is a part of the root *su*. [Response: This too is incorrect, because the elision of the *s* occurs due to the suffix *kvip*, and not because it is an *apṛkta*. Moreover, since the *s* is not a single phoneme (*ekāl*), it cannot be called *apṛkta*. Furthermore, the mention of *apṛkta* is for the sake of excluding forms like *bibharti* and *chinatti*, where the elision of the *t* of the suffix *ti* would otherwise apply; it is not for the sake of excluding the elision of the *s* in *surāsaḥ*. Therefore, the mention of *apṛkta* is indeed purposeful. However, the mention of *hal* [in the rule *suti-sīnāṃ hal*] is for the sake of excluding *bibharti* and the like; it is not for the sake of excluding *surāsaḥ*. Thus, the objection regarding the over-extension is not valid. Consequently, the mention of *apṛkta* is indeed purposeful. But even so, the mention of *hal* is purposeful, because it serves to exclude the elision of the *t* in *bibharti* and the like. Therefore, both [the mention of *apṛkta* and *hal*] are purposeful. That too is not correct, because by virtue of their mutual association (*sāhacarya*), only those case-endings (*vibhakti*) that end in *su* and *ti* are understood; otherwise, as has been stated, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *sic*. Furthermore, between a suffix and a non-suffix, it is the suffix alone that is understood [by the principle of *paribhāṣā*]. Why [specify] "consonant" (*hal*)? [Consider the example: *bibheda*.

But surely the mention of the "first consonant" (*prathamahal*) is redundant, since the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is possible for those [suffixes] following a word ending in a consonant. To this, they say:
For if there were elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (saṃyogāntalopa), the elision of *n* and other such operations would not be established.
Since [the elision] of *t* would occur by that very rule [P. 8.2.23], the elision of the *hal* (consonant) is therefore prescribed [by P. 8.2.23].

For instance, in the word *sakhe*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur, because the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). This might be argued: the elision of a final consonant cluster is not non-existent, as evidenced by the inclusion of the term *sambuddhi* (vocative singular) in the rule *na ṅisambudhyoḥ*. Nor does this imply that the elision of *n* would undesirably apply in cases such as *gomān*; for the indicator (*jñāpaka*) has a specific scope, according to the traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*): "The [elision] is valid only where there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) between the letter *n* and the case-ending."

As for what they say—that because [the word] *he brahman* has a neuter referent, this is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*)—that is not correct. For when [the case-ending] is elided by *luk*, there is an absence of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of rules conditioned by a suffix); yet, since the rule "optionally for neuters in the vocative" (*saṃbuddhau vā napuṃsakānām*) would otherwise be necessary, the mention of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) cannot possibly pertain to the neuter. Thus, the aforementioned indicator remains firmly established. If it is argued that, therefore, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is not the purpose [of the rule], then in this case, in *abhino 'tra*, the substitution of *u* for *r* (*rorutvam*) would not occur. This is precisely what was stated: "the elision of *n* and so forth."
Likewise, in the case of *abibhar bhavān*, the elision of the *t* would not occur, due to the restriction [imposed by] the rule *rātsasya*.

In this regard, the following should be noted: the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is a qualifier only for *su*, and not for *tis* and *tī*, according to the traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). The evidence for this here is the Bhāṣya on this very sūtra, which states: "In this rule, the mention of *dvi-hal-apṛkta* and the mention of *tis* and *tī* need not be made. For if the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* were also qualifiers for *tis* and *tī*, then how could he say that the mention of *tis* and *tī* is unnecessary? As for the argument that *tis* and *tī* are impossible after stems ending in *ṅī* and *āp*: it is true that they are impossible after stems ending in *ṅī*.

However, from a stem ending in *ā* that has been converted by *kvip* for the sake of denoting habitual action (*ācāra*), the suffixes *tip* and *sip* of the *laṅ* indeed occur—as in *agaṅgāt* and *agaṅgāḥ*. Nor is there an intervention by the *śap* augment, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatvena*). Nor does the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) apply here, because this is not a rule concerning what precedes (*apūrvavidhi*).

The essential point here is this: the rule *ṅyāpaḥ suḥ* alone would be appropriate. Nor is there the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the *s* of verbal roots in forms such as *surāḥ* or *surāsau*, because—due to association (*sāhacarya*) with the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp*, and by the maxim *pratyayāpratyayayoḥ*—only the *su* that is a suffix is understood. Furthermore, the elision of *n* in forms such as *rājā* is indeed established by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*. Moreover, the substitution of *u* in *abhino'tra* is also easily explained, because the statement *saṃyogāntalopo rorutve* is recited in the *Siddhakāṇḍa*.

Just as in the case of *harivo medinaṃ tvā*, there is no fault here either in the expression *abibharbhavān*. This is because in the rule *rāt sasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24), the letter *t* is also included by *praśleṣa* (elision/junction), resulting in the analysis *tsasya*. If it is argued that in forms such as *ukhāsrat*, there would be the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) [of the *s*], we say no; for once the substitution of *d* (*datva*) has been applied, that [rule for elision] no longer applies. If it is argued that the substitution of *d* (*datva*) is not established [as a valid operation at this stage], we say no; for in the *Siddhakāṇḍa* section, the rule "the substitution of *d* occurs in the case of *avasvādiṣu*" is recited. If it is argued that the substitution of *d* should not occur because the word-final position (*apadānta*) is lacking, we say no.

This [term *pada*] also applies to that [suffix], because we rely on the alternative view (*pakṣa*). The seed of this [interpretation] lies in the analysis of the rule *asarvanāmasthāne yaci* as *asarvanāmasthāne* *yaci*, which explains that there is no *pada*-status when a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix beginning with *yaC* follows.

Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as *rāja-* (king), once the *naL* elision has occurred, the substitution of *ru* and the subsequent *visarga* would then apply. This is because the specific prescription of the vowel *ā* in the rule *pathimathi-*—which occurs after the rule *ito’t sarvanāmasthāne* has already established the form—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the elision of *su* (*sulopa*) must take precedence. But is this not a non-indicator (*ajñāpaka*), since its purpose is fulfilled in the vocative singular (*saṃbuddhi*), as in *he panthāḥ*, *manthāḥ*, and *ṛbhukṣāḥ*?

If it is argued that in that case, the long vowel [of *rājā*] is excluded by the rule "not in the vocative singular" (*asaṃbuddhau*), and the elision of *n* is prohibited, then let the very sūtra "not before the suffix *ṅi* or the vocative" (*na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ*) serve as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the meaning that the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) occurs prior to the elision of *n*. For instance, the genitive in "before *ṅi* and the vocative" (*ṅisaṃbudhyoḥ*) is not a locative; because the suffix *ṅi* is elided, there is no application of the technical designation "suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, there is a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the phrase "of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*."

Furthermore, a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the vocative suffix *su* cannot be obtained without first applying the elision of the final consonant of the conjunction (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Therefore, there is no objection to the formulation *ṅyāpaḥ soḥ*. However, if the Vārttika "the substitution of *d* for *t* in *vasvādi* [words]" is rejected—since the absence of the long vowel in forms such as *ukhāsrad* would be established by the very mention of *adhātu-* [in P. 6.4.13]—then let the rule be *halṅyāpaḥ soḥ*. As for the fact that the ancient commentators have explained the rule according to its literal form—as meaning "from what ends in a *ṅī*, from what ends in an *āp*, and from what has a long vowel"—[that is a different matter].

That is not so; for it is the *ṅī* and *āp* suffixes themselves that are long (*dīrgha*), not that which ends in them. Nor can the meaning "from that which ends in a long *ṅī*" or the like be obtained from the rule *dīrghān ṅyantāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.69) and so on, because the ablative case in *dīrghāt* cannot be construed [with the suffix]. Furthermore, in a compound, it is impossible to qualify the two subordinate members (*upasarjana*) [of the suffixes] with an adjective. For it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "There is no formation of a compound (*vṛtti*) for those accompanied by qualifiers," and "Once a compound has been formed, there is no connection with a qualifier. By this, the interpretation of the ancient commentators—that "that which does not have the technical name *nadī* is short and ends in *i* or *u*"—is also refuted.

In this rule, *sakhyurasaṃbuddhau*, the term "sarvanāmasthāne" is carried over from the previous rule "ito'tsarvanāmasthāne. That [term] is qualified by the word "asaṃbuddhau. Since the term "ṇit" is carried over from the sūtra "goto ṇit," the seventh case ending is understood as a nominative through grammatical coreferentiality; thus he says: "the sarvanāmasthāna suffixes, with the exception of the vocative. However, the sūtra would have been more appropriately formulated simply as "sakhyurasaṃbuddhiḥ."

The imitation of the words *khi* and *khī*, which have undergone the substitution of *kṛta-aṇ* [i.e., the suffix *aṇ*], by means of the phoneme *khyā*, results in the form *khya*. Similarly, for the words *ti* and *tī*, the result is *tya*. In both cases, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and is not an imitation of a portion of primary words such as *apatya* (descendant). This is because of such grammatical indications (*nirdeśa*) as "for *sakhi*, [the suffix] *ya*" (*sakhyuryaḥ*), "for *pati*, [the suffix] *na*" (*patyurnaḥ*), "of a numeral and that which has a year as its number" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṃkhyasya ca*), and "and of a descendant-formative (*āpatya*) in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)" (*āpatyasya ca taddhite*). Having this in mind, he says: "by the words *khit* and *tit*," and so forth.

The inclusion of the word "subsequent" (*parasya*) is for the purpose of terminating the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "one [element replaces both the preceding and the following]" (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*).

Furthermore, this [rule] is superseded by the preceding rule, "idudbhyām," in the case of those termed *nadī*, and by the subsequent rule, "acca gheḥ," in the case of those termed *ghis*. Therefore, its scope consists of those instances devoid of both designations (*saṃjñā*). Yet, no such *u*-vowel exists; hence he says, "the *u*-vowel. As for what the ancients stated—that [the substitution occurs] after an *i* or *u* that is excluded from the *ghi* and *nadī* designations—that is incorrect, because such an *u*-vowel is unestablished.

Regarding the phrase *samudāyasya* ("of the whole"): even in the case of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), one should not suspect that the word *sakhi*, which provides the object being excluded, possesses the capacity to include [the compound] ending in that [word], because there is no proximate substantive (*viśeṣya*) present. As for what was stated here by Haradatta—"by that which possesses a designation" (*grahaṇavatā*)—and what was stated by Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra *khyatyāt*, that is not correct, because that [rule] pertains to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). Regarding the phrase *gauṇatve 'pi* ("even when [the sense is] secondary"): the intention is that it is like the substitution of *anaṅ* in the case of *asthi* and so forth.

And likewise, regarding the rule *yena vidhiḥ*, Kaiyaṭa states: "In *paramasakhāyau*, it is a *bahuvrīhi*; for if it were a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *ṭac* would have to occur. Similarly, under the rule *dvitīyā śrita-*, Kaiyaṭa, taking up the example *somasakha*, says: "Because it is a *bahuvrīhi*, there is no compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rules *midaco’ntyāt* and *tṛjvatkroṣṭuḥ striyāṃ ca*, as well as in Mādhava’s work on the verbal root *khyā*.

Furthermore, such usages as "anudyukṣo varuṇa indrasakhā" (Varuṇa, friend of Indra, is not exerting himself), "āgneyā hi marutsakhā" (for the Maruts, friends of Agni, belong to Agni), and "tīvraṃ somaṃ pibati gosakhāyam" (he drinks the strong Soma, the friend of the cows), are consistent only in this way; for in those cases, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) characteristic of a *bahuvrīhi* compound is observed, which indicates that [the term *sakhi*] is being used in a figurative sense (*gauṇatvāt*). By this, Haradatta, Nyāsa, and Sakata, who cite "susakhiḥ" (one whose friend is excellent) as an example under the rule defining the technical term *ghi*, along with others following them, are to be disregarded.

The particle *eva* is intended for restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) specifically with respect to the compound itself; otherwise, one might suspect that the meaning is "the husband alone" (*patir eva*). Furthermore, if one were to follow the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) from rules such as "of the root-initial" (*dhātvādeḥ*), there would be an excessive burden on the understanding (*pratipatti-gaurava*).
Now, how is it [to be explained] in the case of: *sītāyāḥ pataye namaḥ* ("Salutation to the husband of Sītā")?

And Parāśara says: "When the husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen [from his caste]... To this it is replied: the word *pati* is derived from the root *pā* (to protect) with the suffix *ṇi*; after the elision of the *ṭi*, the Uṇādi suffix *i* is applied according to the rule "after a vowel, *i*. This word *pati* is not included in the rule "the word *pati* only in a compound," because it is used here in its derivative (lakṣaṇika) sense. By this, the Mahābhārata passage "Arjuna is the friend (*sakhi*) of Kṛṣṇa" and the Rāmāyaṇa passage "by the lord of monkeys, the friend (*sakhinā*)," are explained.

Regarding *bahugaṇa*: the terms *bahu* and *gaṇa* are understood here as nominal stems (*prātipadika*) denoting number (*saṃkhyā*), and not as those denoting a collection (*saṃgha*) or abundance (*vaipulya*), because the technical designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) is prescribed based on the etymological sense of "that by which something is numbered. For this very reason, only the *taddhita* suffix *ḍati* is understood [in the rule], due to its association with *vatu*; it is not the *ḍati* derived from the root *pā*. The mention in the plural—“of the two following after *ṣaṣ*”—is intended to indicate that the meaning (the referent) is primary. The resulting meaning is: “of those two [suffixes] which express the number residing in the referent of *ṣaṣ*.”

Regarding *pratyayalope* (when there is elision of an affix): since this is already established by the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ*, this [present rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). That is to say, when the unique form of an affix is the operative factor, only that grammatical operation occurs upon the elision of the affix, and not an operation common to both affixes and non-affixes. Consequently, in the example *sudṛṣat prāsādaḥ* ("a palace with beautiful stones"), the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] prescribed by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* does not take place. Alternatively, this rule serves as a positive injunction (*vidhyartha*) for cases where the affix is primarily relied upon, even though it is a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*).

Therefore, in the case of *atṛṇeḍ*, even though the *im* augment—prescribed before a *pitt* sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*)—has been elided, it still takes effect [as if present]. However, the rule "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treatment as if a suffix were present) when the operation depends on a phoneme" refers specifically to cases where the phoneme is primary. Consequently, in *go-hitam* ("beneficial for a cow"), the *av* substitution does not occur. Regarding *asmad*: here, the older grammarians also read the word *avyaya* (indeclinable), but that has been disregarded because indeclinables are generally devoid of gender, and even though an *avyayībhāva* compound is neuter, there is no other gender [to distinguish it from].

"In reality," however, means that although [the word] is secondary (*gauṇa*), the substitution of *traya* is logical because there is no plural number (*bahuvacana*) indicating the predominance of the meaning; this is like the case of *anaṅ* in *asthi*, etc.

"The vowel *a* must be stated" means that in the absence of plurality, the word *auḍulomi* ends in *i*; but in the case of plurality, it ends in *a*. One should not be confused by thinking that when the word *uḍulomi* ending in *i* is in the plural, it becomes one ending in *a*. Thus end those [words] ending in *i*.

[The form] *kiditi*. By this, the meaning is that there is elision of the long *ā* according to the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64). Regarding the forms *yayī*, *papyā*, and so on: as for what was stated by the ancients—that likewise there are *devayajyā*, *atilakṣmyā*, and so forth—that is not correct. For in the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who sacrifices to the gods" (*devān yajate*), the word *devayaji* ending in a short vowel is established by Ujjvaladatta and others through the Uṇādi-sūtra "in". Furthermore, the usage in Bhāravi’s poem, "We shall slay those twice-born ones who sacrifice to the gods" (*admo dvijān devayajitīn nihanma*), is explained specifically as referring to the short vowel.

Furthermore, there is no *ī*-suffix prescribed for the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). If it is argued that it may be inferred due to the mention of the term "variously" (*bahulagrahaṇa*), this might indeed be so if an inferential ground were found that could not be established otherwise. However, even in the Veda, only the short vowel is employed—as in: "O Jātavedas, I have sacrificed for you, for Manu" (*āyajiṃ tvā manave jātavedase*). As for the word *atilakṣmī*, because it is a *nadī* (feminine noun ending in long *ī*), when the shortening, the augment *āṭ*, the *nuṭ* augment, and the case-ending *ām* are applied, there is a great difference [in form]; thus, it is not analogous to *vātapramī*. This will become clear in the root-text itself.

Regarding the term *kvibanta*: this is clearly stated in Mādhava’s commentary on the root *māṅ* (meaning "to measure" and "to sound"). In the word *bahuśreyasī*, the suffix *kap* is not applied by the rule *īyasaśca*; nor is there shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasva*), because of the prohibition: *īyaso bahuvrīherna*.

Regarding the statement "the two ending in *ī* and *ū* are called feminine (*stryākhyau*)," there is also the view that here the technical name (*saṃjñā*) applies to the two phonemes alone, as suggested by the natural phrasing of the rule *ācchīnadyornum*. Their status as being called feminine (*stryākhyatva*), however, arises because they are included—either inherently or by virtue of being part of a collection of phonemes denoting a female—in the suffixes beginning with *ṅī*. This is because the status of being the locus where the word-meaning power (*śakti*) resides in its entirety (*paryāptyadhikaraṇatva*) is not intended to be significant. Consequently, the linguistic usage of terms such as "ending in a nadī-suffix" (*nadyantāt*) is not contradicted.

In the same way, regarding the designation *ghisaṃjñā* as well, two alternative views should be understood: either the vowels *i* and *u* are designated as *ghi*, or that which ends in them is designated as *ghi*. If this is a designation of the phonemes (*varṇasaṃjñā*), then the meaning of the term *asakhi* is "that which is a member of something other than *sakhi*," and not "excluding a member of the word *sakhi*. Consequently, forms such as *atisakhinā* are established without objection; this is what should be noted. The word *pūrvam* means "prior to the application [of the rule]. The phrase *vaktavyam* (it should be stated) implies that this is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*) if the designation functions according to its original enunciation (*yathoddeśapravṛtti*), but it must be explicitly stated (*vācanika*) if the system follows the principle of "time of operation" (*kāryakālatva*).

He states that *aci śnu-iha-yv-oh* is a qualification of the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone, and not of *śnu* and *bhṛ*, because there is no deviation [in their application]; thus he says: "of a root ending in an *i*-vowel or an *u*-vowel. However, if one were to explain it as "of the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels of *śnu* and so forth," then the *ṅit*-designation of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would be redundant, and there would be the fault of grammatical discordance (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *kṣipati*, *adyutat*, *didivatuḥ*, and *ūyatuḥ*. The sense is that while adding the qualification "followed by a vowel" (*ac-paratvena*) to the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels avoids this, it results in an awkward construction. "By proximity" (*āntaratamyāt*) means "by position" (*sthānataḥ*).

The author of the *Eranekāca* explains: "In the rule *aci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), although there is a mention of a *dvandva* compound, only the *dhātu* (verbal root) is connected here, and not *śnu* or *bhru*, because the vowel *i* is impossible in those two. Furthermore, the mention of *dhātu* is repeated [to function] as a qualifier for both: for the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) and for the *aṅga* (stem). Thus he explains: 'in a consonant cluster that is a part of a verbal root,' and so forth. In that context, because the *saṃyoga* is qualified by the *dhātu*, *yaṇ* substitution occurs here in *unnyau* and *unnyaḥ*. However, the qualification of the *aṅga* is for the sake of establishing forms such as *harim*, *harī*, and *harīn*."

For if the *aṅga* were not qualified by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then even here in forms such as *praddhyaṃ* and *praddhayaḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitution would occur, overriding both the *pūrvarūpa* and the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*, just as in those examples. This is because the *aṅga* ends in an *i*-vowel that is not preceded by a *saṃyoga* (conjunct consonant) belonging to the verbal root. Regarding the word *vṛścika*: the author of the Bhāṣya has rejected the rule *bhītrārthānām* by relying on a departure (*apāya*) conceived through the intellect; therefore, his intention is that when merely a relationship (*sambandha*) is intended to be expressed, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone is used. Even according to the view of the Sūtra, he says: "belonging to the *vṛścika*."

Regarding the rule *allopayalopau*: one should not argue that the rule *verapṛktasya* would apply here because it is subsequent [in the order of the Aṣṭādhyāyī]; for the author of the Vārttika has stated: "The elision [of the *ya*] by *verapṛktasya* is superseded by the elision [of the *lopa*] before a consonant (*val*), by means of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

As for the phrase *kvau luptam*, the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, the meaning is "elided when *kvip* follows. All of this should also be understood to apply to the case of *kumārī* derived from *kumārīm icchan*.

Regarding the phrase "by way of non-difference": it should be understood that this is because it has already been stated that even in a figurative sense (*gauṇatve*), the operations of *anaṅ* and *ṇittva* do indeed take place. Regarding the phrase "even of the long vowel": the intention is that the mention of the substitution of *yaṇ* was made for this very purpose. If it is argued that the *yaṇ* is mentioned in order to exclude [the rule] from cases where there is scope for *guṇa*, as in *atisakheḥ* and *bhūpateḥ*, let it be so; nevertheless, the application [of the rule] to long vowels remains unavoidable. For there is no authority for the claim that the rule should apply to short vowels but not to long ones.

The formulation of the Sūtra as *vikṛta* (with the vowel lengthened) is appropriate because it serves to exclude both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*), thereby attaining its essential purpose, and because it has been established in the Bhāṣya. As for what the ancients said—namely, "some say *veti*"—and subsequently stated *sakhyuḥ* and so forth; and as for what the commentators of that [work] said, that both of these views are established in the Bhāṣya; and as for the support provided here by the author of the Prasāda: "Pāṇini stated *khyatyāt* for the sake of establishing *sakhyuḥ* and *patyuḥ*;

those who consider this to be common [to all] [cite examples like] *sukhyuḥ*, *sutyuḥ*, *sakhīḥ*, and *sutīḥ*. [Note: The term *sakhyuḥ* is derived from *sakhi-* with the substitution of *kh* for *khy* before the genitive ending *-as*. The rule *khyatyāt parasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.112) prescribes the substitution of *ī* for the *i* of the genitive ending when following a word ending in *khy* or *ty*. The argument is that if this were a general rule, it would apply to *sakhi-* and *pati-* even in secular usage, which some maintain is not the case.]
It is known that for the roots *sukhīyati* and *sutīyati*, which end in the *kvip* suffix,
forms such as *lūni* and *ūrṇuḥ* arise because the substitution [of *i* for *ya*] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it.
"‘Sukhya’ and so forth—both of these are correct because of the weight of the Bhāṣya.
Thus was a verse from the *Vicāracintāmaṇi* cited; let those of refined intellect recognize that all of this is rooted in a failure to thoroughly examine both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa.

As for "śuṣkiya," as for what they have cited as examples—such as *śuṣkyuḥ*, *pakvyuḥ*, *śuṣkyaḥ*, *pakvyaḥ*—and concluded by stating, "this is established in the Bhāṣya," that is due to excessive haste.

*tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ* (A 7.1.95): *kruś* [meaning] "to cry out" forms the word *kroṣṭu* with the suffix *tun* by the rule *sitanigami...* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.70), while the word *kroṣṭṛ* is formed with the suffix *tṛc*. Both denote a jackal. Since both would have been applicable without distinction in usage, these three rules are commenced for the purpose of restriction: that in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* and in the feminine, only the form ending in *tṛc* is used; in the case of vowels beginning with the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), both are used; and elsewhere, only the form ending in *tun* is used. *Kroṣṭuḥ* is the nominative singular from the stem ending in *tun*; *kroṣṭā* is the nominative singular from the stem ending in *tṛc*.

In the rule *tṛjvat*, the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the third case (*tṛjā*). Although an extended application (*atideśa*) is sixfold—concerning cause, designation, identity, scripture, grammatical operation, and form—it is primarily the form that is extended here. Furthermore, this form is not that of just any word such as *pac* and so on, but specifically of *kruś* alone, because it is what is proximate and because of semantic proximity (*āntarya*). With this in mind, he states the result: "in place of the word *kroṣṭṛ*."

"For the sake of restriction" means for the purpose of preventing this [lengthening] from applying to other technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*). Regarding *kroṣṭā*: there is the substitution of *anaṅ*. Because it is subsequent to the elision [of the final vowel] by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* etc., the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*) applies; and although that could have been obtained by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*, nevertheless, because it is subsequent, the rule *aptṛn* is more appropriate. This is because even when *anaṅ* has been applied, the form remains identical to the original through the principle of "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]," and thus it still possesses the character of the suffix *tṛc*. Otherwise, if the substitution were not made, the lengthening would not occur even after the *guṇa* substitution had taken place—this is the intended meaning.

There is another view that the letter *t* is also elided here from the word *rātsasya*. By this, when the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* is reduced to *ṅyāpaḥ sor* (the suffix *su* after a feminine stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or *ā*), forms such as *abibharbhavān* are established. However, in the case of *ajargharta*, because the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) is considered *asiddha* (not yet accomplished), the elision of *t* (*talopa*) does not occur. If it is objected that the form *kīrt* would result from the root *kīrtayati* with the *kvip* suffix, the answer is no; for the *Mahābhāṣya* states: "In the case of unattested usage, one should follow the grammatical rules. By this, the form *avarvart* is also explained.

Regarding the phrase "because it is subsequent": one should not say that *nuṭ* is obligatory; for once the substitution of *tṛjvat* has been applied, *nuṭ* becomes difficult to obtain due to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. This is the intended meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that by the rule *nanu* (P. 1.1.49), everything applicable to its own domain should be sublated, since one resorts to a general consideration of what is to be sublated? And so it will be stated: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa*, the long vowel, and the substitution of *ū*. In this way, because there is no distinction, the augment *nuṭ* would also be sublated by this [rule]. Therefore, how can there be a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)? If you say, "Because such a conflict is impossible between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*"), that is true; however, for that very reason, one should be satisfied with the fact that the Author of the Bhāṣya, having refuted the conflict regarding that portion, stated that *nuṭ* applies on the basis of the *jñāpaka* "na tisṛcatasṛ" (P. 6.4.4). Thus end the words ending in *u*.

"Hūhū" is an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) technical name. Regarding the word "aticamū," however, this is because of the statement: "And [the rule] regarding the mention of the gender of the first [member]. Thus, the intention is that the statement of the ancients—that words such as *aticamū* follow this pattern—is contrary to the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, since the word *varṣābhū* is invariably feminine (*nityastrītvāt*), it would have been more appropriate to state this sūtra only within the section on feminine genders. As for the masculine gender, they explained it as being somehow applicable with the intention of it being a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*), but that is due to haste. For this word *dardura* is indeed masculine.

"Bheka, maṇḍūka, varṣābhū, śālūra, plava, and dardura" (Amara-kośa). Because it is stipulated by that [author] that there is no *dvandva* compound of words with different genders, and because of the Yādava-kośa which states: "In the case of *bhekī*, it refers to the plant *punarnavā* in the feminine; *varṣābhū* and *dardura* are masculine. There is an alternative reading, *dardure ṣaṇī*; *ṣaṇī* is the name used by the ancients for the masculine gender.

Regarding the word *dṛbhati*: the root *dṛbh* meaning "to weave" (*grantha*) belongs to the *tudādi* class. Regarding the statement "it is derived": although Ujjvaladatta read the root as *dṛmph* with the second letter of the labial class (*pa-varga*) and explained that the absence of the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), nevertheless, other commentaries state that the suffix *ḍū* is added to the root *dṛbh* meaning "to weave," and the augment *num* is irregularly inserted. This is clear in the work of Mādhava. In the *Daśapādīvṛtti*, however, it is stated that *darbhaṇam* [weaving] is *dṛmbhūḥ*; here, both the augment *num* and the substitution of the anusvāra are irregularly prescribed.

Since this *ū* is not part of a verbal root (*dhātu*), the substitution *uvaṅ* does not apply; therefore, by the rule "a semi-vowel (*iK*) is replaced by a consonant (*yaṇ*) before a vowel (*aC*)," *yaṇ* occurs. This [application of *yaṇ*] is, however, set aside by the two rules "the preceding form is used before *am*" and "the preceding vowel is homogeneous with the following in the first two cases. With this intention, he provides the examples beginning with *dṛnbhūm*. Nor should one suspect the application of *yaṇ* here to form *dṛnkara*, because in that case only meaningful elements are taken into account. The point is that both this word *dṛn* and the word *bhū* are meaningless (in this context). Thus, it follows that this [word] is like *hūhū*. According to the opinion of Śrīpati, he says: *dṛn*.

Mādhava, however, states that by the rule "andūdṛnbhū... etc., when the word *dṛḍha* is used as an upapada, the suffix *kū* is applied, and the substitution of *dṛn* for the upapada is prescribed; thus he says: *dṛnbhū*. Some say that *taru* is a specific species of snake; others say it is a monkey.

Regarding *dṛṅkara*: here, the reading with the suffix *-n* (*dṛn*) is primary; however, some authorities also accept the reading with the suffix *-m* (*dṛm*). As for the statement "it should be stated": this refers to the rule *varṣābhvaśca*. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. The sense is that what remains unstated must be determined by the authority of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika. Thus, having explained the Vārttika *varṣābhū-punarbhv-aca*, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "This is said too little; it should be stated that [the suffix *ac* applies] after *bhuva* preceded by *varṣāt*, *dṛñ*, and *kāra*."

Vāmana, however, does not read the word *dṛś* at all. This being the case, that which was read by the ancients as *dṛkkāra*, and that which was stated by his grandson (Bhartṛhari) to be a restatement of the Mahābhāṣyakāra’s words in substance—all this is merely the product of rashness. Nor should one be deluded into thinking that even in the Bhāṣya the reading is simply *dṛk*;
for that would contradict Mādhava’s statement that [the root] is prescribed as *andūdṛnbhū*, as well as the works of Kaiyaṭa and others. Thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Regarding the reading *dīrghapāṭhe* (in the long-vowel recension): this is the reading accepted by many works such as the Bhāṣya and the Vṛtti. However, in the *Anusmṛti*, the short vowel is recited. As for what was stated in its commentary—that because a modification of a single part does not alter the identity of the whole, the form with the prefix *kā-* is also established—that is incorrect; for even so, that which is qualified by the suffix *aṇ* remains distinct. Indeed, the suffix *aṇ* itself is not a "modification. Therefore, the distinction is this: in the short-vowel recension, there is *uvaṅ* substitution for the element preceded by *kā-*, whereas in the long-vowel recension, there is *uvaṅ* for the element preceded by *kar-*.

The phrase "like *svayambhū*" [is used]. However, the elder [grammarians] have cited the words *dṛnbhū* and *kārābhū* as being like the word *varṣābhū*; the sense is that this should be disregarded because it lacks a foundation.

And here, from the rule *chandasyubhayathā* ("in Vedic [usage], both ways"), the term *ubhayathā* ("both ways") is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). However, the term *chandasi* ("in Vedic [usage]") has ceased to apply (*nivṛttam*). Consequently, usages such as *cintājarjaracetasāṃ bata nṛṇāṃ kā nāma śānteḥ kathā* ("Alas, what talk indeed of peace for men whose minds are shattered by anxiety? and *nṛṇāmeko gamyastvamasi* ("You alone are accessible to men") are justified. Some, however, maintain that *chandasi* carries over; that is incorrect, because since the matter would already be established by the preceding rule, the rule *nṛ ca* would otherwise be rendered redundant.

As for the claim that they carry forward the terms *atisṛ* and *catasṛ* from the previous sūtra, that too is incorrect, because the option is seen without distinction. For instance, in the mantra "dhātā dhātṝṇām," the Taittirīyas read the short vowel, whereas the Bahvṛcas read the long one; such is the direction [of the argument]. Thus end those [stems] ending in ṛ.

The meaning is that instead of saying *gota*, one should say *ota*. Thus, having raised the objection that in the case of *gām*, since the *vṛddhi* (guṇa) would apply first due to its higher status [in the order of rules], the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) would not occur, the author of the Bhāṣya on the rule "auto'mśasoḥ" stated that the *vṛddhi* is set aside by the *ātva* because the latter is otherwise without scope (*niravakāśatayā*). Kaiyaṭa also says thereon: "It should be read as *ota* in the sūtra, or else it should be explained as having the vowel *o* as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the sound *go*."

Regarding the phrase *smṛtauḥ*: as for what some say—that by the word *gauḥ* (in the sense of the suffix *-auṇādika*), the word *dyauḥ* itself is indicated through similarity, and not merely that which ends in *-au*, and therefore [the forms] *smṛtau*, *smṛtavau*, and *smṛtavaḥ* alone result—this contradicts the Bhāṣya. For if one were to admit that the suffix is *ṇit* only after *gauḥ* and *dyauḥ*, then forms such as *smṛtām* would have scope for the application of the rule *auto'mśasoḥ*.

And thus, in the case of *gām*, since the vṛddhi [substitution] would be unavoidable due to its higher priority, the Bhāṣya’s statement regarding the sublation (*bādhakatva*) and the lack of scope (*niravakāśatva*) for the *ātva* [substitution] would be consistent. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Thus end [the words] ending in *-au*.

The word *rāyaḥ* is masculine according to Amara’s statement, “*artha-rai-vibhavā apī*,” as well as from usages such as “*saṃrāyā bhūyasāsṛjā*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states, “*rā yi chāndasaḥ*” (the form *rā* before the suffix *yi* is Vedic). Kaiyaṭa, on the rule *vānto yi*, explains that this refers to the Vedic nature of the word *rai* when it ends in the denominative suffix *kyac*, and not to the simple word *rai* itself. However, he also mentions another view, namely that the simple word *rai* is also Vedic. Thus end the words ending in *ai*.

"Glau, mṛgāṅka, and kalānidhi" [are synonyms for the moon], according to Amara. That which protects people (*janān*) is *janauḥ*. By the rule "jvaratvara," there is the substitution of *ūṭh*; by the rule "etyedhati," there is *vṛddhi*. Thus, the forms are *janāvau*, *janāvaḥ*, and so forth.
Thus ends the section on base nouns ending in vowels in the masculine gender, composed in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now begins the section on feminine nouns ending in vowels.

It causes delight. By the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding forms specified by gender), [the base] is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) are applied. As for the statement "from one ending in *ā*" (*ābantāt*), and as for what they have explained—that although it is not a nominal stem because it ends in an affix, the meaning is that *ṅī* and *āp* are mentioned separately—this is not correct, because it has already been stated previously that the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* serves another purpose.

Regarding the rule *eṅ-hrasvāt*: because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*) and because it is taught as a specific injunction (*pratipadoktatvāt*), once the substitution of *et* has been applied by the rule *saṃbuddhau ca*, the elision prescribed by *halṅyābbhyaḥ* does not apply. This is because, even though the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would grant it the quality of being an *āp* vowel, it lacks the actual form of the long vowel *ā*. This is because the mention of the long vowel (*dīrghagrahaṇa*) was rejected by including the long vowel *ā* within the term *āp* itself. Furthermore, even according to the literal reading of the rule, the elision by *eṅ-hrasvāt* is more logically appropriate due to its priority. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding *yāṭ*: although it would have been more appropriate to say simply *yaṭ*, and there is no possibility of the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇe*—since that is already precluded by the very purpose of pronouncing the letter *a*—nevertheless, one might suspect that the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. Therefore, *yāṭ* has been formulated for the sake of clarity. As for the rule *vṛddhireci*, as for what was cited by the ancients as *āṭaśca*, that is incorrect; because the *ṭ* of *yāṭ* and *syāṭ* is an indicatory letter (*it*) of the entire complex, there is no occurrence of *āṭ* here.

The suffix *syāṭ* is added to a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and there is also a short vowel; the long vowel is pronounced as before. Regarding this, some say: "The rule should simply be formulated as *sarvanāmno 'suṅ ca* (and *asuṅ* is substituted for a pronoun). In this way, when *yāṭ* follows, because it is marked with *ṅ*, it undergoes substitution at the end [of the stem], and thus forms *sarvasyāḥ* and so forth. The purpose of adding *syāṭ* and prescribing the short vowel should be considered. In this regard, the following consideration arises: if it were stated merely as *asuṅ ca*, forms such as *amuṣmai* would not be established. In reality, however, it is more appropriate to formulate the rule as: *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ yāṭo hrasvaśca* (after a pronoun, *suṭ* is added before *ām*, and *yāṭ* is added, with a short vowel).

And it should be noted that it is not the case that *yāṭ* itself would incur the status of being short (*hrasva*), because of the force of its long pronunciation; for even if it were pronounced short, the substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel *a* could have been prevented simply by the force of that [long] *a*.

Regarding the *vibhāṣā* (optional rule): this option applies because [the previous rule] would otherwise not apply due to its being secondary (*gauṇa*). As for what they say—that it applies when the prohibition "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" has been reached—that is merely superficial; for that [prohibition] pertains to forms like *sarva* occurring within an unformed analytical sentence (*alaukika-prakriyā-vākya*), whereas this [option] pertains to the compound itself. Regarding "that which is north": as for what they say—that "that which is east is its north, thus it is 'north-east' (*uttara-pūrvā*)"—that is due to haste, since it would result in a reversal of the required initial placement (*pūrva-nipāta*).

Regarding the phrase "of the third": this [substitution] is indeed necessary for both the masculine and neuter genders. The sense is that since the desired result is established by this very rule, the sūtra "vibhāṣā dvitīyātṛtīyā" need not be composed.

Regarding the rule *ambārthanadyoḥ*, there is this *vārttika*: "The substitution of *mātaj* for *mātṛ* occurs when it signifies a son worthy of his mother. In the vocative case, the word *mātṛ* undergoes the substitution *mātaj* when the excellence of the son is to be expressed. For example: *gārgīmātṛkaḥ* ("one whose mother is Gārgī"). Its vocative is *he gārgīmāta*. This [substitution] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ap* prescribed by the rule *nadyṛtaśca*. However, where excellence is not to be expressed, but merely the statement of the actual form, the suffix *kap* alone is applied: *gārgīmātṛkaḥ*.

Regarding the statement "an *ā*-ending member [is feminine]," as for what was said by those explaining the rule *yāḍāpaḥ*—"In *atikhaṭvāyā*, there is no *yāṭ* because it is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical operation); likewise, in *atisarvāyā*, there would be no *syāṭ*"—that is due to haste. For the maxim concerning "that which is taught by a rule versus that which is directly stated" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*) does not apply to the domain of extended application (*atideśa*), because that would result in the extended application being rendered useless. Therefore, *yāṭ* is unavoidable. As for *syāṭ*, however, there is no possibility of its occurrence at all, because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) resulting from the fact that [the forms] *saṃjñā* and *upasarjana* are explicitly mentioned in the list. "Some," however, refers to the author of the *Pariśiṣṭa* and others.

In the rule *ṅiti hrasvaśca*, this is an option (*vibhāṣā*) where [the application] was not previously established. For the two short vowels (*hrasva*), since [the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*] was not established, and for the other two, since the prohibition by the rule *neyaṅuvaṅsthānau* had been established, this rule is commenced. Here, the three qualifiers of *ī* and *ū* are: (1) being the substitutes *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*; (2) being different from the word *strī*; and (3) being invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*). However, for the two short vowels, the qualifier is simply "in the feminine" (*striyām*), and does not extend to "being invariably feminine."

Otherwise, even though words such as *iṣu* (arrow) and *aśani* (thunderbolt)—which possess both genders—and those possessing all genders, would be feminine, they would not attain the designation *nadī* (river/feminine noun), because according to Kaiyaṭa’s view they lack "constant femininity" (*nityastrītva*), and even in Haradatta’s opinion, there is no instance to be excluded by the inclusion of the word "constant" (*nitya*) regarding the short vowels. For this very reason, setting aside the mention of "designation" (*ākhyā*) and extracting the mere word "feminine" (*strī*), it is connected [to the rule]; this is what he states: "and the short vowels *i* and *u* when they are feminine."

Regarding the phrase "autve prāpte": the intention is that [the substitution] would otherwise apply by virtue of its being subsequent (paratvāt). As for the explanation given by the ancients (*prāc*) in their commentary on the rule *aut*—namely, that it applies "to those [stems] excluding those designated as *ghit* or *nadī*"—this is not the literal meaning of the words; rather, it is something obtained from the two preceding and following rules. Thus, the omission of the rule *idudbhyām* by the ancients is merely a result of oversight (*prāmādika*).

Regarding the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ guṇadīrghotvānām*: in the example *tisrastiṣṭhanti*, the substitution of *guṇa* [by the rule] *ṛto ṅi* is superseded; in *tisraḥ paśya*, the substitution of the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) [by the rule] *prathamayoḥ* is superseded; and in *priyatisraḥ āgataḥ* and *priyatisraḥ svam*, the substitution of *ut* [by the rule] *ṛta ut* is superseded by the substitution of *rat*. This is the meaning: according to the principle of considering the sublation in its general form (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), there is a sublation of everything that would otherwise apply within its own scope.

In the consideration of specific exceptions (*viśeṣacintā*), however, by the maxim "exceptions [apply] in the middle," there would be a sublation only of the long vowels and the *ut* vowels, but not of the *guṇa*. Furthermore, it is clear in the works of Kaiyaṭa and others that the general and specific positions are established according to the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*), just like the positions regarding universals (*jāti*) and individuals (*vyakti*). As for what they have explained—that the word "exception" (*apavāda*) indicates "sublating power" (*bādhakatva*) and that the intention is that it sublates even the *guṇa* by means of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*)—that is baseless and forced.

As for what was stated by Prasādakṛt—that the meaning is that [the substitution] of *guṇa* is the sublater by virtue of the prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), while [the substitution] of the other two is the sublater by virtue of the subsequent prohibition (*paravipratiṣedha*)—that is not correct, because the rule [for *guṇa*] has not yet fulfilled its purpose. Nor is there fulfillment of purpose for the [substitution of] *ṭau* (the dual case endings), since its purpose is already served by *yaṇ*.

This is because of the qualification of "three or four" (*tricaturau*). For the sense is that, due to being directly heard in the text (*śrutatvāt*), the qualification "in the feminine" (*striyām*) applies specifically to "three or four," and not to the *aṅga* (stem).

Regarding "priyatri": here they explain that since "strī" (feminine) is the referent of the other member (*anyapadārtha*), the *aṅga* (stem) exists there in the form of a *bahuvrīhi* compound; however, because the word "tri" applies only to the masculine and neuter genders, the substitute "tisṛ" does not occur, and so forth.

On this point, the following must be said: if the compound follows the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) theory, the word *tri-* would be meaningless; if it follows the *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) theory, however, it would indeed function as feminine. How, then, can its application to masculine and neuter genders be justified? Herein lies the truth: in this case, the *jahatsvārthā* theory of operation is intended, in accordance with the observed usage (*lakṣya*). Therefore, the statement "the suffix *aṅ* [is applied] when [the base] is feminine" is perfectly correct. As for the word *tri-* denoting masculine and neuter, that is by way of its former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*).

This is because the established doctrinal tenets, such as "the *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the final member as its predominant factor," must be explained in this very manner. Likewise, in the case of *priyatasā pumān* ("a man who has three beloved women"), the application [of the feminine suffix] to the woman occurs only by way of what was previously so. However, according to the view that the compound does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*), the intended sense is "of those two [words] *tri* and *catur*, which convey a number residing in a woman. The textual passage from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "pratyayottarapadayośca" serves as the authority for this point.

Regarding the phrase "because of impermanence": the inclusion of the term *aj* in the rule *iko'ci* (Pāṇini 7.1.73) is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) here. For that [term] was indeed introduced to prevent the application of *num* in the vocative case; for although *num* would occur in the forms beginning with *bhyām*, its subsequent elision is possible there. Furthermore, since the vocative suffix is elided by *luk*, the occurrence of *num* would have to be asserted on the basis of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle (treating the elided suffix as present). And it is clear in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle is difficult to establish without the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the prohibition *na lumatā*.

One should not insist that this impermanence (*anityatva*) has as its object only the qualities of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sambuddhi*), for there is no contradiction in accepting it in other instances as well, in accordance with the requirements of the linguistic forms to be characterized (*lakṣya*). Thus, Kaiyaṭa has justified both forms, *priyatisṛ* and *priyatri*, precisely by the method described above.

As for the phrase "by a prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*), there is no lack of evidence here; the very examples cited in the Bhāṣya, such as *priyatisṛṇi*, serve as proof in this regard.

The meaning is as follows: even though the substitution of *tyadādyatva* (the replacement of *strī* with *t*) is caused by the occurrence of a case-ending (*vibhakti*), it is still the cause for the application of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, because the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the non-disturbance of a grammatical occasion) is not universal and because there is the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the rule "na yāsayoḥ.

Regarding the term *iyādeśa*: the substitution of *iy* prescribed for vowels beginning with *a* applies only to the four [case-endings] beginning with *aus* when the word *strī* is present in the masculine as a secondary member (*upasarjana*), and not elsewhere; this is because it is superseded by the previously mentioned rules such as *guṇa*, the absence of *nābhāva*, and so forth.

The term *sthānau* means "those two that stand (*tiṣṭhataḥ*) in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*"; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). The compound *iyaṅuvaṅ-sthānau* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). He states the resultant meaning as: "those two in which there is the standing (*sthitiḥ*) of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. This prohibition applies only where *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are actually produced. The inclusion of the word *sthāna* (place/standing) is for the purpose of ensuring that this prohibition does not apply where [the substitution] would be overridden by an exception (*apavāda*).

Although the ancient commentators maintain that this [rule] provides an option for the prohibition under discussion, nevertheless, when there is an option regarding a prohibition, it results in an option regarding a prescription. Thus, with the intention that the latter alone is the appropriate meaning of the sūtra due to parsimony (*lāghava*), he says: "Or they are termed *nadī*. The same applies to the sūtra "ṅiti hrasvaśca."

"How then?"—this is the objection: since there is an absence of the designation *nadī* due to the presence of the *uvaṅ* substitute, the short vowel [in *bahvīnām*] is untenable. Regarding the word *bahavaḥ*: some, however, resolve this by carrying over the term *vā* from the rule *vāmi* and relying on a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). That is weak; for if that were the case, the mention of the negative particle *nañ* here and the subsequent rule *vāmi* would both result in being superfluous. Others, however, somehow resolve it by treating it as a neuter used in a general sense (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*).

Regarding the statement "the six [suffixes] do not occur in the feminine," because of the explanation that "that which was mentioned does not exist," it is intended that not only the immediately preceding *ṅīp* but also the separated *ṭāp* are prohibited; with this intention, he says: "*ṅīp* and *ṭāp* are not [used].

As for "rāḥ is like the masculine," the meaning is that the word *rai* is traditionally remembered as being feminine. And thus Kṣīrasvāmī says: "Some say *rāḥ* is a feminine because she bestows (*rāti*) him. Amarasimha states: "In the feminine, *naus*, *taraṇis*, and *taris*."
Thus ends the section on feminine nouns ending in vowels (*ajanta*) in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita.
Now begins the section on neuter gender stems ending in vowels.

Therefore, regarding the rule *amo'm*: the prescription of *am* for *am* is for the purpose of subverting the elision (*luk*). [The interpretation] that "there should be *am*" has been explained in accordance with the views of the Eastern grammarians, or else with the intention that the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) applies when a *jhal* sound follows.

In reality, however, the word division is simply *m*, because of its brevity. In that case, once *sorm* is applied, the form *jñānam* is established. But in the second singular case, after the initial vowel *a* is replaced by *m* according to the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, the desired result is achieved through the elision of the final *m* via *saṃyogāntalopa*.

As for what they say—that if this were the case, there would be lengthening by the rule *supi ca*—that is not so, because it would contradict the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. As for the claim that the *paribhāṣā* does not apply in the rule prescribing lengthening, that too is not correct; for the author of the Bhāṣya has indicated, and Kaiyaṭa has demonstrated, that the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* does indeed apply to the lengthening prescribed by *supi ca* in the context of the two rules *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam* and *śnānnalopaḥ*.

As for what they say—that *atijarasam* would not be established—this too is not correct. For in the second singular case, since the rule *ato 'm* is superseded by *jaras* due to its higher status (*paratva*), the form is clearly established once *jaras* has been applied, as the substitution of *luk* does not occur by virtue of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. However, in the first singular case, *atijarasam* is indeed desired; here, the *jaras* substitute does not apply by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*.

The letter *t* in *ataḥ* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Regarding the phrase "in the designation *bha*": the intention is that because it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule *suḍ anapuṃsakasya*, [the *jaras* substitute applies].

Of that which [consists of] *i* and *a*, namely *yam*. He states this as "of the vowels *i* and *a*. Because of its association with *jas*, *śas* is also understood here as being only a case-ending (*sub*). Therefore, it does not apply here in the example: *kuṇḍaśo dadāti* (he gives by the pot).
The mention of *śi* is a citation without a case-ending. The formation of a technical name (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the sake of following the ancient teachers.

Regarding the phrase *anyatamasya tu*: the sense is that expressions such as *sāmānyādiṣv anyatamam* (one of the general categories, etc. are merely due to negligence. Regarding the statement *sor amādeśe*: as for what was said by the ancients—that *jaras* optionally occurs when *su* is replaced by *am*—that contradicts the Bhāṣya. Consequently, forms such as *ajarasaṃ vartate* and *he ajarasam* are indeed ungrammatical (*apaśabda*). However, the usage *ajarasaṃ paśya* is correct. Nevertheless, the assertion of the ancients that *jaras* occurs when *am* is substituted is itself incorrect, because the substitution of *jaras* is more logically justified by its higher status [in the order of rules], and there is no evidence for a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) in this case.

He explains that *sāntamahataḥ* is a separate word (*pṛthakpada*) with its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*), and that it stands in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the word *saṃyogasya*; thus he says: "of a *saṃyoga* ending in *s*. Regarding the term *upadhāyāḥ*: the mention of *upadhā* here is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the preceding letter [the penultimate vowel] in general, because the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) meaning of *upadhā* is not applicable here.
