Regarding *māsaśchandasī*: the meaning of the rule is that the substitution of *t* for *māsa-* occurs before an affix beginning with *bh*, provided it is in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). An example is: *mādbhiḥ śaradbhirdurodaraṃ tava*.

Regarding the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake*: here, by the mention of the term *hrasva* (short vowel), the word *acaḥ* (of a vowel) is brought to mind. Because this [vowel] qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is an application of the rule to that which ends in it; thus he says, "of that which ends in a vowel. However, it is not explained as "the vowel of the nominal stem," because when a grammatical coreferential relationship (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, a non-coreferential relationship (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is improper, and furthermore, because it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *suvāg-brāhmaṇakula*.

[The author] brings [the arguments] together: the substitution of *y* (yādeśa) made on the basis of the phoneme *a* (avarṇa) would be the cause for its own elision (*tallopah*). This point was hinted at in the Bhāṣya on the sūtras "eoṅ" and "iko guṇavṛddhī," explained by Kaiyaṭa, and established as the final conclusion in the Śabdakaustubha; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. Thus, the sense is that Mādhava’s example of the neuter form *śubhaṃya*—derived from the root *yā* with the suffix *ṅi* after the word *śubhaṃyā*—is not to be respected.

This *luk* (elision) after a neuter [stem] ending in *su* or *am* is an exception by prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the substitution of *at* for *tyad*-type stems and the substitution of *ka* for *kim*. For if the substitution of *at* for *tyad*-type stems were applied later due to its higher status, the form would have been *tat kulam* instead of *taṃ kulam*.

Regarding the phrase "by way of *vṛddhi*, *aut*, and so on": in the example *atisakhīni kulāni*, *vṛddhi* is applicable because of the rule *sakhyurasambuddhau* which causes the stem to behave as if marked with the *ṇit* augment; in *vāriṇi*, however, *aut* is applicable by the rule *acca gheḥ*; and in *priyakroṣṭūni* and similar cases, the substitution of the *tṛjvat* form is applicable.

Now, what is the difference between *num* and *nuṭ*? To this he says: "In the case of *nām*" (*nāmī*). The point is that since *num* is a part of the stem (*aṅgabhakta*), when it is present, the long vowel [of the preceding *ī*] would not occur.

"Regarding the rule *tṛtīyādiṣu puṃvat*" (in the third case and those following, it is like the masculine): this is a prohibition of both *num* and the short vowel, based on the difference in the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). For the word *pīlu*, the ground for application in the sense of a tree is the genus (*jāti*) subsumed under "treeness," whereas in the sense of a fruit, it is either the genus subsumed under "fruitness" or the state of being produced from a specific type of tree. Thus, the meaning is that in both cases, there is no single common ground for application for the masculine and neuter forms.

*asthidadhi*: *atidadhneti* (meaning "having passed beyond the curd"). Regarding the form *priyadadhneti*, some say that although the suffix *kap* would necessarily apply by virtue of the word *dadhi* being listed among the *uraḥprabhṛti* group in the rule "dadhimadhuśalī," it does not occur in the word *priyadadhi* solely due to the usage of the Bhāṣyakāra. That [view] is questionable, because such a reading is not found in many manuscripts of the Bhāṣya. As for the feminine forms *priyadadhnyā* and *priyadadhnyai*, some maintain them; but that is incorrect, because the suffix *ṅīp* cannot apply here due to the *sannipātaparibhāṣā* and the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*.
Therefore, even in the case of the feminine, forms such as *atidadhni* and so forth should be understood just as in the masculine.

Regarding *sudhinī*: because it is subsequent, *iyaṅ* supersedes *num*. Regarding *sudhiyā*: in the alternative view where the masculine form applies (*puṃvadbhāva*), *iyaṅ* occurs due to the absence of *num*.

The family of one who has many excellent [daughters] is *bahuśreyasī*. Here, there is no shortening of the neuter form; for Śrīpati, Puruṣottama, Viśvarūpa, and others maintain that the prohibition "not after a word ending in *īyas*" (Pāṇini 1.2.48) applies only to the shortening of the feminine suffix (*ī*). Others, however, say that only the shortening of the *upasarjana* (the preceding member) is prohibited, whereas the neuter shortening would indeed occur, as in *bahuśreyasi* and *bahuśreyasinī*. The word *sānu* is of both genders, as in the rule "a ridge, a plateau, or a peak (*snu*) is *sānu* in the non-feminine. He states its neuter forms: *snūnī*, *sānūnī*. In the masculine, it is like *śambhu*.
Regarding *priyakroṣṭūni*: as for what the Easterners (*prāc*) stated, namely *priyakroṣṭṝṇi*, that contradicts the Bhāṣya and Vārttika concerning the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior counter-exception).

As for their explanation that this is a counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*) concerning the scope of the rule *vibhāṣā tṛtīyādiṣv aci*, because the Bhāṣya cites *priyakroṣṭune araṇyāya* as the very example [for that rule]; that is not correct, because there is no evidence that an example serves as a restrictive limitation (*saṅkocaka*).

As for what they say—that an example need not be strictly adhered to—furthermore, if the "prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) were restricted solely to the optional *tṛjvadbhāva* (the substitution of the masculine stem *tṛc*), then the mention of *tṛjvadbhāva* there would be entirely redundant; for forms such as *priyakroṣṭunā* could be easily established even without that prohibition, depending on the alternative view. Nor can it be argued that the purpose of the rule is the exclusion of forms like *priyakroṣṭre*; for even in the case where *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine stem substitution) applies, such forms would still be unavoidable, and you yourself have cited them as examples in that very context.

Nor should it be argued that in a collective *dvigu* compound such as *pañcakroṣṭu*, the purpose of the rule is to prevent the application of the *tṛj-vat* substitution (which would apply to *kroṣṭṛ*) because the masculine-like form (*puṃvad-bhāva*) does not occur there; for even so, this would result in an inconsistency with the examples cited in the *Bhāṣya*. If you claim that [the *Bhāṣya* example] is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), then by all means let *priyakroṣṭūni* be taken as the illustration, in order to favor the nominal stem portion (*prātipadika-aṃśa*) as cited in the *Bhāṣya*. This is the direction of the argument. Regarding *sulvā*: in the alternative where the masculine-like form applies, there is no *num* augment, and thus *yaṇ* [substitution] occurs. Regarding *sulunā*: the *num* augment applies here because it is subsequent in the order of rules, thereby overriding the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by the rule *oḥ supi*.

Regarding the term *yadiganta* (ending in /i/ or /ī/): this has been clarified by Mādhava under the root *rā* (in the sense of "giving") in the context of the example *atiri brāhmaṇakulam*. Others, however, maintain that the word *sudyu* is a stem that is marked as having a masculine base (*bhāṣitapuṃska*); since it is now ending in /i/, it remains identical despite the modification of one part (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*), and therefore the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies. Accordingly, the masculine-like treatment is illustrated in works such as the *Rūpamālā*. Therefore, in the opinion of Mādhava, there is no masculine-like treatment for neuter stems ending in /e/ or /ai/, whereas in other opinions there is.
Consequently, forms such as *pradyavā*, *prarāyā*, and *sunāvā*, though previously cited by easterners, are not particularly faulty.
Thus ends the section on neuter nouns ending in vowels (ajanta) in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita.
Now begins the section on masculine stems ending in consonants.

Regarding *liṭ*: [the root] *lih* in the sense of "tasting" takes the suffix *kvip*. Thus we have *liṭ-su* and *liṭ-tsu*. By the rule for *jaś*-substitution, the *ḍh* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule *khari ca*, that *ḍ* becomes *ṭ*. Because that [change to *ṭ*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of the following rule, the augment *dhuṭ* is applied by the rule *ḍaḥ si*. This *dhuṭ* then undergoes *car*-substitution to become *t*. The rule *na padāntāṭṭoḥ* prohibits the application of *ṣṭu*-substitution here. However, the rule *cayo dvitīyāḥ* does not apply in this case, because the *car*-substitution is still regarded as *asiddha*.

By this, the claim made by those explaining the ancient text—that there are forty-one such *pratyāhāras*, and that regarding the *liṭ* suffixes [in the rule] *liṭsu liṭsu*, two forms arise from the *ṭa* and *ṭha* [suffixes]—is refuted. Furthermore, this is consistent with the qualification "not occurring at the end of a word" (*apadānta*) found in the verse of the *Prātiśākhya*: "Some say that the first [consonant] following a sibilant (*ūṣman*), when not at the end of a word, becomes the second [homorganic stop]."

The word "dhātoḥ" (of a root) is repeated [from the previous rule]. Therein, with the intention that one [repetition] indicates the time of instruction (*upadeśakāla*), he says: "In the instruction" (*upadeśe*). He asks about the purpose of the repetition: "What [is the purpose] in the instruction? (*upadeśe kim*)? He states that the purpose is the avoidance of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*), beginning with the words "adho gī" and so forth.

"Regarding *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* [Pāṇini 8.2.37], the phrase *jhal iti nivṛttam* (the condition *jhal* has ceased to apply) is stated. As for what was said by the ancients—that [the rule applies] when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) follows a *jhal* sound and at the end of a word (*padānte*)—that is merely an error, because it would lead to the failure to establish forms such as *adhok*, *adhog*, and *ajarghāḥ*. Furthermore, the mention of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) is not topical here, and in that context, a *jhal* sound cannot function as a cause (*nimitta*). In cases such as *dhugbhyām* and *dhukṣu*, the result is already established simply by the condition "at the end of a word" (*padānte*)."

As for that which was explained by the grandson (Patañjali)—namely, that [the rule] applies only when a *jhali* follows a base (*prātipadika*) and so forth—that too is rootless and fruitless, and thus should be disregarded. Regarding "the substitution of *bhaṣ*": the sense is that because the substitutions of *jaś* and *car* are considered unestablished (*asiddha*), [the *bhaṣ* substitution occurs] prior to those two. Regarding "the substitutions of *ṣatva* and *car*": the sense is that because *car* is unestablished, *ṣatva* occurs first, and after that, *car*.

In the case of *druh*, since it belongs to the *ad* class, the substitution [of *śn*] would apply invariably; for others, it would not apply at all. Therefore, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) covering both cases. Now, one might object: "The roots beginning with *druh* are indeed listed in the *divādi* group in this very order. In that case, let the rule simply be *vā druhādīnām* (or, optionally, for *druh* and the rest). Let the *radhādi* subgroup be within the *puṣādi* subgroup, and the *druhādi* subgroup be within that. This is not correct. For if that were so, the substitution would not occur in the *yaṅluk* formation, because of the prohibition: "That which is specified by its own name or by a group (*gaṇa*) [does not undergo the operation]. Thus, we have *dodhruk* and *dodhruṭ*.

Regarding *igyaṇaḥ yaṇaḥ sthāne*: the intention is that in the context of rules prescribing operations (*vidhipradeśeṣu*), a future designation (*bhāvisaṃjñā*) is resorted to, as in the case of the expression "the cloth of the thread" (*sūtraśāṭaka*).

In the rule *vāha ūṭh*, the term *samprasāraṇa*—which is carried over from the rule *vasoḥ samprasāraṇam*—is a qualifier of *ūṭh*. Consequently, the rule *alo'ntyasya* (P. 1.1.52) does not apply. As for what was stated by the ancients—that [the substitute] belongs to the word *vāh*—that is not the actual meaning of the sūtra; rather, it should be understood as an explanation of the resulting sense arrived at through some interpretive maneuver. Regarding the phrase *chandasyeva*: the intention is that the word *chandasi* is understood from the two rules *chandasi sahaḥ* and *vahaśca*.

As for what was stated by the Easterners (Prācya)—namely, that once *ūṭh* has been applied, there is a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) as in *bhūhaḥ*, *bhūhaḥ*, and so on—that contradicts the Bhāṣya. For instance: let the mention of *ūṭh* be omitted; let only *samprasāraṇa* be prescribed. Once *guṇa* has been applied to the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), the form *viśvauhaḥ* and others are established by the rule "vṛddhireci" (P. 6.1.88). This being the case, the fact that [the rule] is actually formulated [with *ūṭh*] serves to indicate the *paribhāṣā* regarding external elements (*bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*).

For it is established in the *Bhāṣya* that if that [substitution] were present, the internal (*antaraṅga*) *guṇa* would not occur because the external (*bahiranga*) *samprasāraṇa* would be considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*). If it is argued that there would be a difference in form when the root ends in something other than *a* or when the preceding upapada ends in *a*, this is not so; for Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that by the force of the *jñāpaka* stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, one can infer the absence of the *ṇvi* suffix in such cases. By this, usages such as *vāryūhaḥ* and *prauhaḥ* are also refuted. Alternatively, it should be understood that the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *ūh*.

In the rule *vasusraṃsu*, the term *vasu* refers to an affix; therefore, that which ends in it is to be understood. From the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*, the word *sa* is carried over (*anuvartate*). That [word *sa*] qualifies *vasu* alone, and not *sraṃsu* or *dhvaṃsu*, because there is no deviation [in their application]; nor does it qualify *anaḍuh*, because that is impossible. With this intention, he says: "of that which ends in *vasu* and has *s* as its final letter. Regarding "at the end of a word" (*padānte*), the inclusion of *jhal* (consonants other than semivowels and nasals) by the ancient commentators is an error, because it would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *srastam*. For the root *sah*, when it becomes *sāḍ*, the *s* [is replaced by *ṣ*].

*saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.56). Why is *saheḥ* mentioned? [Consider] *saḍaḥ*, meaning "one who exists with *ḍa*," that is, one whose name contains the word *ḍa*, such as *mṛḍa*. The descendant of *saḍa* is *sāḍiḥ*. Thus end those ending in *ha*.

The term *diva* refers to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), whether it is an underived form or one derived by the rule *diver ḍiviḥ* as supplied in the *Nyāsa*, but not to the verbal root *divu* (meaning "to play," etc.), according to the paribhāṣā: "When there is a mention of a form without an *anubandha*, it does not include a form with an *anubandha*. Consequently, [the substitution] does not occur in forms such as *akṣadyūḥ*. The letter *t* in *aut* is for the sake of pronunciation.

Regarding the form *sudyubhyām*: since the vowel *u* is a *samprasāraṇa*, the rule *halaḥ* would have required a long vowel, but this does not occur due to the force of the *tapara* designation (*ut*) in the rule *uto vṛddhir...*. As for what was stated by the ancients—namely, "there is optionally an *ā*-substitution for *div-* before *am*"—that is disregarded, because it is not taught by the three Munis and is therefore fruitless. It should be understood that the form *dyām* belongs exclusively to the word *dyo-*. Thus ends the section on words ending in *vānta*.

Because of the use of the plural number in the rule for the words *ṣaṣ* and *catur*, the predominance of the meaning (*artha*) is intended. And the status of being subsequent to *am* is established through the medium of the word-form (*śabda*). Therefore, even though the rule for "that which ends in [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, the form *paramacaturṇām* occurs only in cases such as this (where *catur* is primary), but not in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. This very point he will state with the words: "But when [the word] is secondary (*gauṇa*), the augment *nuṭ* is not desired," and so forth. Regarding the term *dvitvam*: it is by means of the rule *aco rahābhyām*. [End of section on] words ending in *r*.
Kamalā is Lakṣmī. Thus end those words ending in *l*.

Regarding the rule "mo no dhātoḥ padānte": although the word *jhal* is carried over from previous rules by the ancients, it should nevertheless be disregarded because it does not appear in the *Kāśikā* and other such works, and because its inclusion would be fruitless.

One might object: "Why not simply formulate the rule as *kimaḥ kaḥ*? It will be explained that for the words beginning with *tyad*, the substitute *aḥ* replaces *im*; furthermore, the word *kim* will be recited before *dvi*. Due to the prohibition 'not when [the suffix] is meaningless' (*anarthake*) and by the force of the rule's very commencement, the rule for substitution of the final letter (*alo'ntyavidhiḥ*) will not apply; so what is the need for the substitute *ka*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "even when accompanied by *akac*. For if the *ṭi* were replaced by *a*, the form would be *kak*. Moreover, in rules such as "for *tu* and *hu*, *ku*" (*kutuhoh*), the form *kimaḥ* must necessarily be stated; this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: But in that case, since it would not be the result of a grammatical operation (*gaṇakārya*), would [the substitution] not occur even when [the word *kim*] is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*)? [Reply: Not so; for, by carrying over the word "of *tyad*-etc. (*tyadādīnām*) and modifying the number [to the singular], one explains it as "of *kim*, which begins with *tyad*-etc. Furthermore, by the force of this carry-over, the restriction "only those ending in *dvi*" is abandoned in this rule. Regarding the term "general rule" (*utsarga*): the point is that by this, the commentary statement "In the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau*, what is the purpose of [specifying] 'not final' (*anantyayoḥ*)?"—namely, the examples "O *sa*" (*he sa*) and "O Acyuta, O venerable Acyuta" (*bho acyuta bhavannacyuta*)—is not contradicted. As for the reason why [the form] does not exist here, it is simply the non-observation of frequent usage. As for what they say:
One should understand that the form "this" (idam) refers to what is near, while "this here" (etad) refers to what is even closer;
"that" (adaḥ) refers to what is distant, and "that" (tad) should be known as referring to what is beyond the senses. ||1||

[The opponent argues: "Because of this very statement, such a meaning is unfit to be brought before [the mind]. This is merely superficial; for there is no obstacle to words such as *idam* (this) serving to present the person being addressed, just as there is none for words like *sannikṛṣṭa* (near). Furthermore, we frequently observe that even a distant object, when brought into proximity by the intellect, is addressed. Thus says Bhaṭṭi: "O fair-browed one! Where have you vanished? Alas!"—in this way he lamented much.
Here too, it is the suffix *aka* that forms the pratyāhāra (abbreviation), and not *ṭāp*; this is the intended meaning, because of the qualification "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*).

Regarding the phrase *anabhyāsavikāra* (non-modification of the reduplicated base): by this, the rule for the substitution of *i* in *bhṛñām it* and *artipipartyoś ca* remains applicable as a rule concerning the final letter [of the root]; thus we have *bibharti* and *piparti*. Now, one might raise the objection that because the substitution of *smai* is subsequent [to the rule for *na*], the substitution of *na* would occur; anticipating this, he says: "Because it is obligatory (*nityatvāt*), *ḍeḥ smai* [applies]. The phrase "in order to prescribe an operation" means "in order to make known something not previously established. However, in the verse beginning with *īṣadarthe kriyāyoge*, the meanings such as "slightness" (*īṣadartha*) and so on are not being prescribed, but rather are restated (*anūdyante*). Therefore, the substitution of *enā* does not apply. By this—

"O Rādhā, this man is afraid at night; therefore, you yourself lead him home"—this too has been explained, because the state of being afraid is intended as that which is to be restated (the *anuvādya*). End of those ending in *m*.

Regarding the form *sugāṇ*: the rule "anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ" prescribes a long vowel (*dīrgha*). One should not suspect that, when this long vowel is to be applied, the status of a "substitute" (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies to the elision of the penultimate *a* (*allopa*) or the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*), because such substitution is prohibited in the prescription of a long vowel, and because there is a prohibition regarding operations prescribed for *kvip*. By this, he implies that one should disregard the writings of the ancients who explain *sugaṇṇīśa* as being derived from the root *gaṇ* with the suffix *kvip*.

If there is a persistent insistence that his own work must also be justified, let it be justified in this way: *kvip* is so called because it behaves like *kvip* by means of universal elision (*sarvalopitva*). From the word *kvap*, which ends in the *ācārakvip* suffix, another *kvip* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartari*); thus, its meaning is "one who conquers" (*vijitṛ*). Thus end the words ending in *ṇ*.

Regarding the phrase *upadhādīrgha* ("lengthening of the penultimate vowel"): this is [governed] by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau*. The mention of *ṅau sambuddhau ca* ("in the locative case-ending *ṅi* and in the vocative") is explained in this way in accordance with the views of the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*). However, it would have been more appropriate to explain it as a genitive construction, namely *ṅyantasya sambudhyantasya ca padasya* ("of a word ending in a *ṅī*-suffix or ending in the vocative"). For in that case, the application of the rule regarding the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) would be easily obtained, and thus one would not have to undergo the trouble of following the implications of the prohibition of that specific meaning. Anticipating the objection that there might be the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) even for an operation prescribed after [the original element], he says: *na ca* ("and not").
Regarding the word *ṣāṣṭhīm*: the sense is that because it has been made known in the rule *vāha ūṭh*, it resides in that same location [of the sixth case].

Regarding the phrase *ityasiddhatvāt* (because of its being asiddha): the sense is that this is because the author of the Bhāṣya, in the rule *dyudbhyo luṅi*, has indicated the position that restrictive rules (*niyamasūtra*) function in a positive manner by way of restricting the purport of general rules (*sāmānyaśāstra*). However, it should be understood that under the view that they function in a negative manner, [the asiddhatva] is established by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*. He provides an example of a rule concerning the formation of nominal stems (*subvidhi*) with the words *ātvam* etc.; but in the case of a rule concerning accents (*svaravidhi*), the example is *pañcārmam*.

In the compound *diksaṅkhye saṃjñāyām* ("when a direction and a number [form a compound] in the sense of a name"), once the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) has occurred, the first member (*pūrvapada*) ends in an *a*-vowel. Consequently, the rule *arme cāvarṇaṃ dvyactryac* ("and when [the second member] is *arma*, an *a*-vowel [ending in the first member], whether consisting of two or three syllables, receives the acute accent on its first syllable") would apply; however, because the elision of *n* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), this does not take effect. Regarding the formation of feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), he will explain under the rule *saṃjñāvidhau*: "'Even though the elision of *n* has occurred here in the word *pañca*... etc. But regarding the application of the augment *tuk* before a *kṛt* suffix—as in *vṛtrahabhyām*—the *tuk* prescribed by the rule *hrasvasya piti* ("[the augment *tuk* follows] a short vowel before a suffix beginning with *p*") does not apply. Why "before a *kṛt* suffix"? Consider *vṛtrahacchatram*; here, the *tuk* prescribed by the rule *che ca* ("[the augment *tuk* is added] before the suffix *cha*") would indeed occur.

Regarding *pratidiv*: the suffix *kanin* is applied by the rule "The suffixes *kanin*, *yu*, *ṛṣitakṣi*, *rāji*, *dhanvi*, *dyu*, and *pratidiva*" [Uṇādi Sūtra 1.157]. The form is further modified by the rule "and before a consonant" (*hali ca*) [Pāṇini 6.4.21]. As for what the older commentators have presented as the application of the rule "and before a penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāṃ ca*) [Pāṇini 6.4.7], that is incorrect, because the letter *v* in the root *div* is not a penultimate vowel.
[Furthermore, the rule] "for *in*, *han*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman* before the nominative plural ending" [Pāṇini 6.4.12] applies.

Regarding the word *upadhāyāḥ*: this restriction applies specifically to the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-dīrgha*). Therefore, in the form *vṛtrahāyate*, the lengthening prescribed by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* still takes place. Likewise, in the form *vṛtrahaṇī*, the lengthening that occurs by the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ* is also excluded by this restriction; the point is that the restriction is understood to apply only with respect to the lengthening of the penultimate vowel. He explains the rule *hanteratpūrvasya* through a division of its constituent parts (*yogavibhāga*) as "*hanteḥ*". In connection with this, he provides an example: *prahaṇyāt*. He then states the portion relevant to the present topic:

Regarding the rule *atpūrvasya* and the rule *ekājuttare*: one should not argue that once the elision (*lopa*) of the *ā* has occurred, the condition of being "a single vowel" (*ekāctva*) no longer exists. This is because, even when a grammatical operation is prescribed based on what precedes [the elided element], the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) retains its properties. Nor should one say, "The status of being a substitute does not apply when an operation is prescribed with respect to what precedes an *asiddha* [element]," for it is stated: "The fault [of this rule] applies only in the cases of the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *l* for *r* (*latva*), and the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*)."

As for the statement in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *aṭkupvāṅ*—"vṛtraghnaḥ, srughnaḥ"—which Kaiyaṭa explains by noting that there would be the undesired application of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) under the rule *prātipadikānta*, this should be understood as being intended either to suggest that the compound [of *prātipadika* and *anta*] should not be a genitive (*pañcamī*) compound, or that the mention of *ṇatva* in that context should be omitted. The rejection of the mention of *ṇatva* is hinted at in the *bhāṣya* and explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*.

In reality, however, the application of *ṇatva* here is properly constant by virtue of the rule "kumati ca. Thus it is established that, in any case, the *ṇatva*—whether obtained optionally or necessarily—is restricted by this rule.

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated: "A prohibition must be formulated regarding the substitution of *ha* when there is an intervention by *ku*. What is the purpose? [Examples are: *vṛtraghnaḥ*, *srughnaḥ*, *prāghāni*. Thus, the mention of *atpūrvasya* (‘not preceded by *a*’) in the rule *hanteratpūrvasya* need not be made. This, however, is merely an exposition of the intention behind the Vārttika, and not the actual state of affairs. This is because, rather than rejecting a portion of the Sūtra on the basis of the Vārttika, it is more logical to adopt a word-split (*yogavibhāga*) to incorporate the meaning of the Vārttika; such is the direction of the argument.

It was said by Mādhava: "For his text is as follows: 'In the case of the technical designation *bha* and when there is elision (*al-lopa*), the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) would lack a vowel (*anac*). And since the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply because it is not a rule concerning phonemes (*alvidhi*), there is an absence of the condition of having a single-vowel subsequent member (*ekāj-uttarapadatva*); consequently, the optional application [of the nasal] prescribed by the rule "in the final of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), before *nuṭ*, and in case-endings (*vibhakti*)" occurs—resulting in the forms *vṛtraghnaḥ* and *vṛtraghṇaḥ*.'"

Regarding the phrase "tadbhāṣye": furthermore, the objection that [the rule] does not apply because it is not an *al*-vidhi is inconsistent. This is because the rule "acaḥ parasmin" was indeed introduced for the sake of an *al*-vidhi; thus, if that [rule] were not applicable, some other justification would have to be stated. Moreover, the claim that there is an option (*vikalpa*) is also inconsistent, as one should note that the application of the sūtra "kumati ca" would be unavoidable.

In the rule *maghavā bahulam* ("*maghavā* optionally [before *tṛ*]"), the word *tṛ* is understood from the preceding sūtra *arvaṇastṛsāvanañaḥ*. With reference to that, *maghavā* is in the nominative case used in the sense of the genitive (*maghavaḥ*). Thus he says: "of the word *maghavan*. Regarding the phrase *adhātoḥ*: the meaning is "even when it was previously not a verbal root (*adhātubhūtapūrva*). Indeed, the mention of *añcati* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), namely: "if [the suffix] occurs after a verbal root, then only after *añcati*. Consequently, in examples such as *gomān* (meaning "one who acts like one possessing cows"), although it is currently a verbal root, the mention of *adhātu-* is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartham*).
This will become clear in the root text itself.

One might object: "In cases such as *kurvan*, since the elision of a final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the word would lack the suffix *-n* and thus the lengthening [of the vowel] would not occur. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this case... He explains: "Because of the mention of *bahulam* (‘in various ways’), which means that in some instances something else entirely occurs. He further explains: "By way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*)," meaning that this triad—the substitution of *gh* for the *h* of the root *mahi*, the addition of the augment *avuk*, and the suffix *kan*—is established through irregular derivation. He concludes: "This has been refuted."

And likewise, Kaiyaṭa stated regarding the rule *chandasīvanipau*: "The rule *maghavā bahulam* need not be formulated, because the two forms [maghavā and maghavat] are established even in the common language (*bhāṣā*) by means of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *śvan* and *ukṣan*, and by the suffix *matup* from the stem *magha*.
As for what was said here by the author of the Vārttika: "The forms *arvaṇas-tṛ* and *maghonas-tṛ* need not be taught, for they are Vedic (*chāndasa*)."
"Because of the prescription of the suffixes *matup* and *vani*, and because both are seen in the Vedic language" (Pāṇini 6.1.170).

Furthermore, what Kaiyaṭa stated during the commentary on that [sūtra]—namely, that [the form] is ungrammatical in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*)—refers specifically to the word *maghavan* when it is derived with the suffix *vani* and has the middle syllable as udātta. This is because the suffix *vani* is prescribed only in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Therefore, indicating that there is no contradiction between Kaiyaṭa’s earlier and later statements, he says "in the Vedic language," etc. As for the phrase "but [it is] oxytone,"...

Although initial accentuation (*ādyudāttatva*) is obtained for these words in the case of *śvan* and *ukṣan* by virtue of the authority of Ujjvaladatta and other authors who state that they end in the suffix *kanin*, nevertheless, since the final accentuation (*antodāttatva*) of *ukṣan* and others included in that sūtra is indisputable in instances such as “*ukṣā samudro aruṇaḥ suparṇaḥ*,” “*pūṣā tveto nayatu*,” “*agnirmūrdhā*,” “*nirmajvānaṃ na parvaṇo jabhāra*,” and “*tvamaryamā bhavati yat*,” the suffix *kanip* alone is appropriate; this is the intended meaning.

In the sūtra *maghavā bahulam*, having taken *maghonaḥ* as the illustrative example (*pratīka*), one might suspect the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *ā* of the word *magha-* by the rule *yasya*. Anticipating this, the author of the Nyāsa states: "This is not so; for this is a different, underived nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since its usage is observed even in the common language (*bhāṣā*). Thus, he is in agreement with the view that the word *maghavan* is oxytone and is grammatically correct even in the common language.

This being the case, the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika, while rejecting the substitution of *tra* on the basis of the *matup* suffix, nevertheless accept the long vowel even in the alternative where *tra* is substituted in the word *maghavān*. This is because a rejection [of a rule] is impossible if there is a difference in the resulting form (*phala-bheda*). Therefore, what was stated—that the [substitution of *tra*] is not treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) due to the mention of the term *bahulam*—is indeed in agreement with the Bhāṣya and other authorities. As for what some say—that the intention of the Bhāṣya is that even in the *matup* alternative, there is no long vowel because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*)—that is incorrect, because there is no evidence (*māna*) that a form ending in *matup* is Vedic, and because it contradicts the examples cited by Bhaṭṭi and Kaiyaṭa. Such is the direction of the argument.

By this, Kṣīrasvāmin’s statement that *maghavan*—which is prescribed as a nipātana in the rule *śvan-ukṣan...*—becomes *maghavan* (with a short vowel) due to the substitution of *tr* and the absence of lengthening, is refuted. For the Kātantra-sūtra states: "In the nominative singular (*sau*), [the forms] *maghavān* and *maghavā* [are used]. Furthermore, in the *Vicāracintāmaṇi*, it is stated: "*Maghavān* alone is *maghavā*. Moreover, in the *Kāśikā* as well, only the long vowel is observed; so, enough of this prolixity.

From the root *ṛ*, with the suffix *vic* and the application of *guṇa*, the form *ari* is established; from that, with the suffix *matup*, forms such as *arvantau* and so forth will be successfully derived. By the rule "in the Veda, [the suffixes] *vanip* and *iṣvanip* [are added]," the form *arveti* occurs in the Veda. In common usage (*loka*), however, it will be derived from the root *ṛ* itself with the suffix *vanip*. This is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*), as evidenced by the Amarakośa: "vājī, vāha, arvā, gandharva, haya, saindhava, and sapti. Therefore, there is no difference in meaning.

Nevertheless, since the application of both [forms] ending in *an* would otherwise apply everywhere, this sūtra is intended for the purpose of restriction, like the three sūtras beginning with "tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ. As for what Haradatta stated—that both the words *arvan* and *maghavan* are indeed ungrammatical in the common language (*bhāṣā*) because of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "arvaṇas tṛ maghonaśca"—that is merely superficial, because it has already been explained that the Bhāṣya refers to a specific context. And so Śrīharṣa employed [the word]: "The pride of Indra was shattered by the horses."

Now, one might object: "If the position is that 'phonetic qualities (guṇas) do not cause differentiation,' then even when [the letter] *a* is pronounced without a nasalization (*anunāsika*) in the Sūtra, a nasalized *a* would arise by virtue of being the closest internal correlate (*āntaratamya*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "*ā āditi*" ("[The rule applies] to *ā* and *ā*"). As for what some say: "In this case, there is no nasalization (*anunāsika*), because since it is not an *aṇ*, there is no inclusion of homogeneous letters (*savarṇagrahaṇa*). Nor should it be argued that the rule *taparaḥ tatkālasya* is intended as a positive injunction (*vidhi*) regarding non-*aṇ* sounds; for there is the prohibition: 'A sound being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts. [The author replies: Even if phonetic qualities do not cause differentiation, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because in the Sūtra only a single pure individual instance (*ekavyakti*) is indicated.

In this regard, the following must be said: if there is a doubt that [the rule] "anaṇi" is for the purpose of prescribing [the substitution], then the reply beginning with "bhāvyamāna" is irrelevant; for that [rule] has as its domain the vowels (aṇ).

As they say: "When [the term] 'anitya' and so forth is being considered... Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of a prohibition even in rules such as "coḥ kuḥ". If it is argued that there is no prohibition in that case due to the force of the marker *it* being applied, then what is the point of this effort to catch a crane? Furthermore, in the rule "taparas tatkālasya", the author of the Bhāṣya did not carry forward the mention of "apratyaya" (not being a suffix). Moreover, the statement "of a single pure individual" is inconsistent, because if [the vowel] were non-distinguishing (abhedaka), the fault would be difficult to avoid.

By the statement "only one individual [phoneme] is grasped," the implied meaning is that other individuals are not indicated. And this [implication] is consistent only if the properties (guṇas) serve as differentiators, and not otherwise; let this matter rest for now. By this, the passage from the *Prasāda* commentary—stating that the vowel *ā* is not nasalized because of the prohibition "an *aṇ* being subject to grammatical operation (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)"—is also correctly applied. This is because the root [of that argument] is undermined by the fact that the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is not an *aṇ*.

Both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*), namely *tha* and *nth*, are devoid of vowels (*anackau*). Since the form would be established by the rule *thernth* alone, the explicit statement *ito't* is for the sake of the word *ṛbhukṣin*. Regarding the substitute *nth*: some, however, say it is the substitute *anth*; in that case, the elision of the vowel *a* (the *praśleṣa*) would be redundant.

As for what was stated by the author of the *Nyāsa* and the ancients—that even though [the substitute] consists of multiple consonants (*anekāl*), this is a substitute for the letter *tha* alone, according to the maxim "substitutes apply to that which is not explicitly indicated"—that is not correct; because the specific [element *tha*] does not occur [as a standalone], there is no scope here for the aforementioned paribhāṣā.

He states [the following] as a corollary: "in the feminine," and "supathī. Regarding the form *supathī*, the suffix *kap* is not applied by the rule "inaḥ striyām" (Pāṇini 5.4.152), because the application of suffixes at the end of compounds (*samāsānta*) is not invariably obligatory, and because the form *supathī* appears in the Mahābhāṣya on the sūtra "yuvoranākau" (Pāṇini 7.1.1). Furthermore, this is not the scope of the prohibition "na pūjanāt" (Pāṇini 5.4.69), since it will be stated later that this prohibition applies only to those [words] preceding the root √ṣac. The substitution of *ā* for the final vowel and the replacement of *th* with *nth* in the forms *pathi* and *mathi*, which would otherwise apply to the feminine by the paribhāṣā "liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā," do not take effect here because the feminine base is not grasped when a case-ending follows.

Regarding the word *śau*: as for the explanation given by the predecessors (*prācām*) that the term *suṭ* applies to both rules—"*ita at sarvanāmasthāne*" and "*tho nthaḥ*"—that is incorrect. For it would result in a definition (*lakṣaṇā*) without any basis (*nirbīja*). Furthermore, it would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the neuter form *supathī*, where *auṅ* is replaced by *śī*; and it would entail the impossibility of deriving the form *sapanthāni* in the accusative plural (*śas*). This is the intended meaning.

In this regard, the following should be noted: one who desires a path for oneself is *pathīyati*. From that, the suffix *kvip* is applied; there is elision of the suffix (*alo’paḥ*), and elision of the *y* (*yalopaḥ*). Because a form modified in one part is not considered different from the original, the substitution of *ā* [for the *i*] occurs by the rule *pathimathibhyām* (Pāṇini 7.1.85). The *th* is replaced by *nth*, resulting in *panthāḥ*. The substitution of *ā* by the rule *ito’t sarvanāmasthāne* (Pāṇini 7.1.86) does not take place here, because the *it* in that rule is specified as *tapara* (indicating a short vowel). The substitution of *nth* by the rule *tho nthaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.87) takes precedence over the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82), because it is both subsequent and obligatory (*nitya*). Furthermore, because the *th* is preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), the *yaṇ* substitution does not apply.

*panthiyau*, *panthiyaḥ*, *panthiyam*, *panthiyau*. [In the case of the neuter stem *pathin*: "There is elision of the *ṭi* of a *bha*-stem. Thus: *pathaḥ*, *pathībhyām*, *pathībhiḥ*, and so forth. By this, Haradatta’s statement in his work—that in the rule "ito't sarvanāmasthāne," the addition of the *tapara* marker (*at*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, whether regarding the original element (*sthānin*) or the substitute (*ādeśa*)—is refuted. As for the fact that the author of the Nyāsa and others following him have cited forms such as *pathīḥ*, *pathyau*, and *pathyaḥ* (as if they were *sukhīḥ*, *sutīḥ*), that is questionable; for in the nominative singular (*sāu*), the presence of the vowel *ā* would be unavoidable.

As for the claim that *pathi-mathi-ṛbhukṣām* is an imitation of a base ending in *n*, that too is pointless; for the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) is unavoidable. Furthermore, even in the case of *panthāḥ*, since the substitution of *āt* would necessarily apply first—both because it is a permanent rule and because it is specifically prescribed—the base would no longer end in *n*, and thus the substitution of *nth* would not be applicable.

As for what they say—that because the elision (*allop*) is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitution of *n* for *na* and so forth does not occur—and that the rule "what is elided before *kvip* is not treated as the original element" (*kvau luptaṃ na sthānivat*) is not to be applied here; that too is questionable. For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of applying the *yaṇ* substitution. This is because Kaiyaṭa and others have relied upon the principle "what is elided before *kvip* is not treated as the original element" in order to justify forms such as *sukhīḥ* and *sutīḥ* under the rule *khyatyāt*. Furthermore, this is also consistent with the intention of the author of the Sūtras himself, who employed the marker *t* (as in *itaḥ*) in the rule *ito't* precisely for such cases.

Therefore, it is established that the substitution of *āt* and the replacement by *nth* are indeed correct. By this, forms such as *mathīḥ*, *mathyau*, and *mathyaḥ* are also refuted, because forms such as *manthāḥ*, *manthiyau*, and *manthiyaḥ* alone are logical. As for the forms *ṛbhukṣīḥ*, *ṛbhukṣyau*, and *ṛbhukṣyaḥ*, it has already been stated that the substitution of *āt* is unavoidable before the nominative singular (*su*). Furthermore, the *yaṇ* substitution is impossible in the case of *auṅ* and other endings due to the preceding conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). Therefore, one should understand the forms to be *ṛbhukṣāḥ*, *ṛbhukṣiyau*, *ṛbhukṣiyaḥ*, and so forth.

The statement "those ending in *ṣ* and *n* are six" (*ṣṇāntāḥ ṣaṭ*) is an indication regarding the feminine gender in order to qualify the number. And because of its capacity for such qualification, the author intends that the mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*), though referring to a technical name (*saṃjñā*) in the preceding rule, here becomes a reference to the thing named (*saṃjñin*). With this intention, he says: "the number. As for what the ancients stated—that [the words] end in *ṣ* or *n* at the time of their original instruction (*upadeśa*)—that contradicts his own text, which says, "even when the *n*-elision has been performed in the case of *pañca*," and so forth. If one objects: "Even if they do not end in *ān* now, they did end in *n* during their original instruction; so what is the point of treating [the elision] as 'not established' (*asiddha*)? If you then argue: "But surely this contradiction between earlier and later statements is the same even in the *Kāśikā*," then what of it? [It is of no consequence.]
This is according to the maxim: "When one thing is firmly sublated by its similarity to another, why should the other also not be sublated?

As for what they [the commentators] have explained—that the meaning is "ending with those *ṣ* and *n* sounds which exist at the time of instruction," and that because the connection is with the whole (the compound), it is not an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound where the parts lack mutual expectancy), as in the example "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*)—that is merely superficial. For there is a mutual contradiction in first explaining the connection with the individual parts and then asserting the connection is with the whole. Furthermore, in cases where the subordinate member of a compound has a related referent, there are two ways: one is that even when it possesses a further expectancy (*sāpekṣa*), it may still be compounded.

The primary object itself, such as a potter, has a relation with Devadatta just as it does with his teacher; and that [relation] with the teacher is innate (*utpattigarbha*). However, the relation with Devadatta consists in being produced by that teacher, and thus it is mediated by the teacher (*gurughaṭita*); this is the second type. And it was said by Hari:
"Every relative term is always compounded when it is dependent [on another];
for that very syntactic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) which exists in a sentence is not lost even in a compound."

"And: 'Those things which have a connection with a whole, such as a teacher's family and so forth, come into contact with their parts and are thus joined with that which possesses them. Thus it is said.

In this context, the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is not something that possesses a correlative relation, such that two distinct modes of application could find scope. If it is argued that here too the word *anta* has a meaning involving a correlative relation, we reply: no, because by those who state "the *ṣ* and *n* sounds at the time of instruction," the connection with that [correlative] has been abandoned. Otherwise, one would have to say, "that which has [the sounds] at its end at the time of instruction. In reality, even that is not the case; for the word *anta* is dependent upon a whole (*avayavin*), and not upon just anything whatsoever. Otherwise, there would be the expression "the minister of the wealthy king" (*ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ*), since even the king, as the ruler, is dependent upon the object to be ruled.

According to the lexicon: "The word *rājā* [is used] for a lord, a king, the moon, a Yakṣa, a Kṣatriya, and Śakra. If, however, you say that [the suffix] is not desired when [the word] is *ṛddha*, then the same applies to the present case as well. Regarding the term *saṃnipāta*: thus, the explanation that it refers to "the time of instruction" (*upadeśakāla*) is also fruitless; this is the intended meaning. As for what they say—that because the Paribhāṣā is non-eternal (*anitya*), there would be elision (*luk*)—that is mere rashness. For if it does not apply even in instances where its application is desired, the Paribhāṣā would result in being useless. Furthermore, the claim that it is "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is itself without foundation.

As for what they say—that by the force of the mention of "extremes" (antagrahaṇa), the status of being directly taught (aupadeśikatva) is obtained—that too is not correct; for that force is exhausted by the attraction of the word "number" (saṃkhyā) and by establishing that [the term] refers to the named (saṃjñin).
In the expression "nopadhāyāḥ na," the word "na" is a qualifier of the "base" (aṅga) with its genitive case elided.
As for the phrase "but in the case of being secondary" (gauṇatve tu), the intention is that the mention of the plural number is for the sake of emphasizing the meaning (arthaprādhānya).

Regarding *priyapañca*: there is the letter *ca* between two *ña*s. [The rule] *aṣṭana ā halādau* [is formed]. The word *hali* is drawn down from the subsequent sūtra *rāyo hali*; the intention is that this (*hali*) qualifies the case-ending (*vibhakteḥ*). Consequently, in the form *aṣṭānām*, the substitution of *ā* occurs only after the addition of the augment *nuṭ*, because the Paribhāṣā regarding the loss of causal efficacy (*sannipāta-paribhāṣā*) is not universal; it does not occur before. Otherwise, if the state *aṣṭan ām* were reached, then since the substitution of *ā* would apply by virtue of being both subsequent (*paratvāt*) and obligatory (*nityatvāt*), the stem would no longer end in *n*. As a result, the designation *ṣaṭ* would not apply, and thus the augment *nuṭ* would not occur.

Nor should it be argued that, under the view that the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is assigned according to its enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), the designation "six" (*ṣat*)—having been applied previously due to its being an internal rule (*antaraṅga*)—remains easily available even after the substitution of *āt* by virtue of the maxim of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). The point is that this maxim cannot apply in a rule concerning an *al* (phoneme).

Regarding the statement "auś is substituted for *aṣṭan* when followed by a form ending in *kṛta-ākāra*" (*kṛtākārāt*): one might object, "But was it not stated that the condition *halī* (when followed by a consonant) is elided [from the previous rule]? How then can it be said 'when followed by a form ending in *kṛta-ākāra*'? To this he says: "For *aṣṭabhyaḥ*. This is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the form where the substitution of *ātva* (the change to *āṣṭā-*) has already occurred; it is not an *ātva* produced by the force of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇavaśasampanna*). For if that were the case, since that [substitution] would be optional according to the indicator (*jñāpaka*) to be mentioned later, the author would have simply said "*aṣṭabhyaḥ*" for the sake of brevity—this is the intended meaning. The word "this" (*idam*) means both what is directly heard (*śruta*) and what is inferred (*anumita*).

Regarding the rule *aṣṭano dīrghāt*: a case-ending that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* should be acute (udātta) when it follows the word *aṣṭan* ending in a long vowel (*dīrgha*). For example: *aṣṭābhiḥ*. Why "ending in a long vowel"? Consider *aṣṭabhiḥ*; this word has the acute accent on the middle syllable. This is because the rule *jhalyupottamam* takes precedence over the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādi*. The meaning of that [latter] rule is: "In a word ending in a case-ending beginning with a consonant (*jhal*) following *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, or *catur*, the penultimate (*upottama*) syllable shall be acute. This being the case, the purpose of making the substitution of *ā* (the *ātva*) compulsory would be redundant if it were intended merely to exclude the short vowel. Therefore, the point is that the *ātva* must be established as permanent.

Regarding the phrase "even from the preceding [rule]": the meaning is that in this way, the *ṣṭutva* substitution does not occur in the example *priyāṣṭṇaḥ*, as illustrated by Haradatta. Nor is there a prohibition based on the rule "that which is not established in what precedes is not like the original" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*), because that rule has exceptions, being itself subject to counter-exceptions (*sāpavāda*). If it is argued: "We shall take the *ṇatva* prescribed directly by the rule *raṣābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.4.1], and not that which is obtained through the rule for *ṣṭutva*," we say: "Not so. For according to the view of the Bhāṣya, that [direct prescription] is not applicable here.

For instance, in the rule *raṣābhyām*, the mention of the letter *ṇ* is made by carrying forward (*anuvartana*) the rule *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ*; furthermore, the prohibitive rule *padāntasya* has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. Nor is it easy to maintain a distinction between a *ṇ* produced by the term *mūrdhanya* (retroflex) or by the term *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṣṭu*); since the authority of the sages increases with each successive one, the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) alone is appropriate.

In the *Śabdakaustubha*, a conclusion was reached that the mention of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) in the rule "atasya doṣaḥ" should not be necessary; following that line of reasoning, he says: "in the view of the time of application (*kāryakālapakṣa*). Nor should it be argued that one should instead rely on the view of the locus of origin (*yathoddeśapakṣa*) and allow for *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṣṭu*). The point is that since a difference in results would make a refutation impossible, the view of the time of application alone is appropriate here. For this very reason, one should not harbor any hope for *ṣṭutva* even by supporting the refutation of the compound with the fifth case (*pañcamīsamāsa*).

Since the position that the operation takes place at the time of the effect (kāryakālapakṣa) is more logical for the sake of achieving a single result, the fact that [the condition] is unestablished (asiddhatva) is unavoidable. As for the argument that—on the basis of the indicator (jñāpaka) in the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*—"the status of being as if the original were present (sthānivadbhāva) is not permanent with respect to an operation preceding [the cause], and thus it does not apply here"—the invocation of such non-permanence is indeed improper; however, let this matter rest for now.

Regarding the rule *jaśśasoḥ*: the substitution of *auś* does not occur when [the stem] is secondary (*gauṇatve*), just as elision (*luk*) and the augment *nuṭ* do not; this is because of the use of the plural form in the rule *aṣṭābhyaḥ*. Otherwise, even if the form were an imitation of that which has already undergone the change to *ā*, the author would have indicated it using the singular alone—as in *aṣṭā auś* or simply *aṣṭa*. This point is clear in both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*. Thus, by the force of the mention of the form with *ā* in the prescription for *auś*, it is logical that the *ā*-change itself is intended only in the case of primary application.

And likewise, having raised the objection that in the *jas* [case-ending] there should be only *priyāṣṭānaḥ* and not *priyāṣṭāḥ*, the *Bhāṣya* states: "as prescribed, [it applies] when not used. Kaiyaṭa explains that the meaning is that the substitution of *ātva* does not occur at all in this case. Vāmana also, under the rule *aṣṭābhya auś*, having stated that the term includes those ending in *aṣṭan* (i.e., *paramāṣṭau*), says that because *ātva* is absent in *priyāṣṭānaḥ*, the substitution of *auś* does not take place.

As for Haradatta, however—he having cited the commentary (*vṛtti*) passage from that very same work, "regarding *priyāṣṭānaḥ*," and having promised that he would explain how the substitution of *āt* does not occur when [the word] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatā*) within that very rule—how is it that he stated something contrary to his own prior promise and opposed to the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and other authorities, by saying in the rule "aṣṭana ā vibhaktau" that because of the mention of the singular number, the substitution of *āt* occurs even in a secondary sense, and that there is elision of the *ā* before a case-ending in non-ṅi-vibhakti contexts, as in *priyāṣṭaḥ paśya*?
He alone must be questioned on this matter.

Regarding the phrase "only when [the word] begins with a consonant" (*halādāveva*): although it appears in the Bhāṣya that an explanation could be given even without carrying back the rule *halī* (P. 8.2.77), the point is that its inadequacy has been demonstrated elsewhere. *Priyāṣṭāḥ* is the nominative singular. He summarizes what was stated in the words *priyāṣṭnaḥ*. [This concludes the section on] those ending in *n*.
*bhud* [is derived] from the root *budh* with the suffix *kvip*. [These are] those ending in *dh*.

Regarding *ṛtvig*, *dadhṛk*, and *kiṃcit*: after the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), with *ṛtu* as an upapada, there is the suffix *kvin*. After *dhṛṣ* (to dare), there is reduplication and the udātta accent on the final syllable. After *sṛj* (to emit), there is *kvin* in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the augment *am*. [The same applies] to *diś* (to point) in the sense of the object. After *snih* (to love) preceded by *ud*, there is *kvin*, with the elision of the final vowel of the prefix and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. After *añc* (to bend), there is *kvin* when a *sup*-ending word is the upapada; such is the meaning. Regarding *yuj*: the same applies to *kuñc* (to contract); however, the absence of *nalopa* (the elision of *n*) is additional. Regarding *kan*: the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*); this is the intended sense.

Regarding the phrase *sannihite* (when [the word] is present): as for the claim of earlier scholars that [this refers to] the third section concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), that is incorrect; for in the rule prescribing the suffix *san*, there is no mention of the term *dhātu* to be carried forward to subsequent rules, and thus there is no threefold governing context (*adhikāra*). Regarding the rule *yujerasamāse sarva-*: as for what was stated by the ancients—that [the term *sarvanāmasthāna*] means *suṭ*—that is incorrect, because the term *sarvanāmasthāna* itself is the subject under discussion, and there is no reason to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); furthermore, it would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the dual form *yuñjī* when it is neuter. As for what they say—that in the neuter form *yuñjī* before the suffix *śas*, the augment *num* would not occur—that is also incorrect, because the *num* is possible by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *sulopa*: since the substitution of *k* for *t* (*kutva*) is considered asiddha, the *num* augment occurs first because it applies subsequently; thereafter, the elision of the case-ending occurs according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...*—this is the intended meaning. As for the statement made by the ancients that [the elision of *n*] occurs when a *jhal* sound follows, that is incorrect, because the word *jhalī* is not present in proximity and because such a condition would be useless. As for the explanation given by the grandson (Tatpautra)—that even if *jhalī* is understood to carry over from the rule *jhalo jhali* via the "frog-leap" principle (*maṇḍūkapluti*), there is no fault—that too is incorrect, because it would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *spaṣṭaḥ*. *Khan*: [The form] *khan* is derived from the root *khaj*, meaning "to limp" or "to be lame" (*gativaikalye*). Thus, one who limps is *khan*.

"parau vrajeḥ" and "dīrghaśca. As for what was explained by the ancients—that *viṇ* [is the suffix] and that there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel because of its *ṇit*-character—that is incorrect, because in both the *Pañcapādī* and the *Daśapādī*, only *kvip* and lengthening (*dīrgha*) are prescribed by this rule.

He explains [the phrase] "of *sk* and *k*" as having a dropped genitive case, qualifying [the suffixes] ending in *jhal*—this is shown by the words beginning with "padānte. [The form] *bhṛṭ* is derived from *bhṛjjati* with *kvip*. Regarding "of *s*" (in *sasya*), the meaning is that since the substitution of *jaś* is not yet established (*asiddha*), the substitution of *ścu* occurs first. By this, the contradictory statement of the ancients is refuted.

*Ūrj-*. The root *ūrj* means "to strengthen" and "to give life. From this root, which belongs to the *curādi* class and takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule "bhrājabhāsa... etc. There is the elision of *ṇi*. Furthermore, that [elision] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were present) when the change of *cu* to *ku* occurs, because it is a rule concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*) and because it is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to what precedes it.

Here, among words ending in *j*, *avayāḥ* is not cited as an example; for, having introduced the rule "śvetavahoktha... in the mantra, the suffix *ṇvin* prescribed by "ave yajaḥ" and its exception, the suffix *ḍas* at the end of a word, are both Vedic (*chāndasa*).

As for what was stated by the ancients—"śvetavāḍukthaśāspuroḍāśāvayajāṃ ḍas"—that is incorrect, because the long vowel [required] does not occur in the two roots *vah* and *yaj*, which are the bases (*prakṛti*) of the suffix *ḍas*.

Furthermore, regarding the citation of "avayā" as a marker (*pratīka*), the ancients explained it as being formed by the suffix *ṇvi*; that too is incorrect, because the general rule (*utsarga*) of *ṇvi* does not apply within the scope of the exception (*apavāda*) *ḍas*.

Regarding the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ*: why specify "not being final" (*anantyayoḥ*)? [Consider the example] *he sa*. Due to its higher status (*paratvāt*), the substitution of *sa-* would apply, overriding the substitution of *yatva* for *tyadādi* stems; consequently, after the elision of the case-ending by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, the substitution of *ru* and the visarga would occur. Furthermore, the form *sā* in the feminine would not be possible. However, in reality, the mention of "not being final" (*anantyagrahaṇam*) can be omitted. Nor does the aforementioned fault arise, because when a rule is understood to apply again (*punaḥprasaṅgavijñāne*), the substitution of *yatva* for *tyadādi* stems is indeed possible.

Even in the view that [the rule] applies only once (*sakṛdgatau*), it is possible to explain the rule by dividing the *yoga* immediately after "tadoḥ saḥ sau" as "adasaḥ," thereby establishing that the substitution of *s* occurs only for the *d* of *adas* and not for any other *d*. If it is argued: "In the alternative arrangement (*anyāsa*), the form *sva* would result from the root *dvīyati* with the suffix *kvip*, whereas under the restrictive rule (*niyama*), the form would be *dva*"; we say: do not say so. Since the substitutions of *atva* and *satva* cannot apply to a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense, the form *dvīḥ* alone is what is logically correct.

The phrase *ṅe prathamayoram* is a separate word with its sixth case ending elided. He explains that the word *prathamā* is used figuratively for the collective pair of the first and second [cases] by means of the passage beginning with *ṅe ityasya*. It would be easier to say *ṅe-suṭoḥ am*.

The phrase "with the intention of expressing the locus" (*adhikaraṇatvavivakṣayā*) is used because if *śeṣe* were a qualifier of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), it would be entirely redundant; for in its own domain, the elision (*lopa*) would necessarily be superseded by the specifically prescribed *ātva* and *yatva*. Nor does this result in the position that there is elision of the final letter (*antyalopa*) becoming baseless, because that [elision of the final] is also indicated by the mention of the form with the augment *suṭ* in the rule *sāma ākam*. [The example] is *yuvaṃ vastrāṇi*; here, the elision occurs by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ*.
As for what was stated in the *Kāśikā*:
In this [section], the elision (lopa) is prescribed for the dual endings of the fifth and fourth cases, as well as for those of the sixth and first cases,
when they remain [unreplaced].

Thus, this is with respect to that [secular] language. However, it should be understood that even the nominative dual is indeed within the scope of the elision (*lopa*) of the *śeṣa* in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).
[The question] "Why [is it said] 'of that which ends in *map*'? is a question as to what purpose the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) serves.

Regarding the phrase *aṅgakārye*: by this, the *paribhāṣā* "when an operation has already taken place within the domain of an *aṅga*, there is no further application [of another rule]" is established by implication. Its meaning is as follows: *aṅgavṛtte* means that in which (*yasya*) there is an occurrence (*vṛttaṃ* = *vartanaṃ*) within the section concerning *aṅgas* (*aṅgādhikāre*); when that grammatical rule (*śāstra*) has been applied—that is, when it has become active—and a further application of another [rule] is about to occur, there is "no application" (*avidhiḥ*). It is established in the *Bhāṣya* that this *paribhāṣā* is indicated by both the two rules: *jyādādīyasaḥ* and *jñājanorjā*.

Otherwise, [Pāṇini] would not have stated the vowel *ā* in the rule *jyādād...* [P. 6.4.160]; instead, he would have merely continued the elision (*lopa*) from the rule *bahoḥ lopaḥ* [P. 6.4.158]. Furthermore, since the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] is established by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ dīrghaḥ* [P. 7.4.25], the form *jyāyān* would be correctly derived even without this specific rule. Moreover, he would have prescribed the substitution of *ja* for the roots *jñā* and *jan* [in P. 6.1.197]; then the lengthening would occur by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* [P. 7.3.101]. Nor should it be argued that, in the case of *dvābhyām*, once the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* etc. has taken place, the lengthening required by *supi ca* [P. 7.3.102] would not apply; for the mention of forms such as *dvayoḥ* and *ekasya* indicates that the aforementioned paribhāṣā (the rule regarding the non-application of a subsequent rule when a previous one has already applied) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

As for the claim made by some—that they read "pariniṣṭhitasya" (of that which is fully established) and argue that [the rule] is not fully established without the long vowel in the case of "dvābhyām"—that contradicts the Bhāṣya. For if [the forms] "jyāyān," "jānāti," and "jñāyate" were also not fully established without the long vowel, then even the indication stated in the Bhāṣya would be rendered baseless.

If, however, the reading in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *bhyaso 'bhyam* is indeed *pariniṣṭhitasya*, then it should be interpreted as referring to an alternative view by relying solely on its status as a specific scriptural injunction (*vācanikatā*). Alternatively, let it be that this statement merely expresses the result achieved through the force of [the rule's] non-eternality (*anityatva*), and does not actually enter into the scope of what is to be indicated (*jñāpyāṃśa*). In this way, even the text of the Kāśikā and other works can be somehow reconciled; such is the direction of the argument.

The phrase "immediately following the letter *m*" (*makārāntaram*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should be understood that this is either because, in the rule "jasah śī" (Pāṇini 7.1.17), the letter *s* is elided into the word "jasah" as "jaḥ saḥ," and thus the rule is explained as applying to a *jas* ending in *s*; or because, by carrying forward the mention of "am" from the rule "ato'm" (Pāṇini 7.1.24), the rule is explained as applying specifically to the suffix *am*.

Regarding the term *avibhaktikam*: it was raised as an objection in the *Bhāṣya* that this [rule] serves as a prohibition of the *ām* suffix which would otherwise have been obtained by the preceding rule, "ṅe prathamayoḥ. Nor should it be argued that this [prohibition] could simply be taken as it stands; for in the case of feminine and neuter nouns, the substitution of *n* would not be obtained—as in the examples *yuṣmān brāhmaṇīḥ* or *kulāni*; furthermore, if there were no gender distinction, forms such as *yuṣmān brāhmaṇān* and so forth would result in being unestablished.

In the rule *yo'ci aci*, why is *aci* mentioned? [Answer: *yuvābhyām*. However, if in the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe* the word *hali* is understood as being carried over (*anuvartate*) from the rule *rāyo hali*, then *aci* need not be mentioned here, since the desired result is established by elimination alone. [The meaning would then be: *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [take the augment *āt*] when there is no substitute (*anādeśe*) beginning with a consonant (*hal-ādau*). This is established by elimination because of the mention of *ac* in *yo'ci*. Or rather, it is obtained through the carry-over from *rāyo hali*. [Objection: If this is so, what is the purpose of mentioning *anādeśe*? For there is no substitute that begins with a consonant. [Reply: Not so, because [the substitute] *bhyas* exists [which begins with a consonant]. But in the view where *bhyas* is replaced by *abhyam*, it should be understood that the mention of *anādeśe* is for the sake of carrying it over to the rule *yo'ci*.

Regarding the phrase "in both cases": it should not be argued that in the case of the final elision (*antyalopa*), the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous quality) would apply by overriding the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form), on the grounds of the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the utterance of the letter 'a'. For the utterance of the letter 'a' has its purpose fulfilled by the prevention of the substitution of *et* (the short *e*).

The substitution of *aś* for the genitive case ending (*ṅas*) after the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is marked with the *śit* designation in order to ensure it replaces the entire word. Otherwise, by the rule "ādeḥ parasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), it would replace only the first letter. Nor is this designation redundant, as its purpose is to prevent the application of the *yatva* sandhi (the change of *d* to *y*). One should not argue that even if a portion of the word is replaced, the case ending itself remains unreplaced; for according to the established doctrine, "all [substitutes] are substitutes for the entire word. This very *śit*-designation implies that "all [substitutes] are substitutes for the entire word. The meaning is that the status of being a substitute for an original element (*sthānin*) and an element to be substituted (*ādeśa*) rests only upon meaningful units. However, forms such as *sic*, *caṅ*, and others should be understood to apply even to meaningless elements by virtue of the force of specific grammatical rules.

However, this must be noted: under the view that the final letter is elided (*antyalopa-pakṣa*), the substitution of *sy* would have been applicable [to the final *as*]; it must therefore be prevented by the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*. If one stubbornly maintains that this maxim applies only to operations concerning the *aṅga* itself and not to those merely falling within the jurisdiction of the *aṅga*-heading (*aṅgādhikāra*), then the explanation must be as follows: in the form *aś*, the vowel *a* is understood as being included (*praśliṣṭa*) through the application of *pararūpa* (the subsequent form) according to the rule *ato guṇe*; thus, *aś* remains in the form of the vowel *a* and does not undergo modification. As for the claim that *aś* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *sy*, that is incorrect;
because at the time when the substitution of *aś* is to take effect, the elision of the remainder (*śeṣe lopaḥ*) has not yet occurred, the substitution of *sy* is not even applicable.

Regarding the word *bhāvinaḥ*: the intention is that when the *śeṣe lopaḥ* (elision of the final phoneme) has been applied, the augment *suṭ* would apply because the stem ends in the vowel *a*; however, this is prevented by the force of the designation [of the whole form] as having *suṭ* as its substitute. But according to the view that *śeṣe lopaḥ* means the elision of the *ṭi* (the final phoneme), the mention of *suṭ* would indeed be redundant. The pronunciation of the long vowel in *ākam* is for the sake of the *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening of similar vowels); otherwise, the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) would apply. Nor can it be argued that the pronunciation of the long *ā* is purposeful on its own; for, like in the case of *abhyam*, it serves its purpose simply by preventing the substitution of *et*.

In this context, regarding the two rules "yuvāvau dvivacane" and "tvamāvekavacane," it has been explained that the terms *dvivacana* (dual) and *ekavacana* (singular) do not refer to the suffixes themselves, but rather to their meanings. He demonstrates the result of this [explanation] with the words beginning "samasyamāne" (when being compounded). The phrase "dvyekatva" (duality and singularity) refers to the fact that, according to the view that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five elements, number (*saṅkhyā*) is also included within the meaning of the nominal stem. The term "samāsārtha" (the meaning of the compound) refers to the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*). The phrase "anyasaṅkhyaśced" (if it possesses another number) means: if it possesses a number other than the number inherent in the meanings of the stems *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

The word "are" [in the commentary] means that because one relies on the principle of being directed toward the meaning (*arthaparatva*), one necessarily accepts the understanding of what was previously the case (*bhūtapūrvagati*). However, if there were dependence on the suffix (*pratyayaparatva*), those two [forms] would not occur, and thus there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*). Likewise, in the fourth verse, by the statement "the forms *yuva* and *āva*, as well as *tva* and *ma*, do not [occur]," the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) when there is dependence on the suffix is indicated. Thus, it follows that the principle of being directed toward the meaning has been adopted in order to avoid both under-extension and over-extension.

And there is no contradiction with the principle of the artificial and the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*), because that [principle] is set aside by the very force (*sāmarthya*) of the mention of the word "vibhakti" (in the rule). For otherwise, one would have simply said *dvitvaikatvayoḥ*; since it would have been possible to explain the rule as: "the case-ending (*vibhakti*) which occurs in the sense of duality and singularity—of that, [the suffix] *ām*. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the expression *atitvākam* and *atimākam*: although in the rule *sāma ākam*, the mention of *suṭ* is not a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the substituendum because it is superseded (*bādha*), it nevertheless serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, only that *ām* which is followed by *suṭ* should be replaced by *ākam*. And this is not possible when [the word] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*); thus, *ākam* does not apply. Furthermore, when there is a reference to a whole aggregate (*samudāya*), no third alternative exists apart from being either a qualifier or an indicator.

Furthermore, *suṭ* and *ām* are not here indicated as having separate status as substituends (*sthānin*), because of the absence of the word *ca* and because [the former] is a dual ending. Even if it were explained as a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*)—namely, *s* and *ām*—and *suṭ* alone were understood by the word *s-* through the force of logical fitness, even so, if the mention of *suṭ* were merely an incidental addition (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*), then there would be no compound. However, elsewhere, since the intention is to express their coexistence (*sāhitya*), the occurrence of *ām* alone is impossible.

In this regard, the following must be said: first of all, the rule "suṭ is applied before [the suffix] am" and so forth is sublated, because there can be no connection of *suṭ* with that which has been superseded by *ākam*. If it is argued that *suṭ* applies to *ākam*, then it would have to characterize that very form. If it is argued that it characterizes the original base (*sthānin*) through an indirect relationship mediated by the substitute (*ādeśa*), then alas, *suṭ* would be heard in forms such as *yuṣmām* (for *yuṣmākam*). If it is argued that it is not heard because of the force of the technical designation *sāma*, we say no.

Because the purpose of the grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) is fulfilled by the exclusion of the secondary meaning (*gauṇa*), it lacks the capacity [to establish the desired sense]. Furthermore, the objection raised regarding the formation of a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) on the grounds that it would be taught as a subsequent alternative (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*) is likewise untenable. What remains is merely the claim that a simple [compound] is not applicable because of the intention to express coexistence (*sāhitya*). But even that is not so; for coexistence is accepted precisely through the inclusion of both the *ām* suffix as it exists at the stage of grammatical derivation and the *suṭ* augment—which is imagined as occurring at a later time—within a single conceptual apprehension.

This is like the expression, "the seer of the past and the future. If it is argued that in that case there is a connection between both [past and future] in a single act of seeing, then here too it is the same: there is a connection in a single grammatical operation (*ādeśa*). Thus, regarding the rule *irayoḥ*, in forms such as *dadhre* from the root *dhā*, when the *jha* suffix is replaced by *irec*, and after the elision of *ā* and the substitution of *re*, since that [substitution] has already served its purpose in roots such as *kṛ*, *sṛ*, and *bhṛ*, the augment *iṭ* is applied; then, because of the dual mention in the rule *irayoḥ*, the substitution of *re* is performed again even for that which is derived through a secondary grammatical operation (*lākṣaṇika*). This is established in the original treatise (*ākara*). Furthermore, in *irayoḥ*, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), whereas in *sāma*, there is a *dvandva* (copulative compound). However, the intention to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*) is exactly the same in both cases.
