In reality, however, in the rule *sāma ākam*, the suffix *ām* alone is also indicated by means of *tantra*. Because it possesses the status of being final (*antva*) through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, and because it is accompanied by the augment *suṭ*, the form *sāma* applies [to the word *tvad* and *mad*]. But in the case of secondary (gauṇa) usage, the matter is settled by the very first application [of the rule]. For this very reason, the identity of result is established even with the alternative view that there is elision (*lopa*) in the remainder (*śeṣe*), namely the elision of the *ṭi* portion. In any case, one should not be dogmatic in attempting to justify forms such as *atitvayām* and *atimayām* imagined by some; for forms such as *atitvākam* and *atimākam* have been cited by the author of the Bhāṣya himself. This is the general direction.

Regarding the phrase "of the two [words] qualified by the sixth case, etc.": this is obtained through the governing rule (adhikāra) of the word "pada" (word). However, he will explain that the mention of the term *sthā* (standing/remaining) is for the purpose that [the substitution] should occur only when the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is actually heard (*śrūyamāṇā*), and not when it is elided (*luptā*).
"By all the Vedas... [and so on]: "May Govinda protect you; may Kṛṣṇa always protect us."
However, the reading of the ancient authorities has been rejected, because [the word] "asmān" (us) cannot possibly apply since it does not belong to the same sentence.

Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of *stha*": here, the root *sthā* (to stand) signifies "not abandoning" (*ahāni*). As in the example, "O Sugrīva, stand by your agreement," which is understood to mean "do not abandon the agreement. Therefore, the meaning is that the substitutes [for *tvad* and *mad*] occur only when they do not abandon the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. Thus, in the case of *yuṣmatputraḥ*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the son of you two" (*yuvayoḥ putraḥ*) or "the son of you all" (*yuṣmākam putraḥ*). The word *iti* is used to ensure that [the compound] follows after a word (*pada*). However, this was not employed by the Easterners (*prācām*). In their view, since there would be no status of following a word (*padāt paratvam*), the substitute would not occur anyway; so what is the purpose of the mention of *stha*?

"Not with *ca* and so forth, up to the pentad" means that there is a connection with any one among those five. Regarding the word "yukta," the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) for a neuter noun.

See that for this very reason, by virtue of a grammatical irregularity (nipātana), the suffix *śa* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Thus, *darśanam* becomes *paśyaḥ*. And here, that [term] refers to mere cognition (*jñānamātra*), just as in the rule "the non-perception [of a sound] is its elision" (*adarśanaṃ lopaḥ*). It does not refer exclusively to visual perception, because of the prohibition [in Pāṇini's sūtra] "except in the sense of looking" (*anālocane*). This is what he expresses by saying: "with words meaning non-visual cognition."

Regarding the passage beginning with "bhakta" (devoted), the commentators have explained it as follows: one should construe it thus—"For the very same reason that you are devoted to Hari, I too am devoted. However, if by the word "tena" (by that) the state of being devoted were indicated as the cause for protection, then, because this would involve a dependent prescription (*sāpekṣavidhāna*), there could be no subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) such as "you yourself [should protect] him."

In this regard, the following must be said: first of all, the claim that there is no status as an *anvādeśa* (subsequent mention) when there is a rule dependent on something else is untenable. For an *ādeśa* is indeed a prescription (*vidhi*). An *anvādeśa*, however, is the prescription of another thing after having prescribed something [else]; it does not consist in independence, because that is not the meaning of the word, and because it has not been so defined in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). Nor should it be argued that such a definition is merely inferred from observation of usage, as in:
"His bark was torn away by wild elephants; then the daughter of the Mountain grieved for him."

Since forms such as these are observed even when there is dependence [on another word], and since the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is not explicitly expressed by the word itself—if you say this, we reply: no;
therefore, let this man, who has transgressed the sacred law, be made a guest of the abode of Yama (the God of Death) by your decree.

This is because it contradicts such usages as those found in Māgha. As for the phrase "this [person] is timid by night," this is not an injunction (*vidhi*), but rather a restatement (*anuvāda*); therefore, the expression "him" (*tam imam*) is not contradictory. This being the case, the laborious effort of supplying an unstated relative pronoun (*yacchabda*) in the sense of "by whom you are worshipped" (*yena tvaṃ bhaktaḥ*) is pointless. Rather, the connection is simply "by him he is saved" (*tena trāyate*). Furthermore, since the subject matter has already been introduced, there is no requirement for a relative pronoun; such is the direction of the argument.

In this context, the word *tena* exists; following that is *hariḥ*, ending in the nominative case; and after that comes the substitute (*ādeśa*). Likewise, after the word *trāyate*, there is *saḥ*, ending in the nominative case. One should not be deluded into thinking that *trāyate* belongs to a separate sentence, for through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application), multiple grammatical factors are connected as in "May that Hari protect you. Furthermore, even if one accepts the principle of *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a missing word), the status of being a single sentence—defined by the technical rule "that which contains a single finite verb is a sentence"—is not lost.

Even though the term *āmantrita* (vocative) is used to designate the act of addressing, the inclusion of that which ends in it (*tadanta*) is understood by virtue of the capacity of the formation of a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*). Addressing is *āmantrita*. By metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), the term applies to the means of accomplishing that act. With the intention that one addresses by means of a word ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*) and not by the case-suffix alone, he says: "that which ends in it."

Regarding what was previously stated—that an address (āmantrita) is treated as if non-existent when it precedes [another word]—it was said by some: "With the exception of an address that precedes the qualified noun (viśeṣya) or another address, these substitutes do not occur for the two [words] following a different address. In this regard, the phrase "by some" (kecit) is inappropriate, because the point already stated is established by the two sūtras under discussion. Furthermore, their explanation that "this is the meaning of the three sūtras" is incorrect, because the meaning of the third sūtra is not touched upon by that [explanation].
[The rule] "pādaḥ pat, provided it is a part of that" is obtained through the technical rule (paribhāṣā): "Substitutes apply to that which is being specifically indicated."

Regarding the form *agnimanth* as in "he churns the fire": this very form arises from the roots *mathnāti* and *manthate* with the suffix *kvip*. However, because the root is marked with the *it* augment, there is no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Thus, we have *agniman*, *agnimanthau*, and *agnimanthaḥ*.
"Regarding the letter *ṅ*": the sense is that it is due to the closest similarity (*āntaratamya*).
"Between a short vowel and a consonant": the sense is that for a consonant, a short vowel is slightly similar, whereas a long vowel is dissimilar.

"And it has been stated": the remainder [of the sentence] is "by the author of the Vārttika. However, some cite *amudryaṅ* as an example based on the substitution of *m* for the preceding [nasal]; since that is not mentioned in the Bhāṣya and other such works, it has been disregarded.
This is an exception to [the rule] *uda īt aci*. [The following consonants] end in *c*: [the *c*-group].

Regarding the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ*, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others maintain that the phrase *adhātoḥ* is here separated as a distinct *yoga*. By virtue of this, the prohibition applies only to that which ends in *as* immediately following [the preceding rule], and not to that which ends in *at*. This is what he demonstrates by saying: "of that which ends in *as*, being different from a verbal root.

Since the desired result is already established by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of both [rules]—namely, *abhyastam* and *dve*—he explains that the mention of *ubhe* (both) is for the purpose of understanding them as a collective whole: "both together. Otherwise, in a form such as *nenijati*, the acute accent on the first syllable prescribed by the rule *abhyastānām ādiḥ* would apply optionally to each individual [syllable] in turn.

The six beginning with *jakṣ*—here *jakṣ* is a separate word; by the word *iti*, only the root *jakṣiti* is referred to. The compound "those of which *iti* is the first" (*iti-ādayaḥ*) is a *bahuvrīhi* of the type where the qualities [of the members] are not understood as applying to the whole (an *atad-guṇa-saṃvijñāna*). This is what he states: "the other six roots. They end in *-t*.
The root *gup* means "to protect. When the suffix *kvip* is intended, there is no application of the augment *āya* according to the rule "āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā. [These are] the roots ending in *p*.

Regarding the rule *tyadādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane kañ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.60): [The suffix *kañ* is applied after the root *dṛś* when it occurs with words beginning with *tyad* (pronouns), provided the sense is not that of "perceiving"]. Why say "provided the sense is not that of perceiving"? Consider *tatpaśyatīti taddarśaḥ* ("one who sees that"). Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. Words such as *tādṛśa* and others, however, being conventional (*rūḍhi*) terms, are etymologically derived even though their constituent meaning is non-existent. For this very reason, the statement "after the root *dṛś* in the sense of 'not knowing'" is consistent. In the Bhāṣya, however, the derivation is shown in the sense of the object acting as the agent (*karmakartṛ*): "People see him as if he were that" (*tamivemaṃ paśyanti janāḥ*), or "he sees like that" (*sa ivāyaṃ paśyati*). The meaning is that he becomes an object of cognition.

In this context, although [the term] functions merely as the state of becoming an object (*viṣayatvāpatti*), it is consistent [to say it does not function] as the act of making an object (*viṣayīkaraṇa*), because the meaning is "unknown" (*ajñāta*). Alternatively, the form *naśi* here—even when followed by a *jhal* consonant—is un-Pāṇinian; furthermore, it would over-apply (*atiprasakta*) to forms such as *naṣṭam*.
[The root] *ṇagati* [is used]; the six suffixes (*ṣaḍagakāḥ*) are as before. [The roots] ending in *ś* are finished.

The phrase "even when there is an intervention by *num*, *visarjanīya*, *ś*, or *r*" refers to the application of *ṣṭutva*. When the *s* of *san* has been changed to *ru* and then to *visarjanīya*, the letter *s* optionally remains in one alternative due to the rule "vā śari. Consequently, when there is an intervention by a *śar* sound, the *s* of the *sup* [suffix] undergoes *ṣatva*, and the preceding [letter] undergoes *ṣṭutva*; however, it does not become *ṣ* by the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ," because that is prohibited by the condition "not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya*). This being the case, since the desired result is already established by the mention of *sakāra*, the purpose of mentioning *śar* must be considered.

Regarding the phrase "from the commentary": the statement by Haradatta that [the rule] is impossible is not to be respected, because [the application] is possible in the case of *suhinsu*; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the term *saṃyogānta* (elision of a final consonant cluster): one should not suspect that the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) on the grounds of being "extrinsic" (*bahiraṅga*) when this [elision of the cluster] is to be applied; for the elision of the final cluster is itself extrinsic, as it depends upon the designation of a word (*pada-saṃjñā*). If it is asked: "How then is it previously stated that there is no elision of the final cluster when one is speaking of *kāvyaṃ*, *kalatraṃ*, or *śālvaṃ*?", the answer is: no.

In that context, regarding the two positions—"there is a prohibition of *yaṇ*" and "or rather, not so, because of the elision of the *jhal* [consonant]"—once the absence of elision has been determined in both cases, it is appropriate to accept the principle that "each preceding rule is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than each subsequent one" for the sake of consistency. This is because it is clear that the status of being a word (*padatva*), which is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), and the elision conditioned by it, find their final rest in the portion of the linguistic item (*lakṣya*) preceding them. However, in the present case, since the elision of the final consonant of a cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is evident in the first two positions, it is more logical to maintain the principle that "that which depends on external causes is more external (*bahiraṅga*)," so as to ensure consistency with that. Such is the direction of the argument.

Regarding the passage beginning with *takṣirakṣabhyām* and so forth: as for what some say—that when [words] such as *śukla*, *cakra*, or *śukra* are being taught, there is the elision of the *kal* suffix; thus [one would derive] *śul*, *śuklau*, *śulbhyām*; *caḥ*, *cakrau*, *carbhyām*; *śūḥ*, *śukrau*, *śūrbhyām*, and so on—all of that is refuted by this [rule]. However, this is the distinction: while the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) in the case of *tagrāg* is beyond dispute, in that [other] case, even that [elision] is difficult to obtain.

Regarding *didhagiti*: as for what was stated by Naimiṣīya—that because the substitution of *ḍha* for *dha* [by Pāṇini 8.2.31] is [technically] not established for the purpose of applying the rule "ṣaḍhoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.41), the *ka*-substitution [of *ṭa* for *ḍa*] does not occur, and thus after the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the *jaś*-substitution [of *ḍa* for *ḍha*] results in *didhaḍ*—that is merely an error, because the rule "dāderdhātorghaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.32) which prescribes *gha* remains active as an exception to the *ḍha*-substitution. [The section on] words ending in *ṣ*.
Regarding *vidvān*: from the root *vid*, the suffix *śatṛ* is replaced by *vasu*; due to its being part of the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment.
Regarding *sedivān*: the suffix *kvasu* is applied according to the rule "In the common language (*bhāṣā*), [the suffixes *kvasu* and *kvasuṅ* are used after] the roots *sad*, *vas*, and *śru*."

Regarding the word *seduṣaḥ*: one might object that, by the paribhāṣā "when there is the mention of something with a specific anubandha, that which lacks such an anubandha is not included," it would be proper for the *saṃprasāraṇa* to apply only to the *vasu* of the rule "videḥ śaturvasuḥ" and not to the *kvasu*; this is true. However, the mention of the *ukāra* as an anubandha in *vasuḥ* is for the purpose of including *kvasu* in general, since its status as an *ugit* is established even through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*. Here, the *kvasu* suffix after roots such as *gam* has not been cited because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*), yet poets do employ it.

The passage beginning with "to him who had attained all blessings" and "him standing near the city," and so forth, may somehow be justified by relying on the general indicator (jñāpaka) found in the rule *māsaśchandasi*, which states that "even Vedic forms occur occasionally in the common language (*bhāṣā*)."

It is intended that *asuṅ* [replaces the final vowel] of the word *pums*. Therefore, in the case of *paramapumān*, once *asuṅ* has been applied because it is subsequent, the udātta accentuation of the final member of the compound occurs specifically for the vowel of *asuṅ*. However, if the locative case were interpreted as "subsequent" (*parasaptamī*), this would not be established; for if the vowel *u* of the word *pum̐s* were made udātta even before the emergence of the *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix], then by the rule of substitution of a non-udātta for a consonant characterized by elision (*sraṃsanadharmī*), there would result an udātta substitute for a consonant characterized by elision.

It should not be argued that even though the vowel *u* (in *asuṅ*) has been applied, it will be nullified because it is not final, whereas *asuṅ* itself, being final, will be applied; for the sense is that when the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of the vowel substitution is to take effect, the external operation (*bahiraṅga*) of *asuṅ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). This has been stated in accordance with Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others.

In reality, however, the position of the locative case (*parasaptamī*) is also easily established, since the maxim regarding the non-application of a grammatical operation once its conditions have been met (*akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*) is an exception to the maxim concerning internal operations (*antaraṅgaparibhāṣā*); this is how it should be understood.

[Objection: But surely, even in the absence of compounding, once *asuṅ* has been applied, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) would be superseded by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadikasvara*), which is applied later; thus, the *asuṅ* itself would become acute. However, it is desired that the vowel *ū* [of the suffix] be acute, because in examples such as *pumān*, *pumāṃsam*, and *paripātu*, that is exactly how they are recited. [Response: True. Haradatta and others maintain that by virtue of the fact that the marker *ṅ* is attached to *ḍumsun*, the accent of the nominal stem does not apply. [Objection: But this is incorrect, because the rule "phiṣaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.7) operates only on those items where the division between base and suffix is absent. [Response: True.

In some cases, even when there is a break [in the application of rules], this *liṅga* (indicative mark) is operative. Although this is already established by the rule "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*), nevertheless, the conclusion is that the inclusion of the marker *n* is intended to indicate the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the *paribhāṣā* concerning what is external.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of pronunciation": the sense is that the claim made by the ancients—that the marker *u* is for the purpose of elision (*lopa*)—and the explanation given by his grandson—that the vowel *u* is for the sake of the operations of the *ugit* class—are both incorrect.
In the form "he puman," the long vowel does not occur because of the condition "except in the vocative" (*asambuddhau*).

Regarding the word *puṃsu*: when the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* is elided, the rule *mo 'nusvāraḥ* applies. Since this is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) specifically for the *anusvāra* that replaces *num*, the rule *num-visarjanīya-śar-vasu* does not cause the substitution of *ṣ*. As for the phrase "in the vocative singular" (*asya sambuddhau*): this is based on an explicit statement (*vācanika*). As for what Haradatta and others say—that since it would have been sufficient to state *soḥ ḍe*, the fact that the rule states *anaṅ sāu* indicates that in certain cases *anaṅ* alone is heard, and thus the desired form is established—this has already been refuted. Alternatively, the matter may be resolved by the *paribhāṣā* regarding operations within a stem (*aṅgavṛtta-paribhāṣā*).

[Objection: Let there be the substitution of *au* for *adas* and the elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*)—surely let only *au* be prescribed for *su*. Since the form *asau* is already established through the substitution of *a* for the *tyad*-group stems, what is the purpose of prescribing the elision of *su*? [Reply: Not so. For in the case of *asakau strī*, if the feminine suffix *ṭāp* were applied, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *i* by the rule *pratyayasthāt*. The form *asukaḥ* [is correct]: in the absence of the substitution of *au*, the *tyad*-group substitution of *a* occurs, followed by the substitution of *s* for *d*. However, *amukaḥ* is incorrect, because the substitution of *m* (by *adaso māt*) would block the substitution of *s*. Similarly, forms such as *amukī* and *amukaśarmā* are also incorrect. The only logical forms are *asukā*, *adakaḥ*, *śarmā*, and so forth.

If "plural" (*bahuvacana*) were taken here in its technical sense, then although forms such as *amībhiḥ* would be established, the form *amī* [in the nominative plural] would not be established in the case of *jasi*; for in this instance, the vowel *e* does not have a plural suffix following it. Therefore, he explains: "when expressing a plurality of objects."

He says that *na mu ne* is a locative of the object (*viṣayasaptamī*)—namely, "when *nā* is to be applied. The intention is that otherwise, because the condition of being followed by *ghi* would be absent, the substitution of *nā* would not occur. [Objection: Even if *nā* has been substituted in this way, the rule *supi ca* would cause the lengthening of the vowel, since the substitution of *mu* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the lengthening; therefore, he says: "And when [it has been] done," or it may be resolved by means of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*.

In this regard, the following should be noted: when one ought to say "now as 'amuṣmin'," the statement "na mu ne" (Pāṇini 1.1.14) is intended for the purpose of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule). By means of this, forms such as *rāmaḥ* and *rāmebhyaḥ* are established. Otherwise, since the *ru* [substitute] would be considered *asiddha*, how could the *it-saṃjñā* and its subsequent elision apply to the vowel *u*?

Nor should it be argued that, by virtue of the mention of the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*), the rules for *it*-designation and elision (*lopa*) are not considered *asiddha* (non-existent) [with respect to each other]; for in examples such as *tarumūlam*, the nasalized vowel is specifically mentioned in the rule *ato roḥ* in order to exclude the application of *haśi ca*. Thus, its purpose is fulfilled precisely there. Nor should it be argued that the nasalization need not be present in *ato roḥ*, since the desired result can be achieved simply by taking the term as a *pratipadokta* (explicitly stated) word; for even so, in the case of *deva ruhī*, the nasalization would be unavoidable in the root *rudh*.

Furthermore, in cases such as *rāmaḥ*, it is easy to maintain that the rule finds its purpose (*caritārthatva*) by ensuring the audible pronunciation of the nasalized *r* (*anunāsika*). Thus, when the *sthānivat-sūtra* also applies, the visarga is obtained because of the status of being a word (*padatva*). The indication of [the forms] *pratyayaḥ* and *paraśca*, as well as the inclusion of the term *aś* in the rule for the substitution of *y* (*yatva-vidhi*), serve as the evidence (*liṅga*) here; this is the general direction.
Thus ends the section on masculine nouns ending in consonants in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now begins the section on feminine stems ending in consonants (*halanta-strīliṅga-prakaraṇa*).

It was not stated that *dha* becomes *na*; for if that were the case, in the word *naddham*, the substitution of *na* [for *da*] would occur by the rule "radābhyām," and the rule "jhaṣastathoḥ" would not apply. Here, this should be noted: they have cited *svanaḍvāhī* as an example in a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there are excellent oxen (*suṣṭhu anaḍvāhaḥ*)," but that is questionable because it contradicts the governing rule "anupasarjanāt.

Regarding *gīḥ*: from the root *gṝ* in the sense of swallowing and sound. With the suffix *kvip*, the substitution of *it* occurs by the rule "ṛta it. There is lengthening of the penultimate vowel by the rule "rvorupadhāyāḥ.
Regarding *pūḥ*: from the root *pṝ* in the sense of protecting and filling. There is the substitution of *u* by the rule "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya."

Regarding the forms *āśiṣau*: by the rule "the addition of *kvip* after the root *āśās*" (*āśāsaḥ kvāv upasaṃkhyānam*), the penultimate vowel becomes *i*; then, by the rule "for the roots *śās*, *vas*, etc. (*śāsivasi*), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs.
Thus ends the section on feminine stems ending in consonants in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita.
Now begins the section on neuter stems ending in consonants.

Regarding the term *anvādeśa*, commentators explain that this refers specifically to the pronoun *am*. They state that although this pronoun is elided by *luk*, the designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) still applies due to the force of the explicit statement [in the rule]. In reality, however, this should have been stated directly in the sūtra itself. Forms such as *enam* and *enau* are established through the substitution of *yat* for *tyad*-class stems. In the neuter, even when the case-ending *am* is elided by *luk*, the substitute *ena-* occurs by virtue of the force of the pronunciation of the letter *t* [in the rule *enad-anvādeśe*]. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of applying the same substitute in a form like *etac-chritaḥ*; for since the elision of *su* and *am* (which is internal, being dependent on a single word) has already fulfilled its purpose, the external elision occurring in a compound does not trigger the application of that substitute.

Regarding the statement "it also means day": the form *ahan* was introduced by the Eastern grammarians (*prāc*), but that is inappropriate here; it should somehow be construed as having the sense of *ahobhyām* and so forth. As for the word *asṛk*, this is clear in the work of Kṣīrasvāmin.

The rule *bahūrji* and the rule *antyāt* are both based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "There is a prohibition regarding *bahūrji*; some say that the *num* augment occurs before the final letter. However, in the Bhāṣya, the first Vārttika is rejected by adopting the interpretation that the *num* augment is added to that which ends in a *jhal* consonant following an *ac* vowel. In this way, even for roots such as *urda* (in the sense of measuring) and *garha* (in the sense of censuring), when they take the *kvip* suffix, there should be no occurrence of the *num* augment at all—this being the general direction, since the authority of the sages increases in successive order.

Regarding the term *allopasya*: the rule "that which is elided before *kvip* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*" is not relied upon here, because that rule is only occasional (*kvācitka*). This is clear from the original treatise (*ākara*), as the rule "with respect to an operation [governed] by *kvip*, [the elision] is not *sthānivadbhūta*" is universal (*sārvatrika*).

"Acting as eyes" (akṣibhūtāni) means five hundred and twenty-seven. To explain: in the case of *sau*, there are eighteen forms from the doubling of the final *ñ* of the nine [forms]. In the case of *auṅ*, there are seven from the doubling of *ñ* in three of the four [forms] used for honorific purposes; however, the nasalized (*anunāsika*) form does not occur here because it is a *pragṛhya*. In the case of *jasi*, there are twelve due to the optionality of both the doubling of *ñ* and the nasalization. By summation, this makes thirty-seven. The same applies to the second case (*dvitīyā*). In the case of *ṭā*, there are fourteen.

In the *bhyām* [case-ending], there are forty-eight forms, because of the doubling of the *y* and *m* in *bh-prāg-varṇa*. In the *bhis* [case-ending], there are twenty-four. In the *ṅi* [case-ending], there are seven. However, there is no nasalized (*anunāsika*) form, because this single vowel is not *aṇ*. In the *bhyas* [case-ending], it is like *bhyām*. In the *ṅasi*—that is, in the group of five beginning with *ṅasi*—there are fourteen. In the *sup* [case-ending], for the three [forms] ending in *gati*, there are twenty-four due to the doubling of the *k* and *ṣ* sounds and the nasalization of the *u* vowel. Thus, in the *kuk* alternative, for the six [forms] where *ṅ* and *ṣ* are doubled and the vowel is nasalized, there are forty-eight.

In the absence of *ku* (the first five case endings), there are twelve forms due to the doubling of the nasal *ṅ* and the presence of the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*). [The counts for each suffix are as follows: *su* 18, *au* 7, *jas* 12, *am* 18, *auṭ* 7, *śas* 12, *ṭā* 14, *bhyām* 48, *bhis* 24, *ṅe* 7, [second] *bhyām* 48, [third] *bhyas* 48, *ṅasi* 14, [second] *bhyām* 48, [third] *bhyas* 48, *ṅas*, *os*, *ām*, *ṅi*, *os*, and *sup* are each 14; *sup* totals 48.

In this regard, the following should be noted: in the case of *pūjā* (the second person plural), when the augment *num* is applied and its doubling (*dvitva*) is optionally performed, there are six forms consisting of three *ñ* letters each. Similarly, this applies to *śas* as well; thus, by summation, there are twelve. And so it is said: "The form is called 'planets, fires, and elements' [12]" (verse 539). This refers to the view other than that of the Bhāṣya; such is the direction. As for what they say:
"In this manner, one must infer [the forms] through the optional application of doubling, redoubling, and elision."

"One hundred and seventy-three by the addition of fifty-eight"—this [calculation] is to be reconsidered, because the doubling [of the number] lacks authoritative basis, because it would entail the consequence of an infinite number of forms, and because there is no justification for the addition of fifty-eight; such is the direction [of the critique]. Regarding the term *tiraścī*: due to its being a *bha*-stem, there is elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *acaḥ*; and because of the specific statement "not elision of *al*," the substitution of *tiri* occurs.

*Suvāpī*: This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "a lake (*saras*) in which the waters (*āpas*) are beautiful (*śobhanāḥ*). Although the suffix *a* (as in *ṛkpūḥ*) would normally apply to form the end of the compound, there is a prohibition by the rule "not after a word used for worship" (*na pūjanāt*). As for what the ancients said—that [the suffix] applies because of its irregularity (*anityatvāt*)—that is merely an error. Furthermore, the rule "after *dvi*, *antar*, and prepositions" (*dvyantarupasargebhyaḥ*) does not apply here, because it will be explained later that in that context, the word *apaḥ* is an imitation of the form already containing the compound-ending suffix.

Regarding the form *supumāṃsau*: in the opinion of the ancient grammarians who explain the rule *puṃso'suṅ* as containing the word *suṭ*, this form would not be established in the case of the *śas* ending; furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the *auṅ* ending. However, for us—who state [the rule] exactly according to the sūtra as *sarvanāmasthāne*—all desired forms are established; such is the sense.
Thus ends the section on neuter gender stems ending in consonants in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now begins the section on indeclinables (avyaya).

"An indeclinable is a particle beginning with *svara*": this is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) meaning "the particles beginning with *svara*. *Svar* means in heaven or in the other world; *antar* means in the middle; *prātar* means at dawn; *punar* means in the sense of not being first and in the sense of distinction; *sunutar* means in concealment—these five, ending in the letter *r*, begin with *svara*.

*Uccaiḥ* means "loudly" or "high"; *nīcaiḥ* means "softly" or "low"; *śanaiḥ* indicates slowness of action; *ṛdhak* signifies truth. Others [give it] the meanings of separation, speed, proximity, and lightness. *Ṛte* is used in the sense of exclusion. *Yugapat* means "simultaneously" or "at one time. *Ārāt* denotes both distance and proximity. *Pṛthak* means "separately" or "distinctly. *Hyas* refers to the past day. *Divā* means "by day. *Rātrau* means "at night. *Sāyam* means "at the onset of night. *Ciram* means "for a long time. *Manāk*, *īṣat*, and *kimapi* denote "slightly. *Joṣam* signifies happiness as well as silence. *Tūṣṇīm* means "in silence. *Bahis* and *avas* both mean "outside."

*Samayā* means near or in the middle; *nikaṣā* means in the vicinity; *svayam* means by oneself; *vṛthā* means in vain; *naktam* means at night; *nañ* is used for negation; *hetau* means on account of or as a cause; *iddhā* means in clarity or manifestation; *addhā* means clearly or certainly—some say it denotes reality (*tattva*) and excellence (*atiśaya*); *sāmī* means half or contempt; *vat* refers to the suffix *-vat* prescribed by rules such as "that which is equal to that."

That [suffix] prescribed by the rule "upasargāddhātvarthe" (Pāṇini 5.1.118) is not taken here, as in the example: *yad udvato nivato yāsi* ("when you go from the heights to the depths"). *Sanat* is used in the sense of "giving" (*sanana*) and is obligatory. *Upadha* is used in the sense of "difference. *Tiras* is used in the senses of "disappearance," "sideways," and "contempt. *Antara* is used in the senses of "middle" and "without. *Antareṇa* is used in the sense of "exclusion. *Jyok* is used in the senses of "time," "abundance," "question," "speed," and "immediacy. *Kam* is used in the senses of "water," "head," "censure," and "happiness. *Śam* is used in the sense of "happiness. *Sahasā* is used in the senses of "suddenly" and "without reflection."

*Vineti* is used in the sense of avoidance; *nānā* in the senses of "various" and "without"; *svasti* in the sense of auspiciousness; *svadhā* in the offering to the ancestors (*pitṛ*); *alam* in the senses of ornament, sufficiency, capability, prohibition, and negation; *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *śrauṣaṭ*—these are used in the offering of oblations (*haviḥ*); *anyat* in the sense of "other"; *asti* in the sense of existence; *upāṃśu* in the senses of inaudible utterance and secrecy; *kṣamā* in the sense of forbearance; *vihāyasā* in the sense of the sky; *doṣā* in the sense of night; *mṛṣā* and *mithyā*—these two—in the sense of falsehood; and *mudhā* in the sense of futility.

*Purā* and *itavā* signify "long ago"; *bhaviṣyat* and *āsanna* signify "near future. *Mithas* and *mithas* [are synonyms] in the senses of "mutually" and "in secret. *Prāyas* signifies "for the most part" (majority). *Mahus* signifies "again" (repetition). *Pravāhukam* signifies "simultaneously" and "accomplished purpose. *Pravāhikā* is an alternative reading. *Āryahalam* signifies "by force. Śākaṭāyana, however, says that *ārya* signifies "obstruction," while *halam* signifies "prohibition" and "dispute. *Ābhīkṣṇyam* signifies "frequency" (repetition). *Sākam* and *sārdham*—these two have the sense of "together" (*saha*). *Namah* signifies "bowing" (salutation).

*Hiruk* is used in the sense of exclusion; *dhik* in the sense of censure and reproach; *am* in the sense of speed and smallness; *ām* in the sense of acceptance. Some maintain that suffixes prescribed by rules such as "kimettiṅavyaya" and "kāspratyayāt" are also included here [as indeclinables]. Examples include *papācatarām* and *kārayāmāsa*. *Pratām* is used in the sense of exhaustion; *praśān* has the same meaning as *samāna*; *pratān* in the sense of expansion; *mā* and *māṅ* are used in the senses of apprehension and prohibition.

"An *ākṛtigaṇa* (class of words defined by its form)" means that others should also be understood [as belonging to this class]. For instance: *kāmaṃ* in the sense of "according to one's will"; *prakāmam* in the sense of "excessively"; *bhūyaḥ* in the sense of "again"; *sāmpratam* in the sense of "properly"; *param* in the sense of "but rather"; *sākṣāt* in the sense of "directly" or "manifestly"; *sāci* in the sense of "obliquely"; *satyam* in the sense of "firmly accepting"; *maṅkṣu* and *āśu*, both in the sense of "quickly"; *samvat* in the sense of "in the year"; *avaśyam* in the sense of "certainly"; *sapadi* in the sense of "immediately"; *balavat* in the sense of "excessively"; *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* in the sense of "manifestation."

*Aniśam*, *nityam*, *nityadā*, *ajarām*, and *santatam*—these [words] signify continuity (*sātatya*). *Uṣā* means "at night. *Rodasī* signifies both heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*). *Oṃ* is used for assent and for Brahman. *Bhūḥ* refers to the earth. *Bhuvaḥ* refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). *Jhagiti*, *jhaṭiti*, and *tarasā* signify swiftness. *Suṣṭhu* is used in the sense of praise. *Duṣṭhu* denotes extreme difficulty. *Su* is used for honor. *Aha* expresses wonder. *Ku* is used for contempt and the sense of "slightly. *Añjasā* signifies truth and swiftness. *Mithu* means "two."

*bhājaka* signifies swiftness (*śaighrye*). *Cirāya*, *cirarātrāya*, *cirasya*, *ciram*, *cirāt*, and *cireṇa*—these have the sense of "long" (*cirārthakāḥ*). *Astaṃ* signifies destruction (*vināśe*). *Ānuṣak* signifies succession (*ānupūrvye*). *Anuṣak* signifies following after (*anudāne*). *Amnas* signifies both swiftness and the present moment (*śīghra-sāmpratikayoḥ*). *Sthāne* signifies what is appropriate (*yukte*). *Varam* signifies slight superiority (*īṣad-utkarṣe*). *Sudi* refers to the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣe*), and *vadi* to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣe*), and so forth.

*Vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth: "The particle *vā* may be used in the sense of option (*vikalpa*), comparison (*upamā*), the meaning of *eva*, and also in conjunction. *Ha* denotes well-known fact (*prasiddhi*). *Aha* denotes reverence (*pūjā*). *Eva* denotes restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*). *Evam* refers back to what has been stated (*uktaparāmarśa*). *Nūnam* denotes certainty (*niścaya*) and reasoning (*tarke*). *Śaśvat* denotes repetition (*paunaḥpunya*), eternity (*nitya*), and the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*). *Yugapat* denotes simultaneity (*aikakālya*). *Bhūyas* denotes the sense of "again" (*punarartha*) and excess (*ādhikya*). *Kūpat* denotes inquiry (*praśna*) and praise (*praśaṃsā*). *Kuvid* denotes prosperity (*bhūti*) and praise (*praśaṃsā*).

*ned* is used in the senses of prohibition, doubt, deliberation, and conjunction. *ced* is used in the sense of "if" (*yadī*). *caṇ* is used in the sense of "if" (*ced*) and is marked with the *ṇit* indicatory letter; however, when used in the sense of conjunction and so forth, it is without an indicatory mark (*ananubandha*). *kaccit* is used in an inquiry regarding something desired. *yatra* is used in the senses of impossibility, intolerance, reproach, and wonder—as in: "I do not believe, I cannot tolerate, I reproach, or I find it a wonder, that you would cause a low-born man (*vṛṣala*) to perform a sacrifice. *neha* is used in the sense of a counter-commencement (*pratyārambha*). *hanta* is used in joy, dejection, compassion, and at the beginning of a sentence. *mākiḥ*, *mākim*, and *nakir*—these three are all used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*).

The words *mā* and *nañ* are mentioned among the *svarādi* (words beginning with *svara*) [in the list of indeclinables]. However, their inclusion here is for the purpose of establishing their status as *nipātas* (particles). On this basis, the ancients maintain that their initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is thereby established; yet this is questionable, since the desired result is achieved even by means of the *phiṭ-svara* (the accentual rule for nominal stems). Furthermore, as they also say—that the inclusion in the *svarādi* list is intended to grant the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable) even to words denoting existence—this too is questionable, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the word *mā* (meaning "possessing beauty") also being an indeclinable. Therefore, the purpose of including them in both lists must be considered.

The particle *yāvat* is used in the senses of totality (*sākalya*), limit (*avadhi*), measure (*māna*), and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). In the sense of totality: "As much as the task was, so much has been done. In the sense of limit: "Stay as long as there is to be traveled. In the sense of measure: "As much as was given, so much was eaten. In the sense of restriction: "Invite as many Brāhmaṇas as there are vessels. *Tvai* is used in the senses of distinction (*viśeṣa*) and deliberation (*vitarka*). *Dvai* is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*). *Nvai* is an alternative reading. *Rai* is used in the senses of giving (*dāna*) and disregard (*anādara*). In the phrase *rai karoti*, the meaning is "he gives. "O you, what will you do? (*tvaṃ rai kiṃ kariṣyasi*)?

*Śrauṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* are used in the offering of oblations (*havirdāna*). *Svāhā* is used in the offering to the deities; *svadhā*, to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). The multiple-syllable forms such as *śrauṣaṭ* are listed in both [the consonant and vowel] sections for the sake of distinguishing their accents. *Tum* refers to the sound *tuṅ*. Having uttered *tuṅ*—that is, having uttered *huṅ*—one addresses a superior. Thus it is shown in illustration. *Khalu* is used in prohibition, as an embellishment of speech, and in certainty. *Kila* is used in report and in falsehood. *Atha* is used in auspiciousness, sequence, commencement, inquiry, totality, authority, promise, and conjunction. This [particle] also begins with a vowel.
Thus, although it denotes a blessing (*maṅgala*), its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established. And so says Śrī Harṣa:

"Then, having lifted the golden jars onto the interior of the altar-platform, which was beautiful with its fourfold splendor, the group of matrons bathed the King’s daughter according to family custom."

For here, the meaning of "snapayāmbabhūva" is that he performed an auspicious bathing; however, the particle [“smā”] is auspicious by its very nature, like the sound of a drum. The reading with "suṣṭhu" is for the purpose of distinguishing the accent. "Sma" is used for the past tense and as a verse-filler. "Ādaha" is used in the senses of beginning, injury, and censure.

Regarding the word *avadattam*: here, because it is not a preposition (*upasarga*), the rule "a vowel following a preposition becomes *t* [before *d*]" does not apply. *Aham* is a pseudo-inflected form (*subanta-pratirūpaka*). By this, the phrase "by whom were you two trained in the art of song? (*geye kena vinītau vām*) is explained; for the indeclinable *vām* has the sense of "you two. *Asti* is a pseudo-conjugated form (*tiṅanta-pratirūpaka*). Similarly, *asmi* has the sense of "I," as in "I tell you"; *āha* has the sense of "said" (*uvāca*); *āsa* has the sense of "was" (*babhūva*), and so forth.

*a* is used for addressing, for reproach, and for prohibition; *ā* for sentences and recollection; *i* for addressing, for loathing, and for wonder; *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* for addressing; *paśu* in the sense of "properly" (as in *paśu manyamānāḥ*, "regarding [it] as proper"); *śukam* in the sense of "speedily"; *yathākathāca* in the sense of "indifference"; *pāṭ*, *pyāṭ*, *aṅga*, *he*, *hai*, *bho*, and *aye*—these are used for addressing; *dyā* for violence, opposition, and filling out a verse-line (*pādapūraṇa*); *viṣu* in the sense of "variously"; *ekapade* in the sense of "suddenly"; and *yut* for contempt and cause.

The word *ātaḥ* is used in the sense of "also from this" (*ito'pi*). It is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of particles). For example: *yat* and *tat* are used in the sense of cause (*hetu*); *āhosvit* in the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*); *sima* in the sense of totality (*sarvatobhāva*); *kaṃ* for filling the meter (*pādapūraṇa*); *suka* in the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*); *anukaṃ* in the sense of deliberation (*vitarke*); *śamvaṭ* in the sense of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and facing toward (*ābhimukhya*); *va* for filling the meter and in the sense of "as if" (*ivārtha*); *diṣṭyā* in the sense of joy (*ānanda*); *caṭu* or *cāṭu* in the sense of pleasant speech (*priyavākya*); *hum* in the sense of reproach (*bhartsane*); *iva* in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*); *adyatve* in the sense of "now" (*idānīm*), and so forth.

In this regard, the following should be noted: although there is no distinction between the *svarādi* and *cādi* groups insofar as they both belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class, those words for which the accent of a particle (*nipāta*) is observed in the *cādi* group are to be understood as belonging to the *cādi* group, while others belong to the *svarādi* group. However, those that possess both accents should be understood as belonging to both groups. For example, the word *uta* is in the *svarādi* group, as seen in the usage "īḍyo nūtanairuta" where it has an udātta accent on the final syllable. As for the fact that some, having stated that *uta* belongs to the *svarādi* group, raised an objection regarding its accent as a particle and resolved it by resorting to an *antodātta* (final-accented) nipātana rule—that was done out of haste.

Because *svar* and the others are not indeclinables (*nipāta*), and because it would result in the redundancy of the rule for final acute accentuation (*antodāttatva*) regarding indeclinables. Furthermore, that which was stated in the *Kāśikā*—"*svar*, *śanais*, *ṛdhak*, *divā*, *vṛthā*, *naktam*, and so forth, are acutely accented on the final syllable"—and that which states, "*sanat*, *sanāt*, and so forth, are acutely accented on the initial syllable," all of that is due to negligence. This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdakaustubha*, as these [statements] contradict the observed usage (*lakṣya*) and lack any authoritative foundation (*nirmūlatva*).

"A taddhita suffix that does not take all case-endings" means it consists of the three numbers (singular, dual, and plural). "Not" [in the rule] implies that, rather than taking all endings, only the singular ending is produced; this is the intended meaning. Why specify "taddhita"? [Consider: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *trayaḥ* (one, two, three). Why specify "not all," etc.? [Consider: *aupagavaḥ* (a descendant of Upagu).

Regarding *kṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39), [the example] *jīvase* is formed with the suffix *ase*, according to the rule *tumarthe sesen*. Regarding *pibaddhyai*, the suffix *śadhyai* is applied by that same rule, and the substitution of *piba-* for *pā-* occurs by the rule *pāghrā* (6.1.178). As for what some say—that [the suffix *śadhyai*] occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed—this is due to haste; for the established doctrine is that "suffixes introduced after an indeclinable (*avyayakṛt*) express the action itself (*bhāva*). The inclusion of the word *antam* (in the sūtra) is for the purpose of understanding that [the suffix must be] taught as such [by the rule itself]. Therefore, it does not apply here in cases like *ādhaye* or *cikīrṣave*. This [sūtra] is intended to indicate the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of these two [paribhāṣās]: the one concerning what is taught by a general rule (*lakṣaṇa-ukta*) and the one concerning what is taught by a specific mention (*pratipada-ukta*), as well as the paribhāṣā regarding the non-disturbance of a grammatical operation already in progress (*sannipāta-paribhāṣā*).

Regarding *ktvātosunkasunaḥ*: [the word] *udetoḥ* is derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *ut*, according to the rule: "The suffix *tosun* is applied after the roots *sthā*, *iṇ*, *kṛ*, *vad*, *car*, *hu*, *mi*, *jan*, etc., when indicating a characteristic action (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*). Regarding *visṛpaḥ*: [it is formed] according to the rule: "The suffix *kasun* is applied after the roots *sṛp* and *tṛd*. Regarding the mention of the term *āp* (the feminine suffix): thus there is a Vārttika which states: "'There is no need to state that the elision (*luk*) of *āp* occurs after an indeclinable, because there is an absence of gender [in such cases]. However, the possibility of stating this in the Sūtra itself should be understood as being based on adopting the alternative view in the Sūtra *striyām* that [the suffix applies] "after that which is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with 'feminine'. But that view is not established, because it would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in examples such as *bhūtamiyaṃ brāhmaṇī* ("this Brāhmaṇī woman has become so").

Anticipating the objection that if [the suffix] were not a *liṅga* (gender marker), it would contradict the scriptural statement found in the *Atharvaṇa-vidyā*, he says: "similarly" (*sadṛśam*). Regarding the phrase "liṅga-kāraka": the intention is that the words *vibhakti* and *vacana* refer respectively to *kāraka* (grammatical relation) and *saṃkhyā* (number).

As for the example "as by speech" (*yathā vācā*): some say this is an exhaustive enumeration; others say it is merely an illustration. Regarding the term *vagāha*: only the initial vowel *ā* is elided, not the final one, because of its association with the word *api*.
Thus ends the section on indeclinables in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now begins the section on feminine suffixes.
Regarding *khaṭvā*: [the suffix] *kvan* is applied by the rule "after the roots *aśū*, *pruṣu*, *laṭi*, *khaṭi*, *kaṇi*, and *viśi*, [the suffix] *kvan* [is added].

Regarding *pañcājī*: one should not say that the feminine suffix *ṭāp* does not apply simply because of the absence of the rule for extension to the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*). This is because the inclusion of the term "not preceded by *mahat*" (*amahatpūrvagrahaṇa*) and the governing heading "not being a subordinate member" (*anupasarjanādhikāra*) indicate that, in the case of feminine suffixes, the rule for extension to the end of a compound does indeed apply.

Regarding the word *mūṣikā*: under the governing rule "vṛścikṛṣoḥ kikan," the word *mūṣika* is formed with the suffix *kikan*, which causes the lengthening of the vowel in the root *muṣ*. As for the word *mūṣaka* mentioned by Mādhava—which is derived from the root *mūṣ* (meaning 'to steal') with a long vowel in its penultimate syllable, followed by the suffix *kvun* in the sense of a name—the feminine form here is also made with *ṭāp*. The specific difference, however, is that the substitution of *ī* [for the final *a*] occurs according to the rule "pratyayasthāt. As for the claim that this word ending in *kvun* does not employ the reading in the *ajādi* group [of feminine suffixes], it is because that group is intended for the application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* as a marker of a genus (*jāti*), whereas a proper name (*saṃjñā*) is not a genus; thus they say. But that is questionable, because even in the case of a name like *vyāghrī*, the status of being a genus is not lost despite its being a name.

*bhastrāphalā*: the analysis of this compound is *bhastreva phalāni yasyāḥ* ("that which has fruits like a bellows"). Regarding the rule *ṅyāpoḥ*, this is established in Mādhava’s commentary on the verbal root *phala* (meaning "to produce fruit"); however, in the *Bhāṣya*, the long vowel (*-ā*) is generally read. *pratyakpuṣpā*: this was stated after a careful examination of the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika* on the sūtra beginning with *pākakarṇa*. Therefore, the reading *satprākkāṇḍā* should not be respected.

Regarding the word *śūdrā*: if it denotes a caste (*jāti*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied after the word *śūdra*. However, this does not apply when the word is preceded by *mahat*, provided that the condition "if it denotes a caste" is understood to apply here as well. Regarding the phrase "but in the case of connection with a male" (*puṃyoge tu*): there is no restriction that "connection with a male" must consist solely of the relationship of husband and wife; rather, it also includes the relationship between progenitor and progeny. By this, the rule "from a Kṣatriya [father], the sons of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman are known as Māhiṣya and Ugra respectively" is established. As for *mahāśūdrī*: Amarasimha states, "The term *ābhīrī* is the same as *mahāśūdrī* in both the senses of caste and connection with a male."

In this regard, the following should be noted: in the *ajādi* (ajādigaṇa) list, one should simply read "śūdrā"; the inclusion of "jāti" (caste/class) is redundant. Since the primary meaning of a word is understood first, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is prescribed by the rule for denoting a caste (*jāti*)—will itself block [the application of *ṭāp*]. For the application of a term based on a relationship with a male (*puṃyoga*) is secondary (*gauṇī*). Furthermore, the phrase "not preceded by *mahat*" (*amahat*) and so forth is also redundant; for the word *mahāśūdra* refers specifically to a distinct caste. In that case, because the constituent part [*mahat*] is meaningless [in the context of the compound], there is no possibility for the application of *ṭāp*, as the feminine gender inherent in the meaning of the word *śūdra* is not present. However, where a woman is great and a Śūdra (*mahatī śūdrā*), the form *mahāśūdrā* is indeed desired.

Regarding *kruñc* and so forth: some maintain that these three end in *hal*. However, citing examples such as *kruñcān ālabheta* and *uṣṇihakakubhau*, the *Bhāṣya* accepts them as ending in *a* as well. Regarding the phrase "also in the sense of connection with a male" (*puṃyoge 'pi*): when words like *jyeṣṭhā* refer to one born first and so on, the suffix *ṭāp* is established simply by virtue of their ending in *a*. But when there is the intention to express "the wife of an elder brother" (*jyeṣṭhasya strī*) and so forth, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is prescribed for connection with a male—is applicable; the word *api* is used to indicate that this [suffix] is superseded by the present rule. [The rule applies] after a word beginning with *mūla* when preceded by *nañ*. Why say "after *nañ*"? Consider *śatamūlī*.
*Amūla*: This is a class of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhijāti*).

It is also [a word] ending in an *ugit* vowel. [The suffix] *ṅīp* applies because it is listed among the *sarvādi* group, and it is derived from the root *bhā* with the suffix *ḍvatu*. However, when the suffix *śatṛ* is added, the *num* augment is obligatory by the rule "*śapśyanoḥ*".

*Sutvānam*: [This is formed] from the root *śṛ* with the suffix *vanip*. Once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, although the word ends in a consonant (*haśantāt*), the prohibition of the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* does not apply, because the suffix was not prescribed after a word ending in a *haś* sound.

Regarding "avāveti": the author of the *Nyāsa* states that this prohibition is general (prāyika), and for that reason he says "avāvari"; however, this is not seen in the *Bhāṣya* or other such works. Regarding "in the alternative, by the suffix *ḍāp*": the sense is that in the dual number, there arise three forms—*bahudhīvaryau*, *bahudhīvānau*, and *bahudhīve*.
The suffix *ḍāp* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṅīp* which would otherwise be obtained by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 4.1.5] in the case of the word *ṛc*.

Regarding the phrase "because of its being unestablished" (*asiddhatvāt*): this is according to the view that the time of application [of grammatical rules] is determined by the effect (*kāryakālapakṣa*). However, some say that if the six technical names (*ṣaṭsaṃjñā*) are established according to their original enunciation (*yathoddeśa*), or if the rule *ṣṇānta* is explained as applying at the time of the original instruction (*upadeśakāla*), then the description of its being unestablished is not applicable.

In reality, however, even under the *yathoddeśa* (definition-based) view, the condition of being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*) is indeed applicable; for the rule regarding the substitution of a single part (*ekadeśavikṛta*) is recited in the *sthānivadbhāva* sūtra. Alternatively, by virtue of the mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*), one may explain that even an inferred substitute is treated like the original (*sthānin*), based on the principle that "all [phonemes] are substitutes for all words. In either case, that [rule] does not apply in the case of an operation concerning a vowel (*alvidhi*). This is clear in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*). Regarding the form *bahuyajvānau*: because of the prohibition "not after a conjunct consonant" (*na saṃyogāt*), this is not a case of elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*); therefore, the rule "of that which has elision of the penultimate vowel" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*) does not apply.

[Objection: Surely, since both the suffix *ṅīp* and the suffix *ḍāp* are prohibited [by the rule *ano bahuvrīheḥ*], their optional application (*paryāya*) is established by the very force of the statement [of the prohibition]. [Response: True. However, the rule is divided [into two parts] by the word "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*). In that context, the word "mind" (*manaḥ*) has ceased to apply. Thus, for a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *an*, the suffix *ḍāp* may optionally be used. This is intended to secure an option with respect to the suffix *ṅīp*. As for the rule "for a word ending in *an* which undergoes elision of the penultimate vowel" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*), however, it is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). That is, the aforementioned option applies only to those [words] where there is elision of the penultimate vowel. Consequently, in cases such as *suparvā*, where there is no elision of the penultimate vowel, this [present rule] serves to prohibit [the application of *ḍāp*].

In cases such as *bahurājñī*, however, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "*ṛnnebhyaḥ*" alone; thus, *bahudhīvarī* is established. For in the rule "*ṛnnebhyaḥ*", the suffix *ṅīp* is restated (*anūdyate*) and the phoneme *r* is prescribed in conjunction with it. If *ṅīp* were applied by a rule situated in a different section, this would not be established. If it is argued that the rule "*vano ra ca*" itself should prescribe both *ṅīp* and *ra*, we say no; for there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) in prescribing both simultaneously. Furthermore, even if that were the case, once *ṅīp* is prohibited, *ra* would also be difficult to obtain, because they are taught as being mutually dependent (*sanniyogaśiṣṭatvāt*).

In the Bhāṣya, however, this is resolved by breaking up the sūtras as follows: let there be a sūtra "upadhālopino vā" immediately after "ano bahuvrīheḥ"; let the sūtra located in another place, beginning with "ana upadhā," be omitted; and let the mention of "anyatarasyām" in the ḍāp-sūtra also be omitted.

In this context, with the intention that the term *bahuvrīhi* from the rule "bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ" and the suffix *ṅīp* from the rule "saṃkhyāvyayāderṅīp" both carry over (*anuvartate*), he says "from that which ends in *ann*," and so forth. It has been stated that this [rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Nor should it be argued that, since the option would already be established by the preceding rule, the inclusion of the word *anyatarasyām* here is redundant; for if that were absent, this would be a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) rather than a restriction.

In the rule *pratyayasthātkātpūrvasya*, the vowel *a* in *kā* is for the sake of pronunciation; only the consonant *k* is intended to be expressed. With the intention that, if a specific [vowel] were intended to be expressed, the suffix *akac* would not apply in forms such as *etikāś caranti*, he says: "from the letter *k*" (*kakārāt*). For the suffix *kāra* is prescribed when referring to a specific phoneme (*varṇa*). The fact that it is sometimes used after a whole word—as in the citation "the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is at a higher pitch"—is to be understood as being achieved through a deliberate effort in the form of a specific grammatical instruction.

"Also when *āp* follows": this is a qualifier of the vowel *a*. In that context, by virtue of the logical implication (*sāmarthya*), the change occurs even when there is an intervention by the letters *ka* and *a*; however, it does not occur in cases such as *rathakaṭyā*, where there is an intervention by three or four letters and so on. For this very reason, the change does not occur for the initial *a* in words like *sarvikā*. This is what was stated: "The vowel *i* should replace the vowel *a* when *āp* follows. Had it been intended as a qualifier of the letter *ka*, he would have said: "Of the *a* preceding the letter *ka* that follows *āp*."

As for what the ancients have said—that *āpi* is a qualifier of the letter *k*, and that in cases such as *sarvikā*, although there is an intervention by the vowel *a* due to the status of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) as being like its original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the rule will still apply by virtue of the power of the specific statement—this is not correct, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in forms such as *rathakaṭyā*, since the status of being "subsequent" (*paratva*) is not lost even when there is an intervention. Nor can one find a solution through the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the specific mention), because maxims do not apply in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*). For the meaning of that maxim is: "In the case of qualifiers of that which is being restated... [the maxim does not apply].

And in this regard, the mention of the word *sthāne* (in place of) in the rule *udīcām ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.46) is the *liṅga* (indicative mark). The result, however, is that in the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *vṛddha*, because the *paribhāṣā* concerning *it* does not apply, forms such as *śālīya* are established. As for what they say—that the term *āpi* is a qualifier of the *it* being prescribed [by 1.1.56]—that is too crude. Moreover, it is not even to be suspected that *āpi* is a qualifier of the *aṅga*, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *rathakaṭyā* and *putrakāmyā*.

[The form] *śakā* [is derived with] the suffix *ac* by the rule *pacādyac*. The inclusion of the word *sthā* is for the sake of clarity, since the status of being "situated therein" (*tātsthyalābha*) is obtained simply because there is no suffix consisting of the letter *k* alone.

What is the purpose of the mention of *pūrva* (the preceding)? In examples such as *sarvikā*, it is so that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [of *sarva* + *ā*] does not block the substitution of *kā* for the letter following *ṭāp*; this is because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "That which is taught by reference to what precedes [applies] to what follows. As for the claim that the single-substitute would be blocked by the rule "A grammatical operation (*āṅga*) takes precedence over one based on phonemes (*vārṇa*)," that is incorrect; for, just as priority (*paratva*) is ineffective against an exception (*apavāda*), so too is the aforementioned technical rule ineffective in this case.
In reality, however, the locative indication in "when *ki* stands in a suffix" (*pratyayasthe ki*) alone is appropriate; furthermore, the inclusion of the word *pūrva* could easily be omitted.

Regarding the word *ataḥ*: why is there the specification *taparaḥ* (a short vowel followed by *t*)? [Consider the examples: *dhākā*, *rākā*, and *māmikā*. In the case of *māmikā*, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) beginning with "only in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*) or in Vedic meter (*chandas*)" which applies to words such as *māmaka*.
Regarding the rule *tyaktyapoḥ*: this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the optional rule (*vikalpa*) stated in "the place of the long *ā* for the Northern grammarians."

Regarding the term *dākṣiṇātyikā*: [it is derived as follows] *dakṣiṇā* is that which is near the south (*dakṣiṇasyām adūre*). It ends in the suffix *āc*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "she who exists in the south. As for the analysis provided by the Easterners (*prāc*), namely "she who exists in the southern direction" (*dakṣiṇasyāṃ diśi bhavā*), that is incorrect; because in the rule prescribing the suffix *tyac*, only the word *dakṣiṇā* ending in *āc* is understood due to its association with indeclinables (*avyaya*). Otherwise, there would result the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "in all compound formations involving pronouns" (*sarvanāmno vṛttimātre*). As for the claim that the masculine substitution occurs only in a compound (*samāsa*), we shall state later that this is not so. When the suffix *tyac* is applied, there is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) by the rule "before a *kit* or *ṅit* suffix," etc.; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. Then, in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, the suffix *ka* is added. By the rule "when *ka* follows, [the vowel of] *aṇ* is short," the vowel is shortened, and then *ṭāp* is added again. Thus [is formed *dākṣiṇātyikā*].

Regarding the term *ihatyikā*: [the suffix] *tyap* follows an indeclinable. The author of the *Nyāsa* does not [apply this rule] here to the words *yā* and *sā*. He suggests that this is a prohibition regarding the optional application of the rule "udīcām ātaḥ sthāne" (Pāṇini 4.3.110) to the word *yā*; however, that is not correct, because the specific portion "ātaḥ sthāne" (in place of *ā*) is absent here. With the intention that the mention of *yā* and *sā* is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *yat* and *tat*, he says: "of *yat* and *tat*. He provides examples to show the result when the specific form is not intended to be significant: *yakām* and *takām*. It would have been more appropriate to say simply "of *yat* and *tat*" instead of "of *yā* and *sā*."

Regarding *upatyakā*: according to the rule "the suffix *tyakan* is added after *upa* and *adhi* in the senses of 'near' and 'ascended' [respectively]," and by the rule "and in the case of *kṣipakā* and others," the word *na* (negation) is understood to follow. As for *kṣipakā*: from the root *kṣip*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule governing roots with the marker *i* as an *upadhā*. Then, the suffix *ka* is applied again in the sense of the indefinite (*ajñāta*) and so forth. As for *caṭakā*: from the root *caṭ* (meaning 'to split'), the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule beginning with *pacādyac*, and then the suffix *ka* is applied.

Regarding *tārakā*: it is derived from the root *tṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul*. It refers to a celestial body or a star, as well as the pupil of the eye. *Varṇakā* is a specific type of garment. *Tāntava* is a derivative of threads; [it is formed] by adding the suffix *añ* to the word *otu*. Elsewhere, it is *varṇikā*, which is a commentary on a specific text and one who composes hymns. *Vartakā* means "she who turns" (*vartayati*); in the sense of a bird, there is optionally the substitution of *i* for *u*. Elsewhere, this substitution is obligatory.

The ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) and those deities are the *pitṛdevatās*; the rite for their sake is *pitṛdevatyam*. [This is derived] by the rule "after a word ending in *devatā*, the suffix *yat* is added in the sense of 'for that purpose'. That [day] on which the Brahmins eat is the *aṣṭakā*. [It is formed] by the rule "from the roots *iṣ* and *aś*, the suffix *takan*. As for *aṣṭikā*: "eight" is its measure; [it is formed] by the rule "the suffix *kan* is added after a numeral that does not end in *ati* or *śat*. Having superimposed the femininity residing in the meaning onto the vowel *ā*, there is the feminine designation [of the suffix] by the rule "when preceded by *ya* or *ka*. With the intention that a feminine suffix is thereby obtained, he says: "of the vowel *ā* which is a feminine suffix."

Regarding the term *sāṅkāśyikā*: [The city] *saṅkāśya* is derived from *saṅkāśa* by the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-ādi-sūtra*, specifically *saṅkāśādibhyo ṇyaḥ*. Then, for the sense of "belonging to that" (*tatra bhavaḥ*), the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the rule *dhanvayopadhād vuñ*, and there is the substitution of *a* [for the final vowel]. Since this refers to a woman belonging to Saṅkāśya, the shortening of its vowel (*it-tvam*) would also be optional; therefore, it was stated [in the rule] as *ātaḥ* (from a long *ā*). Now, one might object: "Just as this *a* is not a substitute for a long *ā*, so too it is not a substitute for a feminine suffix (*strī-pratyaya*); thus, this [rule] is deficient in two respects."

On this point, they say: If the rule *ātaḥ* exists, then by the force of the feminine gender indication, it is understood that the vowel *ā* which denotes a female is indeed a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). However, if that [rule] were absent, one would only obtain "the *ā* which denotes a female," and consequently, the undesired application would follow even in the case of *sāṅkāśyikā*.

In this regard, the following must be said: since the word *sthāne* is present in the rule "in place of that which has *ya* as its predecessor" (*yakapūrvāyāḥ sthāne*), how can it be understood as a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*)? Nor can it be argued that this [substitution] occurs in place of the suffix *vuñ*; for although the entire aggregate *ak* might be so [preceded by *ya*], the constituent element *a* is not, and furthermore, *vuñ* itself is not preceded by *ya*. Indeed, in that state, even the elision of the *i* in *yasya* is not applicable. Moreover, when the specifically prescribed feminine suffix is obtained, there is no possibility at all for *vuñ* and the like, which are enjoined in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*). Therefore, the mention of *ātaḥ* is indeed for the sake of clarity.
Regarding *aśvikā*: the followers of Kumāra, however, reading the word *aśva* even in the rule concerning *bhastrā* and others, desire an optional shortening (*it-tva*) for this as well.
*Śubham* is a monosyllabic indeclinable ending in *m*.
*Sunayā* means "she whose guidance is excellent" (*suṣṭhu nayo yasyāḥ*). From that, the suffix *ka* [is applied].
"This is a *bhastrā* [rule], because it follows that. This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). "And thus" refers to what was stated by Haradatta:
"In this context, the phrase 'in place of *āt*' (*ataḥ sthāne*) is a qualifier of the word itself (*svaśabda*)."
For in that case, both presence and deviation exist when the crow and the palm tree are present.
"There is no possibility of [the application of] two [terms], nor is there any deviation elsewhere;
therefore, this rule would not apply to a pronoun that is its own word. Thus [it is said].

In this context, it should be understood that the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is to be supplied immediately after the phrase *svaśabdasya*. This has also been indicated in the root text (*mūla*) itself. Thus, regarding the verse by Śrī Harṣa: "The *haṃsa* residing within the body, moving about like the mental activity of a sage within his own [body]," those who explain that the optional shortening of the vowel occurs here by the rule *bhastraiṣā-* are to be disregarded; such is the intended meaning.

Regarding the term *ātmīyāyām*: the intended meaning is that in the case of one's own kinsmen (*jñāti*) and wealth (*dhana*), the feminine gender simply does not apply. As for what some say—that two forms, *svakā* and *svikā*, are established in the original treatise (*ākara*) for "kinsmen" and "wealth"—that is to be reconsidered, because such an original treatise is unknown and it contradicts the rules of gender instruction (*liṅgānuśāsana*). Furthermore, as for the examples *svakā* and *svikā* cited in the *Kāśikā*, those pertain to technical names (*saṃjñā*) and do not refer to kinsmen.

As for what they have maintained—that "sometimes suffixes added for their own sake (*svārthika*) deviate from the gender and number of the base"—that too must be considered. For even if the feminine suffix *ṭāp* were possible after a word ending in the suffix *ka* according to the method stated, the portion [of the rule] "in place of *ā*" (*ātaḥ sthāne*) would be difficult to justify, because the base itself is not feminine.

Having stated the counter-examples, he states the actual examples, beginning with *nirbhastrikā*: "departed from a bellows" (*niṣkrāntā bhastrāyāḥ*) is *nirbhastrā*. There is shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*), then the suffix *ṭāp*, and then the suffix *ka* in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase *kṛtaṣatve*: the intention is that the irregular formulation (*vikṛtanirdeśa*) in the sūtra refers specifically to the intended scope, and is not a mere incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), as is the case with the rule *na yāsayoḥ*.

Because of the use of the feminine gender in the formulation, only those words beginning with *ajā* that are feminine are understood. Therefore, the following does not apply here: *śubhrājikā*, meaning "one whose goat (*aja*) is white (*śubhra*). Also, *jñaḥ* means "one who knows"; thus, *priyajñikā* means "one whose knower (*jña*) is dear (*priya*)."
He states the result of the explanation [of the rule] by treating the qualifier as non-stated (*abhāṣita*) and prescribed (*vihita*), beginning with the words "of the *bahuvrīhi*.

The word "always" (*nityam*) means that because this option (*vikalpa*) does not apply, the general rule (*utsarga*) "pratyayasthāt" alone operates. The intention is that if [the suffix] were a qualifier of the subsequent member (*para-viśeṣaṇatve*), this option would indeed occur.
The mention of "of the *bahuvrīhi*" is an illustration for the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Therefore, in cases such as *atikhaṭvikā* and *niḥkhaṭvikā*, [the long vowel] occurs always.
Regarding the term *śaiṣike kapī*: the intention is that it refers to the short-vowel alternative under the rule *āpo 'nyatarasyām*.

Regarding the word *abhivyāpya* ("having pervaded"): for this very reason, the ancients say that in the example *bahuyuvā śālā*, the suffix *ti* (from the rule *yūnastiḥ*) does not apply because [the element *yuvan*] is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*).
In this context, the author of the Vṛtti has inserted the suffix *khyun* into the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*.

[Autsi] means "born in a Utsa," according to [Pāṇini 4.1.86]: *utsādibhyo’ñ*. Nor should it be argued that this form is already established by the suffix *ṅīn* [via 4.1.73]: *śārṅgaravādyañ*, because in that rule the term *jāteḥ* ("denoting a genus") is understood as a governing word (*anuvartate*). Otherwise, the suffix would apply even in cases of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). By this, the statement of the ancient commentators—that the explicit mention of the suffix *añ* here is for the sake of clarity—is refuted.

In this context, there are multiple statements; however, because of the interpretation that [the rule applies] from that which ends in the vowel *a* which is not a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*), it does not apply here in the cases: *āpiśalam adhīte* and *āpiśalā brāhmaṇī*. For in these instances, the suffix *aṇ* (denoting "taught by") is subordinate, while the suffix *iṇ* (denoting "one who studies") has been elided. Since the primary status belongs to the phoneme (*varṇa*), the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply; therefore, only the feminine suffix *ṭāp* occurs.

Regarding the term *tācchīlike*: this is the intended meaning—when the suffix *ṇa* occurs in the sense of "habitual character" (*śīla*) by the rule *chatrādibhyo ṇaḥ*, the grammatical operations (*kārya*) pertaining to *aṇ* take place, because of the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *kārmastācchīlye*. For it is by this [rule] that the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) in order to override the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-elision of the stem-final) which would otherwise be enjoined for *aṇ* by the rule *an*.
Thus, *caurī* means "one whose habitual character is thievery" (*curā śīlam asyāḥ*).

Regarding the rule *halas taddhitasya*, [the question is raised]: "But surely, once the *akāra* of the *yañ* suffix has been elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the *yakāra* is indeed followed by an *īkāra*; so what is the purpose of the continued reference to the term 'penultimate' (*upadhā*)? Nor can there be the status of being 'as if present' (*sthānivadbhāva*) for that elision, because that is prohibited in the case of *yalopa*. Do not say so; for when *yalopa* is to be effected, the elision of *akāra* (*allopa*) is considered 'unestablished' (*asiddha*) due to its being an *ābhīya* operation."

Regarding the term *anapatye* (not denoting a descendant): although there is a Vārttika stating that "the mention of *apatya* (descendant) should be made," even so, that refers specifically to [suffixes] prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for descendants. And such [a suffix] is only the *yañ* of the *Garga*-class and not the *yañ* of the *deva*-class, because the latter is recited before the governing rule for descendants. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya has elided the vowel *a* in both the rules "after *kañ*, *kvarap*, and *ayañ*" and "from the *Garga*-class, *yañ*. The same applies to the rule "from the *Yaska*-class, in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*), [there is the substitution of] *ayañ* and *añ*."

The mention of *taddhita* in the rule *prācāṃ ṣpha* is for the purpose of establishing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). [Objection: But surely, even without that, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur by the very power of the inclusion of the marker *ṣ*. [Response: If so, then the mention of *taddhita* indicates that *ṣpha* occurs in some cases even after stems ending in *iñ*. This is because, when a stem ends in *yañ*, the form could be established even by the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution), making the elision of the *i* (by the rule *yasyeti ca*) unnecessary. By this, the upcoming statement "the addition of *āsurī* is to be supplied" is established. In the suffix *āyana*, the vowel *ā* following the letter *ph* is for the sake of pronunciation. There is no substitution of *ī* for the *n* of *āyanī* and *āyanin*, due to the power of the inclusion of the marker *n* in *phin*.

Kauravya: How then [is one to explain] Bhaṭṭi’s usage: "O well-frog, if such is your pride"? On this point, they say: because of its association with *kauravya*, only that form of *māṇḍūka* which ends in a patronymic suffix (*apatyapratyaya*) is understood here. But in this case, since it means "this is the wife of a frog," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam*. Regarding *kumārī*: this word denotes the first stage of life (*prathamavayaḥ*) and is not used merely on account of being unmarried.
