However, the expression *vṛddhakumārī* ("an old maiden") is a figurative (*gauṇa*) usage. Regarding *tryanīkā*: it is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of three armies (*anīka*). Here, because the group beginning with *ajādi* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied; thus, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that *tryanīkā* is the subject of the discussion (*adhikaraṇa*).

Regarding *pañcāśvī*: one might object that here the suffix *ṅīṣ* should not apply by the rule *dvigoḥ*, yet it would indeed occur because the word ends in *ṭhak*. This is not so, because of the interpretation: "*ṭhak* [is replaced] by *ya*, which has an *a*-vowel. *dvibistā*: Amara states, "A *suvarṇa* and a *bista* are measures of gold. "Ten *bhāras* make an *ācita*. *dvikambalyā*: [This means] purchased for two *kambalyas*. A *kambalya* is one hundred *palas* of wool. [The suffix] *yat* is applied by the rule *kambalācca saṃjñāyām*. There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ* which expresses the sense of "purchased."

Regarding *dvyāḍhakī*: from the analysis *dvāv āḍhakau pacati* ("she cooks two āḍhaka measures"), the suffix *kha* is optionally applied by the rule *āḍhakācitapātrāt kho 'nyatarasyām*, and the suffixes *kha* and *ṭhan* are also excluded by the rule *dvigor ṅoṣ ca*. In the absence of these, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the previous rule (*prāgvatīya*), which then undergoes elision (*luk*). By this same reasoning, *dvyācitā* is explained.

A *kāṇḍa* is a staff measuring sixteen cubits (*hasta*) from the end of a section. Although the rule of "extension to the end of the compound" (*tadantavidhi*) is established by the qualifying term itself, if the word "end" (*anta*) were not used, then because of the direct mention of "field" (*kṣetra*), this [term *kāṇḍa*] would qualify only the field and not that which ends in it. Consequently, it would apply here as well: *dvikāṇḍī vaḍavā*, meaning "a mare bought for two fields measured by a *kāṇḍa*. But it would not apply here: *dvikāṇḍā kṣetrabhaktiḥ*, meaning "a field-division of two *kāṇḍas*. Therefore, the word "end" (*anta*) is included.

Regarding the term *mātrac*: as for what was previously stated—that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *dvayasac*—that is not correct, because of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "In my view, the first and the second [suffixes] are intended when measuring height. The example is *dvikāṇḍī rajjuḥ* ("a rope two *kāṇḍas* long"). Now, one might object that here the prohibition by the preceding rule (*parimāṇāntāt*) would apply, since the word *kāṇḍa* refers to length (*āyāma*) and thus does not denote a measure (*parimāṇa*). For a "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is that by which something is measured on all sides—from its height and from its circumference—such as an *āḍhaka* or a *kuḍava*; it is not merely anything that delimits an object in some way. As they say: [The definition of a measure: "That which measures on all sides—in terms of height and in terms of circumference—is a measure, such as an *āḍhaka*, a *kuḍava*, and so forth. It is not simply any instrument of delimitation whatsoever.
"Unmāna is indeed measurement by height; parimāṇa is measurement from all sides; pramāṇa is length; and saṃkhyā is external [enumeration] in every respect. Thus it is said.

For this very reason, there is no application of the suffix *ṅīp* in the expression *dvihastā bhittiḥ* ("a two-cubit wall"). On this point, they say: this [rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), so that the prohibition may apply only to the case of a field (*kṣetra*). Therefore, the result of the rule is precisely the occurrence of *ṅīp* in the expression *dvikāṇḍī rajjuḥ* ("a rope of two sections"). Regarding the rule *puruṣāt pramāṇe* ("after the word *puruṣa*, when denoting a measure"): although the word *puruṣa* denotes a genus (*jāti*), nevertheless, in the sentence *dvau puruṣau pramāṇam asyāḥ* ("two men are its measure"), it indeed functions to denote a measure (*pramāṇa*), because of its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *pramāṇa*. In the resultant compound (*vṛtti*), however, this occurs by its very nature. Thus says the *Śulbasūtra*: "A *puruṣa* is five *aratnis*."

Regarding the term *dvipuruṣī*: here the author of the Nyāsa says that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *dvayasaC* by the rule "the suffix *lo* [is used] after a *dvigu* compound when expressing a measure" (*pramāṇe lo dvigornityam*). That is not correct; for since the word *puruṣa* does not denote a measure, the *Ślokavārttika* rule "the suffix *lo* [is used] when expressing a measure" does not apply there. Indeed, that rule applies only to those things well-known as measures, such as *śama* and so forth, but not even to the word *puruṣa*. Otherwise, there would be elision even in the case of *puruṣadvayasam*.

This is clear from the *Padamañjarī* on the rule *puruṣahastibhyāmaṇ ca*. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the suffixes *-dvayasaC* and *-daghnac* would also not apply after this [word *puruṣa*]; for there is the statement: "*matau mama ūrdhvamāne*" (in my opinion, these two suffixes occur when measuring upwards). Similarly, the application of the rule *puruṣāt pramāṇe* also proceeds by virtue of its own inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).

As for what Haradatta stated regarding the commentary (*vṛtti*) on that very same rule—taking up the phrase "the elision is constant (*nityaṃ luk*) after a *dvigu*"—that "therefore, the elision is prescribed here even though it was not otherwise applicable" (*aprāpta eva... vidhīyate*); that too is questionable, because it contradicts the fact that he is prescribing something not mentioned by the three sages (*munitraya*).

As for what was stated by those explaining the ancient methodology—that there is elision (*luk*) due to another *vārttika* being recited under the rule "puruṣahastibhyām"—that too is merely a rash assertion, since the author of the *bhāṣya* and the *vārttikakāra* did not touch upon the cited sūtra; let that matter rest for now.

In reality, however, in the sūtra "puruṣāt pramāṇe," the phrase "dvigostaddhitaluki" is understood to carry over. By the force of that, elision (*luk*) is also implied. Even the statement of Haradatta should be understood by the discerning as having this very intent, albeit in some indirect manner.
What is the purpose of the word *pramāṇe*? [It is to show: "A cow bought for two men" (*dvipuruṣā gauḥ*).
[This applies] only when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix. In the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), we have *pañcapuruṣī*.
Although the substitution of *anaṅ* could have been accomplished simply by the substitution of *nā*, the specific mention of *anaṅ* is for the sake of the rule "and of *dhanus*" (*dhanuṣaśca*).
Regarding *dāman*: although [the rule] is already established by the fact that it is a qualifier of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of clarity.
Regarding "beginning with a numeral": the intention is that, by the force of its being marked with the *svarita* accent, only the specific portion [of the rule] is carried over.

Regarding "exclusive *āmaka*, etc.": examples include: *addhyasyāṃ māmakī tanū* ("this my own body"), *mitrāvaruṇayorbhāgadheyī* ("the share of Mitra and Varuṇa"), *aniṣevyāstanvaḥ santu pāpīḥ* ("may evil bodies be unapproachable"), *utāparibhyo maghavā vijigye* ("and from all sides the Bountiful One has conquered"), *samānīva ākūtiḥ* ("our intention is as one"), *āryakṛtī* ("the noble deed"), *sumaṅgalī* ("auspicious"), and *śivā rudrasya bheṣajī* ("the auspicious healing medicine of Rudra").
Regarding the phrase "but as a counter-example": the intention is that the counter-example cited by the earlier [author], namely *antarvatī* and *pativatī*, is incorrect.

Regarding the question "how [is it] when [the words] are separate?": the intention is that the explanation given by the earlier author—that there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) even in the case of a compound—is futile. Furthermore, in the word *pūtakratuḥ*, the substitution is the vowel *ai* (the *aikāra*), and not a suffix (*pratyaya*), because the subsequent sūtra specifies that it is "acute-accented" (*udātta*).

"But not so," he says. Otherwise—the word *vṛṣākapi* would result in an acute accent on the middle syllable by the rule "in a word with many vowels (*bahaṣ*), the heavy vowel is acute when followed by a light vowel at the end or by two light vowels. [If this were the case], the treatises of the ancients—which maintain that the three words beginning with *agni* are established simply by the rule "the most similar in place" (*sthāne 'ntaratama*)—would be contradicted; such is the sense. Regarding the statement "the acute *ai*": for the word *manu* has an acute accent on the first syllable, because in the rule prescribing the suffix *man* (namely *śṝ-svṛ-snihi-* etc.), there is the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "acute when added to a word denoting grain" (*dhānye nit*).

By this concise statement, he shows that while the term *udātta* (acute) is understood to carry over, it connects only with *aikāra* due to the continuity of the grammatical connection, and not with *aukāra* as well. Therefore, the claim made by the ancients—that both *aikāra* and *aukāra* are acute—is to be disregarded, because it contradicts the Vṛtti, the Padamañjarī, and other authorities; such is the intended meaning.
[The word] *manāyī* has the acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*). The other two have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
*Etā* means "variegated."
Regarding the term "varṇānām" (of colors): examples include *etaḥ*, *śoṇaḥ*, *śitiḥ*, *pṛśniḥ*, and *pṛṣat*.

Regarding "tryeṇyā": the intention here is that although the final member of the compound is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), the entire compound as a whole is not subordinate. The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs either because it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) or due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

Regarding the word *eke*: since the Bhāṣya states "in Vedic usage" (*chandasi*) here, the ancients maintain that usages in common speech (*loke*) such as "the troop of Asiknīkas has gone quickly" (*gato gaṇas tūrṇam asiknikānām*) are based on error. However, in reality, because of the construction *chandasy eke* ("some [say] in Vedic usage"), the Bhāṣya intends this to apply to common speech as well. Otherwise, it would not have included the mention of *eka*. For no one disputes such usages in Vedic literature as "the young women are grey-haired" (*paliknīr id yuvatayaḥ*).

Regarding the term *viśuddhavācī*: it is because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) that the root *daip* means "to purify. However, the intention is that its usage in the lexicon (*kośa*)—where it says "white, bright, fair"—is based on the common property of purity (*viśuddhatva*). Regarding the word *laghau*: when there is one light syllable at the end, or two light syllables following [the penultimate], a heavy syllable belonging to a word with many vowels (*bahvaṣaḥ*, i.e., a polysyllabic word) shall be acutely accented (*udātta*).
The term *aṣ* is an ancient designation for vowels (*ac*).

Regarding the word *kṛṣṇa*: by the rule *kṛṣeśca*, the suffix *na* is applied [to the root *kṛṣ*], and by the rule *kapeśca*, the suffix *ilac* is applied to the root *kap* mentioned in the sūtra; thus, both *kṛṣṇa* and *kapila* have their final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Furthermore, the word *śvan* is included here among the *ṣid-gaura-ādi* group [of words that take the suffix *ṅīṣ*]. Consequently, the example *śunī* cited by the ancients under the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* is merely an error.

As for what they explain—namely, that in the sense of "he calls out like a dog" (*śvānam ācaṣṭe*) or "he acts like a dog" (*śveva ācarati*), there is either a causative suffix (*ṇic*) or a *kvip* suffix; and because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) when the *kvip* is applied, the *ṅīṣ* suffix does not occur, resulting in forms such as *niḥśunī* (with the *ṅīp* suffix)—that is not correct. For according to the primary view, the stated form is difficult to obtain due to the occurrence of vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the elision of the *ṭi* portion when the causative suffix is applied. In other cases, however, let it be somehow possible. Regarding the phrase "if it is a receptacle" (*āvapanaṃ cet*): it is that in which grain is sown or deposited. Regarding "goṇānyā": this is its arbitrary name.
"Uncontrived" (akṛtrimā) means, for example: "This is that very spot where, while searching for you...
"Artificial" (sthalāni) refers to places prepared by a person; for example: "They collect water from artificial ponds. "Śrāṇā" means cooked.

Regarding the term *ayovikāra*: it is commonly known as a plowshare (*phāla*). Regarding *kuśāni*: the followers of the Sāmaveda (*chandogāḥ*) use the term *kuśā* for the stakes made of *udumbara* wood used for counting the *stotrīya* hymns; this is well-established in the rule *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), in the *Vyāsasūtra* passage *hānau tūpāyana-* (3.3.26), and in the Vedic text *kuśā vānaspatyā stha tā mā pāta*. Regarding *patiṃvarā*: the sense is that because it denotes the longing for taking the hand in marriage, it is an adjective expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*).

Regarding the rule *bahvādibhyaśca*: they say that since the word *bahu* denotes a quality (*guṇavācin*), its inclusion is for the sake of the subsequent rule, as it is already established by the preceding one. In reality, however, both this rule and the subsequent rule *nityaṃ chandasi* are indeed superfluous, because all optional alternatives (*vikalpa*) are restricted to the Vedic language (*chandas*). Regarding *puṃyogāt*: the sense is that [the application of the suffix] is secondary (*gauṇī vṛtti*). But when the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the primary sense according to *tasyedam*, then the form is simply *gopī*.

Some maintain that in this context, *puṃyoga* (connection with a male) refers exclusively to the state of marriage (*dāmpatya*). However, in reality, since there is no evidence for such a restriction, the relationship of progenitor and offspring (*janyajanakabhāva*) is also included. Thus says Bhaṭṭi: "Rāma was easily borne by Kausalyā; thereafter Bharata was born from Kekayī. Here, *kekayī* means the daughter of Kekaya. If the patronymic suffix *añ* were applied according to the rule *janapadaśabdāt*, the form would have been *kaikeyī*. Nor could the elision (*luk*) of that suffix occur by the rule *ataśca*, because of the prohibition in the rule *na prācyabhargādi*. Thus says Kālidāsa: [and so forth].
"The desires of Kaikeyī have borne fruit.

By this, Devakī is explained. A "bad barley" (duṣṭo yavaḥ) is "barley-like" (yavānī); by this, a different species altogether is denoted. This is its very defect: that even in the absence of the stated genus of barley, there is a simulation of its form.

"It should be stated that [the suffix] ṅīṣ [is applied]"—this point was established in the third section of the Bhāṣya under the rule *iṅśca*. How so? As for what they say: "By the force of the long vowel pronunciation, the word *ānuk* is divided as *ā-anuk*. Since the forms of Indra and others would already be established by *ānuk* alone, the force of prescribing the substitution of the vowel *ā* implies that in some cases the suffix is prescribed even from other bases. Thus, the form *brahmāṇī* is established. This is to be considered doubtful, because if *ānuk* were applied, the rule *ato guṇe* would result in the application of the single-substitute (pararūpa) form.

If it is argued that the long vowel will occur by virtue of the power of the utterance of the letter *ka*, for otherwise one would have simply prescribed the augment *nu*—[we reply: No, because [the letter *ka*] serves its purpose by subverting the rule "allopo 'naḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.134). If it is further argued that, as in the case of "patyurno" (Pāṇini 8.2.7), when a substitute (*ādeśa*) is to be applied, the elision of the *a* will not occur precisely due to the power of the utterance of the letter *ka* which serves as a mark (*liṅga*) for the augment (*āgama*)—[we reply: No, because the letter *ka* has its utility in the word *sarva*. For there is no elision there, owing to the prohibition "na saṃyogāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.137).

Therefore, since there is an absence of functional capacity between the letters *ka* and *ā*, the pronunciation of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is necessary for the purpose of subverting the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule. By this, the statement of Haradatta—that "for the sake of brevity, one should simply say *anuk* [with a short vowel]"—is refuted.

Regarding the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*: the suffix *ṅīp* is applied after that which ends in *aṇ*. The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*. As for the form *vastrakrītī*: in the state where the analysis is *vastra-bhis krītaḥ*, before the production of the case-ending (*sup*), the compound ends in *a*; therefore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.

Regarding the phrase "not in some cases": because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely) in the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā*, there is in some instances a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). In that case, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* occurs first because it is *antaraṅga* (internal); subsequently, because the word no longer ends in the vowel *a*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply—this is the intended meaning. Therefore, [the form] *bahvī* [is derived as follows]. This is the underlying idea: the rules prescribing final acute accent (*antodāttatā*) are "bahornañvaduttarapadabhūmni," "nañsubhyām," and "jātikālasukhādibhyo'nācchādanātkto'kṛtamitapratipannāḥ. Since these specify that the accent applies when preceded by a genus-word (*jāti*), it follows by implication that words preceded by *bahu* and others are excluded from this operation.

Since the optionality [of the suffix] for compounds whose prior member is not a *svāṅga* (body part) will be stated later, he says here that only examples where the prior member is a *svāṅga* are given: *ūrubhinnī* ("one whose thighs are split").

Regarding the rule *jātāntāt*: although the formation would be established by the rule *bahuvrīherudāttāt* alone—just as in the case of *varṇādanudāttāt*—the inclusion of the word *anta* (ending in) is for the purpose of conveying the sense of necessity (*nityatva*). The point is that the rule *vā jāte* provides an optional acute accent (*udātta*), whereas this one provides a necessary one. Thus, it should be understood that usages such as *phalamukhī*, *kāraṇamukhī*, and *anavasthā* are based on error.

Regarding the word *uraḥkroḍā*: Haradatta and others maintain that this is feminine. In that case, once the shortening of the *upasarjana* has been applied, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply because the stem ends in *ā*. However, Amarasimha says: "The word *kroḍa*, meaning the space between the arms, is not masculine. Ratnamati, on the other hand, asserts its masculinity. Furthermore, the author of the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi* states that in the [gaṇa] list, only the nominal stem *kroḍa* is recited, not the form ending in *ṭā*. Thus, since there is no distinction made, the examples should be understood as applying to all three genders.

Mādhava, however, states regarding the root *kruḍ* (meaning "to dive") in the *tudādigaṇa*: "The word *kroḍa* [is derived from this]. [With the suffix] *ghañ*, [we have] *kroḍā*, meaning the chest of horses. This word ending in *ṭāp* is by its very nature restricted to a specific domain, because it is listed as ending in *ṭāp* specifically in the *kroḍādi* group. For the word *kroḍa*, which refers merely to the space between the arms, the optional suffix *ṅīṣ*—characteristic of words denoting one's own limbs (*svāṅga*)—does indeed occur in a *bahuvrīhi* compound: *kalyāṇakroḍī* or *kalyāṇakroḍā mayūrī*.

Regarding the statement "the *ṅīṣ* is replaced by *ṅīp*": the sense is that, by the rule "from a word preceded by a direction" (*dikpūrvapadāt*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is substituted for the nominative case (*prathamā*) of the term *ṅīṣ*. If, however, *ṅīp* were independent, it would undesirably apply even to words such as *prāggulphā* (preceded by *prāk*). The sense is that to avoid this, there would be the burden of either carrying over the previously mentioned exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or the prohibitions (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Regarding the example *vṛṣalī*: the sense is that once the status of being a *vṛṣala* (outcaste) is stated with respect to one individual, it is easily understood—even without explicit mention—with respect to their offspring, siblings, and so forth.

In the case of *aupagavī*, this [suffix] *ṅīp*—which is taught later—supersedes the *ṅīp* characterized by the suffix *aṇ*. Thus, the intention is that those who, taking the word *aupagavī* as the illustrative example (*pratīka*) under the section on offspring (*apatya*), explain it as being formed by the *ṅīp* of the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ," are to be disregarded.
Regarding the example *brāhmaṇī*, the sense is that the older examples of *ṅīṣ* are merely due to error (*prāmādika*).

Regarding the word *kurūḥ*: by the paribhāṣā "that which is qualified by gender," it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) are applied. However, the Eastern grammarians, having cited the sūtra "as if preceding and following" (*antādivacca*), stated that the case-endings are applied because of the status of being "like the beginning. Here, this must be said: the status of being "like the beginning" is prescribed with respect to what follows. Consequently, in this case, the prohibition "not when it is a suffix" (*apratyaya*) would apply, and the case-endings would not occur.

As for what they have explained—namely, that "ādi" (beginning) means preceding in relation to the suffix *ūṅ*, and that because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is grasped as a constituent part of that [suffix] due to its having the same status as it, which amounts to saying it possesses the status of being a prior member—that too is strained and contradicts both their own and others' texts. For according to the aforementioned reasoning, even in cases such as *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye*, the suffix *su* would apply by the rule "the singular is the default. To prevent this, if one were to accept a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) in the rule "not a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*), then the fault remains in the present case.

Furthermore, in the case of *śvaśrūḥ*, because there is no single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [operation], the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding forms qualified by gender) is necessary. As for the argument that [the rule] applies here because of the mention of *svādayaḥ* based on the reference "*śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā*," that is not correct, because that reference pertains to the word-form itself, just as in the cases of "*viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*" and "*ṅeryaḥ*".

Regarding the word *śvaśurasya*: although the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been expected by the rule for feminine formation through connection with a masculine (*puṃyogalakṣaṇa*), the suffix *ūṅ* is applied instead. The elision (*lopa*) prescribed in conjunction with that [suffix] applies only to the final vowel *a*, because of its proximity, and not to the initial one. Furthermore, this statement is intended merely to explain the meaning established by the grammatical usage in the rule "the husband is designated by the wife" (*śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā*). Therefore, the elision of the first *a* should not even be suspected. Regarding the phrase "the preceding member expresses the object of comparison": in the example "her thighs are like the foreparts of elephants' trunks (*karabha*) by means of the hands of her nurse (*dhātrī*)," the rule does not apply; for although the word *karabha* denotes the object of comparison, it does not function as the preceding member of the compound.

The term *śaphau* means "two hooves. Although Amara states that "the word *śapha* is neuter, while *khura* is masculine," nevertheless, the masculine gender for the word *śapha* is also widely accepted. This is due to its frequent usage in the Vedic passage "śaphāviva jarbhurāṇā" (like two hooves, quivering), in the works of Nyāsa, Haradatta, and others during their commentaries on the sūtra "grāmyapaśusaṅgheṣu," in treatises such as the *Vācaspatya*, and in accordance with the Mahābhāṣya which states, "Gender is not to be taught, for gender depends upon common usage," as well as the lexicon entry: "śapha, bhuja, guda, ghoṇā."

This is because [the word *ūru*] is listed in the *gaṇa* beginning with *kroḍa* in the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi*, and because Hemacandra’s lexicon (*Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*) states: "The term *śapha* refers to the hoof of cattle and the like, as well as the root of trees. Furthermore, the *Viśvakośa* declares it to be both masculine and neuter. The analysis of the compound is: "she whose thighs (*ūrū*) are beautiful (*vāmau*). In all these cases, since there is no established precedent for such usage, this is a rule providing what was not previously obtained. If so, how is it that Kālidāsa uses the phrase "pīvaroru pibatīva barhiṇam" ("the woman with full thighs drinks, as it were, the peacock")? This is simply an error. Some maintain that the *guṇa* substitution in the vocative is not applied here because the form is based on a specific technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*).

Regarding *sahita*: the word *sahita*, derived from the rule "the root *sam* [is used] with *hita* and *tati*" (*samo vā hitatatayoḥ*), is not intended here; the point is that [the form] is established simply by including *saṃhitā* because it is a modification of one part [of *sahita*].

Regarding "the *a* which follows *añ*": what is the purpose of qualifying the *a* with *añ*? [Consider] *śūrasenī*. Here, after the suffix *añ* [added] to the word for a country according to the rule "from words denoting a country" (*janapadaśabdāt*), there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "and after *at*" (*ataśca*), and then the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the characteristic of a genus (*jāti*).
[Consider] *śārṅgaravī*: the suffix *aṇ* is added to the word *śṛṅgaru* in the sense of offspring (*apatya*).

Regarding the phrase *nṛnarayoḥ*: from the word *nṛ*, the suffix *ṅīp* applies by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*; however, from the word *nara*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have applied by virtue of its being a genus (*jāti*) term, hence this specific statement is made. Now, one might object that in the word *nara*, the *vṛddhi* substitution should apply to the final vowel (*alo'ntyasya*). As for what some say—that because the final vowel is removed by the elision *yasyeti ca*, the *vṛddhi* occurs for the non-final *a* due to proximity (*āntaratamya*), and that according to the maxim *guṇe tvanyāyyakalpanā*, it is more logical to set aside the *paribhāṣā* regarding the final vowel—[this is not so].

That is not correct; for since the *vṛddhi* substitution, which is prescribed in conjunction with the suffix (*pratyaya*), is *antaraṅga*, it is appropriate that it should take effect even before the subsequent elision of the *y* sound (*yasyeti-lopa*), thereby subverting it. Furthermore, even if the elision were to somehow occur, the *vṛddhi* would apply to the *repha* (the *r*) alone and not to the *akāra*, because the *alontya-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning the final letter) takes precedence over the *antaratama-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning the most similar substitute).

Furthermore, the *antaratama-paribhāṣā* excludes a dissimilar substitute (*ādeśa*), but it does not restrict the original element (*sthānin*). Therefore, how could there be an exclusion of the letter *r* from being the *sthānin*? Moreover, the invocation of the maxim "but in the case of a *guṇa*, that which is improper [is excluded]" is quite gross, because there can be no relationship of quality and qualified (*guṇa-guṇibhāva*) between two *paribhāṣās*.

The essential point here is as follows: "nara" is an imitation of the form ending in 'ra' with the vowel 'a' elided, thus [the compound] is *nara-aḥ* = *naraḥ*. It should be explained as "of both *nā* and *nara*. Alternatively, *naraḥ* is *nara-sya aḥ*, where the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) applies as in the case of *katanta*. Then, "of both *nā* and *nara*" refers to *nṛ-narayoḥ*. Furthermore, only the first vowel 'a' of *nara* is taken, and not the second, due to the force of the phonetic conjunction (*praśleṣa*). More details should be understood from the *Śabdakaustubha*.

The word *putra* is cited here [in the rule]. For example: *śailaputrī* ("daughter of the mountain"), "she spreads joy in the heart like a daughter," and "I shall do all that, O daughter of the lord of the earth. One should not fall into the error of thinking that the word *putra* cannot be applied to a girl; for Amarasimha states: "The words *ātmaja*, *tanaya*, *sūnu*, *suta*, and *putra*—all these, when used in the feminine, they say, denote a daughter. It is precisely because of this that the Vārttika, "optionally for *sūtakā*, *putrikā*, and *vṛndāraka*," along with its commentary (*bhāṣya*) and other related texts, is consistent within the section on the substitution of *ī* (by the rule *pratyayasthāt...*).

As for what Haradatta has stated here—that the word *putra* alone does not apply to a female—this should be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya and other works, as well as his own statement within the section on the substitution of *it*. However, this point remains to be considered: for what purpose is the Vārttika, "The suffix *putraḍ* is optionally applied after the word *duhitṛ* following the words *sūta*, *ugra*, *rājan*, *bhojaka*, *kula*, and *meru*," in the rule "When *kāra* follows, [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after *satyāgada*"?

As for what they say—that [the word *putrī*] is for the sake of the accent—that is not so. Because the suffix *ṅīp* is applied due to the *ṭi*-designation, the resulting form is oxytone by the rule regarding the disappearance of the accent (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). Furthermore, even when this *ṅīp*-ending form is part of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it remains oxytone by the general accent rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*); thus, there is no difference in accent. As for the claim that the word *putra* has been interpolated into the *śārṅgarava* group and is not traditional—that too is incorrect, because it contradicts the cited usage and contradicts Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others who, in the Vārttika on "vā sūtakā," support the elision of the vowel *a*. Let this matter rest for now. Regarding *āmbaṣṭhyā*: the suffix *yaṅ* is applied according to the rule "vṛddhetkosalāt."

*Kārīṣagandhyā*: "One who has the smell of *karīṣa* (cow-dung) is *karīṣagandhiḥ*. By the rule "upamānācca," the substitution of the suffix *id* for *gandha* occurs. Her female descendant (*gotrāpatya*) is formed with the suffix *aṇ*. By the rule "aṇiñoḥ," this is replaced by *ṣyaṅ*. Although that [suffix *ṣyaṅ*] is prescribed only for the feminine, nevertheless, by the force of the marker *ṅ*, the suffix *cāp* is applied even after a word ending in it. *Pautimāṣyā*: the word *pūtimāṣa* belongs to the *garga*-class.

The term *taddhitāḥ* (secondary suffixes) is used in the plural to include those secondary suffixes that have not been explicitly mentioned. Furthermore, the use of this grand designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the sake of making the name meaningful: they are called *taddhitāḥ* because they are "beneficial" (*hita*) to those applications (*prayoga*). By this, they shall apply only according to their specific designations. One might object: "Let this governing rule (*adhikāra*) apply prior to the suffix *ṭāp*; let there be no mention of the word *taddhita* in the rule for the suffix *ṣpha*, and let there be no mention of the vowel *ī* in the rule for the elision of the genitive ending *yasya*. This is not so; for in the case of the word *paṭvī*, the substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel *ū* (by Pāṇini 6.4.147) would otherwise undesirably apply.

Regarding the phrase "from the present participle": it is derived from the etymology *yauti* (he mixes) or *pati* (he protects). Some, however, state that the suffix *kat* is an *auṇādika* addition to the root *yu* by virtue of the rule *bāhulaka*. In either case, a collection of young women (*yuvatī*) is called *yauvata*. However, if the suffix *aṇ* were added to the form ending in *ty*, then due to the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), it would simply be *yauvana*. As for the claim that the word does not undergo the masculine substitution because of its inclusion in the *bhikṣādi* list, this interpretation contradicts the *Bhāṣya*, since that reading is rejected in the *Bhāṣya*; such is the direction of the argument.
Thus ends the section on feminine suffixes in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now begins the section on grammatical relations (kāraka).

Regarding the word *mātra*: its meaning is restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Amarasimha states, "The word *mātra* [is used] in the sense of entirety (*kārtsnya*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). By the particle *eva* in the phrase "only those [beginning with] the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), etc., constitute that *mātra*," there is an analysis within the same words (*asvapada-vigraha*). The compound is formed because it belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class and so forth. Regarding the word *kṛṣṇa*: although this term primarily denotes the color blue and is thus of indefinite gender (*aniyata-liṅga*), the point is that when referring to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, it is indeed of definite gender.
Regarding the word *jñāna*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

Regarding the word *droṇa*: it should not be argued that the nominative case-suffix (*prathamā*) should apply to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone. For if that were the case, it would be impossible for the relationship between the delimiting factor (*paricchedaka*) and the delimited factor (*paricchedya*) to appear as a relational mode (*saṃsargavidhayā*), because of the established linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) that the relation between the meanings of two nouns is exclusively one of identity (*abheda*). Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the genitive sense is absent, since the theory of "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted there. Nor does it apply to the meaning of particles (*nipāta*), since their function is accepted as being merely indicative (*dyotakatā*).

Nor should it be argued that even in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*) between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is difficult to find because it is not observed elsewhere; for the sense is that it is indeed observed in cases such as *taddhita* suffixes denoting a deity. "Number" refers to the verbal number (*vacana*), because the ancient grammarians have used the term in that very way.

In this sūtra, it would be sufficient to state simply: "The first [case-ending occurs] in the sense (artha), the object (liṅga), and so forth. Everything else can be dispensed with. For instance, when it is stated that "the first [occurs] in the sense," if there arises the expectation "in whose sense?", it is indeed obtained that "it belongs to that from which the case-endings (svādi) are prescribed. Furthermore, the case-endings are prescribed after nominal stems (prātipadika) and after those qualified by gender-indicators (liṅga-pratyaya). And being for the sake of that [nominal stem] consists precisely in its having a necessary and constant presence (niyatopasthitikatva) [therein].

Furthermore, in cases such as *mṛḍānī*, since the connection with a male [referent], greatness, and so forth are invariably manifested from the word ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, the nominative case is established; this is another favorable point. Under the alternative formulation, however, that [nominative] would not occur.

However, if the word *artha* refers to the domain of grammatical function (*vṛtti*), and *vṛtti* consists of both primary denotation (*śakti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—wherein figurative usage (*gauṇī*) is either included within indication or treated as distinct—and the "triple" (number, gender, and case) constitutes the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then the mention of "gender" (*liṅga*) need not even be included. Even if the indicated meanings (*lakṣyāṇām*) are diverse, there is no harm, because the restrictive portion [of the definition] has been abandoned. Thus, the essence is simply this: "the first case ending occurs when the meaning [of the stem] is to be expressed. Even the expression "a *droṇa* of rice" (*droṇo vrīhiḥ*) is established through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the word *droṇa* to that which is measured by a *droṇa*, just like the expression "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*).

Even the usage of "one," "two," and so forth is established by the very prohibition that "the *prakṛti* [stem] alone should not be employed," because the employment of a mere repetitive suffix (*anuvādaka*) is more logical than the employment of a word whose meaning is unconnected [to the context].

Likewise, the inclusion of the term "mere" (*mātra*) is also redundant, since the first case ending (*prathamā*) does not apply when there is an excess of objects (*karman*) and so on, as indicated by the rule "and in the case of address" (*sambodhane ca*).

As for what was stated by the ancients—that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is "existence" (*sattā*)—and as for its explanation: that meaning which appears merely as "existent" (*san*), and not in the form of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, nor as connected with gender, number, or case-role (*kāraka*), is intended here; such as the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

If it is argued that the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) can only be said to "exist" (*asti*), but cannot be described as being "of such a kind" or "of that kind," we say no. This is because the claim that words such as *uccais* (high) and *nīcais* (low) produce a cognition in the form of "it exists" (*sann iti*) contradicts all established systems of thought; furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with verbs like *asti* is difficult to find in the case of words whose meanings are non-existent; and finally, it contradicts your own statement that [indeclinables] are not connected with gender, number, or case-role (*kāraka*).

If it is argued that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "exists" (*asti*) for that which is presented by another word [in the sentence], we say no; because such a thing does not serve as a differentiator (*avyāvartakatva*), and because it contradicts the remainder of the sentence beginning with "not again" (*na punar*), and because it would result in over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "Kṛṣṇa is Śrī. Nor can its establishment be achieved through the mention of gender (*liṅga*), since the word "only" (*mātra*) excludes anything additional.

As for what was explained by the predecessor—that wherever a word functions without depending on another referent (arthāntara), all that is the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha), which is to say the ground for the application of the word (śabdapravṛttinimitta)—as in the cases of *uccaiḥ* and *nīcaiḥ*; he claims these two, being devoid of gender and number, express their own meaning independently of genus (*jāti*) and so forth—that too is not correct. Here, the ground for the application of the word appears as a qualifier (*prakārībhūya*). And thus, a cognition consisting of that alone is impossible.

If even that were intended, then it would also occur in the case of words such as *ghaṭa* (pot), and consequently, there would be no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with number, case-role (*kāraka*), and so forth.

As for the argument that the word *droṇa* applies to a measure of rice (*vrīhi*) and the like because of the relation "this is that [measure]," and that the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is included [in the definition] because the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhya-nyāya*) would otherwise not apply there—that is not correct. For the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this principle applies to operations on words (*pada-kārya*), not to operations on nominal stems (*prātipadika-kārya*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that expressions such as "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*) could not be established.

As for what they say—that words such as *droṇa* and others never deviate from being measures made of iron or wood, whereas they certainly deviate from the object measured (*parimeya*), and therefore, since that [measure] lacks the status of being the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is necessary even though it was not otherwise obtained—this too is incorrect, because it would result in an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of figurative or metaphorical expressions such as "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*) or "the platforms cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*).

In that regard, if it is argued that even though there is a difference between the qualificand (viśeṣya), such as a young boy (māṇavaka), and the lion, the meaning "one who resembles a lion" is invariably present in the case of secondary indication (gauṇī), then it is equally the case that even though there is a difference between rice (vrīhi) and so forth, the measure "a *droṇa*" is invariably present. Furthermore, because the rule specifically mentions the word "measure" (*mātra*), it would not apply when there is an excess of address; thus, this [sūtra] is commenced. Here, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the vocative is the qualificand with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), but it is an adjectival qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the action (*kriyā*). And it has been said: "That which is a word of address is an adjectival qualifier of the action."
"In 'vrajāni devadatta', there is a *nighāta* (tonal suppression) when that is the case.
And thus, the meaning of the sentence "O Rāma, protect me" is: protection whose object is myself, directed toward [the person] addressed as being related to Rāma. This concludes the first [section].

In the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*, the word *kartuḥ* ("of the agent") is a genitive in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*. The suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the present tense after the desiderative form of the root *āp* (to obtain), by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaś ca*; here, *mati* means "desire" and not "cognition," because the term "cognition" (*buddhi*) is mentioned again later in the rule. Thus, the meaning is: "that which is desired to be obtained by the agent. Furthermore, the "agent" is the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root. When the question arises as to "by what [means] does the agent desire to obtain it?", the answer is obtained by implication: "by means of the activity that serves as the qualifier [of the agent]."

This is what he says with the words "by the action" (kriyayā): the presentness conveyed by the suffix -kta is not intended here. By this, examples such as "he has made a mat" (kaṭaṃ kṛtavān) and "he will make a mat" (kaṭaṃ kariṣyati) are established.

Regarding the term *kārakam*: this is obtained from the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "in the case of a *kāraka*," for there the locative case is used in the sense of the nominative by way of transposition. A *kāraka* designation is prescribed by breaking up the sentence for each individual rule. For example: "that which is fixed (*dhruvam*) in separation shall have the designation *kāraka*. Then, having stated "the *apādāna*," it is meant that the *kāraka* already mentioned shall have the designation *apādāna*. Furthermore, by the force of the recurrence of the word *kāraka*, there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the specific designations.

This designation is etymologically appropriate: that which "acts" (karoti) is an "agent" (kāraka). Consequently, that which is not connected with an action does not [function as an agent], as in the example: "He asks the Brāhmaṇa's son the way. For here, the Brāhmaṇa is a qualifier of the son, but not something connected with the action.

Alternatively, the word *kāraka* refers to action (*kriyā*), based on the etymological derivation: "it is called a *kāraka* because it effects (*karoti*) the designations of agent, object, and so forth. Thus, since the phrase "with respect to an action" (*kriyāyām*) is supplied in the rules prescribing technical terms such as *apādāna*, these specific designations are prescribed only for those things that are connected with an action. However, in rules such as "after a *kāraka* [ending], when *datta* or *śruta* follow," the word *kāraka* is uttered with its accent (*svarita*). Consequently, in this context, only the sixfold group beginning with the agent (*kartṛ*) mentioned under this governing heading (*adhikāra*) is understood. On this view, even in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the meaning of the term *kāraka* is "that which is connected with an action."
In the first alternative, however, the designation "kāraka" (participant) would apply; and it should be explained that this *kāraka* would then bear the designation "karman" (object).

[Objection: But surely, in cases such as *bahupaṭuḥ* ("very clever"), since the meaning [of the suffix] has already been expressed by the prefix *bahu*, the secondary suffixes *kalpa* and so on do not occur; likewise, in cases such as *kaṭaḥ kriyate* ("the mat is being made"), the accusative case will not occur because the meaning has already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so on. Furthermore, the accusative in *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a mat") finds its scope [only there], and in cases like *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"), it will be superseded by the nominative, because [the nominative] is without scope [elsewhere]. Nor can [forms like] *vṛkṣaḥ* ("tree") be considered its scope, because even there, since the tree is the agent with respect to the implied verb "exists" (*asti*), the third case would necessarily follow.

If you argue that in cases such as "this is blue, not red," where the intention is the exclusion of other qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇāntara-nivṛtti*), the nominative case finds its scope because the verb "is" (*asti*) is not necessary; and if you further claim that, due to this conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), let the nominative prevail, and thus the governing rule concerning the "unexpressed" (*anabhihitādhikāra*) is redundant—do not say so. This is because the rule was formulated on the premise that number (*saṃkhyā*) is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*). Thus, the meaning is: when singularity is present in an unexpressed object (*karman*), the singular accusative ending applies.

Furthermore, regarding the non-commencement of the rule [Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.46], the meaning of the sentence is that when there is singularity (*ekatva*) with respect to the object (*karman*), the second case singular suffix *am* is applied. If that were the case, then in examples such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"), even though the mere object is expressed by the *kta*-suffix, the singularity of that object remains unexpressed; consequently, the suffix *am* would be unavoidable. Nor can one argue that the nominative (*prathamā*) applies because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], for in cases like *kartavyaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat is to be made"), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix would apply even more subsequently than the nominative. In the view that the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is the meaning of the case-ending, the rule is rejected in the original treatise (*ākara*).

"One worships Hari" (*hariṃ bhajati*). Since joy arises in Hari through the act of worship, Hari is the object (*karman*) by virtue of being pervaded by the action as qualified by that joy. Alternatively, the meaning of the sentence is the act of worship as qualified by that [joy]. The same applies to the expression "Hari is served" (*hariḥ sevyate*), according to the established doctrine that "the verb (*ākhyāta*) has the action as its primary meaning. The meaning of this doctrine is that the action presented by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), and not a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) as it is with respect to the meaning of a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*).

For this very reason, *pacati vrajati* ("he cooks and goes") is not a single sentence, just as *pācako vrajati* ("the cooker goes") is. For the meaning of *pācaka* and similar forms is "going performed by the agent of cooking. The act of cooking and the act of going, having a single agent, are the distinct meanings of *pacati* and *vrajati*. Consequently, the proclamation of the Naiyāyikas—that cognition has a nominative-ending word as its primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—should not be respected by those who follow the Bhāṣya and other authoritative texts. Yāska also says: "The verb (ākhyāta) has the action as its primary focus; nouns (*nāman*) have the substance as their primary focus."

In expressions such as "see, the deer runs," however, the act of going performed by the deer is the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing, while the act of seeing itself is the primary element. And it has been said: "Just as many nouns (*subanta*) serve as qualifiers for a verb (*tiṅanta*), so too they say that a verb may also serve as a qualifier for another verb."

Thus, the meaning of "pacati bhavati" (he cooks [and it] exists) is that "the act of cooking exists. However, this is the distinction: although an action presented by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) may serve as a qualifier for another action, according to the theory of verbal ellipsis (*śabdādhyāhāravāda*), its status as an object (*karmatva*) is merely a relation (*saṃsarga*) and not a qualifier (*prakāra*), because it is not a word-meaning (*apadārthatvāt*). According to the theory of semantic ellipsis (*arthādhyāhāravāda*), however, even if it were a qualifier, such a conclusion would be acceptable. The same determination applies, depending on the difference of opinion, to the result (*phala*) conveyed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) in expressions such as "pacati" (he cooks).

For this very reason, the occurrence of the second singular case-ending in expressions such as *śobhanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks well"), which are in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with that [verb], and the contingency of the third case-ending in expressions such as *agniṣṭomena yajeta* ("one should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma"), are both logically consistent. Nor should it be argued that, just as in the example, there should be the use of a nominal suffix (*sub-vibhakti*) expressing the objecthood (*karmatva*) etc., from the word providing the qualificand in the illustrated case; for neither the verbal root nor a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For the Naiyāyikas, however, this fault would indeed arise. To explain: just as one might say *dhāvantaṃ mṛgaṃ paśyet* ("one should see the running deer"), one might also say *dhāvati mṛgam* ("the running deer").

Nor should it be argued that such a usage is impossible because the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are obligatory when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a non-nominative case; for even so, the failure of the accusative case to arise remains difficult to justify. If you object: "In that case, there is simply a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), since in the phrase 'paśya' (see), the object 'tam' (him) must be supplied; whereas constructions such as 'pacati bhavati' (he cooks [and] exists) are certainly undesirable in the sense of 'pākaḥ bhavati' (cooking exists)," we say: do not speak thus. For supplying an ellipsis involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and moreover, such a supply would lack authoritative status due to its contradiction with the words of the Sage (Pāṇini). Furthermore, your mere lack of desire to accept this is irrelevant.

Furthermore, in cases such as *apakṣīd devadatto 'vehi*, there is no possibility at all for the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle marker) and the like to apply. Moreover, the status of these as forming a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is accepted by all authorities, including the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vārttika*, and others. Nor should it be argued that in the case of finite verb forms (*tiṅanta*), a cognition of one action qualified by another action necessarily arises; for such a cognition is unavoidable for those who possess the corresponding linguistic competence (*vyutpanna*). Nor can it be said that grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is not desired in such a meaning, because those very same authorities engaged in teaching grammatical correctness have accepted it, and because it is indispensable in examples such as *purīm avaskanda*, which is established under the governing rule *dhātusambandhe pratyayāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.1).

If it is objected: "In the Siddhānta, if agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*) are admitted even for the action denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta*), would not its status as being of the nature of non-existence (*asattvarūpatva*) be compromised? The answer is: No. This is because such a status is established merely through the absence of gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and any *kāraka* other than the agent or the object; furthermore, it is because objecthood is not accepted as a qualifier (*prakāra*). This is explained in detail elsewhere.

Regarding the phrase *abhihite tu* ("but when [the case-role] is already expressed"): if it is objected that, in that case, the accusative would not occur even in the sentence "He eats cooked rice" (*pakvam odanaṃ bhuṅkte*), we say: do not say so. For here, two potencies of objecthood (*karmatva-śakti*) are determined by the roots *pac* (to cook) and *bhuj* (to eat). Of these, the accusative arises by taking up the unexpressed potency as determined by the principal action (*pradhāna-kriyā*). And it has been said by Hari: "Where there are two distinct potencies belonging to a substance in its primary and secondary actions, the potency residing in the subordinate [action] conforms to the principal [action]."
"The capacity whose primary object [is the action] is expressed by the suffix;
when it pertains to a subordinate factor (guṇa), then, like that [primary factor], it is understood even though it is not explicitly stated.
For this very reason, in the expression "Having cooked, the rice is eaten" (*paktvaudano bhujyate*), the nominative case alone is used for the rice, because the act of cooking (*pac*) is subordinate.

In reality, however, in expressions such as *paktvā bhujyate* ("having cooked, it is eaten"), there is a simultaneous verbal (*śābda*) syntactic connection of the object with both the roots *pac* (to cook) and *bhuj* (to eat); yet, this occurs through one [verb] verbally and the other [verb] semantically (*ārtha*). In that case, the nominative and accusative cases are indeed established. For example: *paktvā bhujyate odanaḥ* ("Having cooked, rice is eaten"). What has been cooked? By implication, rice. But when the expression *odanaṃ paktvā bhujyate* ("Having cooked rice, it is eaten") is used, then in the phrase *bhujyate*, "rice" is understood by implication. Thus, depending on the difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣā*), both forms—*pūjayituṃ śakyate hariḥ* ("Hari can be worshipped") and *hariṃ pūjayituṃ śakyate* ("It is possible to worship Hari")—are correct.
"Attained-bliss" (prāptānanda) means one who has become the object of an attainment whose agent is bliss. Regarding what was stated as "generally," he states its result: "in some cases.

As for the phrase "poison-tree": if, however, the connection with either "growing" or "cutting" is intended as the direct object (*karman*), then the accusative case would certainly occur; this is how it should be understood.

"It touches grass": the meaning is that just as there is a connection through action with an object of desire such as the Ganges—which is being touched—because it is the locus of the resulting fruit such as conjunction, so too is there such a connection with an undesired object like grass.

It might be argued: "Let it simply be that action is characterized by possessing a fruit established by a verbal root; what is the use of mentioning separately the 'desired' (*īpsita*) and the 'undesired' (*anīpsita*)? Do not say so. In the sentence *agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati* ("He wards off the boy from the fire"), the status of the boy (*māṇavaka*) as an ablative (*apādāna*) would apply by the rule *vāraṇārthānām*. To set aside that [application], it must indeed be stated: *kartur īpsitatamam* ("That which is most desired by the agent"). Furthermore, for the sake of including both the hated (*dveṣya*) and the indifferent (*udāsīna*), the rule *tathāyuktam* ("that which is connected in the same way") is also necessary. The inclusion of the term *anīpsita*, however, is merely for clarity and is not strictly required.

However, this must be noted: the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding both the desired (*īpsita*) and the undesired (*anīpsita*) is of one and the same form; for although desire (*īpsā*) and lack of desire (*anīpsā*) and so forth are utilized in the application of technical designations (*saṃjñāpravṛtti*), like [the roots] *adhi-śī* etc., they do not enter into the scope of what is expressed by the accusative case (*dvitīyā-vācya*), because only that which cannot be obtained otherwise is the meaning of a word.

Regarding the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the second case suffix [is used] for the object"), all those things for which the designation "object" (*karman*) has been prescribed by various rules are presented in that form. The second case suffix prescribed for them denotes the substratum (*ādhāra*), because of parsimony (*lāghava*), since the action is obtained through the verbal root and the agent through words such as "Devadatta," while properties such as "being most desired" (*iṣṭatamatva*) are not manifested. Furthermore, here there is a relation of identity between the meanings of the base and the suffix. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is the activity conducive to that pleasure which has Hari as its substratum.

Although it is the same in that the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others—prescribed for the object (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)—all have "substratum" (*ādhāra*) as their meaning, nevertheless, a distinction is logically established in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) which results from the fruit, the operation (*vyāpāra*), and both of these mediated through their own substrata. Nor should it be thought that "substratum-ness" (*ādhāratā*) itself is the expressed meaning (*vācya*); for that would entail the excessive complexity (*atigaurava*) of having "substratum-ness" as the delimiting factor of the expressed meaning (*vācyatāvacchedakatā*), and it would result in a violation of the natural sense of sūtras such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*).
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya says:
"The meanings of the nominal suffixes (*sup*) include the object and so forth, as well as number; and likewise for the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).

Nor is it the case that for verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) also, the meaning is merely a property (*dharma*); for otherwise, there would arise an inconsistency among the rules: "The *kṛt* suffixes [denote] the agent," "The *la* suffixes [denote] the object and so forth," and "The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal*-artha suffixes [denote] those two [the agent and the object] alone. Furthermore, in cases such as "Devadatta is a cook" (*pācako devadattaḥ*) or "The rice is cooked" (*pakva odanaḥ*), one must accept that they denote the substratum (*dharmī*) in order to account for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Therefore, in this context, just as with words like "jar" (*ghaṭa*), the expressed meaning is indeed qualified (*viśiṣṭa*).

If, however, one accepts the position of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (that the word denotes the class), then even in all cases there would be merely a property (*dharma-mātra*). In any event, this "half-old-woman" approach (*ardha-jaratīya*)—adopted by the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others—is certainly to be rejected. Indeed, the distinction between verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and nominal suffixes (*kṛt*) is not easily established. We have explained this at length in the *Śabdakaustubha*, so let us stop here. Regarding the phrase "an enumeration": the intention is that, by this [enumeration], there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in examples such as *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("he hears from the actor").
In *gāṃ dogdhi* ("he milks the cow"), the meaning is the act of milking which has milk related to the cow as its object (*gosambandhi-payah-karmaka-dohana*).

It might be argued that this is already covered by the two sūtras: "The object most desired by the agent is the *karman*," and "Likewise, that which is connected [with the action] though not desired. For instance, the meaning of *duh* (to milk) is the causing of abandonment (*tyājana*), subordinate to the act of abandoning (*tyajana*); the meaning of *yāc* (to beg) is the causing of giving (*dāpana*) and the accepting (*aṅgīkaraṇa*); and the meaning of *pac* (to cook) is the softening (*vikledana*) and the turning away (*nivartana*), and so forth. And thus, it is perfectly clear that cows and other such entities possess the status of being the substratum (*āśrayatva*) for those acts—abandoning, giving, accepting, and so on—which have become the objects of the operations expressed by the verbal roots.

For this very reason, since the status of the agent as the object (*karmatva*) when the root is in the *ṇic* form is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*), the ancient masters maintain that the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi* (P. 1.4.52) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). It is for this same reason that the statement in the Bhāṣya on the *ākaḍāra* rule—"In the case of *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*, the designation of 'object' (*karmasaṃjñā*) applies because it is subsequent [to the designation of 'ablative']"—is consistent.

If one holds the position that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) consists of five factors, then this [rule] applies when there is a simultaneous intention to express both the state of being the limit (*avadhitva*) and the state of being the locus of the result (*phalāśrayatva*). The meaning would then be: "the instigation residing in the cow, which has as its object the activity conducive to the flowing of milk that resides in that cow which serves as the limit. If it is argued that, in such a case, the rule *akathitaṃ ca* ("and that which is not otherwise mentioned") is redundant, it is replied: when the object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case would apply—as in the example "one should not eat beans" (*na māṣāṇām aśnīyāt*). This rule is intended to set aside that [genitive].

Thus, it is established here that the meaning of the accusative case is merely a general relation (*sambandha-mātra*), just like the genitive. However, when there is an intention to express the status of the *apādāna* (ablative) alone, the ablative case ending alone is used. When the cow is a qualifier of the milk, however, the genitive is used; therefore, the usage *goḥ payo dogdhi* ("he milks the milk of the cow") is indeed correct. This should be inferred in subsequent cases as well. As for what was stated by the ancients: "The object of the roots *duh*, *aci*, *rudh*, *pracch*, *ci*, *brū*, *śās*, and *ji* is joined [with the sixth case]."

"nī-hṛ-kṛṣ-manth-vah-daṇḍ-grah-muṣ-pac [are] karmabhāk (possessing two objects). Regarding this, the following must be said: the inclusion of *grah* (to seize) is without authority (*nirmūla*). Consequently, the example "jagrāha dyutaruṃ śakram" (he seized Indra by the tree of lightning) is also incorrect. Although the status of the others as *dvikarmaka* (taking two objects) is authoritative, there is nevertheless a purity of context (*saṃdarbhaśuddhi*). To explain: having listed the roots beginning with *duh* and those beginning with *ni* here in two groups, in the supplement to the section on the formation of the *bhāva* and *karman* (passive/impersonal) voices, when the question arises—"Will the suffixes *la*, *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal-artha* apply to the primary object (*mukhya karma*) or the secondary object (*gauṇa karma*) after *dvikarmaka* roots?"—the author himself has stated:

"Roots such as *ni* (to lead) and others, when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and having the sense of motion without an object, take the suffix [denoting the agent] in relation to the primary object;

roots such as *duh* (to milk) do so in relation to the secondary object; but others [take it] according to their specific character. If this were the case, then the suffix would also apply to the primary object in the cases of *daṇḍi* (to fine) and *manthi* (to churn). Consequently, the Bhāṣya statement, "Let the Gargas be fined a hundred," would be contradicted. For here, the hundred is the principal element, not the Gargas, as indicated by the supplementary statement: "Kings become seekers of gold. Furthermore, in this context, the root *daṇḍ* has the sense of seizing (*grahaṇa*), not of punishing (*nigraha*). For the same reason, the suffix would also apply to the primary object in the case of *manthi*. However, it is desired that it apply to the secondary object. And thus says Bhāravi:
"By whom the ocean, whose serpent-dwellings were burst open by the cast-up waters,
was churned for nectar by the gods and asuras.
In this [verse], "nectar" (amṛta) is primary because it is the intended object, whereas "ocean" (ambunidhi) is secondary.

As for what the commentators have said—that the reading of *pac* among transitive (two-object) verbs is unauthoritative—that is due to haste. For instance, the transitivity of *pac* is established in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*, in the Vārttika *duhipacyorbahulaṃ sakarmakayoḥ*, and in its Bhāṣya. This has been made clear by Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta in that very context. Mādhava also stated: "Of *ji*, *kṛṣ*, *manth*, *muṣ*, *gaṇḍ*, and *pac*," and so forth; and he cited as an example: *taṇḍulān odanaṃ pacati* ("He cooks rice grains into boiled rice").

As for what was stated by Haradatta regarding the rule *akathitaṃ ca*: "If the word *akathita* were taken to mean 'that which is not primary,' then in the example *pāṇinā kāṃsyapātryāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* ('he milks milk with his hand into a bronze vessel'), the [karmasañjñā] would apply to both the hand and the bronze vessel. However, [the karmasañjñā] would have no scope for the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), since roots such as *pac* (to cook) take precedence there, and because this [karmasañjñā] applies only to the specific enumeration of roots beginning with *duh*. This was said with reference to another opinion; otherwise, there would be contradictions with the examples cited in one's own and others' works. Let that matter rest for now.

"He conquers a hundred" (*śataṃ jayati*). The root *ji* means "to overcome" (*abhibhave*). As for the explanation that *ji* means "to win" (*jaye*), that is not correct, because that [meaning] is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Although roots such as *jayati* are not explicitly listed in the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa maintains that they are nevertheless included by virtue of the particle *ca*. Regarding the phrase "based on meaning" (*artha-nibandhanā*): it does not depend on the formal shape (*svarūpa*) of the word. The point is that even in the Bhāṣya on the *Tad-rāja* sūtra, the root *cud*, which is a synonym for *pracch* (to ask), is seen to be transitive (*dvikarmaka*), as in the statement: "I too shall raise this unobjectionable objection. And so Bhaṭṭi says: "With a smiling face, he spoke to the one standing firm in battle."
Mārīca spoke these words of great significance in a loud voice;
and Kālidāsa also [wrote]:
"Even the mountain, out of affection for the protector of the earth, seemed to speak that very same meaning aloud."
And Bhāravi [says]:
"The noble-minded king was addressed by Dvaipāyana as 'Mountain' (giri), which is itself a noble [term].
In this way, many verbs such as *nāth* and others should be understood as taking two objects (*dvikarmaka*).

Regarding the term *deśa* (place): only [specific locations] such as Kuru, Pañcāla, and so forth are understood by this; therefore, rules such as *adhi-śīṅ-sthāsām* do not become redundant. Regarding *godoha* (the milking of cows): here, [the application of the rule] is not established on the basis of time (*kālatva*), because in common usage only things well-known as units of time, such as months and the like, are grasped as time. Consequently, expressions such as *ghaṭam āste* ("he sits for a pot") do not occur. As for what was stated by the ancients—"some say that when used in conjunction with intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the second case is employed after words denoting place, time, distance, and state"—examples such as *nadīm āste* ("he sits by the river") are cited.

In this regard, the following must be said: since the designation of "object" (*karman*) has not been explicitly stated here, the *l*-affixes and others would not occur in the sense of an object, as in the example *māsa āsyate* ("a month is sat through"). Furthermore, the claim made by some—that "a country (*deśa*) consists only of a collection of villages, such as those ending in *kur*, *vāra*, etc., and not merely a portion thereof; therefore, [the rule] does not apply in the case of *grāmaṃ svapiti*"—is also inconsistent, because of the statement in the authoritative source (*ākara*): "A country is not merely a part. Moreover, the term *adhvan* ("way") is too restrictive, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one could say *adhvānaṃ svapiti*. For this very reason, in the authoritative source, "way" is specified as "that which is to be traversed"; it is explained as being well-known as something to be traversed and having a fixed extent, such as a *krośa* or similar distance.

*Gati*, *buddhi*, and *pratyavasāna* [mean] movement, cognition, and eating, respectively. Regarding the phrase "of those whose object is sound" (*śabdakarmakāṇām*): the meaning is "those for whom sound is the objective factor (*karmakāraka*). However, in this context, the word *karman* does not refer to an action (as it does in the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*), because grammatical operations apply to technical terms (*kṛtrima*) and because of the force of including the term *karman*. Otherwise, he would have simply said, "of those whose meaning is movement, cognition, eating, and sound."

The ancient scholars maintain that this sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). That is to say, if [the agent] of the action denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇij*) is to be designated as the object (*karman*), it occurs only when the root has the sense of "motion" (*gati*) and so forth, and specifically when it is the agent of the action itself. Consequently, in the example *pācayati devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook"), since the status of being the agent with respect to the meaning of the base root remains uncontradicted in the prompted one (*prayojya*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is established. And it has been said: "Because of independence in the subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*), [the prompted one] attains the status of an object (*karmatā*) in the act of instigation; yet, due to the restrictive rule regarding the technical designation 'object,' it is expressed according to its own inherent property (*svadharmeṇa*)."

"By the agent's own action"—the meaning is "by the third case ending. Now, an objection: since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) with respect to the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is set aside by the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), this is established simply because it is more powerful (*paratva*) and because it is more internal (*antaraṅgatva*). For an action qualified by its own factors of action (*kāraka*) is connected with the meaning of the causative suffix, since the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed when there is a causal agent (*hetumat*), and the cause is the instigator of the agent. Therefore, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is indeed that which must be presupposed (*upajīvya*). And thus:
"Because it is more powerful, more internal, and also because it is that which must be presupposed..."
Let the person to be prompted possess agency; however, the injunction is appropriate for the act of going and so forth.

If this is argued, let it be so, for the object (*lakṣya*) remains uncontradicted. If it is asked, "What then is the status of those treatises (*grantha*) which state that this is a restrictive rule (*niyamasūtra*)?", listen: by prioritizing the verbal predominance (*śābdapradhānya*) of the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*)—which follows that predominance—is more powerful; thus, there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) at all. It is possible for the treatises to make such a statement with the intention that even if [the other factor] is internal (*antaraṅga*) or a basis of subsistence (*upajīvya*), it does not cause predominance with respect to the primary element. However, it should be understood that if one prioritizes the predominance of the actual meaning (*arthapradhānya*), then it is more appropriate to regard it as an original injunction (*vidhāyaka*).

Regarding the word "śatrūn" (enemies): the meaning is that the activity residing in [the agent] which is conducive to that movement—whose object is heaven and which resides in the enemies—is "Śrī Hari is my refuge. Now, one might ask: how can heaven be the object (*karman*) here? For an object is that which is most desired by the agent (*kartṛ*), and the enemies are not the agents; rather, they would be objects by virtue of the rule *gaty-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 1.4.52). Do not say so. For in the definition of the technical term "object," the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that which is independent (*svatantra*). And independence consists precisely in being the locus of the activity expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

And that [agency] exists for the prompted agent even when the prompter is present. Nor is there a lack of evidence for its being a secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), because the author of the Bhāṣya himself provides the proof for this by stating: "For roots with two objects, they say that the *l*-affixes and so forth denote the primary object; for roots such as *duh* [they denote] the non-primary object," and then saying, "[In the case of causative forms (*ṇyanta*)], the agent of the causative is also [treated as] the object. For without figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the status of having two objects cannot be obtained for causative forms, whereby the statement "the agent of the causative" would have no scope.

If it is asked, "How can there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for that which was conventionally assigned (*saṅketita*) only to its own independent form?"—understand this: it occurs only with respect to the independent form itself, which is common to both that [form] as qualified by another name and that [form] unqualified by another name.

Regarding the rule *nīvahyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.39): although the meaning of these two roots is "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*) and not "going" (*gati*), nevertheless, since "going" also enters into "causing to reach" as a qualifier, the prohibition is stated simply on the basis of this inclusion.

Regarding *niyantr* (Pāṇini 1.4.48): a "driver" (*niyantṛ*) is one who impels animals, and not merely a charioteer. By this, the form *vāhayati balīvardān yavān* ("he makes the oxen carry the barley") is established.

Regarding the term *aniṣedha*: the resulting meaning is that it should be stated that the object (*karman*) is the one to be employed (*prayojya*). Regarding the term *sūta*: "The driver, the charioteer, the controller, the *sūta*, the *kṣattṛ*, and the charioteer [are synonyms].

Regarding the term *ādayati*: when the fruit of the action does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*), the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is used according to the rule "after all [roots], in the sense of the agent. However, when the fruit benefits the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) applies by the rule "and after roots ending in ṇic. This is because the exception to that rule—"also after roots meaning swallowing and moving"—is itself prohibited by the rule "there is a prohibition for the root *ad*."
Regarding the word *sasyam*: the injury (*hiṃsā*) should be understood as occurring when barley standing in a field is being eaten, because at that stage they possess sentience (*cetana*).

Regarding the phrase "it causes him to remember" (*smārayati*): as for the example given under the rule *ṇeraṇau*, namely, "the thicket of forest bushes causes him to remember by itself," one should understand the status of the object (*karmatva*) there solely on the basis of the usage in the Bhāṣya.
Regarding the root *śabdāyate*: in the sense of "he makes a sound," the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied according to the rule *śabdavaira...*, and from that, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added.

Regarding the phrase *dhātvarthe* (in the sense of the root-meaning): by this, those who employ the accusative case in the example "śabdāyayati sainikairipūn" (he causes the enemies to sound with his soldiers) are refuted. As for what the ancients stated—"there is no [accusative] after *ay*, *krand*, *śabdāya*, and *hveñ*"—the mention of *ay* therein is entirely baseless. As for *krand* and *hveñ*, there might be a possibility of their application based merely on their being actions involving sound; however, it has been stated that such is not actually the meaning of the rule.

As for the statement that [the roots] *śru*, *grah*, and *dṛś* take two objects (*dvikarmaka*), therein the inclusion of *dṛś* is indeed authoritative. As for *śru*, its status as taking an object is established because it has sound as its object. Regarding *grah*, although its being *dvikarmaka* is accepted by Sudhākara and others, it is nevertheless not accepted by many. For this very reason, they have explained the usage in Bhāravi’s *Bhaṭṭikāvya*, "janako 'jigrahattaṃ dhanustat" (Janaka made him grasp that bow), as meaning "he made him understand" (*ajigrahat bodhitavān*).
