Likewise, in the verse: "The Mountain was indeed unable to make the God of Gods accept his daughter when she was not asked for," the word *grāhayitum* means "to cause [him] to understand [the act] as one of marriage. And this is logical; for if the root *grah* were inherently transitive (taking two objects), then in the phrase *jāyāpratigrāhitagandhamālyām*, the cow—which is the prompted agent (*prayojya*)—would have to be expressed by the past passive participle (*kta*), according to the rule: "In the case of a causative (*ṇyanta*), there is the expression of both the agent and the object. Consequently, the construction would have to be *jāyayā gandhamālye pratigrāhitām*.

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she by whom the perfume and garland were accepted. The meaning is: she who is the agent of that acceptance which has the perfume and garland as its object and is the domain of an instigation directed toward one's wife. This is because the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is postulated through the inclusion of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) and precisely through the reversal of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
Regarding the rule *abhivādidṛśoḥ*: this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*); it is not applicable for the root *abhivādayati*, whereas it is applicable for the root *dṛś*.

Regarding the reversed order of utterance when *abhini* should have been placed first according to the rule that the shorter member comes first: he states that this is for the purpose of intending the specific compound (*saṃghāta*), saying "of that which is preceded by the compound. Therefore, it does not apply here in the verse: "If the tip of a grain awn enters into the foot... As for the phrase "not in some cases," the usage in the *Bhāṣya*, "of those who are intent (*abhiniviṣṭānām*) upon these meanings," serves as the authority here. He states the case-ending of the subordinate word (*upapada-vibhakti*) with the rule beginning "ubha-sarvatasoḥ," etc. The term *ubhasarvatasau* refers to the forms *ubha* and *sarva* ending in the suffix *tasi*; the meaning is that the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) must be employed when in conjunction with words ending in those two.
On this point, the ancients say: "By the word *ubha*, the word *ubhaya* is indicated (*lakṣyate*), because otherwise [the suffix] *tas* would be impossible.

However, in reality, even though *ayac* is applied in the context of a compound formation (*vṛtti*), there certainly exists that which ends in *tas* derived from the word *ubha*; therefore, it is correct according to the literal text.

The ancients held that *dhik* is an indeclinable citation, just as in the case of *gavityayamāha*. This is not correct; for if that were so, because it would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*), there would be the undesirable consequence that, just as the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* does not apply in the example, the rule for *jaś*-substitution (*jaśtva*) would likewise fail to apply in the case being illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*). Nor should one be deluded into thinking that this [form] ends in the letter *g*, for if it did, the example *dhakiditi* in the rule *kasya ca daḥ* would result in being inconsistent. Therefore, *dhik* is indeed [the form] ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*). By the extended application (*atideśa*) "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), the case-suffix (*sup*) is elided.

"Black on both sides" means on both flanks of the black [horse]. The suffix *tasi* is used here according to the rule for the group beginning with *ādi*; the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive. This should be understood in all instances of the case of the subordinate word (*upapada-vibhakti*).
In all sentences, the relationship between two nouns is established in only two ways:
either by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or, in some cases, by way of the genitive case.

Thus, when the Elder [Vasubandhu] stated [the rule], the mention of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its apodotic case as well. The statement "in two ways" is to be understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), or alternatively, by taking the genitive and its apodosis as a single category.

"Fie upon one who is not a devotee of Kṛṣṇa!"—the meaning is that such a person is to be censured. How is it that [in the example] "Fie, you fool! [the word *dhik* is used]? It has already been stated that a vocative word connects with a verb; therefore, there is no connection with the word *dhik*. Furthermore, whether a verbal form is explicitly heard or implied is another matter altogether. Thus, the sentence-meaning is that the prohibited conduct and so forth of the fool being addressed is censured. By this, expressions such as "Alas, father! and "Alas, Queen, be firm! are also explained.

As for what they say—"The case ending denoting a *kāraka* is stronger than the case ending of an appositional word (*upapada*)," and thus the nominative alone occurs in the vocative because the vocative word expresses the agent *kāraka*—that is weak, because there is no possibility of such a statement [if the vocative were truly an agent]. If it is argued that in cases such as "O King, be gracious," the king is in fact the agent, this does not by itself establish that it possesses the status of a *kāraka* case ending. Furthermore, in examples such as "O King, I worship you" or "They worship you," the person being addressed does not even possess actual agency; let this matter rest for now.

Regarding the term *uparyupari*: how then is one to understand the expression "the cognitions of Īśvara move above the cognitions [of others]" (*uparyuparibuddhīnāṃ carantīśvarabuddhayaḥ*)? It is said in reply: the meaning is that they move above those whose cognitions are higher, that is, those whose cognitions are more elevated. And thus, because there is no reduplication (*āmreḍitatva*), the accusative case does not apply.

Alternatively, the rule "uparyadhyadhasaḥ sāmīpye" (Pāṇini 8.1.7), which prescribes reduplication, is understood here; therefore, when reduplication occurs due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), this rule does not apply.
It has been stated, "it is also seen elsewhere," and he demonstrates this with the examples "abhitaḥ" and "paritaḥ."

Regarding the word *pratibhāti*: this prefix *prati* is an *upasarga* because it qualifies a verb, and not a *karmapravacanīya*. Regarding the phrase *antarā tvāṃ mām*: the meaning is "in the middle between you and me.
Regarding the expression *sāmarthyāt*: the sense is that for this very reason, even the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) is accepted as an object within the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

In *nadīm anu*, the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is "relation" (*sambandha*). And here, that [relation] takes the form of "concomitance" (*sāhitya*), which is indicated by the prefix *anu*. In *lakṣaṇettham*—as in *vṛkṣaṃ prati*—the meaning is "illumination" (*dyotana*) related to the tree. Furthermore, the prefixes such as *prati* indicate that this relation is one of "the indicator and the indicated" (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*). In *bhakto viṣṇuṃ prati*, the relation of "object and subject" (*viṣaya-viṣayi-bhāva*) between Viṣṇu and devotion is what is indicated by *prati* and the other prefixes.
Regarding the word *lakṣmīḥ*: there is a relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) between the portion that is Lakṣmī and Hari.

Regarding *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam*: here, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is indicated solely by the reduplication; the prefix *pari*, however, is connected with the action. The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object (*karman*). Because the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya* subordinates the designation of *upasarga*, the substitution of *ṣ* (in *pariṣiñcati*) does not occur. It is explained in the *Ākara* (the *Mahābhāṣya*) that "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth are mentioned as the scope [of *karmapravacanīyas*] precisely for this reason. The rule *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ* does not apply here, because of its association with the word *apa* when it has the sense of exclusion (*varjana*).

*Mamābhiṣyāt* means "may there be a portion for me. The ancients also cite *mām abhiṣyāt*, which there means "may it reach me"; because the root *as* (to be) becomes transitive by virtue of the prefix (*upasarga*), the second case ending is used in *mām*, and here the meaning ultimately resolves to "a portion for me. Since the status of being a *karmapravacanīya* is prohibited by the word *abhāge*, the rule *upasargaprādurbhyām* applies, resulting in the cerebral *ṣ*. Regarding the phrase *pūjāyāṃ ca*: the mention of "worship" (*pūjā*) is drawn over from the preceding sūtra, *suḥ pūjāyām*.

Regarding *kālādhvanoḥ*: *atyanta* means that which has transcended (*atikrānta*) the end (*anta*), i.e., the cessation (*virāma*). That which is such [an *atyanta*] is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), meaning uninterrupted proximity (*nirantarasannikarṣa*). It is taught that the second case (*dvitīyā*) should be used; this is because of the explicit mention [in the rule], and thus it applies only to those [words] denoting time (*kāla*) and distance (*adhvan*). As for the example *māsasya*, some say that the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used here by the rule *kṛtvo'rthaprayoge kāle'dhikaraṇe*. This is not correct; for in that rule, due to the continued application of the term *śeṣa*, the result is simply the non-application of compounding with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, as in the example *dvirahno bhojanam*. Therefore, the truth is that in this instance, the genitive is used solely by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*. Thus ends the section on the second case.

The agent (*kartṛ*) is independent (*svatantra*). Independence with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which is the primary factor, consists in being its substratum (*āśrayatva*). And it has been said: "The status of being an agent is always intended for that *kāraka* whose action is expressed by the verbal root. The instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which is most effective (*sādhakatama*). It is "most effective" because the accomplishment of the action follows immediately after its operation. And it has been said:
"The accomplishment of an action is that from whose operation [the result] is intended to be described immediately thereafter;
that which is so intended at a particular time and place is then remembered as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
By the word "is intended" (*vivakṣyate*), he indicates that even things such as a cooking pot (*sthālī*) possess the status of an instrument by virtue of intention.
And it is said: "In reality, that [agent] is indefinable, for no entity is fixed [as a permanent agent],
since we observe the intended meaning [of agency] expressed as 'the pot cooks'."

The meaning is this: the status of being a *kāraka* and the sixfold set of [roles] such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth do not remain fixed within a particular entity in the same way that the relationship between qualifier and qualified does. For it cannot be rightly said that "a cow is a cow for everyone, and never a non-cow for anyone," in the same manner that one can say "a qualifier is indeed a qualifier."

And thus, when an object is presented by some particular individual instance of a verbal root (dhātu), in response to the question "What is the agent and so forth?", the agent is that which is intended as the locus of the operation (vyāpāra) conveyed by that specific individual instance of the root; the object (karman) is the locus of the result (phala) which is non-co-referential with the operation; and the locus (adhikaraṇa) is the locus through a relationship mediated by the agent or the object. Furthermore, the operation expressed by the meaning of the root is manifold.

And thus, when the act of cooking (*pacati*) has as its primary intention the placing [of the pot] on the fire, the pouring in of rice, the adding of fuel, and so forth, then Devadatta, as the locus of those [actions], is the agent (*kartṛ*). When its intention is the blazing [of the fire], the fuel (*edhas*) is the agent. When it is intent upon the holding of the rice, the pot (*sthālī*) is the agent; when it is intent upon the separation of parts [of the rice], the grains of rice are the agents. In the expression "he cooks with a pot" (*sthālyā pacati*), although the pot is the locus of the operation denoted by the instrumental case-ending, it is merely an instrument (*karaṇa*) and not the agent, because the operation of Devadatta and others alone is what is expressed by that verbal root.

Likewise: when the meaning is conveyed by roots such as *ādi* (to eat) and *khādi* (to eat), the agent (*kartṛ*) is the grammatical participant; when that same meaning is conveyed by the root *bhakṣayi* (to eat), the object (*karman*) is the participant. When the meaning is conveyed by roots such as *śīṅ* preceded by the prefix *adhi*, the locus (*ādhāra*) is the object; when conveyed by those same roots used alone, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the participant, and so forth.

By this, the objection that there is a contradiction between the agent and the object (*kartṛ-karmavirodha*) regarding the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition is refuted; for in perception and other means of knowledge, agency and the like—which are conditioned by specific linguistic factors—cannot possibly be expressed. By this, those who attempt to refine the definition of "object" (*karman*) as "that which possesses a result produced by an action inherent in another," fearing over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the ablative (*apādāna*), and instead define it as "that which possesses a result delimited by the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthatāvacchedakaphalaśālin*), are also answered; for such a definition would fail to apply to the goer in cases such as "he causes Devadatta to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gamayati devadattam*).

In that view, even though "going" (gamana) is the meaning of the base (prakṛti), it does not delimit the essence [of the action]; therefore, in that case, the causative suffix (ṇic) has the meaning of "operation" (vyāpāra), not the base. Or, if it were so, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to the prompted agent (prayojyakartṛ) in expressions such as "he causes to cook" (pācayati).

If you argue that the technical status of being an object (*karmatva*), which is useful for grammatical instruction, is established by the force of the specific rule, then consider this: it follows that such a status does not exist even in the case of the *apādāna* (ablative), because within the governing heading of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), a designation with no scope (*anavakāśā*) sublates one that has scope (*sāvakāśā*). For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya*, having raised the objection that in examples such as "he kills himself by himself" (*ātmānam ātmanā hanti*), the designation of object (*karmasaṃjñā*) is sublated by the subsequent designation of agent (*kartṛsaṃjñā*), the solution is provided by resorting to a distinction between the Self (*ātman*) as qualified by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by Rāma": although in this context the factors of action (*kāraka*) presented by case-endings function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the action, nevertheless those presented by a *kṛt* suffix function as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), because of the statement: "Nouns (*nāman*) have substance (*sattva*) as their primary meaning. Furthermore, even in the case of the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) presented by a verbal root (*dhātu*), there is a reversal of the qualifier-qualificand relationship when they are used in conjunction with a *kṛt* suffix denoting the object. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: Vālī is the substratum of the separation of life, which is to be accomplished by the operation of an arrow that is the object of the operation [of killing] desired by Rāma.

As for what was stated by the Mīmāṃsakas in the section on the Vājapeya—"it might even be said that 'cooking is done with wood'"—that is swallowed up by the acceptance of the very point we desire. This is because, as the wise should discern, there is no possibility of expressing such things without the syntactic connection of a *kāraka* (participant in action) with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) of a *kṛt*-suffix, according to rules such as "the agent and the instrument [are compounded] frequently with a *kṛt*" and "the agent and the object [are compounded] with a *kṛt*."

What is the purpose of the condition *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed")? [Consider: *hariḥ karoti* ("Hari does"). *Jīvanaḥ* ("one who lives by this") and *śābdikaḥ* ("a grammarian")—the suffix *ṭhak* is applied here according to the rule *śabdāduraṃ karoti*. In *kṛtaviśvāḥ* ("by whom the universe was made"), the meaning is "one who has the act of making the universe as its object"; this is because a different derivation is accepted for a *bahuvrīhi* compound that does not have the sense of the genitive case (*aṣaṣṭhyartha*). This will be explained further below. Regarding the rule *prakṛtyādibhyaḥ*: this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). Therefore, examples such as *nāmnā sutīkṣṇaścaritena dāntaḥ* ("sharp by name, self-controlled by conduct") should be understood.

The combination of two *droṇas* is *dvidroṇam*. Due to its inclusion in the *pātrādi* group, there is an absence of the feminine gender; the meaning is "grain related to two *droṇas*. Regarding the word *ca* ("and"): since the term *karaṇa* (instrument) is understood from the preceding rule, or because the option (*anyatarasyām*) found in the subsequent sūtra—"the recipient [is called *saṃpradāna*] in the case of hiring"—is drawn back [to this rule], the two technical terms would otherwise be optional alternatives. The particle *ca* is used to ensure their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*). Consequently, in the example *manasādevaḥ*, both are established: the suffix *aṇ* by virtue of the [rule for] the object, and the instrumental case ending by virtue of the instrument. [Furthermore,] there is no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case ending in *manasaḥ* by the rule "in a name [formed with a suffix beginning with a consonant], after *manas*."

Furthermore, regarding the example *kiṃ cākṣair devayate yajñadattena*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the root is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the agent of the *aṇ* [causative] does not become the object of the *ṇic* [causative]; nor does the *parasmaipada* ending apply by the rule "aṇāvakarmakāt".

As for the explanation given by the ancients (*prāc*) that the [agent] may optionally receive the designation of "object," that should be disregarded due to its contradiction with the authoritative sources (*ākaravirodha*).

It might be argued as follows: there is scope for the designation *karaṇa* (instrument) in the case of "the dice are for gambling" (*devanā akṣāḥ*), where the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument; whereas there is scope for the designation *karman* (object) in the case of "the dice are being played with" (*dīvyante akṣāḥ*), where the suffix *laṭ* is applied in the sense of an object. Thus, in the expression "he plays with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*), when there is a conflict between two operations prompted by these two designations, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) alone would apply because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], and not the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*). To this, they reply: according to the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that the rule applies at the time the operation is to be performed), the application of the rule "the second case-ending is used in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) occurs at that specific point; since its application is then without any other occasion (*anavakāśatva*), the second case-ending indeed prevails.

Objection: In the case of *akṣā dīvyante* ("the dice play"), even though the object (*karman*) is expressed, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not expressed; therefore, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) should occur. Likewise, in *devanā akṣāḥ* ("dice for playing"), although the instrument is expressed by the suffix *lyuṭ*, the object is not expressed; therefore, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) should occur. Reply: Not so. For in this context, there is only one single power (*śakti*) which serves two designations (*saṃjñā*). Thus, in both instances, there is indeed expression (*abhidhāna*), and not non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).

In the example *sahayukte*—as in *putreṇa* ("with the son")—the father's connection to the action is expressed by the word (*śābda*), whereas the son's connection is understood through the sense (*ārtha*); thus, the son is subordinate. It would have been possible to omit the mention of "subordinate" [in the rule]. Nor does this result in the occurrence of the third case ending for the father as well; for in that case, the nominative arises first because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) as it pertains merely to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Furthermore, in examples such as *pitur āgamanam* ("the coming of the father"), the case ending denoting the grammatical relation (*kāraka-vibhakti*) possesses greater force.

Regarding the phrase *yenāṅgavikāraḥ*: the word *aṅga* ends in the suffix *ac* according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas* (Pāṇini 5.2.127), hence he says *aṅginaḥ*. By the pronoun *yena*, it is precisely the limb (*avayava*), which constitutes the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), that is grasped, due to its proximity. And that [limb] is necessarily modified, for a modification of the body cannot occur through an unmodified limb. This is what he means by saying *yenāṅgena vikṛtena*. Regarding *saṃjānīte*: the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied by the rule *sampratibhyāmanādhyāne* (Pāṇini 1.3.46). Due to its higher priority, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in connection with a *kṛt* suffix, as in *pituḥ saṃjñātā*.

As for what Haradatta stated—that because [the action] is directed toward another (*paratva*), the genitive case is applied by the rule *adhīgartha* (Pāṇini 2.3.52) as in "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ saṃjānāti*)—that is not correct, because in that instance the governing heading is *śeṣa* (the residual relation).

Regarding "substance and so forth" (*dravyādi*): it has been said—"The *hetu* (cause/efficient cause) has substance and so forth as its object; the *karaṇa* (instrument) is that whose action is restricted."

"And when the operation (*vyāpāra*) is not [explicitly] relied upon, the cause (*nimitta*) is accepted as the *hetu*," so it is said. And this also applies to the "result" (*phala*). This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *pratyaya*. Thus, this third case (*tṛtīyā*) is optionally used alongside the fourth case (*caturthī*) expressing purpose (*tādarthya*). For example: *adhyayanāya vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of study"). However, there is this distinction: the relation with the result of the study is one of identity (*abheda*), whereas the relation with the state of being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*) is one of definition (*nirūpakatā*). Regarding the term "implied" (*gamyamāna*): the sense is that there is no insistence that [the word] must be explicitly heard (*śrūyamāṇa*).

Regarding the word *sādhana*: the sense is that one understands the meaning of the stem portion (*prakṛtibhāga*) in the case of *sādhya*. However, in the example "He dismissed the attendants with the words 'Do not be fickle,'" the word *yatadhvam* ("strive") is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

As for the term *aśiṣṭa* ("unrefined"): this is made known by the rule *dāṇaśca sā ceccaturthyarthe* ("and [the suffix *tumun* is used after] *dāṇ*, provided that *sā* [the object] is in the sense of the dative").
Thus ends the third [section].

He states [the definition] by the force of a term that corresponds to its meaning: "of giving" (*dānasya*). The intention is that, by this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "he leads the goat to the village" (*ajāṃ nayati grāmam*) or "he places his hand on the tree" (*hastaṃ nidadhāti vṛkṣe*).

Giving (*dāna*) consists in the production of another's ownership preceded by the cessation of one's own ownership, for the purpose of non-reacquisition. For this very reason, [the designation does not apply] in cases such as "he gives the washerman's clothes" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*), because in that instance the verb *dadāti* ("gives") is used figuratively. And this is the opinion of the author of the Vṛtti.

In the view of the Bhāṣya, however, there is no insistence on the term being etymologically descriptive (*anvarthatā*), because of the usage: "The teacher Khaṇḍika gives a slap to his pupil. As for the expression "he gives the cloth to the washerman," this should be understood as intended to express the status of being a *śeṣa* (a subordinate or beneficiary). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence in the case of "he leads the goat to the village," because by the statement "whom he intends [to benefit]," the one indicated by "whom" (*yam*) is understood to have the status of the *śeṣin* (the principal), while the object (*karman*) has the status of the *śeṣa*. The village does not possess the status of a *śeṣin* with respect to the goat. Regarding the suffix *-anīya*: it is added in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*) by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).

For roots meaning "to please" (*rucyarthānām*), the one who is being pleased (*prīyamāṇaḥ*) [is called *saṃpradāna*]. The root *prīñ* means "to satisfy. Here, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). In the example *haraye rocate* ("It pleases Hari"), this rule is stated because the designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) would otherwise have applied. Why say "being pleased"? Consider: *devadattāya rocate modakaḥ pathi* ("A sweetmeat pleases Devadatta on the road"). Here, it should not apply to the "road" (*pathin*). Regarding *ślāgh-hnuṅ*: *ślāghā* means praise. *Kṛṣṇāya ślāghate* ("He praises Kṛṣṇa"); the meaning is that he praises Kṛṣṇa. Others, however, say the meaning is: "He speaks of himself or another as praiseworthy to Kṛṣṇa. In the first case, since the status of "object" (*karman*) would apply, and in the second case, since it would be a mere "remainder" (*kārakaśeṣa*) and thus the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply, this rule is stated.

Regarding *hnute*: the meaning is that she who is excluding [the black garment] from her co-wives makes him understand that very same matter, namely the black one; or it means she excludes it from anyone at all. Regarding *tiṣṭhate*: the meaning is that by her standing, she makes her intention known. The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending occurs here according to the rule "in the senses of making manifest and designating a fixed position.
This statement is made because, in the case of the root *dhṛ*, the creditor would otherwise have been subject to the genitive case.

Regarding the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ*—it is stated [as such] because of its subsequent position. By this, forms such as *paraspareṇa spṛhaṇīyaśobham* ("mutually possessing desirable beauty") and *spṛhaṇīyaguṇair mahātmabhiḥ* ("by great souls whose virtues are desirable") are established. However, when there is an intention to express the status of a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), then the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used. By this, the form *kumārya iva kāntasya trasyanti spṛhayanti ca* ("like maidens, they tremble and yearn for their beloved") is established. All of this has been stated according to the system of Haradatta and others.

In the *Vākyapadīya* and the work of Helārāja, however, it is established that "this designation of *sampradāna* (recipient) sublates both the designation of *karman* (object) and the genitive of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) when used in connection with the root *spṛh*. According to that view, in the expression *spṛhaṇīyam*, the *kṛtya* suffix denotes the recipient, just as in the word *dānīya*. As for the phrase *kumārya iva*, it should be explained by changing the case-ending [to the dative] as *kāntāya spṛhayantī* ("longing for a lover").

*Krudhadruha-*: *krudh* means anger, *druh* means malice, and *īrṣya* means envy. *Asūya* is a root ending in the *ya*-suffix belonging to the *kaṇḍvādi* class. The meaning is that those verbal roots whose meanings are like the meanings of these [four]. Among them, anger (*krodha*) is intolerance; malice (*droha*) is doing harm; envy (*īrṣyā*) is intolerance of another's excellence; whereas censoriousness (*asūyā*) is the attribution of faults to virtues. Since *krudh* and *druh* are intransitive, the sixth case (genitive) would apply when they are used in conjunction with their objects; since the other two are transitive, the second case (accusative) would apply.

Regarding the phrase "the *kāraka* of *rādhīkṣyoḥ*": the claim that it is the "object *kāraka*" (*karmakāraka*) is an error of the ancient grammarians, because of the rule governing the application of only one technical designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*). Nor can the designation "object" (*karman*) be applied merely on the basis of its initial occurrence; for if one accepts the meaning as "he reflects upon the auspicious and inauspicious pertaining to Kṛṣṇa," then the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone would be required. In the examples *anuprati-gṛṇaḥ* and *hotre*, the genitive is used because they are citations of forms ending in the suffix *śnā*. In the case of *hotre*, the genitive occurs because the [object] status (*karmatva*) has been superseded.

In the context of *parikrayaṇa* (hiring), "purchase" (*kraya*) refers to the absolute acquisition [of a person] through the surrender of wealth and so forth; the prefix *pari-* expresses its proximity [to that purchase]. And he explains that this [hiring] is for a fixed period because it is less than that [absolute acquisition], stating: "for a fixed time. "By wages" (*bhṛtyā*) means by means of salary and the like.

Regarding the term *tādarthye*: that which is for the sake of a particular effect is *tadartha*—that is, the cause; the state of being such is *tādarthya*. By means of the suffix *ṣyañ*, a relationship characterized by being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*) is expressed, according to the established principle that "from primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds, the notion of a relationship is conveyed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). And this state of being a benefactor is manifold. Therefore, it occurs even in cases such as *brāhmaṇāya dadhi* ("curd for the Brahmin").
In the phrase *bhaktir jñānāya* ("devotion for the sake of knowledge"), the meaning is that it transforms itself into the nature of knowledge.

When one intends to express a distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*), the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used after a word denoting the modification; however, when non-distinction is intended, the nominative (*prathamā*) alone is used because it is of higher priority, as in *bhaktir jñānaṃ kalpate* ("devotion becomes knowledge"). But when, according to the rule *janikartuḥ*, the status of being the source (*apādānatva*) is intended for devotion, then—since the agency is already expressed—the nominative alone is used, as in *bhakteḥ jñānaṃ kalpate* ("knowledge arises from devotion"). With the intention that the term *klṛpī* refers to the general sense [of becoming], he says "it becomes" (*sampadyate*), etc.

Regarding "by a portent" (*utpātena*): a portent (*utpāta*) is a transformation of the elements that indicates the good or bad fortune of living beings; the meaning is that the fourth case is used after a word expressing an object indicated by such a portent.

"For *vātāya*": the meaning is that it is an indicator (*jñāpika*) of [the rule regarding] *vāta*. "It is beneficial" (*hitā*): the sense is that this is known from the rule prescribing the compound. The same should be understood in the case of connection with *sukha*. With the intention that, by the power of the sūtra "The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* [are used] when there is another action," an accompanying word (*upapada*) denoting an action results in being expressive of an action itself, he says "action" (*kriyā*). The meaning is: having an action as its fruit, and having a verbal root expressing an action as its base. The mention of "*tumun*" is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *ṇvul*; for there is no obstacle to explaining "he goes for fruits" (*phalebhyo yāti*) as "one who brings fruits" (*phalānyāharakaḥ*).

Regarding the term *karmaṇi*: the intention is that this [sūtra] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the second case ending (*dvitīyā*). As for the explanation given by the ancients—that the sūtra is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) so that the [karmasañjñā] applies only when the object is not explicitly mentioned (*aprayujyamāna*), but not when it is mentioned (*prayujyamāna*)—that is incorrect, because a restriction cannot apply to what has not already been established. Nor is there establishment [of the karmasañjñā] by the rule "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*); for the act of going is not for the sake of the fruit (the goal), but rather for the sake of bringing [it]. That bringing, however, has the fruit as its object; this is a separate matter.

Since the sense of "for that purpose" (*tādarthya*) is already established by the very mention of *tumun*, which expresses the state of being (*bhāva*), the further inclusion of the term "expressing a state of being" (*bhāvavacana*) is for the sake of selecting specific rules; thus he says, "by this rule. Nor should it be suspected that the meaning is already covered by [the rule] *na ca tādarthye* alone, because if only "expressing a state of being" were used, the sense of "for that purpose" would be indicated precisely as it is by *tumun*, and consequently, the nominative case (*prathamā*) would undesirably apply even when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).

As for what was stated by the ancients—that this sūtra is for the sake of restriction so that [the genitive] occurs only after words expressing an action (bhāvavacana), and not after a word ending in *ṇvul* such as *pācako vrajati*—that is incorrect. This is because in a word ending in *ṇvul*, the agent (*kartṛ*) is primary, and there is no sense of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) toward the agent; furthermore, the act of going (*yāna*), which has become subordinate, cannot be construed with the meaning of the case-ending. If it is asked, "But why [mention] the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as well?"—one might suspect that the genitive alone should suffice, and that the word *alaṃ* should be understood only in the sense of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) rather than its other meanings. Anticipating this objection, he says: "it prevails over that" (*tasmai prabhavati*).

"But you [are] like a blade of grass," and so forth. Now, one might object: since it is like a blade of grass and the like, the dative case ought to occur after the word *yuṣmad* as well when it functions as the subject (*pakṣa*). This is not so; for the phrase "in disregard" (*anādare*) is a qualifier of the object (*karman*)—meaning, that object which indicates disregard. Such an object is indeed a blade of grass, but not the referent of *yuṣmad*. Thus ends the section on the dative case.

Regarding the word *dhruvam*: the root *dhru* means "motion" (*gati*) and "steadiness" (*sthairya*). From this root, which belongs to the *kuṭādi* class, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*. However, if the reading is *dhruva* in the sense of "steadiness," then the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *igupadhalakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*. *Dhruvam* means "steady. It is that which, while not being engaged in the motion expressed by the verb in question, is the substratum of the disjunction produced by that motion. Since this [status] logically applies only to the limit (*avadhi*), he says: "that which has become the limit" (*avadhibhūtam*).

Regarding the example *dhāvataḥ* ("of the two running"): here, even though the horse is qualified by an action, its status as the point of departure (*avadhi*) with respect to the action expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛtadhātu*) is not contradictory. In the case of *parasparasmān meṣāv apasarataḥ* ("the two rams move away from each other"), since both movements are expressed by the root *sṛ*, the fact that one is the point of departure for the movement residing in the other is not contradictory. And it has been said: "That which is indifferent to the separation—whether moving or unmoving—is called the point of departure (*apādāna*), because it remains fixed and is not involved [in the action itself]."
Since the horse is certainly the cause of the falling man, and since that man falls from the horse,
the wall or other such object is likewise considered the certain cause of that horse's falling.
"The state of being a limit (avadhitva) for each of the two rams is distinct, depending on their respective actions;
and the state of being an agent (kartṛtva) for each of the two rams is also distinct, depending on their own actions.

In the case of the expression "he falls from the horse falling from the mountain," the meaning is that the horse is the locus of the falling which has the mountain as its limit, while Devadatta's falling has that [horse] as its limit.

In the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*), with the relation of non-difference (*abhedena saṃsargeṇa*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is the qualifier, while the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) resides in the action; moreover, that [meaning of the suffix] is the substratum (*dharmī*) and not a mere property (*dharmamātra*), because there is no dispute regarding the fact that a *bahuvrīhi* compound, prescribed in the sense of a case-ending, has the substratum as its primary referent. For in the example "the pot from which rice has been removed" (*uddhṛtaudanā sthālī*), the meaning is "that which has become the limit (*avadhibhūtā*) for the removal whose object is the rice. As for the word *jugupsā*: the author of the *Bhāṣya*, however, maintains that words such as *jugupsā* indicate a cessation preceded by that [aversion], and asserts that this is established by the rule itself. The same applies to the subsequent rules as well.

Regarding the fear [expressed in the question]: "How then [is this to be explained]?"—as for the *Rāmāyaṇa* passage, "From whom do even the gods fear when he has become enraged in battle?", they say: "[The answer is] 'from whom in battle' (*kasya saṃyuge*). Nor does it follow that "battle" (*saṃyuga*) alone would incur the technical designation of the ablative (*apādāna*), because it is superseded by the subsequent designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa*). However, when the status of being a locus is not intended to be expressed, the desired result indeed follows. As for "from study" (*adhyayanāt*), the meaning is "weariness related to study."

Regarding *janikartuḥ*: birth (*janana*) is arising (*janir utpattiḥ*). The suffix *iñ* is applied to the root *jan* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) by the rule *iñ ajādibhyaḥ*, or alternatively, the suffix *iṇ* is applied by the *uṇādi* sūtra *janighasibhyām iṇ*. The prohibition of *vṛddhi* is applied by the rule *janivadhyośca*. The compound is formed with the genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "the agent of that [birth]. Thus, it applies even when connected with another verbal root, as in the example: "From limb after limb you are born. This is what he expresses by saying: "of that which is being born" (*jāyamānasya*).

The point is that by this [explanation], the authors of the Mīmāṃsā-vārttika—who, relying on the rule "ik-śtipau dhātunirdeśe" (P. 3.3.108) to maintain that this is a reference by means of the vowel *i*, raised objections regarding the contingency of the elision of the penultimate vowel in "gamahana" (P. 6.4.98), the lack of semantic coherence, and the impossibility of forming a compound—are thereby resolved.

In this sūtra, the author of the Vṛtti holds that the mention of *prakṛti* (material cause) refers only to the instrumental cause (*hetu*), as illustrated by the example: "Joy arises from a son. However, the opinion of the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa is that it refers only to the material cause (*upādāna*). He provides an example common to both views: "From Brahman... Here, *Brahmā* refers to Hiraṇyagarbha; he is indeed only the instrumental cause and not the material cause. Furthermore, *Brahman* is the one variegated with *māyā*, for it is the established Vedāntic doctrine that this is the material cause of all effects.

"Bhū" is the act of becoming (*bhavana*); the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) because it belongs to the class beginning with *sampad*. He says "of the agent of *bhū*" (*bhūkartuḥ*), because the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*), although specified in a compound in the preceding rule, is understood here due to its being marked as *svarita*. "Source" (*prabhava*) means that from which something originates;
the phrase "due to the elision of *lyap*" (*lyablope*) means that the suffix *lyap* is not actually employed because its meaning is already implied.

Regarding the phrase *yataśca*: the meaning is "from that which," referring to that which is relied upon as a limit (*avadhi*) for the construction or delimitation (*pariccheda*) of a path or time. Consequently, the nominative and locative case endings are employed after words denoting the path being constructed, by virtue of their connection through the sense of the word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*).
Regarding the rule *kālāt*: the phrase *tadyuktāt* ("connected with that") is to be understood as required.

As for the phrase *prapañcārtham* ("for the sake of elaboration"): one should not argue that this refers to the sense of "low" (*nīca*) based on Amara’s statement, "the other [meaning of *itara*] is 'different' and 'low'," because—as in examples such as *asmāttāro mandro vā*—this is already established by the rule *pañcamī vibhakte*.

As for the claim that the word *itara* is employed only when it has a correlate (*pratiyogin*) explicitly indicated—as in "Caitra is brave, the other is cowardly"—and therefore this [usage] does not have another meaning; that is weak, because the requirement for a correlate is equal in both cases and because it contradicts the cited lexicon. [Regarding the example] "except for Kṛṣṇa" (*ṛte kṛṣṇāt*), how then is one to explain "without the propitiation of the Person" (*puruṣārādhanamṛte*)? Some say this is a mere error.

Others, however, state that because of the inclusion of the root *dṛś* (to see) in the rule *ubhasarvatasoḥ*, the accusative case is also correct when used with *ṛte* (without/except), just as in examples such as *caitraṃ yāvacchītam*. This is indeed logical, based on the Cāndra Sūtra: *ṛte dvitīyā ca* ("with *ṛte*, the accusative as well"). Regarding the phrase "in connection with words having the sense of *prabhṛti* (starting from)": this means in connection with words whose meaning is *prabhṛti*. Thus, while commenting on the Mahābhāṣya passage *kārtikyāḥ prabhṛti*, Kaiyaṭa employed the expression: "the meaning is 'starting from that' (*tata ārabhya*)."

Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of *vacana*": the intended meaning is that, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), only the limit (*avadhi*) is intended to be expressed; the sense is that the qualifying portion, namely "without that" (*tena vinā*), is not intended. Alternatively: the term *maryādāvacana* refers to that in which the word *maryādā* is mentioned—namely, the rule *āṅmaryādābhividhyoḥ*. The meaning is that the *āṅ* seen therein is given the aforementioned designation. Regarding *pari hareḥ*: according to the Vārttika "the mention of *pari* is optional when expressing exclusion (*varjana*)," there is, in one alternative, an absence of reduplication.

Regarding *pariratra*: here, the intention is that when the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is prescribed, it is due to the association with *apa* in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). Regarding "in the case of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) and an exchange (*pratidāna*)," they say that the fifth case occurs in connection with these two precisely because of this very rule. A substitute (*pratinidhi*) is that which is taken up in the absence of the primary object; an exchange (*pratidāna*) is the returning of what has been given. "When not denoting the agent (*akartari*)"—the fifth case shall apply. This is an exception to the third case (*tṛtīyā*).

Regarding the word *śatena*: here, "hundred" (*śata*) is called a debt (*ṛṇa*) because it is to be held by the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). By the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca*, the technical designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) is also applied.
Regarding the phrase "due to a separation of the yoga" (*yogavibhāgāt*): this is clear in the commentary of Haradatta on the rule *hetumanuṣyebhyaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase *striyāṃ ca* ("and in the feminine"): the indication in the Vārttika—*bāhulakaṃ prakṛtestanudṛṣṭeḥ* ("there is diversity because the original forms are seen to be few")—is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in this context.

The phrase "pṛthag-vinā—samuccayārtham" (pṛthag and vinā for the sake of conjunction) means that the sense is that particles have multiple meanings. Regarding "pañcamī" (the ablative case): there, the ablative is applied by the "maṇḍūkapluti" (frog-leap) principle; however, the accusative is already present [by the previous rule]. Examples are: *dūram*, *dūrāt*, or *dūreṇa*. Here, the locative will also be mentioned. Furthermore, because the sūtra "dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.34) is carried over to the subsequent rules as well, one should understand that these four case-endings are applicable to these words even when expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, it is employed: *dūrād āvasathān mūtram* ("urine from afar from the dwelling"), meaning "far from the dwelling."

The term *asattva* means "the state of not being a denotation of a substance" (*sattva*), which is to say, "having that [substance] as its qualificand. In this way, a case where the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is the qualificand by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is excluded. This is what he states with the example: "dūraḥ panthāḥ" (the path is far). By this, the passage of the ancient commentators on the rule *karaṇe ca stoka-*—"What is the purpose of [mentioning] *karaṇe*? It is so that [the designation of accusative] does not apply to an adverbial object (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*); for instance, in 'stokaṃ pacati' (he cooks slightly), the action is not a substance"—is explained.

As for what was said—having restated that [position], they claimed it must be reconsidered because action, being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), necessarily possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*)—that very point is what must be reconsidered; for it is well-established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that the action denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*) is of the nature of non-existence (*asattva*). Nor is there any inconsistency in its being a qualificand, since such status is possible simply by virtue of its lack of connection with gender, number, and so forth, just like a "state" (*bhāva*) expressed by a *kṛt* suffix.

Although the *Bhāṣya* accepts the connection with number in examples such as "those who have been killed lie down" (*hataśāyikāḥ śayyante*), and the connection with agency and objectivity in examples such as "he cooks and [the action] comes to be" (*pacati bhavati*), nevertheless, the absence of gender and other *kārakas* remains entirely uncontradicted. And it has been said:
"The action is not joined with gender, nor with the action itself, nor with the *kārakas* which do not serve as its substratum;
let this very nature of its being non-substantial (*asattvarūpatā*) be firmly established."
Thus ends the fifth [chapter].

In the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the genitive case occurs only from the subordinate element (*apradhāna*) because the meaning of the suffix (the possessor) is primary with respect to the meaning of the base (the person). And that meaning [of the suffix] serves as a qualifier for the "man. However, the genitive does not occur from the primary element, because that would contradict the aforementioned rule and because there is no "remainder" (*śeṣa*). For the word *puruṣa* functions either solely in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) or in the sense of a grammatical relation (*kāraka*). But when it is not so [i.e., when it does not function as a mere stem-meaning or a *kāraka*], then the genitive indeed occurs even after the word *puruṣa*.

As for the claim that "the subordinate is the *śeṣa* (remainder)," that is not correct; for in cases such as "a white jar" (*śuklo ghaṭaḥ*), where there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*pratipadikārtha*), there would result the undesirable application of the genitive case to the qualifier. Nor can it be argued that the nominative case is sublated [by the genitive], because the nominative has already fulfilled its function when denoting predominance (*prādhānya*). The phrase "of the object and so forth as well" means that just as one uses the form "possessing color" (*rūpavān*) when there is no intention to specify a particular quality, whereas when such specification is intended, one employs forms such as "blue" (*nīlaḥ*) or "yellow" (*pītaḥ*), so too this [application of the genitive] is established by logical principle (*nyāya*). This is the intended sense.

Regarding the phrase "of the wise" (satām): the point is that the rules cited from the works of the ancients—"when used with a *kta*-suffix in the neuter sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), provided there is a desire to express [the relation] as a residual category (*śeṣatva*)"—and "after verbs meaning 'to satisfy,' the sixth case may optionally be used for the instrument (*karaṇa*)"—are not novel statements.

Regarding "of ghee" (*sarpiṣaḥ*): the group of eight sūtras beginning with *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe*, *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi*, *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne*, *rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānām ajvareḥ*, *āśiṣi nāthaḥ*, *jāsiniprahaṇanāṭakrāthapiṣāṃ hiṃsāyām*, *vyavahṛpaṇoḥ samarthayoḥ*, and *kṛtvo'rthaprayoge kāle 'dhikaraṇe* has not been explained here, because its purpose is the prevention of compound formation (*samāsa-nivṛtti*).

For instance: there, the word *śeṣe* (in the sense of the "remainder") is understood to carry over. And when the [factors] such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) are intended to be expressed as the "remainder," the genitive case is already established. Thus, the meaning here is this: in these instances, only the genitive occurs and not its elision (*luk*). Consequently, the compound (*samāsa*), which is the cause for that elision, does not occur at all. Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "And because it is prescribed by a specific rule," and so forth. And Hari says:
"When [a factor] is designated by a kāraka [term] and the action is explicitly heard, the genitive is prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*) in order to prevent compounding."

Therefore, when the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣatva*) is intended, forms such as *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee") and *mātuḥ smaraṇam* ("the remembrance of the mother") are correct only when they remain uncompounded. However, forms such as *harismaraṇam* ("remembrance of Hari") are to be understood as compounds formed with the sixth case ending used for the *kṛt*-suffix connection (*kṛdyoga-ṣaṣṭhī*), since the sense of "remainder" is not intended there. In that case, because it is preceded by a *kāraka*, the accentuation is that of the base of the final *kṛt*-member; whereas if it were a compound with the sixth case of "remainder," it would have an udātta accent on the final syllable, which is undesirable. Thus, the ultimate conclusion is that this group of eight sūtras is for the sake of regulating accent (*svarārtha*).

Furthermore, in examples such as *mātuḥ smṛtam* ("remembered by the mother"), the absence of a compound is also a result [of the prohibition]. For in those cases, the genitive of the *kāraka* (agentive/active case) is not available, because of the prohibition by the rule *na loke*. And it has been said:
"The genitive referring to the object (*karman*) is prohibited when used with a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*);
in that case, a compound with a genitive characterized as 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) is not desired."

This being the case, Haradatta and others maintain that whatever *tiṅ*-ending forms appear as examples (*udāharaṇa*) or counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) in works such as the *Vṛtti* and other commentaries within this treatise, all of them should be understood as being illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the rule "and the third case after a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca*), the word "pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ*) here is in the genitive case; thus he says, "in the employment of a pronoun. The intention is that if it were in the ablative case, the sixth and third cases would not occur after the word *hetu*. He illustrates the purpose of including the term "synonym" (*paryāya*) with the words beginning with "thus" (*evam*).

The author of the *Prācīna* (Purushottama) has cited "kimartham" as an example. In that case, the neuter gender of *kimaḥ* is difficult to justify; it must somehow be explained by resorting to the neuter gender for general reference (*sāmānye napuṃsakatā*) and by assuming a compound. Regarding the term *asarvanāmnaḥ*: although the *Vārttika*—"In the sense of cause, motive, or reason, all [case endings] are generally seen"—was indeed mentioned here by the author of the *Vṛtti*, it was nonetheless read by the author of the *Bhāṣya* under the rule "hetau. Consequently, it applies even when a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is not used. However, because of the inclusion of the word "generally" (*prāya*), the meaning is that only the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth occur there. Vardhamāna, however, maintains that the nominative (*prathamā*) also occurs.

Regarding the rule "the sixth case [is used] when joined with a suffix having the sense of *atas* or the fifth case": how then is it that we have *tataḥ paścāt* ("after that")? Because of the usage in the Bhāṣya, "he will fall away or perish after that" (*tataḥ paścāt sraṃsyate, dhvaṃsyate ca*), the fifth case is also used in connection with *paścāt*. The mention of the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is of doubtful utility. How then is it that we have "our house is to the north of the house of the Lord of Wealth" (*tatrāgāraṃ dhanapatigṛhād uttareṇāsmadīyam*)? It should be understood that *uttareṇa*, ending in the third case, is in grammatical apposition with *toraṇena* (which is implied).

The inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") with words meaning "far" (*dūra*) and "near" (*antika*) is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*). By that [term], the fifth case (*pañcamī*), though remote, is also conjoined according to the commentary; however, the sixth, second, and third cases are not. This is what he states: "and the fifth case. By the word *tat* ("that") in the phrase *divastadarthasya*, the two terms *vyavahṛ* and *paṇa* are referred to; and since those two have the same meaning as gambling (*dyūta*) and the transaction of buying and selling (*krayavikrayavyavahāra*)—having been understood from the previous rule—he says: "in gambling."

Regarding the term *karmaṇi*: the sense here is that the word *śeṣe* ("in the remaining cases") does not apply, because of the commencement of the two subsequent sūtras. For this very reason, he provides an example of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) within this group of three sūtras: *śatasya dīvyati* ("he plays for a hundred"). Regarding *preṣyabruvoḥ*: the form *preṣya* is the second person singular imperative of the root *iṣ*, belonging to the *divādi* class and meaning "to go. Due to its association with that, *brū* is also understood as being in the same form (the second person singular imperative). For this very reason, the mention of *śeṣa* is not connected here, because the formation of a compound with a finite verb is otherwise impossible.

Regarding the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), it has been said: "The genitive case is fixed when [the relation] is with respect to the primary [factor], but it may be either way when [the relation] is with respect to the subordinate. In the example *kṛtapūrvī*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is *kṛtaṃ pūrvamanena* ("that which was done previously by him"). The meaning is "one who has done it before. Since the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarmaka*), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). The compound is formed according to the rule *sup supā*. The suffix *ini* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by the rules *pūrvādiniḥ* and *sapūrvācca*; for in that specific rule, the word *anena* is understood as being carried over from the preceding sūtra *śrāddhamanena*.

Now, how is it that Bhaṭṭi says, "dhāyairāmodamuttamam"? On this point, they say: this [rule] is not universal (*anitya*), because of the specific mention in the rule "tadarham". Regarding the phrase "of the two feminine suffixes": how then is the commentary on the sūtra "suṭtithoḥ" to be understood when it states, "there is no sublation of *si* and *yuṭ* by *suṭ*"? Understand that the instrumental case is used here because there is an intention to express the instrument (*karaṇatva*). Regarding the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā...": the analysis of the compound is "u and uka are 'ūk'; la and ūka are 'laukā'. Because the suffix *u* (from *uka*) serves as a qualifier, the rule applies to that which ends in it; thus he says: "desiring to see Hari" (*didṛkṣuḥ*) or "wishing to adorn" (*alaṃkariṣṇuḥ*).

Regarding the rule "the genitive is used for the remaining cases": by this, such passages as "For the success regarding the difficult-to-attain goal of the Ikṣvākus depends on you" and "Or, even the speech of the Lord of Speech might cause wonder at that which is difficult to utter," are explained. Alternatively, the construction is "the successes of the Ikṣvākus" and not "the difficult-to-attain [goal] of the Ikṣvākus"; likewise, the construction is "wonder caused by the Lord of Speech" and not "that which is difficult to utter by the Lord of Speech."

How then do Kālidāsa [use] "tulāṃ yadārohati dantavāsasā" (when he ascends the scale with Dantavakra) and Māgha [use] "sphuṭopamaṃ bhūtisitena śambhunā" (clearly comparable to Śambhu who is white as ash)? It is said: the third case ending is used according to the rule "sahayukte 'pradhāne" (the third case is used for that which is not the principal when joined with *saha*). This is as in the example: "svabālabhārasya taduttamāṅgajaiḥ samaṃ camaryeva tulābhilāṣiṇaḥ" (desiring a comparison with the hair of his own head, like a yak with the hair on its own back). For it has been stated: "The third case occurs even without connection to that [word].

The meaning is that because of this explanation, the word *artha* in the sūtra is also a separate cause [for compounding]; thus, it is indeed a *dvandva* compound, and not a *bahuvrīhi* with the word *artha*.
Thus ends the sixth [chapter].

"The substratum (ādhāra) is threefold"—this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule *saṃhitāyām*. "Four [cases]"—the intention is that this refers to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārthamātra*). Furthermore, since the rule *dūrāntika* is also understood to apply here, these [four cases] should be understood as including the locative (*adhikaraṇa*) as well. "Of that which ends in *kta*"—the meaning is: that *kta*-suffix for which words ending in *in* or *inn* constitute the domain, that is, the basis of their application.

Regarding "the third case [is used] in the sense of cause," one should also understand that "the fourth case [is used] in the sense of being for the sake of that (tādarthya). As for "sīmā" and so forth, this was stated by Kulacandra in his *Durgavākyaprabodha*. Medinīkāra also says:
"The word *sīmā* [is used] in the feminine gender to denote a boundary, a state, a field, and egg-shells."
And thus [it is said]: "Then Puṣkalaka, the musk deer, [struck] the two mendicant stakes.
However, Haradatta and others say that *puṣkalaka* means a stake (*śaṅku*), and that it was "struck"—meaning driven or buried—in the boundary for the purpose of knowing the boundary.

And for that [action]—an action whose time is known serves as the *lakṣaṇa* (indicator) for an action whose time is unknown, because it delimits its time. This seventh case (*saptamī*) indicates the agent and the object which are the substrata of those two actions. Among these, "having gone while the Brāhmaṇas were studying" is an example where the agent is indicated. Regarding the object, he says: "among the cows. Here, the status of being an indicator (*lakṣaka*), which is perceived in the Brāhmaṇas who are studying and the cows which are being milked, finds its rest in the actions of studying and milking, which serve as qualifiers.
The meaning is: "it is indeed a distinction," and not that they are subsumed under a general form conveyed by another word.

Regarding "māthurāḥ": for here, as in the case of "gavāṃ kṛṣṇā" and so forth, there is no relationship of general and particular; rather, there is simply a contradiction between the two properties expressed by the words. Regarding "nipuṇo rājñaḥ": when employing a correct word (*sādhuśabda*), the locative case indeed occurs even without *arcā* (reverence), according to the Vārttika rule: "and [the locative is used] in connection with the employment of correct and incorrect words. Regarding "prasitaḥ": Amara states that *prasita* and *āsakta* both mean "intent upon" (*tatpara*).

Regarding the word *mūlena*: [the suffix] *aṇ* [is applied] by the rule "time joined with a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*), and this *aṇ* is elided by the rule "elision when there is no distinction" (*lubaviśeṣe*).

Regarding the word *paryāyeṇa*: the word *īśvara* is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*). One explanation is that it refers to the lordship (*īśvaratva*) of a master (*svāmin*). Here, "of whom" (*yasya*) points to the property (*sva*). Another explanation is that it refers to the master of a property; here, "of whom" (*yasya*) points to the property (*sva*). Thus, due to these different interpretations, the case ending is used alternately (*paryāyeṇa*). And the meaning is that this [genitive] functions like the sixth case (genitive) because it is a qualifier. This concludes the seventh [case].
Thus ends the section on *kāraka*s in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
Now begins the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds.

Regarding the phrase *samarthāśrita*: the intention is that the word *samartha* (capable/competent) in the Sūtra is used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*). Regarding the phrase *katipaya*: although the author of the Vārttika stated in the section on compulsory composition (*nityādhikāra*) that there is a compound of a finite verb (*tiṅ*) with another finite verb that possesses an acute accent (*udāttavat*) or motion (*gatimat*), nevertheless, that is not an absolute rule (*niyata*), because we do not observe such compounds in instances like *ya ānayat* or *abhiprabharadhṛṣate*. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya established this by means of a formal split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *saha*. The implication is that among the sages, authority increases in successive order.

And as for the word *sa* (he): this too is obtained precisely because the purpose of the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is to establish the desired result. This is clear in the *Padamañjarī* on the sūtra defining the technical term *sampradāna*. For if [the suffix] were to occur even in common usage (*loka*), then in cases such as *abhipraiti*, the case-endings (*svādi*) would have to appear after the compound, just as they do in *pacatikalpam* and similar forms following a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Nor can the matter be resolved by accepting the universal gender (*liṅgasarvanāma*) of the neuter, because in *prakurute* and similar forms, a short vowel (*hrasva*) would result, and in *prakurvīran*, the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) would occur.

Regarding the phrase "because of being specifically taught": otherwise, even though there is no distinction in both being taught first, because the designation *upasarjana* (secondary member) is based on its actual meaning (*anvartha*), the word *pūrva* alone would have been placed first; this is the intended sense. Regarding the rule "with *iva*": this compound also occurs only occasionally (*kvācitka*) as in the previous case. Consequently, the reading by the Taittirīyas as separate words in examples such as "jīmūtasyeva" is justified, and the use of separate words in examples such as "udbāhuriva vāmanaḥ" is also consistent.
[The rule] "of a secondary member that ends in *go* or a feminine suffix" refers to that which is a *upasarjana*.

As for what was stated by the predecessors—that [the rule applies] when the two members ending in *go* and a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) are *upasarjana*s—that is incorrect. For in examples such as *citraguḥ*, although the word *go* is an *upasarjana*, it is not the end of that [compound]; furthermore, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *gaurīpatiḥ*.

If one asks: "How then do we account for *sugokulam* and *rājakumārīputraḥ*? Listen: because an *upasarjana* is inherently relative (possessing a correlative), the shortening occurs only when the two words functioning as the final member (*uttarapada*) have become subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) with respect to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) for which the shortening is prescribed.

Regarding the phrase "diśayoḥ": even when analyzed with the word ending in a consonant as "diśoḥ," the form remains the same. This is because the word *diś* takes the suffix *ṭac* due to its inclusion in the *śarad-ādi* group. As for the expression "by the force of the statement": since the term *vibhakti* (case-ending) refers to that very case-ending which forms part of the nominal stem (*subanta*) with which the compound is formed—due to proximity—the sense is that the particle *adhi* indicates the meaning of that [case-ending]. However, in the *Parishishta*, two alternative views are maintained: that this compound is formed either with a nominative (*prathamānta*) or a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) ending.

As for what was stated by the ancients—that in the analysis (*vigraha*) "having *hari* as the subject" (*harim adhikṛtya*), the form "in *hari*" (*harau*) is established—that is not correct, because an analysis is impossible due to its being an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). As they say: "An obligatory compound is one that lacks an analysis. If it is argued: "But even an analysis with non-co-referential members (*asvapadavigraha*) is accepted, as in 'he makes a jar' (*kumbhaṃ karoti*); let this [compound] be like that too, since the gerund ending in *-lyap* in *adhikṛtya* exists outside the compound," we reply: No. For it is impossible for that which does not convey even a trace of the meaning of the compound to enter into its analysis.

As for what they have explained: "The term *vigraha* is like a *vigraha*; it is merely an explanation of the meaning. Therefore, because it is not an actual compound (*avigrahatva*), its status as a permanent compound (*nityasamāsa*) is not contradictory. For this very reason, he shows another non-worldly sentence (*alaukika-vākya*) which serves as the basis for the compound: "It remains as *harau adhi*."

In this regard, the following must be said: the phrase "as in a vigraha" (at the stage of analysis) is inappropriate, because the sentence that expresses the meaning itself constitutes the *vigraha*, and thus there is no difference between them. Nor is it correct to say "merely the expression of the meaning," for by using a form ending in the suffix *-lyap* (in *adhītya*), one fails to touch upon the actual sense of the compound. Furthermore, as for the claim that the form *harau adhīti* is *alaukika* (non-occasional/analytical), that too is incorrect; for in that case, it is precisely the form *hari ṅi* that enters into the process, according to the maxim "even internal [rules may be superseded]. Otherwise, the vowel *i* belonging to the word *hari* would be difficult to obtain within the compound.

As for what they have explained—that because it is *alaukika* (non-ordinary), the locative case (*saptamī*) occurs even though it has already been expressed by the prefix *adhi*, otherwise it would not occur due to the governing rule *anabhihite*—that too is merely superficial. For *alaukikatva* indeed means "the state of being not yet finalized because it is the object of another obligatory rule," but on this basis alone, it is not easily established that the locative case, which is not [otherwise] prescribed, should enter into that context, as it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

As for that which was explained by his grandson—that because of the restrictive enumeration (*parigaṇanā*) in the rule *tiṅkṛttaddhitasamāsaiḥ*, the seventh case (*saptamī*) occurs even when the sense [of location] is already expressed by the prefix *adhi*—that is not correct. For such an enumeration has been rejected in the original treatise (*ākara*), and he himself stated the same in the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā*; furthermore, it would contradict usage such as "he recognized him as Nārada in due order" (*kramādamuṃ nārada ityabodhi saḥ*). Regarding the phrase "of the second and fifth cases" (*dvitīyāpañcamyoḥ*), this is clear in the work of Rakṣita.

As for what they say—that in cases such as *caitrasya vanād ārāt* ("from near the forest of Caitra"), because the compound would be ungrammatical due to the presence of a relative (*sāpekṣatva*), and since its purpose is already served by the non-compounding, there is no force in the rule [prescribing it]—that is to be considered. For if an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) were logical, the very employment of qualifiers such as *caitrasya* would be impossible. Indeed, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "There is no connection with a qualifier for that which has already undergone composition (*vṛtta*)."

If it is objected that the *Bhāṣya* also states, "There is no compounding of words accompanied by qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇānām*)," this is true; however, that refers to the domain of non-obligatory compounds (*anityasamāsa*). If obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*) were also excluded from application when qualifiers are present, then forms such as *mahataḥ kumbhasyopa* would result. As for what the ancients said—namely, "of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasyopa*)—and what their commentators explained, saying "when such an analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) stands," both of these are merely due to oversight (*prāmādika*), according to the reasoning stated previously. *Samprati*: the indeclinable *samprati* means "now."
According to Amara, *etarhi*, *samprati*, *idānīm*, *adhunā*, and *sāmpratam* all mean "now.

Since these words primarily denote the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), they are fit to be construed with a verbal action alone; even a negation pertains only to an action. Thus he says: "it is appropriate" (*yujyate*). Regarding the term *asamprati*: in a compound formation (*samāsa-vṛtti*), the action of "joining" (*yujikriyā*) is internalized, just as the action of sprinkling (*sekakriyā*) is internalized in the compound *dadhyodana* ("rice with curd").

As for what was stated by the ancients—that "asamprati" means the absence of the present, and by this, the negation is made of that very time which belongs to the object of enjoyment—this is not correct, because the logical connection of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to the negation is contrary to all systems of logic. Indeed, no one accepts that the phrase "there is no jar on the ground" negates the ground itself, nor is such a view consistent with reason; so let us leave it at that.

Regarding the expression *itihari*: there is a compound of the word *iti*, which has the sense of "thus" (*prakāśārtha*), with the word *hari* ending in the genitive case, which refers to its own essential nature (*svarūpapara*).

Regarding the word *pratiśabdasya*: as for what some say—that in the example *grāmasya vṛkṣaṃ prati*, the prescription of the second case (*dvitīyā*) has its scope because the compound is precluded due to the presence of a correlative (*sāpekṣatva*)—that has already been refuted. Haradatta, however, says: the sentence *artham arthaṃ prati* is also correct because of the usage by the author of the Bhāṣya; or rather, the indeclinable here does not function through repetition (*vīpsā*), but rather, by virtue of being a *karmapravacanīya*, it delimits a relationship. Repetition, moreover, is indicated by the doubling of the word. In the example *sahapūrvāhṇam*, the *avyayībhāva* compound occurs in the sense of totality (*sākalya*).

Regarding the phrase "even when it is subordinate": the intention is that if the word *sādṛśye* ("in the case of similarity") were not used, then [the compound] would occur only where similarity is the primary element, because in an *avyayībhāva* compound, the predominance of the indeclinable's meaning is the general rule (*autsargika*).

Regarding the word *anta*: here, "end" (*anta*) is intended to mean completion (*samāpti*) in relation to the extent of the portion of the text that has been determined as the limit for study—namely, "this much of the section must now be studied. Since such an end occurs even when the study is incomplete, it is mentioned separately from "completeness" (*sākalya*). The word *agni* refers to the treatise (grantha) concerning its subject matter; it is compounded with the third case ending. Although the usage *agninā saha* (with Agni) would indeed be appropriate, such a form is used merely to indicate accompaniment (*sāhitya*). However, when the intention is to express the sense of "end," the compound is obligatory. For this very reason, the analysis *agnigrantham* is shown as an *asvapadavigraha* (an analysis where the constituent words do not appear in the compound).

As for the claim that there is an analysis (*vigraha*) as "he whose end is fire" (*agniranto'sya*) using the nominative case, or that there is a compound (*samāsa*) with the genitive case ending [in *agneḥ*], that is incorrect. This is because the word *saha* does not denote "end" (*anta*). Furthermore, "end-ness" (*antatva*) is even more impossible to obtain [as the meaning of *saha*]. Moreover, it would lack syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the act of studying (*adhyayane*). Also, the instrumental case is logically required when joined with *saha*.

Finally, just as in the expression *satṛṇam atti* ("he eats everything down to the grass"), where completeness (*sākalya*) is expressed by the accompaniment (*sāhitya*), so too in *sāgnī*, "end-ness" is expressed by that accompaniment; therefore, having accepted a compound with the instrumental ending in that case, to abandon it here is groundless.

Regarding the phrase *yāvacchlokam*: the indeclinable *yāvat* is compounded. However, it should be understood that because the analysis (*vigraha*) is performed with a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), there is no co-occurrence of the same word-forms (*asvapadatvam*). Regarding the statement *vibhāṣā etat*: this is an indication of a grammatical principle (*liṅgadarśana*) for a matter already established by logic. Since the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) is as invariably applicable as the designations *ṭi*, *ghu*, *bha*, and so on, the optionality of these designations—just like other rules—cannot be obtained without an explicit statement.

It might be argued: "In that case, the rule *sup-supā* would also be compulsory. This is not an acceptable consequence, as it would contradict established doctrine. For instance, in the commentary on the *caraṭ*-sūtra, the author of the Vṛtti stated: "One who has previously been [something] is called *bhūtapūrva*; this is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā*."

Similarly, regarding the *Śākala-sūtra*, the *Bhāṣya* states: "In the rule *'sinnityasamāsayoḥ śākalapratiṣedhaḥ'* (the prohibition of the *Śākala* [substitution] applies to *si*-stems and obligatory compounds), the mention of 'obligatory' (*nitya*) is unnecessary; this [form] is also established: *vāpyāmaśvaḥ* or *vāpyaśvaḥ*. Kaiyaṭa explains this as follows: "*Vāpyaśvaḥ* is a compound formed by the rule *'sup supā'* (Pāṇini 2.1.4). Since the compound is obligatory by the rule *'saṃjñāyām'* (Pāṇini 2.1.44), the prohibition is established. This is likewise clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on such rules as *'anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam'* (Pāṇini 6.1.158) and *'asiddhavadatrābhāt'* (Pāṇini 6.4.22).

Therefore, he says: "By [the rule] *sup-sup-eti*, it is a compound (*samāsa*). Although the formation of the compound is established by the very analysis of the rules (*yogavibhāga*), its re-enactment in subsequent rules regarding compounds indicates that the former [rule] applies only occasionally (*kvācitkatā*). And thus, because the compounding with *iva* is also occasional, forms such as *udbāhuriva vāmanaḥ* ("like a dwarf with uplifted arms") are established. As for the Vārttika *ivena*, although it is recited under the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, Kaiyaṭa states that it is merely a reminder (*smārita*) of that which belongs to the rule *sup-sup-eti* within the context of the permanent governing rule (*nityādhikāra*).

This being the case, those who postulate that the compound with *iva* is Vedic in character are refuted; for although the Bahvṛcas accept the compound in the phrase *jīmūtasyeva*, the Taittirīyas read it as an uninflected (analytic) expression—this is the general direction of the argument. By this very same indicator (*jñāpaka*), the ablative case is employed in connection with *bahiḥ*. However, what is established by an indicator does not apply everywhere. By this, the expression "the hand of the trunk is outside" (*karasya karabho bahiḥ*) is justified.

Regarding the phrase *ābālam*: as for the expression used in the *Kiraṇāvalī*, "from the atom (*paramāṇu*) up to the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*)," that is due to a scribal error (*prāmādika*), because the use of the particle *ca* within a compound is impossible. It should rather be read as *ābhūgolakāt*. Regarding the phrase *yaṃ padārtham*: in the sūtra, the word *yat* is neuter in the sense of generality (*sāmānya*). Since this is already established by the rule "the indeclinable [is used] in the sense of case-endings" (*avyayaṃ vibhakti*), the present sūtra is for the sake of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*). By means of this, one may optionally cite *vanasyānu* as an example.

Regarding the term *anugaṅgam*: here, the suffix *an* indicates both length (*āyāma*) and the state of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*). The object to be defined (*lakṣya*), however, is the meaning of the compound itself. For this very reason, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Vārāṇasī. This being the case, he states the resulting conclusion: "the length of the Gaṅgā," etc. Regarding *vārāṇasī*: *varānaḥ* means that which possesses excellent water (*vara* = best; *āna* = water); [the city] is situated not far from that. By the rule "and that which is situated not far from [something]," the suffix *aṇ* is applied, followed by initial *vṛddhi*. The substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "after a word ending in a consonant, when a name is formed. Since it ends in *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.

And here, by the mention of "rivers" (*nadībhiḥ*) in the plural, there is no inclusion of the actual form, the name, or the river itself; rather, it refers to the meaning. Furthermore, that [meaning] does not itself constitute a technical name (*saṃjñā*); therefore, this compound applies to those words which denote that meaning. And these are not only particular terms, but also general terms.

"An obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). This is clear in the *Vṛtti*. Kaiyaṭa’s intent regarding the *Śākala-sūtra* is also thus. If it is argued that, by parity of reasoning, the *bahuvrīhi* would also be an obligatory compound, this is not so; for the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is understood through the juxtaposition of other words such as "of whom" (*yasya*). For this very reason, it is stated [in the commentary] "because the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not apprehended," and not "because the meaning of another word is not apprehended. What is the purpose of [the mention of] "technical name"? [Example: "The region of Śīghragaṅga. Now, he states the specific compound-endings (*samāsānta*) for the *avyayībhāva*:

Regarding the phrase *avyayī-samāsānta*: this means the final member (*caramāvayava*) of either the compound as a whole or of the final member that constitutes the meaning of the compound. By this rule, the suffix *am* is established in *upaśaradam* by the rule *nāvyayībhāvāt*, and the suffix *ṅīp* is established in *dvipurī* and similar forms by the rule *dvigoḥ*. The rule *jarāyāḥ* is a *gaṇasūtra* (a rule belonging to the list of words).
Regarding *pratipara*: [the word] *akṣṇaḥ param* means "beyond the range" (*aviṣaya*). In the context of syntactic function (*vṛtti*), the word *akṣi* refers to the sense organ in general.

Regarding the word *samakṣam*: it means "suitable for the eyes" (*akṣṇoḥ yogyam*). In the case of *nadī*, here there is the inclusion of the actual form itself (*svarūpa*) and not the technical name (*saṃjñā*), because *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī* are mentioned separately [in the rule]. In *upanadī*, due to the absence of the suffix *ṭac*, the neuter short vowel occurs. However, this must be noted: it has been stated that in the rule *nadībhiśca*, there is an inclusion of the actual form as well as of specific instances (*viśeṣa*), since there is no evidence to suggest that only specific instances are intended. By this, the form *pañcanadam* is established. And in this case, the vowel *ac* is compulsory. As it has been said:
"And if [the number] is greater than that of the river Godāvarī," so it is said.
And this is established by the division of the rule (yogavibhāga) into "ac" and "praty-anv-ava" within the rule *ac-praty-anv-ava*.
The phrase "for the sake of honor" means that the option (*anyatarasyām*) is understood from the context of the preceding rule.
Thus ends the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita.
